questions.stem: A patient suffers a traumatic injury to the articular cartilage of the knee joint. Why is this specific cartilage highly limited in its ability to undergo appositional repair to heal the defect?

choices.A: The high concentration of type I collagen at the articular surface actively inhibits the cellular pathways required for appositional growth.
choices.B: Articular cartilage lacks a perichondrium, so there is no local source of progenitor cells to form new chondroblasts at the surface.
choices.C: The chondrocytes of articular cartilage are locked in an exceptionally dense calcified matrix, preventing them from dividing mitotically.
choices.D: Articular cartilage is elastic cartilage whose perichondrium is too thin to supply enough chondroblasts to rebuild the surface by appositional growth.
choices.E: Articular cartilage is highly vascularized, causing immune cells to quickly form scar tissue that blocks appositional growth.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Appositional growth of cartilage relies entirely on the perichondrium (specifically its inner cellular layer containing progenitor cells) to add new layers of matrix to the surface. Articular cartilage has no perichondrium, meaning it cannot repair itself via appositional growth.
  - Supporting Quote:  "An important exception to this is that articular cartilage (the hyaline cartilage that covers the articular surfaces of bones in a joint) does NOT have a perichondrium." (Page 5-6, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

      - "Appositional growth occurs on the surface of the cartilage. In this case, cells of the inner cellular layer of the perichondrium (fibroblasts or chondroprogenitor cells) differentiate into chondroblasts..." (Page 4, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: Not a thin perichondrium: articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage with no perichondrium at all (Cartilage & Bone study guide).

questions.stem: How does the structural matrix of fibrocartilage differ from hyaline cartilage to accommodate areas subject to high mechanical shear and directional stress?

choices.A: It contains an abundant network of elastic fibers that permits rapid recoil under mechanical stretching.
choices.B: It organizes its chondrocytes into massive, circular isogenous groups that prevent cell compression in all directions.
choices.C: It lacks a perichondrium and features thick bundles of Type I collagen fibers aligned parallel to the direction of functional stress.
choices.D: It keeps a thin perichondrium but replaces most ground substance with randomly oriented Type II collagen fibrils that resist compression from every direction.
choices.E: It relies on a specialized basal lamina connected to dense regular connective tissue via integrins rather than standard collagen fibers.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Fibrocartilage is a structural hybrid. It lacks a perichondrium and features dense bundles of Type I collagen oriented in the direction of mechanical stress to withstand high physical force.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Fibrocartilage: This is a hybrid tissue... It does NOT have a perichondrium." (Page 8, Cartilage and Bone Guide)
      - "In H&E, fibrocartilage looks like chondrocytes in lacunae... surrounded by dense collagen fibers (Type I) which are aligned in the direction of functional stress." (Page 9, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: Fibrocartilage has no perichondrium, and its Type I collagen bundles run parallel to the stress, not randomly (Cartilage & Bone study guide).

The fibers cannot be seen without a special elastic stain.

questions.stem: An experimental drug selectively blocks the proton ($H^+$) pumps on the ruffled border of active osteoclasts. What is the immediate physiological consequence of this drug on bone remodeling?

choices.A: Osteoclasts can no longer synthesize or secrete collagenase, leaving the organic osteoid completely intact.
choices.B: Osteoclasts cannot acidify their lysosomes, so cathepsin K stays inactive and the collagen persists while the mineral phase is still dissolved normally.
choices.C: Osteoclasts fail to fuse from their monocyte precursors, reducing the overall number of multinucleated cells in Howship's lacunae.
choices.D: The local microenvironment remains alkaline/neutral, preventing the dissolution of the inorganic mineral portion of the bone.
choices.E: Osteoblasts are signal-blocked from transitioning into mature osteocytes, halting the production of new bone matrix.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Osteoclasts dissolve the inorganic (mineral) portion of bone by actively pumping protons ($H^+$) into their sealed subosteoclastic microenvironment to create an acidic space. Blocking these pumps prevents acid production, leaving the mineralized matrix intact.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Osteoclasts dissolve bone. To dissolve the mineral (inorganic) portion of bone, they create an acidic microenvironment... To dissolve the organic portion (collagen and proteoglycans) of bone, they release lysosomal enzymes (especially collagenase) into the space." (Page 13, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: Without the proton pump the sealed zone never acidifies, so it is the mineral that stays undissolved; acid secretion is what dissolves the inorganic phase.

A.passage: stick with “zone of degeneration” terminology instead] Zone of ossification: Osteoblasts move in and secrete their organic matrix (osteoid) in the area le# by the degenerated cartilage. Over time this becomes mineralized, and now we have a longer bone!
A.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

B.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

C.passage: Another type of cell found in bone is the osteoclast . These cells are of the monocyte/macrophage lineage, and their job is to digest and resorb bone. Osteoclasts are a type of giant cell, which happens when many macrophages join cell bodies to form one large cell with many nuclei. Osteoclasts live along the inner surface of the bone. Where they sit against the bone, they have a convoluted, ruffled cell membrane, which can be appreciated on electron microscopy.

questions.stem: In compact bone, how do osteocytes located in the outer concentric lamellae of an osteon receive oxygen and nutrients if they are sealed within a calcified matrix far from the central Haversian canal?

choices.A: They rely on active vesicular transport across the interstitial lamellae via specialized endocytic pathways.
choices.B: They periodically migrate out of their lacunae, travel to the Haversian canal to absorb nutrients, and return to their home matrix.
choices.C: They depend on perpendicular Volkmann's canals that directly penetrate every single individual lacuna.
choices.D: Nutrients diffuse directly through the calcified lamellae, which stay porous to small solutes because the hydroxyapatite crystals are loosely packed.
choices.E: Nutrients diffuse from the Haversian canal through a continuous network of tiny canaliculi, utilizing physical cell processes joined by gap junctions.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: The osteon's calcified matrix is impermeable to standard diffusion. Osteocytes survive by extending thin cytoplasmic processes through microscopic tunnels (canaliculi), where they form gap junctions with neighboring cells to share nutrients diffusing from the central Haversian canal.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "The previously discussed canaliculi run from the Haversian canal to the innermost ring of lacunae, and then from lacuna to lacuna, for diffusion of nutrients and oxygen to the outermost osteocytes of the osteon. Recall that osteocytes also extend cell processes along these canaliculi for communication with other osteocytes." (Page 24, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: The calcified matrix does not allow diffusion; osteocytes depend on canaliculi that link their processes by gap junctions (Cartilage & Bone study guide).

A.passage: In which zone of the epiphyseal plate is interstitial growth of cartilage occuring?
A.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

B.passage: The Haversian canal is a small channel running parallel to the long axis of the bone, containing very small blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics. Each Haversian canal supports a “cylinder” of osteocytes around it. A canal with its associated osteocytes is referred to as a Haversian system or an osteon.
B.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

C.passage: Volkmann’s canals run perpendicular to the long axis of the bone, intersecting Haversian canals, and also carry very small vessels and nerves.
C.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

D.passage: and can grow, repair, and regenerate. By weight, a little more than half of the matrix is organic and contains type I collagen and macromolecules. The macromolecules of bone, particularly the glycoproteins, attract and bind calcium. The inorganic portion of the matrix consists of calcium, phosphorus (often complexed as “hydroxyapatite crystals”), and other trace minerals.
D.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

E.passage: Nutrients can also flow through the canaliculi, and thus be distributed widely through the tissue.
E.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

questions.stem: During the primary step of endochondral ossification, what is the exact mechanism that triggers the calcification of cartilage and the subsequent death of chondrocytes in the center of the diaphysis?

choices.A: Hypertrophic chondrocytes secrete VEGF that draws in the periosteal bud, and the invading vessels then deposit the calcium that kills the chondrocytes.
choices.B: The chondrocytes run out of glycogen reserves, triggering a programmed apoptotic cascade that releases calcium into the extracellular matrix.
choices.C: Mesenchymal cells secrete high levels of calcium ions directly into the articular surface, which crystallizes the entire model from the outside in.
choices.D: The development of a bony periosteal collar around the diaphysis cuts off the diffusion of nutrients to the deep cartilage.
choices.E: The invasion of the periosteal bud directly delivers osteoclasts that eat away the living chondrocytes.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: The very first step of endochondral ossification is the creation of a bone collar on the surface of the diaphysis. This collar acts as a physical barrier to diffusion, causing the internal chondrocytes to undergo hypertrophy, calcify the matrix, and die.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Endochondral ossification begins with a hyaline cartilage model... first step is the development of a bony collar around the diaphysis of the cartilage model. The bony collar prevents nutrients from diffusing into the cartilage in the center of the diaphysis, and this cartilage begins to calcify and the chondrocytes there die." (Page 15, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: Calcification and chondrocyte death come first; the periosteal bud invades cartilage that is already calcified and dying (Cartilage & Bone study guide).

A.passage: and then settle down to become chondrocytes and just maintain the matrix around them. In doing this, new cartilage tissue is created.
A.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

B.passage: Resting zone: Chondrocytes are at rest in the hyaline cartilage, waiting for a signal to grow. Proliferation zone: Chondrocytes multiply (interstitial growth) and become arranged in parallel columns. This is the main zone responsible for gain in bone length. Zone of hypertrophy: Chondrocytes hypertrophy (cells swell, indicates insult due to lack of nutrients) and stop synthesizing collagen and proteoglycans. Zone of degeneration: Chondrocytes die and degenerate, leaching their contents into the matrix. The matrix becomes mineralized and appears darker.
B.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

C.passage: On the outside of bones is a thin, tough fibrous layer called
C.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

D.passage: A hyaline cartilage model of the skeleton has already been established in the fetus. The mesenchymal (undi"erentiated, primitive) cells adjacent to the future diaphysis di"erentiate into osteoblast cells that begin to deposit bone matrix in the mesenchyme. (thus this step is intramembranous ossification). This eventually forms a belt or collar of bone around the cartilaginous sha#. The bone belt/collar blocks di"usion of oxygen and nutrients to the cartilage it is encircling, and the chondrocytes become unstable and begin to die. Blood vessels penetrate into the middle of the dying cartilage.
D.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

E.passage: Of note, bone is basically in a continual state of remodeling, with both osteoclasts and osteoblasts working all the time to some degree, and both cell types are usually found on a random slide of bone. Both osteoblasts and osteoclasts can also be activated by the endocrine system if calcium needs to be stored away (osteoblast activity) or released to the bloodstream (osteoclast activity).

questions.stem: Which zone of the epiphyseal plate is characterized by chondrocytes that physically swell, accumulate glycogen, and actively secrete vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) to initiate blood vessel invasion?

choices.A: Zone of proliferation
choices.B: Zone of ossification
choices.C: Zone of hypertrophy
choices.D: Zone of reserve (resting) cartilage
choices.E: Zone of calcified cartilage

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: In the Zone of Hypertrophy within the epiphyseal plate, chondrocytes stop dividing and instead enlarge (swell) physically. They accumulate glycogen in their cytoplasm and release VEGF to signal blood vessel invasion.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "3. Zone of hypertrophy: the chondrocytes swell, accumulate glycogen, and secrete VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor - a signal for blood vessels to invade)." (Page 17, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: In the zone of ossification osteoblasts lay bone onto calcified cartilage spicules; swelling, glycogen and VEGF belong to the hypertrophic chondrocytes.

questions.stem: Which of the following outlines the correct cellular progression during intramembranous ossification?

choices.A: Osteocytes dedifferentiate $\rightarrow$ Form a periosteal collar $\rightarrow$ Osteoblasts invade via Volkmann's canals $\rightarrow$ Woven bone is synthesized.
choices.B: Chondrocytes hypertrophy $\rightarrow$ Matrix calcifies $\rightarrow$ Osteoclasts drill tunnels $\rightarrow$ Osteoblasts lay down lamellar bone.
choices.C: Fibroblasts secrete Type I collagen $\rightarrow$ Transform into chondroblasts $\rightarrow$ Appositional growth creates a cartilage template $\rightarrow$ Direct replacement by bone occurs.
choices.D: Mesenchymal cells condense $\rightarrow$ Differentiate into chondroblasts $\rightarrow$ Build a hyaline template $\rightarrow$ Osteoblasts from a periosteal collar replace it.
choices.E: Mesenchymal cells group $\rightarrow$ Differentiate into osteoblasts $\rightarrow$ Secrete uncalcified osteoid $\rightarrow$ Cells become trapped and calcify into osteocytes.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Intramembranous ossification does not use a cartilage model. Instead, mesenchymal cells condense directly in vascularized connective tissue, differentiate into osteoblasts, and deposit osteoid which subsequently calcifies and traps them as osteocytes.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Intramembranous ossification: This occurs in flat bones... Mesenchymal cells group together... and differentiate into osteoblasts. These osteoblasts secrete osteoid... Eventually, the osteoblasts get completely surrounded by osteoid and calcify, becoming osteocytes." (Page 14, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: A cartilage template replaced from a periosteal collar is endochondral ossification; intramembranous bone forms directly from mesenchyme with no cartilage model.

A.passage: Volkmann’s canals run perpendicular to the long axis of the bone, intersecting Haversian canals, and also carry very small vessels and nerves.
A.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

B.passage: Of note, bone is basically in a continual state of remodeling, with both osteoclasts and osteoblasts working all the time to some degree, and both cell types are usually found on a random slide of bone. Both osteoblasts and osteoclasts can also be activated by the endocrine system if calcium needs to be stored away (osteoblast activity) or released to the bloodstream (osteoclast activity).
B.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

C.passage: Appositional growth of cartilage involves adding to the cartilage from the edges of an existing piece, where the perichondrium is located. The perichondrial cells differentiate into chondroblasts, which make matrix until they settle down as chondrocytes. This growth pattern helps generate the immature fetal skeleton.
C.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

D.passage: condense to form an ossification center. Some of these mesenchymal cells are osteoprogenitor cells, which then differentiate into osteoblasts and begin secreting the organic part of bone matrix (osteoid) directly into the surrounding tissue. Once the osteoblasts are entrapped in their matrix, they are considered mature osteocytes. Inorganic ion deposition follows, resulting in hardening of the matrix. This type of ossification is seen in the flat bones of the cranium, the clavicle, the patella (kneecap), and sesamoids (small bone niblets found in hands and/or feet of some individuals).
D.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

E.passage: the periosteum , which contains progenitor cells that can differentiate into osteoblasts if needed. Lining the insides of bones there is a thin layer called the endosteum , that also contains progenitor cells that can differentiate into osteoblasts.
E.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

questions.stem: When analyzing a slide of mature compact bone, you observe irregular patches of lamellar bone with osteocytes that do not form complete concentric circles around a central Haversian canal. What do these "interstitial lamellae" represent?

choices.A: Specialized anchoring zones that connect the outer periosteum directly to the endosteum.
choices.B: Pathological woven bone structures caused by a localized lack of calcium.
choices.C: Circumferential lamellae laid down by the periosteum that became trapped between newer osteons as the bone grew in diameter.
choices.D: Remnants of older, partially destroyed osteons left behind after osteoclast-mediated bone remodeling.
choices.E: The very first uncalcified osteoid laid down by osteoblasts during early development.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Bone remodeling is a continuous process where osteoclasts tunnel out old osteons and osteoblasts build new ones. The fragments of the older, partially consumed osteons remain in the matrix as interstitial lamellae.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "[Of note, there are some osteocytes that are not included as part of an osteon – these are called “interstitial.” They persist as remnants of prior osteons that have been remodeled over...]" (Page 24, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: Circumferential lamellae line the outer and inner bone surfaces; interstitial lamellae are the leftovers of older osteons after remodeling.

A.passage: the periosteum , which contains progenitor cells that can differentiate into osteoblasts if needed. Lining the insides of bones there is a thin layer called the endosteum , that also contains progenitor cells that can differentiate into osteoblasts.
A.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

B.passage: crowded, the collagen fibers of the matrix are disorganized, and matrix mineralization is low. Because of the irregular collagen arrangement, it is also sometimes called “woven” bone by pathologists.
B.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

C.passage: seen as a dense white rind of bone around the marrow space and the more delicate spongy bone. Compact bone accounts for about 80% of the total mass of the adult skeleton. Compact bone has a specialized microarchitecture called “osteons” or “Haversian systems” – more on this below.
C.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

D.passage: Bone’s matrix is hard and partially inorganic, but is not static
D.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

E.passage: The area where the osteoblasts very first start making bone within the diaphysis is the “primary ossification center.” Eventually they will ossify the entire shaft. This ossification mainly takes place during fetal development. Around the time of birth, “secondary ossification centers” appear in the epiphyses of the long bones; the process is similar, with osteoblasts migrating into and growing over dying cartilage.
E.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

questions.stem: What is the precise biophysical mechanism that allows the extracellular matrix of hyaline cartilage to act as an effective shock absorber resisting compression?

choices.A: The cross-linking of elastic fibers with type I collagen creates a rigid, unyielding cage.
choices.B: Negatively charged GAGs on aggrecan attract sodium ions, which pull in water to form a turgid, hydrated gel.
choices.C: The perichondrium acts as a pressurized membrane that compresses the internal matrix mechanically.
choices.D: Type II collagen fibrils bind calcium ions and stiffen into a rigid lattice that resists compression without needing a high water content.
choices.E: Chondrocytes constantly pump calcium ions out of their cytoplasm, maintaining a high osmotic pressure in the lacunae.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: The shock-absorbing quality of hyaline cartilage is due to its highly hydrated proteoglycan matrix. Aggrecan molecules contain highly negatively charged GAGs that attract sodium, which osmotically binds massive amounts of water to resist compression.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Aggrecan consists of a core protein with many highly charged GAGs attached... Because the GAGs are highly negatively charged, they attract sodium ions, which in turn attract water molecules... This high water content allows cartilage to resist compression (act as a shock absorber)." (Page 3, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: Compression resistance comes from water held by the negatively charged GAGs on aggrecan; type II collagen fibrils mainly resist tension.

B.passage: The main cell is the chondroblast/chondrocyte. The main fiber is collagen type II; the fibers are delicate and cannot be seen with the regular microscope. The macromolecules are specialized to attract and hold a lot of water, which lends cartilage a particular bounciness that is good for shock-absorption.
B.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

The perichondrial cells differentiate into chondroblasts, which make matrix until they settle down as chondrocytes. This growth pattern helps generate the immature fetal skeleton.

The macromolecules of bone, particularly the glycoproteins, attract and bind calcium. The inorganic portion of the matrix consists of calcium, phosphorus (often complexed as “hydroxyapatite crystals”), and other trace minerals.

questions.stem: Which structural transition marks the official transformation of an active osteoblast into a mature osteocyte?

choices.A: The cell retracts all of its cytoplasmic processes, breaking its gap junctions with neighboring cells to enter dormancy.
choices.B: The cell synthesizes Type II collagen and shifts its physical location to the perichondrium.
choices.C: The cell stops secreting osteoid, flattens, and remains on the bone surface as a quiescent bone-lining cell connected to its neighbors.
choices.D: The cell becomes completely surrounded by its own synthesized osteoid matrix, which subsequently calcifies, trapping the cell in a lacuna.
choices.E: The cell begins to express multinucleated properties and forms a ruffled membrane border.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Osteoblasts build the organic matrix (osteoid). Once an osteoblast becomes completely entombed in its own secreted osteoid and the matrix calcifies, its phenotype transitions into a mature osteocyte.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Osteoblasts synthesize the organic matrix of bone (osteoid)... As the osteoblast makes more osteoid, it eventually becomes completely surrounded by it. The matrix eventually calcifies, and the osteoblast (now completely trapped in its lacuna) is called an osteocyte." (Page 11, Cartilage and Bone Guide)

Tempting but wrong: An osteoblast that stays on the surface becomes a bone-lining cell; it becomes an osteocyte only when its own calcified matrix entombs it in a lacuna.

A.passage: The primary cell in bone, responsible for generating, secreting, and maintaining the organic part of the matrix (called the “osteoid”) is called an osteoblast while immature, and an osteocyte when mature. These cells live in lacunae in the matrix, similar to the arrangement in cartilage. However, osteocytes also have long, thin cytoplasmic processes that remain extended through the matrix in tiny tunnels called canaliculi. These processes reach out to and meet processes of other osteocytes, and the cells can communicate.
A.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

B.passage: The matrix of bone contains collagen fibers; what type of collagen is it?
B.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

C.passage: Another type of cell found in bone is the osteoclast . These cells are of the monocyte/macrophage lineage, and their job is to digest and resorb bone. Osteoclasts are a type of giant cell, which happens when many macrophages join cell bodies to form one large cell with many nuclei. Osteoclasts live along the inner surface of the bone. Where they sit against the bone, they have a convoluted, ruffled cell membrane, which can be appreciated on electron microscopy.
C.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

D.passage: stick with “zone of degeneration” terminology instead] Zone of ossification: Osteoblasts move in and secrete their organic matrix (osteoid) in the area le# by the degenerated cartilage. Over time this becomes mineralized, and now we have a longer bone!
D.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

E.passage: When activated, the osteoclast secretes acids and enzymes in the region of the ruffled border, facilitating decalcification and digestion of the bone matrix. The ruffled border provides a large surface area for resorbing/consuming the now-digested matrix components. On light microscopy, the ruffled border can’t be seen, but the osteoclast appears to be sitting in a shallow pit with a gap

questions.stem: If a neuron is exposed to a toxin that selectively inactivates the motor protein dynein, which cellular process is most directly and immediately compromised?

choices.A: The retrograde transport of trophic factors and worn-out organelles from the axon terminal back to the soma.
choices.B: The physical assembly of microtubule tracks within the dendritic arbor.
choices.C: The anterograde transport of newly synthesized neurotransmitters from the soma to the axon terminal.
choices.D: The slow axonal transport of cytoskeletal proteins such as neurofilaments and tubulin from the soma toward the axon terminal.
choices.E: The local translation of ribosomal proteins within the axon hillock.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Axonal transport relies on motor proteins walking along microtubules. Kinesin drives anterograde transport (away from the soma), while dynein drives retrograde transport (toward the soma) to return signaling molecules, trophic factors, and organelles for degradation.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "• Retrograde transport... uses a motor protein called dynein... Retrograde transport is used to transport trophic factors and other signaling molecules, and to return worn-out organelles to the cell body for recycling." (Page 3, Nervous System Guide)

Tempting but wrong: Slow transport of cytoskeletal proteins runs away from the soma (anterograde, kinesin); dynein carries cargo back toward the soma.

A.passage: Neurons are made up of a cell body, one or more long processes called dendrites, and an axon.

C.passage: Structural Components of a Neuron: 1. Dendrites, which can be described as the “input ends”; they bear receptors to neurotransmitters. Neurons vary in the number of dendrites that they have. 2. Cell body, which contains the nucleus and cytoplasmic organelles. 3. an Axon, the longest cell process, which is capable of transmitting (propagating) electrical nerve activity (action potentials).

E.passage: Dendrites → Neuron cell body → Axon Input → Integrate → Output

questions.stem: Histological analysis of a motor neuron reveals extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes (Nissl bodies) throughout the soma and dendrites. Why is there a complete absence of Nissl staining in the axon hillock and the axon itself?

choices.A: The protein synthesis machinery is restricted to the soma and dendrites because axons do not contain Nissl bodies.
choices.B: Axons rely entirely on adjacent Schwann cells or oligodendrocytes to physically inject pre-translated proteins into their cytoplasm.
choices.C: Nissl bodies are present in the axon but stain only with silver impregnation methods, not with the basic dyes used for the soma.
choices.D: Axonal proteins are synthesized locally on specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum instead.
choices.E: The axon hillock contains high concentrations of lysosomes that rapidly degrade any ribosomes entering the space.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Nissl bodies consist of rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes, representing the protein synthesis machinery of the neuron. While they are abundant in the cell body and dendrites, they do not enter the axon hillock or the axon, leaving the axon unable to synthesize its own proteins.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "the cell body contains lots of rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes... collectively referred to as Nissl bodies... Nissl bodies are found in the cell body and the dendrites, but NOT in the axon hillock or the axon." (Page 2, Nervous System Guide)

Tempting but wrong: Nissl substance is basophilic RER and free ribosomes; it is absent from the axon hillock and axon, not just unstained (Nervous System slides).

A.passage: Neurons are made up of a cell body, one or more long processes called dendrites, and an axon.

B.passage: Oligodendrocytes • Form myelin around axons in the CNS (analogous to Schwann cells in the PNS)

E.passage: Dendrites → Neuron cell body → Axon Input → Integrate → Output

questions.stem: How does the myelination pattern of a single oligodendrocyte in the Central Nervous System (CNS) differ fundamentally from that of a single Schwann cell in the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)?

choices.A: Oligodendrocytes wrap axons in Type IV collagen sheets, while Schwann cells wrap them in lipid-rich cell membranes.
choices.B: One oligodendrocyte myelinates a single segment of a single axon, whereas one Schwann cell can myelinate up to 50 different axons.
choices.C: One oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of multiple axons (up to 50), whereas one Schwann cell can only myelinate one segment of one axon.
choices.D: Each oligodendrocyte myelinates one segment of one axon, just like a Schwann cell, but CNS myelin has no nodes of Ranvier between segments.
choices.E: Oligodendrocytes only myelinate unmyelinated axons, whereas Schwann cells selectively target nodes of Ranvier.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: In the CNS, a single oligodendrocyte has multiple processes that can myelinate segments of up to 50 individual axons. In the PNS, a single Schwann cell can only wrap around a single segment of a single axon.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Oligodendrocytes: these are the myelin-producing cells of the CNS. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of multiple axons (up to 50)." (Page 7, Nervous System Guide)
      - "Schwann cells: these are the myelin-producing cells of the PNS... One Schwann cell can only myelinate one segment of one axon." (Page 8, Nervous System Guide)

Tempting but wrong: CNS myelin still has nodes of Ranvier, and one oligodendrocyte sends processes to segments of many axons (up to 50).

A.passage: Astrocytes Oligodendrocytes and Schwann Cells Microglia Ependymal cells

B.passage: Oligodendrocytes • Form myelin around axons in the CNS (analogous to Schwann cells in the PNS)

C.passage: Neurons are made up of a cell body, one or more long processes called dendrites, and an axon.

D.passage: CNS Microglia Native immune cells in the brain (mesodermal origin) Astrocyte many functions, e.g. helps form blood- brain barrier via interactions with vessels, nutritional support, etc. Oligodendrocyte myelin-forming cells in CNS

E.passage: Schwann cells (the PNS counterpart of oligodendrocytes) Schwann cells in the PNS (peripheral nervous system) serve the same purpose as oligodendrocytes in the CNS-- they form myelin sheaths. In addition, they also have phagocytic activity and help clear cellular debris.

questions.stem: What is the structural and functional relationship between astrocytes and brain capillaries that is critical for the maintenance of the blood-brain barrier (BBB)?

choices.A: Astrocytes act as phagocytic macrophages that consume any molecules attempting to exit the capillary lumen.
choices.B: Astrocytes physically block capillaries by secreting thick sheets of dense regular connective tissue over them.
choices.C: Astrocytes secrete vasodilators that force endothelial cells to stretch, closing physical fenestrations in the capillary walls.
choices.D: Astrocytic end-feet are sealed to one another by tight junctions, forming the barrier layer around a leaky, fenestrated capillary endothelium.
choices.E: Astrocytic perivascular feet wrap the capillaries and induce and maintain the tight junctions between endothelial cells.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Astrocytes extend cytoplasmic processes ending in perivascular feet. These feet physically envelop capillaries and produce the essential signals that stimulate the vascular endothelial cells to form and maintain the tight junctions that constitute the Blood-Brain Barrier.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Astrocytes have cytoplasmic processes... end in expansions called 'perivascular feet' that wrap around capillaries... critical for the formation and maintenance of the blood-brain barrier (BBB)." (Page 7, Nervous System Guide)

Tempting but wrong: The BBB tight junctions are between the capillary endothelial cells; astrocyte end-feet induce and maintain them but are not the sealed layer.

A.passage: Microglia Microglia are specialized brain macrophages that are derived from blood-borne monocytes (mesodermal origin). They are phagocytic cells that act as the “first line of defense” against foreign invaders.

B.passage: Astrocytes Oligodendrocytes and Schwann Cells Microglia Ependymal cells

C.passage: Astrocytes Astrocytes are found only in the CNS. They are the largest of the neuroglia, and are the most abundant neuroglial cells. They have many long processes that help anchor neurons to their blood supply. They are therefore believed to play an important role in the blood-brain barrier, which serves a protective filter against pathogens and toxins.

questions.stem: Which connective tissue sheath in a peripheral nerve serves as a highly protective, metabolically active diffusion barrier, and what cellular specialization makes this barrier possible?

choices.A: The perineurium, due to layers of epithelial-like cells joined together by tight junctions.
choices.B: The mesoneurium, due to the presence of continuous vascular fenestrations.
choices.C: The epineurium, due to thick bundles of parallel Type I collagen fibers.
choices.D: The endoneurium, due to a dense network of fibroblasts secreting ground substance.
choices.E: The endoneurium, because the basal laminae of its Schwann cells fuse into a continuous sheet sealed by tight junctions.

questions.explanation:

  - Supporting Quote:

Tempting but wrong: The endoneurium is loose connective tissue around single fibers; the tight-junction-linked epithelioid cells are in the perineurium.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs the embryological origin and primary functional role of microglial cells in the central nervous system?

choices.A: Ectodermal origin; myelination of small diameter central axons.
choices.B: Neuroectodermal origin (from the neural tube, like astrocytes); resident phagocytes that clear debris from sites of injury.
choices.C: Endodermal origin; acting as structural physical anchors to hold neurons in place.

questions.stem: How do modified ependymal cells physically contribute to the production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the brain's ventricles?

choices.A: They undergo holocrine secretion, breaking down entirely to form the bulk fluid of the CSF.
choices.B: They use long, flagellum-like stereocilia to mechanically filter blood plasma into the ventricles.
choices.C: They cooperate with loose connective tissue and capillaries to form the choroid plexus, actively regulating fluid transport into the ventricles.
choices.D: They line the central canal and ventricles and secrete CSF by absorbing it back from the venous sinuses through their apical cilia.
choices.E: They synthesize large amounts of myelin that liquefies into CSF in response to mechanical pressure.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Ependymal cells line the ventricles. In specialized regions of the ventricles, modified ependymal cells interact directly with underlying capillaries and loose connective tissue to form the choroid plexus, which actively filters blood to produce CSF.
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Within the brain's ventricles, modified ependymal cells, loose connective tissue and capillaries together form the choroid plexus, which produces CSF." (Page 10, Nervous System Guide)

Tempting but wrong: CSF is reabsorbed into venous sinuses by arachnoid villi; modified ependymal cells produce it as part of the choroid plexus with capillaries and loose connective tissue.

A.passage: Glial cells cannot transmit nerve impulses themselves, and do not form synapses. However, they form the myelin sheaths around axons, and they are able of dividing (they are therefore the source of nervous system tumors).

B.passage: Astrocytes Astrocytes are found only in the CNS. They are the largest of the neuroglia, and are the most abundant neuroglial cells. They have many long processes that help anchor neurons to their blood supply. They are therefore believed to play an important role in the blood-brain barrier, which serves a protective filter against pathogens and toxins.

C.passage: Ependymal cells These are cuboidal or low-columnar cells that form a single layer lining the internal cavities (ventricles) of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord. The apical surfaces of ependymal cells are covered with cilia, which helps to circulate the CSF through the ventricles and central canal. Within the brain's ventricles, modified ependymal cells, loose connective tissue and capillaries together form the choroid plexus, which produces CSF.

D.passage: Ependymal Cells • Line cerebral ventricles and central canal of spinal cord

E.passage: 🩺Clinical correlation: CSF Abnormal accumulations of CSF can lead to expansion of the ventricular spaces within the brain, also known as hydrocephalus. There are different ways of classifying hydrocephalus: congenital vs. acquired , communicating vs. non-communicating, high vs normal pressure. Refer back to the Panopto lecture recording for further details on this topic when studying for the exam.

choices.B: Multiple sclerosis; Oligodendrocytes

choices.E: Guillain-Barré syndrome; Schwann cells

- Mechanism: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune condition characterized by demyelination in the Central Nervous System (brain and spinal cord). The myelin-producing cells of the CNS are oligodendrocytes.

Tempting but wrong: MS spares peripheral nerves because it targets CNS myelin made by oligodendrocytes; Schwann cells myelinate the PNS.

They have many long processes that help anchor neurons to their blood supply. They are therefore believed to play an important role in the blood-brain barrier, which serves a protective filter against pathogens and toxins.

questions.stem: During saltatory conduction in a myelinated nerve fiber, why does depolarization occur exclusively at the Nodes of Ranvier rather than along the entire length of the axon?

choices.A: Myelin insulates the internodes, and voltage-gated potassium channels clustered at the nodes depolarize the membrane to regenerate the impulse.
choices.B: Schwann cells actively depolarize the internodal segments, leaving only the nodes to be depolarized by the axon itself.
choices.C: Potassium leakage channels are blocked at the nodes, forcing sodium to accumulate in those areas.
choices.D: Myelin prevents any extracellular fluid from touching the axon, and voltage-gated sodium channels are highly concentrated only at the unmyelinated nodes.
choices.E: The nodes are the only sites where dynein motors can actively pump sodium ions across the axolemma.

questions.explanation:
- Mechanism: Myelin acts as an electrical insulator, preventing ions from crossing the membrane along the wrapped segments. Depolarization is forced to "jump" along the axon because voltage-gated sodium channels are highly concentrated exclusively at the unmyelinated gaps (Nodes of Ranvier).
  - Supporting Quote:

      - "Myelin is a lipid-rich layer that acts as an electrical insulator... Nodes of Ranvier are the unmyelinated gaps... concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels is very high at the nodes... action potential 'jumps' from node to node... saltatory conduction." (Page 11, Nervous System Guide)

Tempting but wrong: Depolarization at the nodes is carried by voltage-gated Na+ channels concentrated there; K+ channels repolarize.

A.passage: Oligodendrocytes These glial cells are found in the CNS and are smaller than astrocytes. They surround (wrap around) the axons of neurons forming a “myelin sheath” which insulates and supports neural conduction. questions.stem: If an axon in the PNS is classified as "unmyelinated," how does it physically interact with Schwann cells?

choices.B: It is completely engulfed by a Schwann cell that wraps around it dozens of times without producing myelin lipids.
choices.C: Each unmyelinated axon has its own Schwann cell, which forms a single thin loop of membrane around it without compacting into myelin.

questions.stem: During clinical blood collection, why does centrifuging a tube without an anticoagulant yield serum, whereas centrifuging a tube containing citrate or heparin yields plasma?

choices.A: Heparin and citrate bind fibrinogen and pull it out of solution, so plasma lacks clotting factors while serum keeps all of them.
choices.B: Without an anticoagulant, clotting consumes fibrinogen and other clotting factors into the clot; the liquid left over is serum.
choices.C: Citrate and heparin act as enzymes that synthesize extra albumin, transforming the liquid phase into plasma.
choices.D: Anticoagulants force the plasma proteins to precipitate out of solution, leaving only serum at the top of the tube.
choices.E: Anticoagulants chemically destroy the red blood cells, releasing intracellular fluid that dilutes serum into plasma.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: When blood is collected without an anticoagulant, the clotting factors are activated and form a fibrin meshwork (clot) that traps the cellular elements. The fluid remaining after this clot is removed is serum, which is depleted of clotting proteins (like fibrinogen). If anticoagulants are present, clotting is blocked, and the liquid obtained after centrifugation is plasma (which still contains clotting factors).
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Serum: the liquid portion; no longer contains clotting factors. Blood clot: a fibrin-containing network trapping blood cells and clotting factors" (Mather PDF, Page 5)
      - "If blood is collected in a tube containing an anticoagulant (like citrate, heparin, or EDTA) and then centrifuged, it will separate into three distinct layers... plasma... buffy coat... red blood cells" (Blood Cells study guide, Page 2)

Tempting but wrong: It is the reverse: anticoagulated plasma still contains fibrinogen and clotting factors, while serum has lost them to the clot.

B.passage: Serum: the liquid portion; no longer contains clotting factors

C.passage: The major proteins in blood are albumin (which maintains osmotic pressure), the globulins (α, β, γ), and fibrinogen.
C.file: 25_08_14 - Blood Cells study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

D.passage: Blood is composed of cellular elements suspended in plasma (a solution of salts and proteins dissolved in water). The cellular elements are red cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes), and platelets (thrombocytes).
D.file: 25_08_14 - Blood Cells study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

E.passage: SERUM -VS- PLASMA Collect blood in tube with or without anticoagulant

questions.stem: What specific membrane skeletal proteins allow erythrocytes (RBCs) to dynamically deform as they squeeze through narrow splenic sinusoids, and then return immediately to their characteristic biconcave shape?

choices.A: Tubulin and dynein
choices.B: Actin and myosin II
choices.C: Spectrin and ankyrin
choices.D: Integrin and cadherin
choices.E: Spectrin and dystrophin

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The structural integrity and remarkable flexibility of the erythrocyte membrane are maintained by a specialized cytoskeleton composed of spectrin filaments anchored to transmembrane proteins by ankyrin. This allows the cell to withstand significant shear forces in microvessels and return to its original shape.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "The biconcave shape provides a high surface-area-to-volume ratio... The cell membrane is associated with a cytoskeletal network containing spectrin and ankyrin, which maintains the cell's shape and provides the flexibility required for the cells to squeeze through small capillaries." (Blood Cells study guide, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: Dystrophin anchors actin to the sarcolemma in muscle; the RBC membrane skeleton is spectrin anchored to the membrane by ankyrin.

questions.stem: During a bacterial infection, neutrophils undergo "respiratory burst" to destroy pathogens. What biochemical weapon is synthesized within their azurophilic (primary) granules during this event, and what is its substrate?

choices.A: Lysozyme, which specifically targets the bacterial cell membrane's lipid bilayer.
choices.B: Myeloperoxidase, which utilizes hydrogen peroxide ($H_2O_2$) and halide ions to generate highly toxic hypohalite radicals.
choices.C: Gelatinase, which cleaves Type IV collagen in the bacterial wall.
choices.D: Elastase, which digests elastin in the bacterial capsule using hydrogen peroxide ($H_2O_2$) as its co-substrate.
choices.E: Lactoferrin, which binds and sequesters essential copper ions.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Neutrophil granules contain diverse antibacterial enzymes. The azurophilic (primary) granules are characterized by myeloperoxidase (MPO), which catalyzes the production of hypohalites (like hypochlorous acid/bleach) from hydrogen peroxide and halides during the respiratory burst. Secondary granules contain lactoferrin to sequester iron.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Azurophilic granules (primary granules): large lysosomes containing myeloperoxidase (MPO)..." (Blood Cells study guide, Page 7)
      - "Specific granules (secondary granules): smaller, contain enzymes such as collagenase, phospholipase, and lactoferrin (sequesters iron, an essential nutrient for bacterial growth)" (Blood Cells study guide, Page 7)

Tempting but wrong: Elastase is an azurophilic-granule protease but does not use H2O2; myeloperoxidase turns H2O2 and halides into hypohalite.

C.passage: ACUTE response to injury (aka "acute inflammation ") through phagocytosis & bacterial destruction.

questions.stem: An experimental model demonstrates that a target cell cannot defend against a parasitic helminth (worm) infection. Under normal conditions, which specific cationic protein is released by eosinophils to disrupt the parasite's membrane, and what enzyme do they release to limit secondary tissue damage?

choices.A: Major basic protein (MBP) to damage the parasite; heparin to anticoagulate the surrounding tissue and limit clot-driven damage.
choices.B: Myeloperoxidase to damage the parasite; collagenase to digest the surrounding extracellular matrix.
choices.C: Major basic protein (MBP) to damage the parasite; histaminase to degrade histamine and limit allergic inflammation.
choices.D: Eosinophilic cationic protein (ECP) to damage the parasite; myeloperoxidase to synthesize toxic bleach.
choices.E: Histamine to damage the parasite; heparin to degrade local blood clots.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Eosinophils are highly specialized for defense against parasites. Their large pink granules release Major Basic Protein (MBP) to damage the parasite membrane. To prevent excessive inflammatory damage to surrounding tissues, they also release histaminase to break down local histamine.

questions.stem: What is the functional consequence of basophil degranulation into the bloodstream during an acute hypersensitivity reaction?

choices.A: Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability of venules mediated by the release of histamine.
choices.B: Extensive local tissue destruction driven by the sudden activation of myeloperoxidase.
choices.C: Rapid vasoconstriction of large elastic arteries mediated by direct calcium release.
choices.D: Immediate formation of a dense fibrin network to isolate the allergen.
choices.E: Vasodilation of arterioles with decreased venular permeability, mediated by the release of heparin onto vascular smooth muscle.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Basophil granules are packed with histamine and heparin. Upon activation, they release these contents (degranulate), with histamine acting on local blood vessels (specifically venules) to cause rapid vasodilation and increased permeability, leading to the swelling and redness of an allergic reaction.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Activated in inflammatory & hypersensitivity reactions... Note that basophil degranulation releases a significant amount of histamine into peripheral blood." (Blood Cells study guide, Pages 9-10)
      - "Basophils... Heparin, Histamine... Vasoactive mediators -> vasodilation, increased vascular permeability" (Mather PDF, Page 20)

Tempting but wrong: Heparin is an anticoagulant; histamine is what dilates vessels and makes venules leaky.

Tempting but wrong: Fibrinogen and vWF are alpha-granule cargo and serotonin is dense-body cargo, so any pairing that mixes them is wrong.

questions.stem: How do mature platelets physically form within the bone marrow before entering peripheral circulation?

choices.A: They are nucleated cells that undergo rapid mitotic division to form fragments.
choices.B: They are synthesized in the plasma of the bone marrow sinusoid from raw lipid aggregates.
choices.C: They are shed from the cytoplasm of large precursor cells called megakaryocytes.
choices.D: They form when megakaryocyte nuclei fragment and each nuclear fragment is wrapped in its own membrane.
choices.E: They represent the remnants of old erythrocytes that have been degraded by macrophages.

  - Supporting Quotes:

Tempting but wrong: Platelets are anucleate fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm; nuclear fragments do not become platelets.

questions.stem: What biochemical and physical transformations occur as a circulating monocyte transitions into a functional macrophage in the connective tissue?

choices.A: It enlarges and builds lysosomes while still circulating, so only fully mature macrophages cross the endothelium into the tissue.
choices.B: After entering the tissue it enlarges, expands its lysosomes and protein synthesis machinery, and becomes actively phagocytic.
choices.C: It fuses with adjacent Schwann cells to form a multi-nucleated glial syncytium.
choices.D: It synthesizes specific granules containing myeloperoxidase to undergo respiratory burst.
choices.E: It decreases in size, condenses its chromatin, and switches to anaerobic glycolysis.

      - "monocytes enter connective tissue and differentiate into macrophages... once in the tissue, they increase in size, and increase their capacity for phagocytosis and protein synthesis." (Blood Cells study guide, Page 8)

Tempting but wrong: Monocytes differentiate into macrophages after they leave the blood and enter the connective tissue.

questions.stem: Why can't T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes be distinguished from one another under a standard H&E-stained peripheral blood smear, despite having distinct immunological functions?

choices.A: B-lymphocytes only exist in the lymph nodes and are never found in peripheral blood smears.
choices.B: B-lymphocytes completely lack a nucleus, while T-lymphocytes have a bi-lobed nucleus.
choices.C: T-lymphocytes are packed with large pink eosinophilic granules, whereas B-lymphocytes are packed with purple granules.
choices.D: Both are small round cells with a condensed nucleus and a thin rim of cytoplasm; only surface-marker staining separates them.
choices.E: B-lymphocytes are noticeably larger with abundant basophilic cytoplasm, so only T-lymphocytes need surface marker staining to be identified.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Under light microscopy with H&E or Wright-Giemsa stains, all small lymphocytes look essentially identical: they are small cells with a round, highly condensed nucleus surrounded by a very narrow rim of pale blue cytoplasm. Identifying them as T-cells, B-cells, or NK cells requires antibody staining for specific cluster of differentiation (CD) markers.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Lymphocytes... Small, round cells... Nucleus is round and intensely stained with condensed chromatin. Cytoplasm is a thin, pale blue rim" (Mather PDF, Page 27)
      - "T-cells and B-cells look identical under the light microscope on a typical H&E stained slide. Special stains or techniques (such as immunohistochemistry or flow cytometry) are needed to identify the different cell types based on specific proteins on their cell surfaces." (Blood Cells study guide, Page 5)

Tempting but wrong: Small B and T lymphocytes look the same on a smear; neither can be told apart without surface-marker staining.

questions.stem: What physical and structural properties of erythrocytes (RBCs) maximize their capacity for rapid gas exchange ($O_2$ and $CO_2$) across alveolar membranes?

choices.A: The presence of dense networks of rough endoplasmic reticulum that actively pump oxygen.
choices.B: Their spherical shape, which minimizes their overall surface area.
choices.C: Their anucleate status and biconcave disc shape, which maximizes their surface-area-to-volume ratio and decreases diffusion distance.
choices.D: Their large size ($12\text{--}20\ \mu\text{m}$), which slows their velocity in capillaries.
choices.E: Their abundant mitochondria and biconcave shape, which supply the ATP needed to actively load oxygen onto hemoglobin.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Mature erythrocytes are structurally optimized for gas transport. The loss of their nucleus and organelles, combined with their biconcave shape, maximizes the surface area available for gas diffusion and ensures that no cell volume is far from the membrane.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "The biconcave shape provides a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, which is optimal for gas exchange." (Blood Cells study guide, Page 3)
      - "Anucleated biconcave disk... High surface area to volume ratio... Small diffusion distance" (Mather PDF, Page 9-10)
Part 2: Skin Answers

Tempting but wrong: Mature RBCs have no mitochondria (they rely on glycolysis), and oxygen loading is passive diffusion, not ATP-driven.

B.passage: Lymphocytes • Second most common WBC in blood • Mononuclear cells with spherical nucleus • Chromatin is condensed à intense staining with scant rim of cytoplasm • Lifespan: months to years

C.passage: Mature RBCs are anucleate biconcave discs with a diameter of 7-8 μm (you do NOT need to memorize the specific sizes of the blood cells, but be aware of relative differences in size between RBC/WBC/platelets). The biconcave shape results in a 20-30% increase in surface area (as compared to a sphere). The very large surface area to volume ratio allows for efficient gas transfer.
C.file: 25_08_14 - Blood Cells study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

D.passage: • About same size as neutrophil; • “Bi-lobed” nucleus • Large eosinophilic granules

E.passage: discs that appear pale in the middle and darker along the edges (biconcave)

questions.stem: Histological examination of the stratum spinosum under standard light microscopy reveals cells with prominent "spines" projecting from their borders. What physical processing artifact and structural specialization explain this appearance?

choices.A: Cellular shrinkage during tissue processing while the cells remain firmly anchored to one another via desmosomes linked to keratin tonofibrils.
choices.B: The secretion of thick lipid droplets via cytocrine secretion.
choices.C: Rapid mitotic division stretching the lipid bilayer.
choices.D: Intracellular accumulation of water that causes the cytoplasm to balloon outwards between cell junctions.
choices.E: Cellular shrinkage during tissue processing while the cells stay anchored to one another by tight junctions linked to actin filaments.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The "spiny" appearance of the cells in the stratum spinosum is a classic histological artifact. During tissue dehydration and preparation, the cytoplasm of these cells shrinks. However, because they are held together tightly by numerous intercellular desmosomes connected to internal keratin filaments, the cells remain attached at these discrete points, creating microscopic "spines."
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Stratum spinosum... This layer gets its name from the 'spiny' appearance of the cells when seen under a light microscope. The spines are actually an artifact of tissue preparation - as the tissue is prepared, the cells shrink slightly, but remain attached to neighboring cells via numerous desmosomes. Keratin filaments (called tonofibrils in this layer) are abundant..." (Skin study guide, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: The spines are desmosomes holding keratin tonofibrils, not tight junctions (Skin slides).

A.passage: Stratum Granulosum: Substance from the keratohyalin granules combines with the tonofibrils converting them to keratin

B.passage: Melanin is synthesized from tyrosine, a reaction catalyzed by tyrosinase. It is stored in melanosomes, which move through the processes, and are “injected” into keratinocytes (bonus fact: a process called cytocrine secretion). They migrate to an apical, perinuclear location in the keratinocyte.

C.passage: In Stratum Granulosum, the lipid contents are extruded into the intercellular spaces. Waterproofing occurs here.

questions.stem: How do cells in the stratum granulosum cooperate to establish the epidermal water barrier that prevents life-threatening dehydration?

choices.A: They undergo rapid cell division, creating a tight physical wall of nucleated cells that water cannot penetrate.
choices.B: They synthesize a thick layer of Type IV collagen that blocks the passage of water.
choices.C: They secrete major basic protein to kill any water-consuming bacteria.
choices.D: They produce keratohyalin granules containing filaggrin to aggregate keratin filaments, and exocytose lipid-rich lamellar granules to form an intercellular hydrophobic envelope.
choices.E: They produce lamellar granules containing filaggrin to bundle keratin filaments, and exocytose keratohyalin granules whose lipids seal the spaces between cells.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The epidermal water barrier is established in the stratum granulosum. It has two essential parts: an insoluble protein envelope formed by keratin filaments aggregated by filaggrin (from keratohyalin granules), and a lipid envelope formed by the exocytosis of lamellar granules containing lipids.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Stratum granulosum... Keratohyalin granules: these granules contain proteins (such as filaggrin) that bind to and aggregate keratin filaments... Lamellar granules: these are membrane-bound granules containing lipids. The lipids are released by exocytosis into the extracellular space between the stratum granulosum and stratum corneum, forming a lipid barrier that prevents water loss..." (Skin study guide, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: Filaggrin comes from keratohyalin granules and the lipid sealant comes from lamellar granules; this option swaps them.

With aging, collagen synthesis decreases and collagen crosslinks form. Additionally, elastic fibers are lost, so skin becomes more fragile and less supple

D.passage: Stratum Granulosum: Substance from the keratohyalin granules combines with the tonofibrils converting them to keratin

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the correct molecular pathway of melanin synthesis, transport, and delivery within the epidermis?

choices.A: Melanocytes make melanin from tyrosine via tyrosinase, package it in melanosomes, and pass them to keratinocytes (cytocrine secretion), where they cap the nucleus.
choices.B: Melanocytes secrete raw DOPA directly into the dermis, where fibroblasts convert it into a protective pigment matrix.
choices.C: Melanosomes synthesize tyrosine in the stratum corneum, then migrate basally to be absorbed by melanocytes.
choices.D: Keratinocytes convert tyrosine to DOPA via tyrosinase, package melanin into melanosomes, and pass them to melanocytes of the stratum basale, which cap their nuclei.
choices.E: Keratinocytes synthesize melanin and inject it into the cytoplasm of melanocytes to protect the melanocyte stem cells.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Melanocytes live in the stratum basale and synthesize melanin from tyrosine (via tyrosinase) inside melanosomes. They extend long dendritic processes to transfer these melanosomes into neighboring keratinocytes. Once inside the keratinocytes, the melanin pigment aligns on the sunny side of the nucleus to shield the cell's DNA from damaging UV radiation.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Melanocytes: these cells are derived from neural crest cells... The synthesis of melanin occurs in melanosomes, which are membrane-bound organelles... Tyrosinase converts tyrosine to DOPA, which is then converted to melanin... Melanosomes are transported to the tips of the melanocytes' dendritic processes, where they are transferred to neighboring keratinocytes (this process is called cytocrine secretion). Once inside the keratinocytes, the melanin pigment accumulates over the nucleus, acting as a 'shield' to protect the cell's DNA from UV radiation." (Skin study guide, Pages 6-7)

Tempting but wrong: Melanocytes, not keratinocytes, make melanin; keratinocytes receive melanosomes by cytocrine secretion and cap their own nuclei.

A.passage: Melanin is synthesized from tyrosine, a reaction catalyzed by tyrosinase. It is stored in melanosomes, which move through the processes, and are “injected” into keratinocytes (bonus fact: a process called cytocrine secretion). They migrate to an apical, perinuclear location in the keratinocyte.

B.passage: Melanocytes secrete melanin in the basal layer and extend their processes up between the cells of the basale and spinosum layers.

C.passage: 5. Stratum Corneum • Consists of 15-20 layers of non- nucleated, keratinized cells. Stratum corneum

D.passage: The nuclei of keratinocytes are shielded from uv radiation by melanin produced by melanocytes.

E.passage: Keratinocytes (with melanin surrounding nuclei to protect DNA from UV damage)

questions.stem: From a cellular and molecular perspective, how does the pathological mechanism of vitiligo differ fundamentally from that of albinism?

choices.A: Albinism involves a complete loss of keratinocytes; vitiligo involves the overproduction of lamellar granules.
choices.B: Albinism is characterized by an autoimmune destruction of melanocytes; vitiligo is a genetic defect in tyrosinase.
choices.C: Albinism is a genetic absence of melanocytes from the epidermis; vitiligo is a genetic lack of functional tyrosinase in otherwise normal melanocytes.
choices.D: Albinism: normal melanocyte numbers but no functional tyrosinase (genetic); vitiligo: autoimmune destruction of the melanocytes.
choices.E: Albinism is caused by UV damage to melanocytes; vitiligo is caused by a nutritional lack of tyrosine.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Albinism is a genetic disorder where melanocytes are present in normal numbers, but they cannot produce melanin because they lack a functional tyrosinase enzyme. In contrast, vitiligo is an autoimmune disease where the body's immune system actively destroys the melanocytes, resulting in a physical decrease or loss of these cells in affected patches of skin.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Albinism: This is an inherited (genetic) condition... normal numbers of melanocytes, but they are unable to synthesize melanin due to a lack of functional tyrosinase enzyme." (Skin study guide, Page 7)
      - "Vitiligo: In contrast to albinism, in vitiligo the number of melanocytes is affected. Melanocytes are destroyed... because vitiligo is an autoimmune disease..." (Skin study guide, Page 8)

Tempting but wrong: In albinism melanocytes are present in normal numbers but lack functional tyrosinase; vitiligo is autoimmune destruction of melanocytes.

A.passage: Keratinocytes start to produce membrane coating granules contain GAGS and Lipids

B.passage: Albinism If tyrosinase is absent or deficient, the reaction that generates melanin does not occur, resulting in lack of pigmentation or albinism. Note that the number of melanocytes may be normal, but their function is impaired. This is a congenital disorder that affects all vertebrates, and is characterized by the complete or partial absence of pigment in thethe skin, hair, and eyes due to the absence or defect of tyrosinase. Mutations in the TYR gene cause albinism through the inhibition of melanin production.

D.passage: In contrast to albinism, in vitiligo the number of melanocytes is affected. Melanocytes are destroyed, resulting in irregularly shaped white patches on the skin. A widely accepted view is that the depigmentation occurs because vitiligo is an autoimmune disease – possibly due to cytokines that alter and kill melanocytes. Another theory is that melanocytes may self-destruct, leading to decreased numbers.

E.passage: - melanocytes are destroyed, resulting in irregularly shaped white patches on the skin - A widely accepted view is that the depigmentation occurs because vitiligo is an autoimmune disease – possibly due to cytokines that alter and kill melanocytes. Another theory is that melanocytes destroy themselves.

questions.stem: What anchoring systems prevent the epidermis from mechanically shearing away from the underlying dermis when subjected to lateral physical force?

choices.A: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) connecting keratinocytes to the papillary dermis.
choices.B: Desmosomes (using cadherins) anchoring basal cells to the basal lamina, supported by anchoring fibrils of Type IV collagen.

Basal cells of the stratum basale attach to the underlying basal lamina via hemidesmosomes (utilizing transmembrane integrin proteins).       - "The interface between the epidermis and dermis is highly irregular... forming dermal papillae... Anchoring fibrils (type VII collagen) help to anchor the basal lamina to the underlying dermis." (Skin study guide, Page 5)

Tempting but wrong: Basal cells attach to the basal lamina by integrin-based hemidesmosomes with Type VII collagen anchoring fibrils; desmosomes join keratinocyte to keratinocyte.

questions.stem: Why do sebaceous glands require a continuous rate of mitotic division at their basal layer to maintain their secretory function?

choices.A: They utilize apocrine secretion, where the apical half of the cell is lost and must be rebuilt.
choices.B: They utilize holocrine secretion, meaning the entire cell fills with lipid product, disintegrates to release sebum, and must be completely replaced.
choices.C: They use merocrine secretion of lipid droplets, but the sebum they release is toxic to the secretory cells, which must constantly be replaced.
choices.D: They utilize merocrine secretion, but the high osmotic pressure of sweat destroys the cells.
choices.E: They are endocrine glands that constantly shed cells directly into the local capillaries.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Sebaceous glands are classical holocrine glands. The secretory process involves the entire cell filling with lipid product, dying, and disintegrating completely to release the sebum. Consequently, the gland must have a highly active mitotic basal layer to constantly generate new cells to replace those that are lost.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "In holocrine-type glands, the cells make intracellular product, and then the whole cell falls apart into the duct - HOLocrine releases the wHOLe thing\! Example of holocrine gland: sebaceous of skin" (Epithelium study guide, Page 8)
      - "Sebaceous glands: These glands are associated with hair follicles... They are holocrine glands... cells at the periphery of the gland divide mitotically to replace cells that are lost as sebum is released." (Skin study guide, Page 8)

Tempting but wrong: Sebaceous glands are holocrine: the whole cell becomes the secretion, so the basal layer must keep dividing (Skin slides).

A.passage: A specialized type of sweat gland in the skin of the axilla and groin is of the apocrine type (i.e. pieces of the gland cells break off and are lost with the secretory product).

B.passage: Sebaceous glands (holocrine) Sebaceous glands are small holocrine-type glands associated with hair follicles in the skin. They secrete an oily, waxy matter called sebum into the hair follicle lumen to lubricate the skin and hair. They are found in greatest abundance on the face and scalp, though they are distributed throughout all skin sites, except the palms and soles. Sebum is secreted as the whole cell (holocrine secretion). The sebaceous glands are highly influenced by hormones and are especially active around puberty and adolescence.

C.passage: Specialized skin structures/appendages - glands, nerves, hair There are 3 subtypes of exocrine secretory glands in the skin: eccrine (aka merocrine), apocrine, and holocrine. These subtypes refer to mechanisms by which secretory products are released.

D.passage: Sweat glands (eccrine and apocrine) Most sweat glands are eccrine (merocrine) type, i.e. they don't lose cytoplasmic components during secretion, in contrast with apocrine type noted below. Eccrine glands are simple, coiled tubular glands that produce a mixture of water, salt, urea, NH3 (aka the precursor to sweat, which is an ultrafiltrate of plasma). Eccrine sweat glands are found at border between dermis and hypodermis, and play a role in regulation of body temperature via evaporative cooling.

E.passage: Exocrine glands 1. Eccrine glands 2. Apocrine glands 3. Sebaceous glands

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs the specialized non-keratinocyte cell of the epidermis with its correct embryonic origin and primary physiological function?

choices.A: Langerhans cell: endodermal origin; secretes sebum to lubricate the hair follicle.
choices.B: Merkel cell: ectodermal origin; functions as a high-sensitivity mechanoreceptor associated with sensory nerve endings.
choices.C: Merkel cell: mesodermal origin; acts as an antigen-presenting immune cell.
choices.D: Merkel cell: neural crest origin; synthesizes melanin and transfers it to neighboring keratinocytes.
choices.E: Langerhans cell: neural crest origin; synthesizes pigment to protect against UV radiation.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Merkel cells are sensory cells of ectodermal origin located in the stratum basale. They associate closely with expanded terminal endings of afferent sensory nerve fibers (Merkel discs) to serve as sensitive mechanoreceptors for light touch.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Merkel cells: these cells are found in the stratum basale... derived from ectoderm... function as mechanoreceptors and are associated with sensory nerve endings. They are most abundant in areas where sensory perception is highly acute (such as the fingertips)." (Skin study guide, Pages 5-6)

Tempting but wrong: Neural crest origin and melanin synthesis describe melanocytes; Merkel cells are mechanoreceptors associated with sensory nerve endings.

A.passage: Hair and hair follicles (skin appendages) The base of the hair follicle is the hair bulb. A dermal papilla inserts into the base of the hair bulb; it contains a capillary network (which sustains the hair follicle). Hair grows from the germinativum (basale) layer and consists of a medulla and cortex covered with cuticle.

B.passage: Nerve Supply • There are several types of nerve endings that serve as sensory receptors, including mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors and nociceptors (pain receptors).

C.passage: • Keratinocytes • Melanocytes • Langerhans cells: APCs • Merkel cells: slow adapting touch receptors

D.passage: Pigmentation is due to melanin, produced by melanocytes at a rate that is genetically controlled. Melanocytes, derived from neural crest, are located amongst keratinocytes of the stratum basale, and in hair follicles.

E.passage: Functions of the Skin •Barrier Function -general wear and tear -protection against infection -protection against UV radiation

questions.stem: How does the histological structure of the papillary dermis differ from that of the reticular dermis to support its specific metabolic and mechanical demands?

choices.A: The papillary dermis is dense regular connective tissue aligned along tension lines, while the reticular dermis is loose areolar tissue that holds the capillary loops feeding the epidermis.
choices.B: Both layers are dense irregular connective tissue, but the papillary dermis holds the capillary loops and Meissner corpuscles while the reticular dermis has thicker Type III collagen to resist stretch.
choices.C: The papillary dermis is composed of dense irregular connective tissue with thick Type I collagen, while the reticular dermis is composed of loose connective tissue containing capillary loops.
choices.D: The papillary dermis contains abundant subcutaneous fat, while the reticular dermis contains the sebaceous glands.
choices.E: The papillary dermis is loose connective tissue with thin collagen and capillary loops that nourish the epidermis; the reticular dermis is dense irregular tissue with thick Type I collagen.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The dermis is divided into two layers with distinct roles. The superficial papillary layer consists of loose connective tissue, allowing blood vessels (capillary loops) to come close to the avascular epidermis to provide metabolic support. The deeper reticular layer is made of dense irregular connective tissue with thick Type I collagen fibers to provide multi-directional mechanical tensile strength.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Papillary layer: This is the superficial layer of the dermis... composed of loose connective tissue... contains capillary loops that extend into the dermal papillae... Reticular layer: This is the deeper, thicker layer... composed of dense irregular connective tissue... characterized by thick bundles of collagen fibers (primarily type I) and elastic fibers..." (Skin study guide, Page 5)

Tempting but wrong: The papillary dermis is loose connective tissue; only the reticular dermis is dense irregular, with thick Type I collagen.

A.passage: Dermis • The connective tissue layer subjacent to epidermis. • Exerts an inductive effect on overlying tissue, which develops into epidermis characteristic of the area of the dermis’ origin (i.e. sole, palm

B.passage: 1. Meissner’s corpuscles are encapsulated nerve endings in the dermal papilla of skin-- they are mechanoreceptors, sensitive to light touch. 2. Pacinian corpuscles are mechanoreceptors that sense vibration. These are found deep in the dermis and in the hypodermis.

With aging, collagen synthesis decreases and collagen crosslinks form. Additionally, elastic fibers are lost, so skin becomes more fragile and less supple
