questions.stem: What prevents blood vessels from penetrating into the epidermal layers of the skin, and how do epidermal cells survive without direct vascularization?

choices.A: The tight junctions of the stratum corneum block blood vessel growth; epidermal cells rely on active transport from the subcutaneous fat.
choices.B: Melanocytes secrete angiostatin, which keeps the epidermis vessel-free; cells survive by digesting dead stratum corneum cells.
choices.C: The epidermis is avascular; its cells survive on nutrients delivered by lymphatic capillaries that run up between the dermal papillae.
choices.D: High hydrostatic pressure in the stratum basale pushes vessels back; epidermal cells survive by synthesizing their own nutrients from sebum.
choices.E: The epidermis is an avascular tissue; cells survive via the diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from capillary loops located in the dermal papillae.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Like all epithelia, the epidermis is completely avascular. Blood vessels do not cross the basement membrane. To survive, the living layers of the epidermis rely entirely on the passive diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the microvascular capillary loops situated in the dermal papillae.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Epidermis: The superficial, cellular layer... It is avascular, meaning it does not have its own blood supply. The cells of the epidermis rely on diffusion of nutrients from blood vessels in the underlying dermis." (Skin study guide, Page 2)
      - "Papillary layer... contains capillary loops that extend into the dermal papillae... to provide nutrients to the avascular epidermis." (Skin study guide, Page 5)
Part 3: Vascular System Answers

Tempting but wrong: Nutrients diffuse from blood capillary loops in the dermal papillae, not from lymphatics.

A.passage: 5. Stratum Corneum • Consists of 15-20 layers of non- nucleated, keratinized cells. Stratum corneum

B.passage: 1. stratum basale (proliferative layer) 2. stratum spinosum (cell adhesion) 3. stratum granulosum (anti-dessicant) 4. stratum lucidum (transition to dead cells) 5. stratum corneum (dead cells sloughing off)

C.passage: Dermis This is the mesodermal connective tissue layer deep and adjacent to epidermis. It exerts an inductive effect on overlying ectodermal tissue, influencing development of skin characteristic to a particular area (i.e. sole, palm, etc.) The basal lamina between (i.e. at the interface of) the epidermis and dermis follows the contour of the dermal papillae, which has ridges that increase surface area for adhesion. Hemidesmosomes are very plentiful at this interface.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the direct physiological effect of vasoactive factors secreted by endothelial cells on the smooth muscle of the adjacent tunica media?

choices.A: Nitric oxide stimulates the synthesis of Type I collagen, while endothelin-1 degrades the internal elastic lamina.
choices.B: Endothelium-derived factors act purely as physical insulators and have no chemical influence on smooth muscle cells.
choices.C: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin stimulate smooth muscle contraction, while endothelin-1 stimulates relaxation.
choices.D: Nitric oxide and endothelin-1 both stimulate smooth muscle relaxation (vasodilation), while prostacyclin is the main endothelial vasoconstrictor.
choices.E: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin stimulate smooth muscle relaxation (vasodilation), while endothelin-1 stimulates smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction).

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The endothelium is a highly active metabolic barrier. It synthesizes and secretes several vasoactive molecules that diffuse into the adjacent tunica media to regulate smooth muscle tone: nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin act as potent vasodilators (relaxing smooth muscle), whereas endothelin-1 is a powerful vasoconstrictor (contracting smooth muscle).
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "The endothelium is not just a simple physical barrier... It secretes vasoactive agents that regulate the tone of the underlying smooth muscle cells: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin (which cause vasodilation)... Endothelin-1 (which causes vasoconstriction)..." (Vascular study guide, Page 2)

Tempting but wrong: Endothelin-1 is the endothelial vasoconstrictor; NO and prostacyclin both relax smooth muscle.

A.passage: Elastic fibers: The arterial side of the circulation is subject to repetitive distension with each stroke of the heart, and elastic fibers help the artery recoil once the blood bolus has passed by. Elastic fibers can be found in dense bands called lamina; the internal elastic lamina is found in the tunica intima, and the external elastic lamina is found in the outermost layers of the tunica media. There also may be elastic fibers interspersed throughout the tunica media. In general, the larger the artery, the more elastic is found.

B.passage: Through the vasculature, endothelial cells are not simply heart and vessel liners; they actively produce factors that prevent blood clotting, factors that cause adjacent smooth muscle cells to contract or relax, and factors that initiate inflammation at sites of damage or infection.
B.file: Circulatory System - SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS.pdf

D.passage: adjacent tissue. Endothelial cells also make and store compounds that promote blood clotting; these are released when the endothelial cell is damaged (much more on this later). The heart The heart muscle proper is composed entirely of cardiac muscle cells, with a small amount of loose connective tissue and collagen type III present between cells to support the small vessels within the muscle. As you’ve already learned, some of the muscle cells are specialized to conduct impulses (the Purkinje fibers). All of the inner surfaces of the chambers are lined by endothelium.

E.passage: The tunica media is the middle layer and is composed of a variable number of smooth muscle cells arranged in a circular pattern around the lumen. The smooth muscle cells allow for constriction or dilation of the lumen. There are also a small number of fibroblasts, collagen fibers, and ground substance. In some vessel types (discussed below), there may also be elastic fibers.

questions.stem: What structural adaptation in the wall of elastic arteries (such as the aorta) is essential for maintaining steady blood flow and pressure during diastole, and what clinical pathology results if this structure degrades?

choices.A: Concentric fenestrated sheets of elastic fibers (elastic lamellae) in the tunica media; degradation leads to aneurysm formation.
choices.B: Thick layers of longitudinal smooth muscle in the tunica adventitia; leads to atherosclerosis.
choices.C: Continuous capillaries within the tunica intima; leads to varicose veins.
choices.D: Concentric fenestrated elastic lamellae in the tunica media; degradation of these lamellae leads to atherosclerotic plaque formation.
choices.E: An exceptionally thin tunica media with no elastic fibers; leads to venous thrombosis.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Elastic arteries (such as the aorta) have a highly specialized tunica media containing numerous concentric elastic sheets (lamellae). During systole, these elastic sheets stretch to accommodate high blood pressure, and during diastole, they recoil to maintain continuous pressure and forward flow. Loss or damage to these elastic elements weakens the wall, allowing it to balloon outward, forming an aneurysm.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Elastic arteries (large arteries)... The tunica media of these vessels is very thick and contains many concentric sheets of elastic fibers, called elastic lamellae... The elastic features allow the vessel to stretch during systole... and recoil during diastole... Clinical correlation: Aneurysm... a weakness in the wall of an artery (often due to damage to the elastic/muscle layers of the tunica media)..." (Vascular study guide, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: Atherosclerosis is an intimal disease; loss of the medial elastic lamellae weakens the wall and leads to aneurysm.

A.passage: Elastic fibers: The arterial side of the circulation is subject to repetitive distension with each stroke of the heart, and elastic fibers help the artery recoil once the blood bolus has passed by. Elastic fibers can be found in dense bands called lamina; the internal elastic lamina is found in the tunica intima, and the external elastic lamina is found in the outermost layers of the tunica media. There also may be elastic fibers interspersed throughout the tunica media. In general, the larger the artery, the more elastic is found.

B.passage: I am a vessel (hi!) and I have a thick tunica media, elastic fibers in my tunica media, inner and outer elastic lamina, and vasa vasorum in my tunica adventitia. Who am I?

C.passage: Vessels: General structure Arteries and veins (but not capillaries) share a general structure, consisting of three layers: the tunica intima, the tunica media, and the tunica adventitia.

D.passage: The largest are the elastic arteries , and are close to the heart (e.g. aorta, pulmonary artery); these experience widely fluctuating high pressure, and in addition to having internal and external elastic lamina, they contain large amounts of elastic fibers throughout the tunica media. These are arranged in sheets (lamellae) that alternate with layers of smooth muscle and collagen fibers in the media. The wall is overall thick, too thick for the whole wall to get nutrients from the blood

E.passage: Veins experience relatively low pressures as compared to arteries, and their walls are considerably thinner, largely due to a thin tunica media. This results in them being somewhat “floppy,” and on histologic sections they often appear collapsed. There is not much elastic tissue on the venous side of the system; the largest vein (the vena cava) has a very thin internal elastic lamina.

questions.stem: Why are arterioles classified as the primary "resistance vessels" of the cardiovascular system?

choices.A: Their small lumen and 1–2 layers of medial smooth muscle can contract or relax to regulate blood pressure and organ perfusion.
choices.B: They have a wide lumen and a tunica media of many smooth muscle layers that stores elastic recoil energy to keep blood pressure steady during diastole.
choices.C: They contain valves that physically resist the backward flow of blood into capillaries.
choices.D: Their walls consist of a massive tunica adventitia that resists external physical compression.
choices.E: They are highly resistant to atherosclerotic plaque formation due to their high velocity of blood flow.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Arterioles have a small lumen and a tunica media consisting of only 1 or 2 layers of smooth muscle. Because of their strategic position and ability to significantly alter their diameter in response to sympathetic or local signals, they provide the primary peripheral resistance in the circulatory system, regulating blood pressure.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Arterioles (very small arteries)... The tunica media has only 1-2 layers of smooth muscle cells... Arterioles are the primary resistance vessels of the vascular system; they regulate systemic blood pressure and direct blood flow to specific organs..." (Vascular study guide, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: Arterioles have a small lumen and only 1–2 smooth muscle layers; storing recoil energy for diastole is the job of elastic arteries.

A.passage: The tunica media is the middle layer and is composed of a variable number of smooth muscle cells arranged in a circular pattern around the lumen. The smooth muscle cells allow for constriction or dilation of the lumen. There are also a small number of fibroblasts, collagen fibers, and ground substance. In some vessel types (discussed below), there may also be elastic fibers.

B.passage: Elastic fibers: The arterial side of the circulation is subject to repetitive distension with each stroke of the heart, and elastic fibers help the artery recoil once the blood bolus has passed by. Elastic fibers can be found in dense bands called lamina; the internal elastic lamina is found in the tunica intima, and the external elastic lamina is found in the outermost layers of the tunica media. There also may be elastic fibers interspersed throughout the tunica media. In general, the larger the artery, the more elastic is found.

C.passage: The venous side of the system is low-pressure and does not require recoil; however, elastic fibers are found in the valves (more on valves below).

D.passage: Vessels: General structure Arteries and veins (but not capillaries) share a general structure, consisting of three layers: the tunica intima, the tunica media, and the tunica adventitia.

E.passage: Clinical correlation: Atherosclerosis is the formation of “plaques” (cholesterol, debris, and macrophages) within the tunica intima of arteries, thickening the intima. Over time, a plaque can also “eat into” the underlying tunica media, thinning it, and weakening the artery. Atherosclerotic plaques often narrow the lumen of the artery, which can compromise efficient blood flow. Additionally, sometimes bits of a plaque can break off, travel downstream, and lodge in a smaller artery or capillary, completely blocking it.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Blood/Skin/Vascular, Q23

questions.stem: Continuous capillaries must balance their protective barrier function with the metabolic transport needs of surrounding tissues. How do they transport large, water-soluble macromolecules across their endothelium without disrupting their tight junctions?

choices.A: By passing macromolecules through fenestrae closed by thin protein diaphragms that admit large solutes but not cells.
choices.B: By forcing macromolecules through large open fenestrations in the endothelial cell body.
choices.C: By temporarily dissolving the zonula occludens to allow paracellular flow.
choices.D: By utilizing retrograde dynein motors to walk the molecules along the basal lamina.
choices.E: By utilizing pinocytotic vesicles to transport macromolecules across the cell cytoplasm via transcytosis.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Continuous capillaries have tight junctions (zonula occludens) that seal the space between endothelial cells, preventing paracellular leakage of large molecules. To transport larger macromolecules, they utilize pinocytotic vesicles that bud from the luminal surface, traverse the cell cytoplasm, and fuse with the basal membrane to release their cargo (transcytosis).
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Continuous capillaries... characterized by a complete endothelial lining with tight junctions (zonula occludens) between cells... transport of large, water-soluble molecules occurs via pinocytotic vesicles, which transport substances across the cytoplasm of the endothelial cell (a process called transcytosis)." (Vascular study guide, Page 5)

Tempting but wrong: Diaphragm-covered fenestrae belong to fenestrated capillaries; continuous capillaries move macromolecules in pinocytotic vesicles (transcytosis).

A.passage: nanometers) in their bodies (like sliced baby swiss cheese). The basal lamina forms a continuous layer. Fenestrated capillaries are found in areas where more rapid exchange of larger molecules is needed – for example in the intestines, endocrine organs, and in parts of the kidneys. There are two types of fenestrated capillaries – those with diaphragms and those without. Fenestrated capillaries with diaphragms – The small openings in the endothelial cells are bridged by a diaphragm, which is comprised of macromolecules and is thinner than a plasma membrane.

B.passage: Capillaries are classified as three structural and functional types, with features that allow different degrees of molecular or even cellular exchange: (1) continuous capillaries with many tight junctions so that all exchange must occur through the cells; (2) fenestrated capillaries with small pores or fenestrations through the cells; and (3) discontinuous capillaries, or sinusoids, with larger lumens, large spaces between the endothelial cells, and a discontinuous basal lamina.
B.file: Circulatory System - SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS.pdf

C.passage: Terminal arterioles branch into metarterioles, in which smooth muscle sphincters contract to resist blood flow and relax cyclically to allow pulsatile flow of blood into an anastomosing capillary bed, where metabolic exchange with surrounding cells occurs.
C.file: Circulatory System - SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS.pdf

D.passage: Fenestrated capillaries without diaphragms – The small openings in the cell bodies are not bridged by a diaphragm, and substances moving from bloodstream to tissue only have to pass through the basal lamina. However, the basal lamina is unusually thick and has special characteristics. This capillary type is found only in the glomerulus of the kidney and is related to urine production (more details in histology of the kidney).

E.passage: Tight continuous capillaries are characterized by numerous tight/occluding junctions between the endothelial cells, and a continuous layer of basal lamina between the endothelial cells and the tissue proper. Tight continuous capillaries are found in parts of the body where exchange from the blood to the tissue needs to be highly regulated – for example in skeletal muscle, in the thymus, and in the central nervous system. While some materials can diffuse across the wall, larger substances are moved by active transport or by pinocytotic vesicles.

questions.stem: What is the functional significance of the difference between fenestrated capillaries with diaphragms and those without diaphragms, and where is the latter type uniquely located?

choices.A: Capillaries with diaphragms are found only in large muscular arteries; capillaries without diaphragms are found in the tunica adventitia of veins.
choices.B: Diaphragms act as mechanical valves; capillaries without diaphragms are found only in the liver.
choices.C: Diaphragms provide a thin protein barrier across pores; capillaries without diaphragms allow high-volume filtration and are located uniquely in liver sinusoids and endocrine glands.
choices.D: Diaphragms provide a thin protein barrier across pores; capillaries without diaphragms allow high-volume filtration across a thick basal lamina and are located uniquely in the kidney glomerulus.
choices.E: Capillaries with diaphragms allow cellular migration; capillaries without diaphragms restrict transport to ions and are found in the brain.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores (fenestrae) in their endothelial cells. In most tissues (like endocrine glands and the intestine), these pores are bridged by thin, membrane-like diaphragms that act as selective filters. Uniquely, the capillaries of the kidney glomerulus lack these diaphragms, allowing high-volume fluid filtration across an unusually thick basal lamina to produce urine.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Fenestrated capillaries with diaphragms - The fenestrae are closed by a thin diaphragm... found in tissues where rapid exchange of substances is needed... Fenestrated capillaries without diaphragms - The small openings in the cell bodies are not bridged by a diaphragm... This capillary type is found only in the glomerulus of the kidney and is related to urine production..." (Vascular study guide, Pages 5-6)

Tempting but wrong: Fenestrated capillaries without diaphragms are unique to the renal glomerulus; liver sinusoids are discontinuous capillaries.

questions.stem: Why do the liver, spleen, and bone marrow utilize discontinuous capillaries (sinusoids) instead of continuous or fenestrated capillaries?

choices.A: To maintain a high hydrostatic pressure that forces blood to flow rapidly through these organs.
choices.B: To allow exchange of large proteins and blood cells across an intact, continuous basal lamina that sieves cells by size as they cross the endothelium.
choices.C: To prevent the entry of systemic hormones, isolating these organs metabolically.
choices.D: To prevent blood cells from escaping into the tissue spaces, protecting the organs from internal hemorrhage.
choices.E: To let large proteins and whole blood cells (old or newly made) cross through large gaps and an incomplete basal lamina.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Discontinuous capillaries (sinusoids) possess large open fenestrations, no diaphragms, and an incomplete basal lamina. This highly open architecture is necessary in the liver (for metabolic screening of blood), spleen (for removal of old red blood cells), and bone marrow (to allow newly formed red and white blood cells to enter circulation).
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Discontinuous capillaries, have endothelial cells that are fenestrated, but the holes in the body of the cell are larger... There are no diaphragms, and the basal lamina is incomplete, with holes in it. These are found in areas where extensive exchange between blood and tissue is needed, such as the liver, spleen, and bone marrow." (Vascular study guide, Page 6)

Tempting but wrong: Sinusoids have large gaps and an incomplete basal lamina; that discontinuity is what lets cells and large proteins cross.

A.passage: CAPILLARIES – the “microcirculation” The microcirculation deals with the flow of blood from the arterioles, through capillaries, into venules. Meta-arteriolar precapillary sphincters control the flow of blood between the arteriole and capillaries. When the sphincters are closed, blood is not allowed to travel into capillary beds. This allows blood to be distributed where most needed. In some cases there may be a channel directly connecting the arteriole to the venule (arteriovenous anastomosis), allowing the blood to simply bypass the bed entirely and circulate back to the heart.

B.passage: Tight continuous capillaries are characterized by numerous tight/occluding junctions between the endothelial cells, and a continuous layer of basal lamina between the endothelial cells and the tissue proper. Tight continuous capillaries are found in parts of the body where exchange from the blood to the tissue needs to be highly regulated – for example in skeletal muscle, in the thymus, and in the central nervous system. While some materials can diffuse across the wall, larger substances are moved by active transport or by pinocytotic vesicles.

D.passage: Veins have valves, which are thin connective tissue extensions of the wall that help prevent backflow of blood. The connective tissue portion is thin and contains some elastic fibers, and is entirely covered with endothelium. Valves are found periodically along the length of a vein and may sometimes be seen on histologic sections.

E.passage: Capillaries are classified as three structural and functional types, with features that allow different degrees of molecular or even cellular exchange: (1) continuous capillaries with many tight junctions so that all exchange must occur through the cells; (2) fenestrated capillaries with small pores or fenestrations through the cells; and (3) discontinuous capillaries, or sinusoids, with larger lumens, large spaces between the endothelial cells, and a discontinuous basal lamina.

questions.stem: Which of the following outlines the correct sequence of cellular and molecular events during the initiation of atherosclerosis?

choices.A: Endothelial damage $\rightarrow$ LDL enters the tunica intima and oxidizes $\rightarrow$ Macrophages engulf LDL to become foam cells $\rightarrow$ Smooth muscle cells migrate and form a fibrous cap.
choices.B: Valves fail in the tunica media $\rightarrow$ Blood pools in the intima $\rightarrow$ Fibroblasts secrete Type II collagen $\rightarrow$ Plaque ruptures.
choices.C: Smooth muscle cells die $\rightarrow$ Elastin lamellae calcify $\rightarrow$ Endothelium thickens $\rightarrow$ Adventitia detaches.
choices.D: Vasa vasorum hyper-proliferates $\rightarrow$ Intima is compressed $\rightarrow$ Endothelial cells undergo holocrine secretion.
choices.E: Endothelial damage $\rightarrow$ Smooth muscle cells migrate and form a fibrous cap $\rightarrow$ LDL enters the tunica intima and oxidizes $\rightarrow$ Macrophages engulf LDL to become foam cells.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Atherosclerosis begins with chronic endothelial damage, which allows low-density lipoproteins (LDL) to enter the subendothelial space (tunica intima) and become oxidized. Macrophages migrate in and phagocytose the oxidized LDL, turning into "foam cells." Eventually, smooth muscle cells migrate from the media into the intima, proliferating and laying down matrix to form a fibrous cap over the lipid core.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Clinical correlation: Atherosclerosis... initiated by damage to the endothelium. This damage allows low-density lipoproteins (LDL) to enter the tunica intima, where they become oxidized. Monocytes/macrophages enter the intima and phagocytose the oxidized LDL, becoming 'foam cells' (lipid-laden macrophages). Smooth muscle cells then migrate from the tunica media into the intima, where they proliferate and secrete collagen, forming a fibrous plaque..." (Vascular study guide, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: The fibrous cap forms last, after LDL oxidation and foam-cell formation have built up the lipid core.

A.passage: Vessels: General structure Arteries and veins (but not capillaries) share a general structure, consisting of three layers: the tunica intima, the tunica media, and the tunica adventitia.

B.passage: I am a vessel (hi!) and I have a thick tunica media, elastic fibers in my tunica media, inner and outer elastic lamina, and vasa vasorum in my tunica adventitia. Who am I?

C.passage: Macroscopically visible blood vessels have three major layers or tunics: (1) The intima includes the endothelium, connective tissue, and an internal elastic lamina in larger vessels; (2) the media contains alternating layers of smooth muscle and collagen or elastic lamellae; and (3) the adventitia (or externa) contains connective tissue, small vessels (vasa vasorum), and nerves.
C.file: Circulatory System - SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS.pdf

D.passage: in the lumen, so out in the tunica adventitia are small vessels to help feed the outer layers of the wall; these are called the "vasa vasorum" or the "vessels of the vessels." The muscular arteries are all those smaller than the elastic arteries. They have less connective tissue in the tunica intima, may have internal elastic lamina, and there are often some scattered elastic fibers in the media. Most have an external elastic lamina, but the smallest ones might not. The thickness of the tunica adventitia is variable, and there may be "vasa vasorum" present.

E.passage: adjacent tissue. Endothelial cells also make and store compounds that promote blood clotting; these are released when the endothelial cell is damaged (much more on this later). The heart The heart muscle proper is composed entirely of cardiac muscle cells, with a small amount of loose connective tissue and collagen type III present between cells to support the small vessels within the muscle. As you’ve already learned, some of the muscle cells are specialized to conduct impulses (the Purkinje fibers). All of the inner surfaces of the chambers are lined by endothelium.

questions.stem: How do the histological properties of veins differ from those of corresponding arteries, and how does this relate to their function as capacitance vessels?

choices.A: Veins have a much thicker tunica media with tightly packed smooth muscle to pump blood back to the heart.
choices.B: Veins have larger, irregular lumens and thinner walls, but the tunica media is their thickest layer, so smooth muscle contraction actively pumps the stored blood back toward the heart.
choices.C: Veins completely lack an endothelial lining, permitting blood to contact the subendothelial collagen.
choices.D: Veins have smaller lumens, thicker walls, and lack a tunica adventitia.
choices.E: Veins have larger, irregular lumens, thinner walls (with the tunica adventitia typically being the thickest layer), and lower internal pressure, allowing them to hold a large volume of blood.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Veins have larger, irregular lumens and much thinner walls compared to their companion arteries. The tunica media is relatively thin, and the outer tunica adventitia is typically the thickest layer. This structure allows veins to expand easily to act as a low-pressure reservoir (capacitance vessels) for blood.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Veins are thin-walled vessels with relatively large, irregular lumens... Veins function as capacitance vessels; they hold a large volume of blood under low pressure... In general, the tunica media of veins is much thinner than that of companion arteries, and the tunica adventitia is the thickest layer." (Vascular study guide, Pages 4-5)

Tempting but wrong: In veins the tunica adventitia is typically the thickest layer; venous return relies on valves and low pressure, not a thick pumping media.

A.passage: Vessels: General structure Arteries and veins (but not capillaries) share a general structure, consisting of three layers: the tunica intima, the tunica media, and the tunica adventitia.

B.passage: Veins experience relatively low pressures as compared to arteries, and their walls are considerably thinner, largely due to a thin tunica media. This results in them being somewhat “floppy,” and on histologic sections they often appear collapsed. There is not much elastic tissue on the venous side of the system; the largest vein (the vena cava) has a very thin internal elastic lamina.

C.passage: VEINS Veins are not strictly categorized and are usually just referred to by large, medium, and small. A very small vein that is just exiting a capillary bed can be called a venule.

D.passage: I am a vessel (hi!) and I have a thick tunica media, elastic fibers in my tunica media, inner and outer elastic lamina, and vasa vasorum in my tunica adventitia. Who am I?

E.passage: Veins usually have a thicker adventitia to help hold them in place within the surrounding tissue, and this is needed since they are floppy/have inconsistent shapes. Veins may display vasa vasorum in the adventitia.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Blood/Skin/Vascular, Q28

questions.stem: Why do large blood vessels require a "vasa vasorum" in their tunica adventitia, and why is this structure absent in smaller-caliber vessels?

choices.A: Large vessels require continuous lymphatic drainage to prevent local edema; small vessels drain directly into the adjacent veins.
choices.B: The vasa vasorum acts to synthesize extra elastic fibers for large vessels; small vessels do not require elastic properties.
choices.C: Large vessel walls are too thick for diffusion from the lumen to reach the outer layers; small vessel walls are thin enough to be fed from the lumen.
choices.D: The walls of large vessels are too thick for luminal oxygen to reach the deep layers, so the vasa vasorum supplies the tunica intima; small vessels have no intima to supply.
choices.E: Large vessels undergo higher physical stretching, requiring a nervous system to coordinate relaxation; small vessels contract autonomously.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Cells in the walls of small-caliber vessels are close enough to the central lumen to receive oxygen and nutrients by direct diffusion through the endothelial surface. However, the walls of large, thick vessels are too thick for diffusion to reach the outer layers. These vessels require a dedicated network of small blood vessels (vasa vasorum) in their adventitia to nourish their outer cells.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Tunica adventitia... In larger vessels, this layer contains small blood vessels, called the vasa vasorum... The vasa vasorum functions to supply blood to the cells in the outer layers of the vessel wall, which are too far from the lumen to receive oxygen and nutrients by diffusion." (Vascular study guide, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: The vasa vasorum supplies the outer wall (adventitia and outer media); the intima next to the lumen is fed by diffusion from the lumen.

A.passage: The largest lymphatic vessels, the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, both with walls having tunics like those of veins, return lymph to the circulatory system by joining veins near the heart.
A.file: Circulatory System - SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS.pdf

B.passage: in the lumen, so out in the tunica adventitia are small vessels to help feed the outer layers of the wall; these are called the "vasa vasorum" or the "vessels of the vessels." The muscular arteries are all those smaller than the elastic arteries. They have less connective tissue in the tunica intima, may have internal elastic lamina, and there are often some scattered elastic fibers in the media. Most have an external elastic lamina, but the smallest ones might not. The thickness of the tunica adventitia is variable, and there may be "vasa vasorum" present.

C.passage: The outermost layer is the tunica adventitia , which is composed of connective tissue and a variable amount of elastic fibers. Depending on location, this connective tissue may merge imperceptibly with the surrounding tissues. In blood vessels where the wall is too thick for the luminal blood to nourish the entire thickness of the wall, the tunica adventitia also contains small vessels for blood supply to the outer layers of the wall. These small adventitial vessels are referred to as the vasa vasorum (vessels of vessels).

E.passage: Macroscopically visible blood vessels have three major layers or tunics: (1) The intima includes the endothelium, connective tissue, and an internal elastic lamina in larger vessels; (2) the media contains alternating layers of smooth muscle and collagen or elastic lamellae; and (3) the adventitia (or externa) contains connective tissue, small vessels (vasa vasorum), and nerves.
E.file: Circulatory System - SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS.pdf

questions.stem: What structural landmark defines the boundary between the tunica intima and the tunica media in a muscular artery, and why does this landmark appear highly folded or scalloped in routine histological sections?

choices.A: The basement membrane; it appears folded because of the high concentration of desmosomes.
choices.B: The external elastic lamina; it appears folded because of the high pressure of blood within the living tissue.
choices.C: The internal elastic lamina; it looks folded because the medial smooth muscle contracts after death and during fixation.
choices.D: The internal elastic lamina; it appears folded because it is laid down in pleats so the artery can expand during systole without tearing.
choices.E: The vasa vasorum; it appears folded to allow capillary loops to reach the endothelium.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The internal elastic lamina is a fenestrated sheet of elastic tissue that physically separates the tunica intima from the tunica media. In histological preparations, it classically appears as a highly wavy, scalloped, or folded line. This occurs because the smooth muscle of the media contracts during tissue fixation and death, compressing and folding the elastic layer.
  - Supporting Quotes:

      - "Tunica intima... In muscular arteries, the outer boundary of this layer is defined by a distinct, fenestrated sheet of elastic tissue called the internal elastic lamina... In histological sections, the internal elastic lamina often appears highly folded or wavy due to post-mortem contraction of the smooth muscle in the tunica media." (Vascular study guide, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: The folds are a fixation artifact: post-mortem contraction of the medial smooth muscle crumples the internal elastic lamina.

B.passage: The largest are the elastic arteries , and are close to the heart (e.g. aorta, pulmonary artery); these experience widely fluctuating high pressure, and in addition to having internal and external elastic lamina, they contain large amounts of elastic fibers throughout the tunica media. These are arranged in sheets (lamellae) that alternate with layers of smooth muscle and collagen fibers in the media. The wall is overall thick, too thick for the whole wall to get nutrients from the blood

C.passage: Elastic fibers: The arterial side of the circulation is subject to repetitive distension with each stroke of the heart, and elastic fibers help the artery recoil once the blood bolus has passed by. Elastic fibers can be found in dense bands called lamina; the internal elastic lamina is found in the tunica intima, and the external elastic lamina is found in the outermost layers of the tunica media. There also may be elastic fibers interspersed throughout the tunica media. In general, the larger the artery, the more elastic is found.

D.passage: in the lumen, so out in the tunica adventitia are small vessels to help feed the outer layers of the wall; these are called the "vasa vasorum" or the "vessels of the vessels." The muscular arteries are all those smaller than the elastic arteries. They have less connective tissue in the tunica intima, may have internal elastic lamina, and there are often some scattered elastic fibers in the media. Most have an external elastic lamina, but the smallest ones might not. The thickness of the tunica adventitia is variable, and there may be "vasa vasorum" present.

E.passage: I am a vessel (hello!) that has only a couple of layers in my tunica media; I don't have any elastic in my walls, and I don't need any vasa vasorum in my adventitia. I am responsible for controlling flow through a capillary bed. Who am I?

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Blood/Skin/Vascular, Q30

questions.stem: What mechanical mechanism regulates the entry of interstitial fluid and large macromolecules into lymphatic capillaries during local tissue swelling?

choices.A: Active ATP-driven endocytic pumps on the luminal surface of endothelial cells.
choices.B: Endothelial cells sealed by tight junctions open only when the smooth muscle of the lymphatic capillary contracts and sucks fluid in through the gaps.
choices.C: Elastic fibers contract to compress the vessels, creating a negative vacuum pressure inside the capillary lumen.
choices.D: High hydrostatic pressure within the lymph vessels forces tight junctions to unzip.
choices.E: Overlapping endothelial cells act as micro-valves, while anchoring collagen filaments pull the endothelial cells open as tissue fluid volume increases.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Lymphatic capillaries are uniquely designed for fluid collection. Their endothelial cells lack tight junctions and overlap, acting as one-way micro-valves. They are held in place by collagen anchoring filaments. When interstitial fluid accumulates, it pulls these filaments, expanding the capillary lumen and opening the overlapping junctions so fluid, proteins, and cells can enter.
  - Supporting Quote: "lymphatic capillaries: these are blind-ended vessels... composed of a single layer of endothelial cells... no tight junctions... overlapping endothelial cells... anchor filaments (collagen) attach to the endothelial cells and surrounding tissue... as interstitial fluid volume increases, the filaments pull the endothelial cells open, allowing fluid to enter." (Lymphatic system study guide, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: Lymphatic capillaries have no tight junctions or smooth muscle; overlapping endothelial flaps pulled open by anchoring filaments let fluid in.

A.passage: -Epithelial surface has deep crypts (increases surface area for antigen contact!)

B.passage: continue as vessels interrupted by lymph nodes on their path back to the venous system. Lymphatic endothelial cells line these lymphatic vessels. Interstitial fluid forms at the arterial end of the capillaries because of the higher pressure of blood there; most of it returns to the venules. The rest (~10-20%) enters the lymphatic capillaries as lymph, a watery, clear liquid with the same composition of interstitial fluid. The lymphatic vessels ultimately converge on the Right Lymphatic Duct and the Thoracic Duct. These return blood to the venous system by way of the superior vena cava.

D.passage: Lymphatic fluid moves to the lymph nodes via afferent lymphatic vessels, while efferent lymphatic vessels move filtered lymphatic fluid from lymph nodes to other downstream lymph nodes or into the venous system.

E.passage: Bonus facts (will not be tested on exam): Note that splenic sinusoids have a special wall configuration called ‘barrel hoop’ wherein endothelial cells (stave cells) are longitudinal, and reticular fibers form transverse “hoops” that surround the endothelium. The endothelial cells are separated by gaps, so they appear (in transverse section) as cuboidal cells arranged loosely with intervening gaps.

questions.stem: Which of the following outlines the correct structural components of the blood-thymus barrier in the thymic cortex, and what is its physiological purpose?

choices.A: Fenestrated capillaries, a thick reticular lamina, and Type VI epithelioreticular cells; it allows circulating self-antigens to freely enter the cortex to promote negative selection.
choices.B: Continuous capillaries, an endothelial basement membrane, a perivascular space with macrophages, and Type VI epithelioreticular cells joined by desmosomes; it lets self-antigens reach cortical T-cells for negative selection.
choices.C: Discontinuous sinusoids, a fenestrated basement membrane, and follicular dendritic cells; it facilitates rapid export of mature T-cells into the bloodstream.
choices.D: Continuous capillaries, Hassall's corpuscles, and Langerhans cells; it synthesizes major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules.
choices.E: Continuous capillaries, an endothelial basement membrane, a perivascular space with macrophages, and Type I epithelioreticular cells with tight junctions; it prevents circulating antigens from reaching developing T-cells.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The blood-thymus barrier in the cortex prevents blood-borne antigens from reaching developing T-lymphocytes. It is composed of a continuous capillary endothelium, its thick basement membrane, a perivascular space containing macrophages (to destroy any leaking antigens), and a sealing layer of Type I epithelioreticular cells joined by tight junctions.
  - Supporting Quote: "Blood-thymus barrier in cortex... Continuous capillaries, endothelial cell basement membrane, perivascular space with macrophages, and Type I epithelioreticular cells with tight junctions... prevents circulating antigens from reaching developing T-cells." (Lymphatic system study guide, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: The cortical barrier is sealed by Type I epithelioreticular cells with tight junctions and keeps antigens out; negative selection happens in the medulla.

A.passage: Thymocytes: These precursor-T cells are derived from stem cells produced by the bone marrow. In the thymic cortex, they are surrounded by the epithelial reticular cell framework and they undergo an intense selection process through interactions with the epithelioreticular cells. Most cells die in the cortex; less than 5% of the lymphoid progenitors that originally entered the thymus from the bone marrow will mature, leave the thymus, and enter the peripheral immune system. Note that several thymic growth factors (such as thymosin) control the maturation of T cells.

B.passage: Cords = lymphoid tissue; B-cells, plasma cells, macrophages Sinuses: spaces bridged by reticular cells and fibers; contain lymph, lymphocytes, macrophages. Contiguous with cortical sinuses. 38

C.passage: (follicles) containing B cells. The paracortical zone houses T- cells. The medulla contains “cords”of cells (with plasma cells, macrophages, reticular cells, fibers, and dendritic cells) and spaces in between cells called sinuses (note that the lymph fluid percolates through the sinuses).

D.passage: Hassall’s corpuscles: These unique-looking structures are found in the medulla of the thymus; they appear as eosinophilic swirls, and are composed of flattened, keratinized epithelial- reticular cells. The presence of Hassall’s corpuscles is diagnostic of thymic tissue.

E.passage: In the thymic parenchyma, a “blood-thymic barrier” is formed because thymic capillaries are continuous, tight vessels and they have a surrounding sheath of reticuloepithelial cells external to their basal lamina. The function of this blood-thymic barrier is to protect developing T-cells from circulating antigens.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q2

questions.stem: How do the molecular interactions and anatomical locations of T-cell positive selection differ from negative selection within the thymus?

choices.A: Positive selection is in the cortex (recognizing self-MHC on Type II/III epithelioreticular cells); negative selection is in the medulla (strong self-antigen binders removed by dendritic cells and Type V/VI cells).
choices.B: Positive selection occurs when B-cells migrate into the cortex to present antigen; negative selection occurs in Hassall's corpuscles.
choices.C: Positive selection occurs in the medulla mediated by dendritic cells; negative selection occurs in the cortex mediated by Type I epithelioreticular cells.
choices.D: Positive selection eliminates any T-cell that binds to self-antigens; negative selection promotes the survival of T-cells that bind to foreign antigens presented by macrophages.
choices.E: Positive selection occurs in the medulla, where T-cells must recognize self-MHC on Type V and VI epithelioreticular cells; negative selection occurs in the cortex, where T-cells binding self-antigen too strongly are removed by Type II and III epithelioreticular cells.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: T-cell education requires two distinct steps. Positive selection occurs in the cortex, where T-cells must recognize self-MHC on Type II/III epithelioreticular cells. Negative selection occurs in the medulla, where T-cells that bind self-antigens too strongly are destroyed by dendritic cells and Type V/VI epithelioreticular cells.
  - Supporting Quote: "T-cell education... Positive selection occurs in the cortex (cells must recognize self MHC; mediated by type II and III epithelioreticular cells). Negative selection occurs in the medulla (cells must not recognize self antigens; mediated by dendritic cells, and type V and VI epithelioreticular cells)." (Lymphatic system study guide, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: Positive selection (self-MHC recognition) is cortical and negative selection (strong self-antigen binding) is medullary; this option swaps them.

A.passage: Thymocytes: These precursor-T cells are derived from stem cells produced by the bone marrow. In the thymic cortex, they are surrounded by the epithelial reticular cell framework and they undergo an intense selection process through interactions with the epithelioreticular cells. Most cells die in the cortex; less than 5% of the lymphoid progenitors that originally entered the thymus from the bone marrow will mature, leave the thymus, and enter the peripheral immune system. Note that several thymic growth factors (such as thymosin) control the maturation of T cells.

B.passage: Hassall’s corpuscles: These unique-looking structures are found in the medulla of the thymus; they appear as eosinophilic swirls, and are composed of flattened, keratinized epithelial- reticular cells. The presence of Hassall’s corpuscles is diagnostic of thymic tissue.

C.passage: Immunity Cellular immunity (or cell-mediated immunity) is mediated by T cells. It is the arm of the adaptive immune system that does not involve antibodiesor complement, but rather involves the activation of T lymphocytes, macrophages, and Natural Killer cells (NK cells), and the release of various cytokines in response to an antigen.

D.passage: Big picture: Lymphatic/Lymphoid system The general functions of the lymphatic system are to provide the sites for the differentiation of lymphocytic cells (including their ability to recognize “non-self” or foreign cells or invaders; as well as their ability to distinguish “self” from “non-self”) and to provide regions for blood and lymph filtration.

E.passage: Cells Cells in the lymphatic system include B & T lymphocytes and Antigen-presenting cells (APCs).

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q3

questions.stem: High Endothelial Venules (HEVs) are crucial for lymphocyte homing. What is the characteristic morphology of their endothelial cells, and how do they physically facilitate lymphocyte entry into the lymph node parenchyma?

choices.A: Simple columnar epithelium with motile cilia; they sweep lymphocytes from the bloodstream into the subcapsular sinus.
choices.B: Simple cuboidal epithelium; chemokines open wide fenestrations between the cells so lymphocytes slip through without having to adhere first.
choices.C: Simple cuboidal epithelium; apical glycoproteins and integrins attract lymphocytes, which then exit the blood by diapedesis.
choices.D: Simple squamous endothelium; they open wide intercellular fenestrations to allow passive filtration of lymphocytes.
choices.E: Stratified cuboidal epithelium; they undergo holocrine secretion, shedding whole sheets of lymphocytes into the paracortex.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: High Endothelial Venules (HEVs) are found in the paracortex of lymph nodes and have a unique cuboidal endothelium. They express specialized surface glycoproteins that bind circulating lymphocytes, signaling them to migrate across the venule wall (diapedesis) to enter the lymph node.
  - Supporting Quote: "Lymphocytes enter the lymph node from blood via HEVs (high endothelial venules) whose endothelium is cuboidal. Bonus fact: The glycoproteins and integrins on the apical surfaces of this specialized endothelial cell lining attract lymphocytes back to the lymph nodes." (Lymphatic system study guide, Page 8)

Tempting but wrong: Lymphocytes enter through HEVs by binding apical glycoproteins and integrins and then crossing by diapedesis, not through fenestrations.

A.passage: In this drawing (from this link): yellow = subcapsular sinus, green = cortex, blue = medulla

B.passage: B-cells: form from bone marrow sites; generate memory cells and plasma cells; account for approximately 10-20% of circulating lymphocytes T-cells: approximately 70-80% of circulating blood lymphocytes. NK (Natural Killer) cells: comprise remainder of circulating lymphocytes APCs: Antigen presenting cells – these include macrophages, Langerhans cells (in the skin), dendritic cells, and B-cells.

C.passage: Lymphocytes enter the lymph node from blood via HEVs (high endothelial venules) whose endothelium is cuboidal. Bonus fact: The glycoproteins and integrins on the apical surfaces of this specialed endothelial cell lining attract lymphocytes back to the lymph nodes.

E.passage: There are palatine tonsils (located in the lateral wall of the oropharynx and covered by a stratified squamous epithelium, lingual tonsils (situated in the lamina propria at the root of the tongue and also covered by stratified squamous epithelium), and pharyngeal tonsils (located in the upper part of the throat and covered by pseudostratified ciliated epithelium).

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q4

questions.stem: What is the functional difference between the "open" and "closed" blood circulation pathways within the red pulp of the spleen?

choices.A: Closed circulation allows blood to bypass the red pulp completely; open circulation dumps blood directly into the white pulp follicles.
choices.B: Closed circulation empties directly into the sinusoids; open circulation empties into the cords of Billroth, so cells must squeeze through slits in the sinusoid wall to get back into the blood.
choices.C: Closed circulation is exclusive to T-cells; open circulation is reserved entirely for old erythrocytes.
choices.D: Closed circulation dumps blood into the splenic cords of Billroth for filtering; open circulation delivers blood straight into the sinusoids, so only closed-circulation cells must squeeze through the endothelial slits.
choices.E: Closed circulation is mediated by lymphatic capillaries; open circulation relies on fenestrated capillaries with diaphragms.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The spleen's red pulp filters blood. In closed circulation, capillaries connect directly to splenic sinusoids. In open circulation, blood is dumped directly into the splenic cords (of Billroth). Blood cells must then squeeze through the narrow slits between the elongated, rod-shaped endothelial cells of the sinusoids to re-enter circulation, a process that filters out old or damaged erythrocytes.
  - Supporting Quote: "In open circulation, penicillar arterioles dump blood directly into the red pulp cords (cords of Billroth)... blood cells must then squeeze between the elongated endothelial cells of the sinusoids to return to circulation." (Lymphatic system study guide, Page 6)

Tempting but wrong: Open circulation empties into the cords of Billroth and forces cells through the sinusoid slits; closed circulation goes straight into sinusoids.

A.passage: The Red Pulp is composed of a network of reticular fibers bearing lymphocytes, macrophages and APCs. These cells make up the splenic cords or “Cords of Billroth” and interspersed among these are blood-containing sinuses. The red pulp is the site of filtration of blood. The White Pulp consists of lymphoid tissue that responds to blood-borne pathogens/antigens. White pulp includes 2 components:

B.passage: The splenic circulation is an important part of understanding this organ. The pathway of splenic circulation on this slide is high yield for the exam.

D.passage: Red Pulp of the Spleen • Splenic Cords (“Cords of Billroth”) - network of reticular cells and fibers - B and T lymphocytes - macrophages - plasma cells - blood cells (rbc, neutrophils, platelets)

E.passage: Lymphatic vessels The lymphatic vessels can be considered to be a “one-way street back to the Superior Vena Cava”. They originate as “blind” lymphatic capillaries in connective tissue beds and
