questions.stem: How do specialized Microfold (M) cells in the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) physically deliver foreign luminal antigens to the immune system?

choices.A: They sample luminal antigens and transcytose them to antigen-presenting cells waiting in a basolateral pocket.
choices.B: They undergo continuous apoptosis, shedding their cytoplasm into the lamina propria to release captured antigens.
choices.C: They secrete major basic protein into the lumen to break down the antigen before absorbing it via active transport.
choices.D: They use long, flagellum-like cilia to physically push the antigen into the adjacent lymph nodules.
choices.E: They phagocytose luminal antigens, digest them in lysosomes, and present the peptides on MHC II directly to T-cells in the lamina propria.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Microfold (M) cells are specialized epithelial cells that cover lymph nodules in the GI tract (MALT/Peyer's Patches). They sample antigens from the lumen and transport them across the cell via transcytosis, delivering them directly to antigen-presenting cells waiting in a unique basolateral pocket.
  - Supporting Quote: "M cells sample antigen directly from the lumen and deliver it to APCs that are located in a unique pocket-like structure on their basolateral surface via 'transcytosis'." (Lymphatic System I and II slide deck, Page 61)

Tempting but wrong: M cells transcytose antigen to the antigen-presenting cells in their basolateral pocket; they are not themselves the presenting cells.

A.passage: M cells sample antigen directly from the “Microfold lumen and deliver it to APCs that are located in a unique pocket-like structure on cells” their basolateral surface via “transcytosis”.

B.passage: In the thymic parenchyma, a “blood-thymic barrier” is formed because thymic capillaries are continuous, tight vessels and they have a surrounding sheath of reticuloepithelial cells external to their basal lamina. The function of this blood-thymic barrier is to protect developing T-cells from circulating antigens.

C.passage: that do enter the GI tract encounter macrophages, dendritic cells, and B and T lymphocytes in Peyer’s patches and other GALT tissues. M cells are specialized cells found in the epithelium covering Peyer’s Patches--they help to “sample antigen”. M cells function by sampling antigen directly from the lumen of the gut and deliver it to APCs and lymphocytes that are located in a unique pocket-like structure on their basolateral surface. Tonsils The tonsils are accumulations of lymphoid tissue surrounding the openings of the digestive and respiratory tracts.

D.passage: Lymphoid Follicles (nodules) - the sites of antigen encounter and proliferation/differentiation of B cells.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q6

questions.stem: Which anatomical region of the spleen is rich in T-cells, and how is it organized relative to the splenic microvasculature?

choices.A: The marginal zone, which surrounds the white pulp at its border with the red pulp.
choices.B: The splenic cords of Billroth, which form thick nets surrounding the trabecular veins.
choices.C: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS), which physically surrounds the central arteriole in the white pulp.
choices.D: The germinal centers of the splenic nodules, which are centered around penicillar arterioles.
choices.E: The marginal zone, which forms a continuous barrier of epithelioreticular cells around the splenic capsule.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The white pulp of the spleen is organized around central arterioles. The immediate sleeve of lymphoid tissue surrounding these arterioles is the Periarteriolar Lymphoid Sheath (PALS), which is highly enriched in T-lymphocytes.
  - Supporting Quote: "White pulp... Periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS) - rich in T-cells... surrounds the central arteriole" (Lymphatic system study guide, Page 5)

Tempting but wrong: The marginal zone lies between white and red pulp; the T-cell sleeve wrapped around the central arteriole is the PALS.

A.passage: The Red Pulp is composed of a network of reticular fibers bearing lymphocytes, macrophages and APCs. These cells make up the splenic cords or “Cords of Billroth” and interspersed among these are blood-containing sinuses. The red pulp is the site of filtration of blood. The White Pulp consists of lymphoid tissue that responds to blood-borne pathogens/antigens. White pulp includes 2 components:

B.passage: Spleen Blood Supply: Splenic artery → Trabecular artery → Central artery (surrounded by lymphoid tissue – PALS) → Penicillar arterioles → sinuses → trabecular veins – Splenic vein)

C.passage: lymphoid nodules (containing B cells) and the Periarteriolar Lymphoid Sheaths (PALS), a sheath of T lymphocytes surrounding the central arterioles. While you do not need to visually recognize the histology of PALS, red pulp, or white pulp for the exam, be familiar with the descriptions above.

D.passage: proliferation of B cells in lymphoid nodules present at intervals along the path of PALS (though the B-cell containing nodules are not part of PALS!). When the arteriole subdivides to the point that the PALS is lost, the arterioles tend to run in bundles – at this location they are called penicillar arterioles; they deliver blood to the red pulp. Blood from the penicillars then enters the cords of the red pulp –in an “open” fashion, or it continues in a “closed” fashion, passing directly into the splenic sinuses.

E.passage: The splenic circulation is an important part of understanding this organ. The pathway of splenic circulation on this slide is high yield for the exam.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q7

questions.stem: What cellular and structural changes characterize the post-pubertal involution of the thymus?

choices.A: The epithelial reticular network is completely replaced by dense regular collagen fibers, leading to a rigid calcified organ.
choices.B: The thymus undergoes hyperplasia, transforming entirely into a secondary lymphoid organ packed with B-cell nodules.
choices.C: Most of the lymphatic tissue is replaced by fat, but epithelioreticular cells and Hassall's corpuscles persist.
choices.D: Most of the lymphatic tissue is replaced by adipose tissue, and the epithelioreticular cells and Hassall's corpuscles disappear along with it.
choices.E: The blood-thymus barrier breaks down completely, allowing the thymus to filter blood similarly to the spleen.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Following puberty, the thymus undergoes involution, during which its active lymphatic tissue is gradually replaced by adipose tissue. However, the basic epithelial structure, including Hassall's corpuscles, remains identifiable.
  - Supporting Quote: "Involution of the thymus... Post-pubertal thymus undergoes involution, in which the functional lymphatic tissue is replaced by fat. However, the epithelioreticular cells and Hassall's corpuscles are still present." (Lymphatic system study guide, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: Epithelioreticular cells and Hassall's corpuscles persist in the involuted thymus even as fat replaces the lymphatic tissue.

A.passage: • Cells: – B Lymphocytes and plasma cells – T Lymphocytes – APCs (macrophages, dendritic cells, and B lymphocytes) – Reticular cells (fibroblastic cell that produces the network of Type III collagen fibers, or reticular fibers that support all lymphatic tissues except thymus) – Epithelial reticular cells (only in thymus) 10

B.passage: Lymphoid Structures common to many secondary lymphoid organs:

C.passage: Hassall’s corpuscles: These unique-looking structures are found in the medulla of the thymus; they appear as eosinophilic swirls, and are composed of flattened, keratinized epithelial- reticular cells. The presence of Hassall’s corpuscles is diagnostic of thymic tissue.

D.passage: Lymphatic vessels The lymphatic vessels can be considered to be a “one-way street back to the Superior Vena Cava”. They originate as “blind” lymphatic capillaries in connective tissue beds and

E.passage: What is the main function of the blood-thymic barrier present in the thymus?

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q8

questions.stem: What structural transitions occur within an outer cortical lymph nodule (follicle) of a lymph node upon exposure to a foreign antigen?

choices.A: The nodule changes from a primary to a secondary nodule whose pale germinal center is a site of T-lymphocyte proliferation for cells arriving from the paracortex.
choices.B: The nodule's reticular fibers degrade completely, transforming it into a fluid-filled medullary sinus.
choices.C: The nodule loses all of its B-cells and is completely colonized by T-cells arriving from the paracortex.
choices.D: The nodule transitions from a primary nodule to a secondary nodule containing a germinal center, which represents a site of active B-lymphocyte proliferation and differentiation.
choices.E: High endothelial venules (HEVs) proliferate within the nodule to turn it into an endocrine-like gland.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Unstimulated lymph nodules are "primary." Upon antigen exposure, they transform into "secondary" nodules, which develop a pale-staining germinal center at their core. This germinal center is a highly active zone of B-lymphocyte proliferation, somatic hypermutation, and selection.
  - Supporting Quote: "Cortex... contains lymphatic nodules (or follicles), which are rich in B-cells. Primary nodules do not have a germinal center. Secondary nodules have a pale-staining center called a germinal center, which is a site of active B-lymphocyte proliferation..." (Lymphatic system study guide, Page 7)

Tempting but wrong: Germinal centers are sites of B-lymphocyte proliferation and differentiation; T cells occupy the paracortex.

A.passage: Secondary follicles develop after an antigen has been encountered. A germinal center (the site of B cell proliferation) develops. B cells then differentiate as plasma cells or memory B-cells. 26

B.passage: CT = connective tissue of the capsule T = trabeculae extending from capsule throughout the lymphoid tissue LN = lymphoid nodules MS = medullary sinuses MC = medullary cords 37

C.passage: (follicles) containing B cells. The paracortical zone houses T- cells. The medulla contains “cords”of cells (with plasma cells, macrophages, reticular cells, fibers, and dendritic cells) and spaces in between cells called sinuses (note that the lymph fluid percolates through the sinuses).

D.passage: Primary follicles contain small, naïve lymphocytes, with no germinal center

E.passage: Lymphocytes enter the lymph node from blood via HEVs (high endothelial venules) whose endothelium is cuboidal. Bonus fact: The glycoproteins and integrins on the apical surfaces of this specialed endothelial cell lining attract lymphocytes back to the lymph nodes.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q9

questions.stem: Trace the exact anatomical pathway of lymph fluid as it percolates through a lymph node from entry to exit.

choices.A: Afferent lymphatic $\rightarrow$ subcapsular sinus $\rightarrow$ medullary sinuses $\rightarrow$ paratrabecular (trabecular) sinuses $\rightarrow$ efferent lymphatic at the convex capsule.
choices.B: High endothelial venules $\rightarrow$ trabecular sinuses $\rightarrow$ germinal centers $\rightarrow$ afferent lymphatic.
choices.C: Subcapsular sinus $\rightarrow$ medullary cords $\rightarrow$ efferent lymphatic $\rightarrow$ paracortex.
choices.D: Medullary sinuses $\rightarrow$ paratrabecular sinuses $\rightarrow$ convex capsule $\rightarrow$ afferent lymphatic.
choices.E: Afferent lymphatic $\rightarrow$ subcapsular sinus $\rightarrow$ paratrabecular (trabecular) sinuses $\rightarrow$ medullary sinuses $\rightarrow$ efferent lymphatic at the hilum.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Lymph enters the node via afferent lymphatic vessels on the convex outer surface. It drains into the subcapsular sinus, passes through paratrabecular (trabecular) sinuses into the medullary sinuses, and finally exits the node via efferent lymphatic vessels at the concave hilum.
  - Supporting Quote: "Afferent lymphatics bring lymph to the lymph node via its convex surface; the lymph drains into the subcapsular sinus, through the paratrabecular sinuses into the medullary sinuses, and is finally drained by the efferent lymphatics exiting at the hilum." (Lymphatic system study guide, Page 8)
Part 2: Connective Tissue Answers

Tempting but wrong: Lymph runs subcapsular → trabecular → medullary sinuses and leaves by the efferent lymphatic at the hilum, not the convex surface.

B.passage: Lymph Node: Summary Function: Filtration of lymph, “Conference Centers” for immune reactions (sites of antigen encounter; proliferation/differentiation of B cells) Unique Histologic aspects: - Capsule - Afferent lymphatics → subcapsular sinus → trabecular sinuses → medullary sinuses → efferent lymphatics - Blood supply – HEV: site of lymphocyte entry - Cortex: Follicles (B-cells) +/- germinal center - Paracortical areas: T cells - Medulla: cords, sinuses (plasma cells) - Overall make-up: ~60% T cells, ~40% B cells 39

C.passage: CT = connective tissue of the capsule T = trabeculae extending from capsule throughout the lymphoid tissue LN = lymphoid nodules MS = medullary sinuses MC = medullary cords 37

E.passage: Afferent lymphatics bring lymph to the lymph node via its convex surface; the lymph drains into the subcapsular sinus, through the paratrabecular sinuses into the medullary sinuses, and is finally drained by the efferent lymphatics exiting at the hilum.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q10

questions.stem: Why does a deficiency in Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) directly disrupt collagen synthesis within the recombinant pathways of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER)?

choices.A: Vitamin C is required as a co-factor for lysyl oxidase; without it, tropocollagen molecules cannot be cross-linked into stable fibrils outside the cell, even though the triple helix forms normally.
choices.B: Vitamin C physically cross-links tropocollagen molecules into mature collagen fibrils at the cell surface.
choices.C: A lack of Vitamin C blocks glycosylation of hydroxylysine residues in the Golgi, so procollagen cannot be packaged into secretory vesicles and accumulates inside the fibroblast.
choices.D: Vitamin C is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases; without hydroxylated proline and lysine, the alpha chains cannot form a stable procollagen triple helix.
choices.E: Vitamin C is the primary energy substrate used by procollagen peptidases to cleave registration peptides in the extracellular space.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Inside the rER, individual alpha chains of collagen must undergo hydroxylation of their proline and lysine residues. This crucial step, catalyzed by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, requires Vitamin C as an essential cofactor. Without it, the chains cannot form stable triple helices (procollagen), leading to scurvy.
  - Supporting Quote: "Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which hydroxylate proline and lysine in the rER... without this step, unstable triple helix procollagen forms, which is degraded... Scurvy: bleeding gums, loose teeth, poor wound healing." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 7)

Tempting but wrong: Extracellular cross-linking is done by lysyl oxidase (a copper enzyme); vitamin C is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases inside the rER.

A.passage: The helices are packaged in the Golgi and secreted to the extracellular environment. Once outside the cell, the terminal registration peptides are cleaved, and the helix becomes insoluble and is called “tropocollagen.” These can now polymerize and form true fibers of collagen.

B.passage: Which step of collagen formation fails if Vitamin C is lacking?

C.passage: Which of the following diseases results from lack of Vitamin C in the diet?

D.passage: Alpha chain polypeptides are initially formed – these alpha strands are then modified in the rER. Hydroxylation of the strands occurs next, and requires vitamin C as a co-factor. The next step is glycosylation of the alpha chains. Di"erent carbohydrates added in this step can result in di"erent collagen types. The alpha chains have terminal “registration” peptides on both ends, which helps orient them to now form triple helices in the rER. The triple helix is now called “procollagen.” The registration peptides remain attached; these allow the triple helix to remain soluble inside the cell.

E.passage: Intracellular (mostly in rER): - procollagen alpha strands formed - hydroxylation (vitamin C is cofactor) - glycosylation - procollagen triple helices formed (soluble) - soluble triple helices packaged and secreted Extracellular: - registration peptides cleaved→ insoluble - polymerization

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q11

questions.stem: What biochemical cleavage step prevents collagen from prematurely self-assembling into large fibrils inside the Golgi apparatus or secretory vesicles of a fibroblast?

choices.A: The preservation of non-helical registration peptides (propeptides) on both ends of the procollagen molecule, which are only cleaved extracellularly by procollagen peptidases to form tropocollagen.
choices.B: The continuous phosphorylation of collagen chains by Golgi-resident kinases.
choices.C: The binding of tropocollagen to cytoplasmic actin filaments during transport.
choices.D: The physical encapsulation of procollagen in highly acidic lipid vesicles that inhibit fibrillogenesis.
choices.E: The hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues is delayed until the molecule reaches the extracellular space, where hydroxylases finally let the triple helices pack into fibrils.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Fibroblasts synthesize procollagen with non-helical registration peptides (propeptides) at both the N- and C-termini. These bulky propeptides keep the molecule soluble and prevent premature self-assembly into fibrils inside the cell. Once exocytosed, extracellular procollagen peptidases cleave these propeptides, producing tropocollagen, which spontaneously self-assembles.
  - Supporting Quote: "Procollagen is secreted into the extracellular space... procollagen peptidases cleave registration peptides... to form tropocollagen, which self-assembles into fibrils." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 6)

Tempting but wrong: Hydroxylation happens inside the rER; premature assembly is blocked by the registration peptides, which procollagen peptidases remove only outside the cell.

A.passage: Intracellular (mostly in rER): - procollagen alpha strands formed - hydroxylation (vitamin C is cofactor) - glycosylation - procollagen triple helices formed (soluble) - soluble triple helices packaged and secreted Extracellular: - registration peptides cleaved→ insoluble - polymerization

B.passage: • Collagen synthesis is similar for all types of collagen – Types can differ by amino acids or post-translational modifications • Each collagen molecule is triple helix – All three strands of helix are the same in any particular collagen type • Collagen synthesis has intra- and extracellular steps

C.passage: The helices are packaged in the Golgi and secreted to the extracellular environment. Once outside the cell, the terminal registration peptides are cleaved, and the helix becomes insoluble and is called “tropocollagen.” These can now polymerize and form true fibers of collagen.

E.passage: Collagen itself is a triple helix protein consisting of three polypeptide alpha strands. The alpha strands are each a repetitive string of three amino acids. Three strands form triple helices inside the cell; once they are discharged to the extracellular space they undergo final modification and can then polymerize into long fibers.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q12

questions.stem: What is the structural relationship between fibrillin and elastin during the assembly of elastic fibers, and what disease state results from a genetic mutation in this scaffolding system?

choices.A: Elastin is deposited first and fibrillin microfibrils then wrap it as an outer sheath; mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene cause Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.
choices.B: Fibrillin acts to degrade excess elastic fibers; mutations lead to Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.
choices.C: Fibrillin microfibrils act as a structural scaffold or template upon which elastin is systematically deposited; mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene cause Marfan Syndrome.
choices.D: Elastin molecules are enzymatically converted into fibrillin by lysyl oxidase; mutations lead to Scurvy.
choices.E: Elastin forms a rigid outer template that is slowly filled with fibrillin; mutations lead to Osteogenesis Imperfecta.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Elastic fibers are composed of two main structural elements: a microfibrillar scaffold made of the glycoprotein fibrillin, and an amorphous elastin core deposited onto this scaffold. A genetic defect in the fibrillin-1 gene prevents proper elastic fiber assembly, causing Marfan Syndrome.
  - Supporting Quote: "Elastic fibers... Fibrillin microfibrils act as a scaffold... Elastin is deposited... Marfan syndrome: mutation in fibrillin-1." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 8)

Tempting but wrong: Fibrillin microfibrils are laid down first as the scaffold for elastin, and fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome; Ehlers-Danlos involves collagen.

A.passage: Clinical correlation: Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are a cluster of diseases that involve gene mutations affecting steps of collagen formation, such as genes for the alpha strands, or the gene for the hydroxylation enzyme, etc. Symptoms are varied, depending on the specific mutation, but skin and joints are often involved. You’ll learn more about these later in the systems blocks.

B.passage: • Ehlers-Danlos syndromes – Cluster of diseases relating to poor collagen production – Various gene mutations described, such as: • Alpha chain, collagen type I • Alpha chain, collagen type III • Enzyme of hydroxylation step

C.passage: • Marfan’s syndrome – mutation in fibrillin-1 gene → defective, fragmented elastic fibers

D.passage: To make elastic fibers, the main cell secretes two components - tropoelastin and fibrillin. The fibrillin forms a mesh, and the coiled tropoelastin molecules sit on the fibrillin mesh, and many of these cross-link to form an elastic fiber. Elastic fibers will stretch when stress is applied, but will snap back to the more coiled position once the stress is released.

E.passage: • Osteogenesis imperfecta – Several types with different mutations – All affect collagen type I formation in bone – → malformed/brittle/bendable bones

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q13

questions.stem: What physical property of Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) and proteoglycans allows the ground substance of connective tissue to resist compressive forces and act as a structural shock absorber?

choices.A: They are highly negatively charged due to sulfate and carboxyl groups, which repel water and pack the GAG chains tightly against collagen fibrils into a dense, dehydrated lattice.
choices.B: They are highly positively charged, attracting chloride ions that dehydrate the matrix.
choices.C: Their hydrophobic lipid tails form a dense oil-like barrier that repels water.
choices.D: They are highly negatively charged due to sulfate and carboxyl groups, attracting sodium ions which osmotically bind large volumes of water, creating a highly hydrated, turgid gel.
choices.E: They form covalent ester bonds directly with collagen fibrils, locking them into a rigid crystalline lattice.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are long carbohydrate chains rich in negative charges (sulfate and carboxyl groups). This high negative charge density attracts sodium ions ($Na^+$), which are highly osmotically active, pulling in water to form a highly hydrated, turgid gel that effectively resists physical compression.
  - Supporting Quote: "Because the GAGs are highly negatively charged, they attract sodium ions, which in turn attract water molecules... This high water content allows cartilage to resist compression (act as a shock absorber)." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 11)

Tempting but wrong: The negative charges attract Na+ and with it water; the hydrated gel, not a dry lattice, is what resists compression.

A.passage: DENSE REGULAR connective tissue –densely packed type I collagen

C.passage: • Loose – supportive, flexible, weak – Delicate, inconspicuous collagen fibers, inconspicuous fibroblasts – Provides space for immune cells to live, move, communicate – Good examples are found supporting the epithelium in GI tract • Dense regular – handles strong unidirectional force – Dense collagen in parallel bundles – Examples are ligaments (bone-bone), tendons (muscle-bone) • Dense irregular – handles strong multidirectional forces – Short dense collagen bundles running in different directions – Good example is dermis of skin

E.passage: • Collagen synthesis is similar for all types of collagen – Types can differ by amino acids or post-translational modifications • Each collagen molecule is triple helix – All three strands of helix are the same in any particular collagen type • Collagen synthesis has intra- and extracellular steps

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q14

questions.stem: How do the adipocytes of brown (multilocular) adipose tissue generate heat instead of ATP during exposure to cold temperatures?

choices.A: They contain abundant lysosomes that degrade lipids via an exothermic hydrolytic pathway.
choices.B: Mitochondrial thermogenin (UCP-1) lets protons bypass ATP synthase, so the energy of the proton gradient is released as heat.
choices.C: They pack their abundant mitochondria with extra ATP synthase and burn the surplus ATP in futile cycles of glycolysis, releasing the energy as heat.
choices.D: They store lipid in a single large droplet that peroxisomes oxidize, and the breakdown of the resulting hydrogen peroxide releases heat in place of ATP synthesis.
choices.E: They use specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum to oxidize glucose anaerobically.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Brown adipocytes are specialized for non-shivering thermogenesis. They contain abundant mitochondria expressing thermogenin (Uncoupling Protein-1 or UCP-1). Thermogenin allows protons to flow back across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase, which dissipates the proton motive force directly as heat.
  - Supporting Quote: "Brown fat... uncoupling protein-1 (UCP-1) or thermogenin... uncouples proton flow from ATP synthesis... energy dissipated as heat." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 18)

Tempting but wrong: Brown-fat heat comes from thermogenin (UCP-1) letting protons bypass ATP synthase, not from making and burning extra ATP.

A.passage: Macrophages: These are phagocytic immune cells that live in tissue; they are derived from immune cells called monocytes which circulate in the blood. Macrophages endocytose particles (of anything they encounter) for digestion in lysosomes. They are important in first-line immune defense, as they can communicate discovery of potentially dangerous molecules (antigens) to other immune cells.

B.passage: large amounts in hibernating animals. It can function as a quick heat source – the adipocytes in brown fat can activate the enzyme thermogenin, which uncouples the electron transfer system in mitochondria, allowing the energy to be released as heat. Only small residual amounts of brown fat are found in adult humans.

E.passage: Which of the following cells can be found in many tissues and is specialized to ingest debris?

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q15

questions.stem: What structural and mechanical organization makes dense regular connective tissue different from dense irregular connective tissue, and where is the former typically located?

choices.A: Dense regular connective tissue contains random, multi-directional collagen fibers to resist forces in all directions (located in the dermis).
choices.B: Dense regular connective tissue consists of closely packed collagen fibers woven in alternating perpendicular layers to resist stress from several directions (located in the dermis and organ capsules).
choices.C: Dense regular connective tissue is characterized by a high concentration of active macrophages and mast cells (located in the lamina propria).
choices.D: Dense regular connective tissue consists of closely packed, parallel collagen fibers aligned in the direction of unidirectional mechanical stress (located in tendons and ligaments).
choices.E: Dense regular connective tissue features a massive volume of amorphous ground substance with very few fibers (located in the umbilical cord).

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Dense regular connective tissue consists of closely packed collagen fibers aligned in a parallel, highly organized arrangement designed to withstand mechanical pull in a single, predictable direction. This tissue forms tendons (connecting muscle to bone) and ligaments (connecting bone to bone).
  - Supporting Quote: "Dense regular CT: consists of closely packed, parallel bundles of collagen fibers... aligned in the direction of unidirectional functional stress (e.g., tendons, ligaments)." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 12)

Tempting but wrong: Fibers in dense regular tissue run parallel in one direction (tendons, ligaments); multidirectional packing is dense irregular tissue such as the dermis.

A.passage: • Loose – supportive, flexible, does NOT handle forces well • Dense – strong, handles forces well Regular – unidirectional forces Irregular – multidirectional forces

B.passage: DENSE IRREGULAR connective tissue - short, thick bundles of type I collagen, oriented randomly, forming a three-dimensional network. It is strong, and resists stresses in multiple directions. Often contains supplementary elastic fibers, and may have some type III collagen sprinkled in. Skin dermis is a good example.

C.passage: Mast cells – these are scattered in connective tissue near interfaces with epithelium throughout the body (skin, GI tract, upper respiratory tract). They generate and store mediators of inflammation (e.g. histamine, heparin, proteases, leukotrienes, etc). They have Mast cell membrane-bound receptors for IgE (an antibody made by plasma cells). Mast cells degranulate, or dump their granule contents, into the extracellular space when stimulated. Clinical correlation: Mast cell degranulation results in “type I hypersensitivity reactions” which include localized swelling, redness, and itching.

D.passage: DENSE REGULAR connective tissue –densely packed type I collagen

E.passage: There are two main classes of macromolecules in the ground substance – glycoproteins and proteoglycans.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q16

questions.stem: What cellular events occur during the primary degranulation pathway of mast cells when they encounter an allergen to which they have been previously sensitized?

choices.A: The granules release pre-formed leukotrienes and prostaglandins immediately, while histamine and heparin are synthesized only after the allergen has been internalized.
choices.B: Antigen cross-links IgG molecules bound to Fc-gamma receptors on the mast cell membrane, triggering calcium influx and new synthesis of histamine and heparin that is secreted over the following days.
choices.C: Antigen cross-links IgE molecules bound to high-affinity $Fc\epsilon RI$ receptors on the mast cell membrane, triggering calcium influx and the rapid exocytosis of pre-formed granules containing histamine and heparin.
choices.D: Mast cells convert into plasma cells, which secrete large volumes of soluble collagenase into the matrix.
choices.E: Intracellular IgG antibodies bind directly to the nucleus, forcing the cell to undergo necrosis and release cytokines.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Mast cells express high-affinity IgE receptors ($Fc\epsilon RI$) bound with IgE antibodies. When a multivalent antigen (allergen) binds and cross-links these IgE molecules, it triggers an intracellular signaling cascade involving calcium influx, causing the rapid exocytosis of cytoplasmic granules containing histamine and heparin.
  - Supporting Quote: "Mast cells... express high-affinity IgE receptors on their cell surface... when antigen binds, it cross-links the IgE, triggering degranulation... Histamine (vasoactive, increases vascular permeability), Heparin (anticoagulant)..." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 15)

Tempting but wrong: Mast cells are sensitized by IgE on Fc-epsilon-RI, and histamine and heparin are pre-formed in granules released within seconds.

A.passage: Extensive release of mast cell granules can result in anaphylactic shock. Mast cells are moderate sized, have a central bland nucleus and pink granules; they can be very difficult to find in a tissue section.

C.passage: • Numerous cytoplasmic granules • Granules store chemical mediators of inflammation (Histamine, heparin, proteases eosinophil chemotactic factor, leukotrienes) • Have membrane-bound receptors for IgE (more on this in immuno-) • Degranulate when attached IgE is bound by an allergen → Type I hypersensitivity reactions (allergic reactions, hives, anaphylactic shock)

D.passage: Mast cells – these are scattered in connective tissue near interfaces with epithelium throughout the body (skin, GI tract, upper respiratory tract). They generate and store mediators of inflammation (e.g. histamine, heparin, proteases, leukotrienes, etc). They have Mast cell membrane-bound receptors for IgE (an antibody made by plasma cells). Mast cells degranulate, or dump their granule contents, into the extracellular space when stimulated. Clinical correlation: Mast cell degranulation results in “type I hypersensitivity reactions” which include localized swelling, redness, and itching.

E.passage: • Found in CT and in lymph nodes • Derived from B lymphocytes • Synthesize/store antibodies, release when triggered

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q17

questions.stem: How can an active fibroblast be cytologically distinguished from an inactive fibrocyte under light microscopy?

choices.A: The active fibroblast is a multinucleated giant cell with a prominent ruffled membrane.
choices.B: The active fibroblast has a small, elongated, heterochromatic nucleus and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm because its rough ER has been replaced by smooth ER.
choices.C: The active fibroblast is smaller, with a highly condensed pyknotic nucleus and no visible cytoplasm.
choices.D: It has a larger, oval, euchromatic nucleus with a prominent nucleolus and more basophilic cytoplasm (abundant rough ER and Golgi).
choices.E: The active fibroblast contains massive lipid vacuoles that compress the nucleus to the periphery of the cell membrane.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Active fibroblasts are actively synthesizing extracellular matrix proteins. They feature abundant rough ER and a prominent Golgi apparatus, which imparts cytoplasmic basophilia, and a large, euchromatic nucleus with a visible nucleolus. Inactive fibrocytes are smaller, spindle-shaped cells with dark, heterochromatic nuclei.
  - Supporting Quote: "Fibroblast (active): larger cell, oval euchromatic nucleus, prominent nucleolus, abundant basophilic cytoplasm... Fibrocyte (inactive): smaller cell, spindle-shaped, dark heterochromatic nucleus, sparse cytoplasm." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 5)

Tempting but wrong: A small, dark, elongated nucleus with scant pale cytoplasm describes the inactive fibrocyte; the active fibroblast is euchromatic with basophilic cytoplasm.

A.passage: Ruffled cell membrane → high surface area to encounter particles and engulf them

B.passage: • Appears tan-brown grossly • Many small fat globules in cytoplasm, “multilocular” • Nucleus fits between small globules, not pushed to side

C.passage: The primary cell – the FIBROBLAST The primary cell found in all basic connective tissue (but not in the specialized types) is the fibroblast. The fibroblast synthesizes,

D.passage: • Moderate in size • Eccentric nucleus with chunky chromatin – Sometimes referred to as “clock-face nucleus” • Pale region beside nucleus = prominent Golgi

E.passage: Microscopically, usually only the nucleus of the cell can be seen

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD1 Lymph/CT/Small groups, Q18

questions.stem: Why do mature white adipocytes appear as empty, ring-like "signet ring" structures on standard H&E stained histology slides?

choices.A: Alcohol and xylene used in routine processing dissolve the stored triglyceride, leaving an empty space inside a thin rim of cytoplasm.
choices.B: The lipid droplet is fixed by osmium during routine H&E processing and then washed out by the eosin step, leaving a clear vacuole with the nucleus pushed to one side.
choices.C: Adipocytes are hollow cells that contain only air under normal physiological conditions.
choices.D: The massive unilocular lipid droplet is highly basophilic, which completely repels both hematoxylin and eosin dyes.
choices.E: The nucleus of the adipocyte undergoes rapid autolysis immediately after tissue excision, so the cytoplasm collapses into a thin ring around an empty central cavity.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: White adipocytes contain a single, large, unilocular lipid droplet composed of neutral triglycerides. During routine histological slide preparation, the tissue is dehydrated using alcohols and cleared with organic solvents (like xylene), which completely dissolves the lipids, leaving a large, empty white vacuole.
  - Supporting Quote: "White fat cells... one large droplet of fat in the cytoplasm... Of note, the lipids themselves are melted away during the process of making a slide, so the white space of the cytoplasm is actually where the lipids used to be." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 17)
Part 3: Small Group 1 Answers

Tempting but wrong: Osmium is a special stain that preserves lipid; routine H&E loses the triglyceride to alcohol and xylene, which is why the cell looks empty.

A.passage: adipocyte, and contains a large amount of fat in the cytoplasm – this is melted away during processing to make slides, so the blank “white” cytoplasm in fat cell represents where lipids used to be.

B.passage: • Appears white on microscopic sections (is yellow grossly) • Has one big fat vacuole (“unilocular”), nucleus pushed to side

C.passage: Brown fat adipocytes have multiple small droplets of fat instead of one large droplet (hence the name “multilocular fat.”). Because of this, the nucleus is not as compressed to the side as in white fat adipocytes, and often sits centrally.

questions.stem: In the clinical case of Pemphigus Vulgaris, what specific cell junction is target-damaged by autoantibodies, and what is the resulting clinical and histological presentation?

choices.A: Hemidesmosomes are damaged (autoantibodies against BP180); leads to intraepidermal blistering because basal keratinocytes separate from one another (acantholysis).
choices.B: Tight junctions are damaged; leads to rapid leakage of interstitial fluid across the stratum corneum without any physical cell separation.
choices.C: Hemidesmosomes are damaged; leads to deep subepidermal blisters where the entire epidermis cleanly detaches from the dermis.
choices.D: Desmosomes are damaged (specifically autoantibodies against desmogleins); leads to intraepidermal blistering because keratinocytes separate from one another (acantholysis).
choices.E: Gap junctions are damaged; leads to complete loss of metabolic communication between the stratum basale and the stratum spinosum.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Pemphigus Vulgaris is an autoimmune disease where antibodies are produced against desmoglein, an adhesion molecule found in desmosomes. This impairs cell-to-cell adhesion in the epidermis, causing the keratinocytes to pull apart (acantholysis) and form intraepidermal blisters.
  - Supporting Quote: "Pemphigus vulgaris... autoimmune disease where antibodies are made against desmoglein, a cadherin protein... cells separate from one another (acantholysis)... target junction: Desmosomes" (SG1 post-session answers, Page 2)

Tempting but wrong: Pemphigus vulgaris targets desmogleins in desmosomes; BP180 and hemidesmosomes are the target in bullous pemphigoid (Small Group 1).

Hemidesmosomes (half-desmosomes), attach to cytoskeleton (keratins) and anchor to the basal lamina; primary proteins are integrins. The basement membrane is basal lamina + reticular lamina (from fibroblasts). (Basal infoldings too, but not all epithelial cells have them)

questions.stem: How does the pathological mechanism of Bullous Pemphigoid differ from Pemphigus Vulgaris, and what specific junctional proteins are targeted?

choices.A: Bullous Pemphigoid targets desmosomes via autoantibodies against desmoglein 3; this splits keratinocytes from one another and produces fragile, flaccid intraepidermal blisters with acantholysis.
choices.B: Bullous Pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes (autoantibodies against BP180 or BP230), lifting the whole epidermis off the dermis as tense subepidermal blisters without acantholysis.
choices.C: Bullous Pemphigoid is a defect in Type IV collagen synthesis; Pemphigus Vulgaris is an autoimmune attack on fibroblasts.
choices.D: Bullous Pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes via autoantibodies against BP180 or BP230; the damage splits the stratum spinosum, producing flaccid intraepidermal blisters with acantholysis like pemphigus.
choices.E: Bullous Pemphigoid is a genetic lack of keratin production; Pemphigus Vulgaris is an infectious disease that destroys melanocytes.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Bullous Pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes (autoantibodies against BP180/BP230), which anchor the basal cell layer of the epidermis to the basal lamina. Because the attachment of the entire cellular sheet to the basement membrane is destroyed, the entire epidermis detaches from the dermis, producing large, tense subepidermal blisters.
  - Supporting Quote: "Bullous Pemphigoid... autoantibodies against BP180 or BP230 (proteins of the hemidesmosome)... entire epidermis detaches from dermis... no oral blisters." (SG1 post-session answers, Page 2)

Tempting but wrong: In bullous pemphigoid the split is beneath the epidermis (tense subepidermal blisters, no acantholysis); acantholysis is the pemphigus vulgaris pattern.

B.passage: Low-power border between epidermis and dermis is really uneven and diving down in one area. There are large nests of cells in the dermis that look like the ones in the epidermis.
B.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

questions.stem: What molecular motor defect is responsible for immotile cilia syndrome (Kartagener's Syndrome), and how does this defect directly cause chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis?

choices.A: A defect in myosin II, which halts the contraction of the actin-based terminal web.
choices.B: A genetic loss of tubulin proteins, which prevents the structural assembly of the basal bodies.
choices.C: A lack of nexin links between the central pair of microtubules in the axoneme, which lets cilia beat but in random directions; mucus is moved too slowly, predisposing the patient to chronic respiratory infections.
choices.D: A defect in kinesin motors along the axonemal microtubules, which blocks anterograde transport of tubulin to the ciliary tip so cilia form short and stiff, leaving mucus to pool in the airways.
choices.E: A lack of inner and outer dynein arms in the axoneme stops ciliary beating, so the mucociliary escalator cannot clear mucus and bacteria, causing chronic airway infection.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Cilia require microtubule-associated dynein motors to slide microtubules past one another, generating the force for ciliary bending. In Kartagener's Syndrome, a genetic lack of inner and outer dynein arms halts ciliary motility, leading to chronic infections from a non-functional mucociliary elevator.
  - Supporting Quote: "immotile cilia syndrome (often called Kartagener's syndrome)... cilia are abnormal because they lack outer and inner dynein arms... clinical triad of: chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, situs inversus" (SG1 post-session answers, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: Kartagener syndrome is a loss of the inner and outer dynein arms, which stops ciliary beating altogether (Small Group 1).

B.passage: connexon with connexin subunits) 2. Review and briefly describe the features found at the basal aspect of epithelium. Hemidesmosomes (half-desmosomes), attach to cytoskeleton (keratins) and anchor to the basal lamina; primary proteins are integrins. The basement membrane is basal lamina + reticular lamina (from fibroblasts). (Basal infoldings too, but not all epithelial cells have them)
B.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

C.passage: 3) What might be the effect of this mutation on a patient’s respiratory tract? Their cilia won’t work, can’t move pollutants/mucus/etc away, it accumulates and can end up deeper in the lung.
C.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

D.passage: 2) What is cilia's function in the large airways? Sweep pollutants/mucus/etc off the epithelial surface
D.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

E.passage: 7) Now back to your patient: why might they be at increased risk for this condition? Their cilia won't move the debris/mucus/bacteria away, and this can get deep into lung, resulting in bacterial pneumonia. Patients with ciliary dysfunction easily and frequently develop bacterial pneumonia.

questions.stem: During the progression of cutaneous melanoma, what anatomical landmark must tumor cells cross to transition from the "radial growth phase" to the "vertical growth phase," and why does this transition increase the risk of metastasis?

choices.A: They must penetrate the basement membrane and spread laterally along the dermal-epidermal junction, where Langerhans cells carry them into the bloodstream for systemic spread.
choices.B: They must cross from the papillary dermis into the reticular dermis, because only the reticular dermis contains blood vessels and lymphatics that can carry tumor cells away.
choices.C: They must invade the hair follicle sheath to access sebaceous glands, which transport tumor cells to the subcutaneous fat.
choices.D: They must penetrate the basement membrane and invade the underlying dermis, which contains blood vessels and lymphatic capillaries that provide pathways for systemic metastasis.
choices.E: They must cross the stratum corneum to access the external environment, allowing them to spread via physical contact.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Melanoma cells first spread horizontally within the avascular epidermis (radial growth phase), during which they cannot metastasize. However, once they acquire the ability to invade vertically, they break through the epithelial basement membrane and enter the underlying dermis, gaining access to lymphatic and blood vessels.
  - Supporting Quote: "The tumor cells got into lymphatics and probably went to lymph nodes, but then kept going and landed in other organs, and starting growing there too... invaded through basement membrane into dermis." (SG1 post-session answers, Pages 4-5)

Tempting but wrong: Vertical growth means invading down into the dermis, whose blood and lymphatic vessels give tumor cells a route to metastasize; Langerhans cells do not carry tumor cells.

B.passage: Low-power border between epidermis and dermis is really uneven and diving down in one area. There are large nests of cells in the dermis that look like the ones in the epidermis.
B.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

C.passage: 1) Review the names and approximate locations of the layers of the skin. Epidermis, dermis (superficial/papillary and reticular/deep), subcutaneous fat.
C.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

D.passage: 4) What layers of the skin appear to be involved? Epidermis, superficial dermis, maybe into the deep dermis though some of the deep dermis looks OK. The subcutaneous fat looks OK.

questions.stem: Based on the path of lymphatic metastasis discussed in Small Group 1, how do invading melanoma cells physically reach and colonize regional lymph nodes?

choices.A: They enter dermal blood capillaries, travel through the veins and arteries, and leave the circulation through high endothelial venules in the paracortex to colonize the node.
choices.B: They enter dermal lymphatic capillaries, travel via efferent lymphatic vessels to the lymph node, enter the node at the hilum, and proliferate in the medullary cords.
choices.C: They enter dermal lymphatics, travel in afferent lymphatic vessels, enter the node at the subcapsular sinus, and grow there, disrupting its architecture.
choices.D: They cross the blood-brain barrier and travel via cerebrospinal fluid into the thoracic duct.
choices.E: They are physically carried into the node by active Schwann cells via the peripheral nerves.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Metastatic melanoma cells enter dermal lymphatic vessels. They travel with the lymph fluid and enter regional lymph nodes via afferent lymphatic vessels on the convex surface. They first pool in the subcapsular sinus before invading the parenchyma, proliferating, and replacing normal lymphoid tissue.
  - Supporting Quote: "sentinel lymph node... cancerous cells got into a lymphatic vessel, traveled to the node, entered the node via the subcapsular sinus, and then decided to hang out here and grow." (SG2 post-session answers, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: Lymph, and tumor cells carried in it, reach a node through afferent lymphatics and enter at the subcapsular sinus; efferent vessels leave at the hilum.

A.passage: 2) Take this opportunity to review how lymph and blood flow through this organ.
A.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

B.passage: Now examine this slide of an abnormal lymph node surgically removed from a patient's axilla. It has been bisected. [this a lymph node with metastasis from a breast cancer]
B.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

C.passage: The node receives lymph draining from local tissues. If a cancer cell gets into a lymphatic, it will enter the node via the subcapsular sinuses and then start growing in the node. This node was excised from the axilla of a patient with breast cancer.
C.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

E.passage: Lymph enters via the subcapsular sinus. Blood enters/exits via the hilum. Lymphocytes traveling in the bloodstream can get out of the vessel and into the node via the high endothelial venules (these are difficult to visualize).

questions.stem: What is the cellular and molecular mechanism of Scurvy, and how does it explain the clinical presentation of bleeding gums and poor wound healing?

choices.A: It is an autoimmune destruction of desmosomes in the oral mucosa.
choices.B: It is a genetic mutation in the fibrillin gene that prevents elastic fiber recoil in capillaries.
choices.C: Without Vitamin C, proline and lysine in procollagen are not hydroxylated in the rER; the unstable triple helices are degraded, so collagen in vessels and healing tissue is defective.
choices.D: Vitamin C deficiency blocks lysyl oxidase cross-linking of tropocollagen outside the cell, so collagen fibrils form with normal helices but lack covalent cross-links, leaving vessels and wounds weak.
choices.E: A lack of Vitamin C prevents the hydroxylation of proline and lysine in fibrillin within the rER; the resulting elastic fibers cannot recoil, so capillaries over-stretch and bleed, and wounds heal slowly.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Scurvy is caused by a nutritional deficiency of Vitamin C. Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes require Vitamin C as a cofactor to stabilize collagen triple helices. Without it, newly synthesized collagen is structurally unstable and rapidly degraded, causing tissue fragility, bleeding gums, and poor wound healing.
  - Supporting Quote: "Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which hydroxylate proline and lysine in the rER... without this step, unstable triple helix procollagen forms, which is degraded... Scurvy: bleeding gums, loose teeth, poor wound healing." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 7)

Tempting but wrong: Scurvy is defective collagen: vitamin C is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases that stabilize the collagen triple helix, not fibrillin or lysyl oxidase.

A.passage: 2) From what you’ve learned, what could be affected if cadherin is defective/lost? Adherens junction and desmosomes
A.file: SG1_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

questions.stem: Which genetic and structural defects characterize Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS), and what are its classic clinical presentations?

choices.A: Defects in elastin synthesis or in the fibrillin scaffold that carries it; presents with loose, hyperextensible skin and joints that recoil poorly, but normal collagen in vessels and tendons.
choices.B: A defect in ciliary dynein arms; presents with chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and situs inversus.
choices.C: A mutation in the gene encoding tyrosinase; presents with complete loss of skin pigmentation and visual defects.
choices.D: A mutation in the fibrillin-1 gene that weakens elastic fibers; presents with tall stature, long limbs, lens dislocation, and aortic root dilation or dissection.
choices.E: Defects in collagen synthesis or processing (such as lysyl hydroxylase deficiency or mutations in Type I, III, or V collagen); presents with hypermobile joints, hyperextensible skin, and tissue/vascular fragility.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome is a heterogeneous group of inherited disorders caused by defects in the synthesis, processing, or assembly of collagen fibrils (such as mutations in Type I, III, or V collagen). This leads to a severe loss of tensile strength, presenting as hyperelastic skin, hypermobile joints, and tissue fragility.
  - Supporting Quote: "Clinical correlation: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome... group of inherited disorders... defect in collagen synthesis or processing... hypermobile joints, hyperelastic skin, tissue fragility." (Connective Tissue study guide, Page 7)

Tempting but wrong: Ehlers-Danlos is a family of collagen defects (lysyl hydroxylase, collagen I, III, V); fibrillin and elastic-fiber defects describe Marfan syndrome.

questions.stem: Why is the articular cartilage of a joint exceptionally limited in its ability to undergo repair or regeneration following mechanical injury?

choices.A: The tissue is completely avascular and lacks a perichondrium (which would normally harbor chondroprogenitor stem cells); thus, there is no blood supply or source of new cells to facilitate repair.
choices.B: Chondrocytes constantly secrete vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) to destroy any invading blood vessels.
choices.C: The matrix is calcified throughout, so chondrocytes trapped in their lacunae cannot divide or migrate toward the injury, even though nearby blood vessels can supply repair cells.
choices.D: The tissue is richly supplied by synovial blood vessels but lacks a perichondrium; new chondroblasts can be recruited from the blood but cannot attach to the smooth articular surface.
choices.E: The cells are multinucleated and cannot undergo mitosis; the high density of elastic fibers blocks the diffusion of all growth factors.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces. Unlike other cartilage, it lacks a perichondrium (which contains progenitor cells), and like all cartilage, it is completely avascular. Consequently, there is no blood-borne or local stem-cell source to facilitate significant regeneration after mechanical injury.
  - Supporting Quote: "articular cartilage... does NOT have a perichondrium... avascular... very limited ability to repair itself." (Cartilage and Bone study guide, Pages 5-6)

Tempting but wrong: Articular cartilage is avascular and lacks a perichondrium, so it has neither a blood supply nor a local source of new cells for repair.

questions.stem: What cellular imbalance is responsible for the skeletal remodeling pathology seen in Osteoporosis?

choices.A: Bone resorption by osteoclasts exceeds bone deposition by osteoblasts, leading to a net loss of bone mass and destruction of trabecular microarchitecture.
choices.B: Osteoblasts differentiate directly into chondrocytes, replacing the bone matrix with hyaline cartilage.
choices.C: Bone deposition by osteoblasts exceeds resorption by osteoclasts, but the new osteoid fails to mineralize, leaving soft, poorly calcified bone and bowing deformities.
choices.D: Osteoclasts become largely inactive, so old bone is never remodeled and accumulates as dense, brittle bone with microcracks that cause fractures.
choices.E: Osteocytes break their gap junction connections and undergo rapid, synchronized apoptosis, leaving empty lacunae throughout the osteons.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Bone is dynamically remodeled by the opposing actions of osteoblasts (bone deposition) and osteoclasts (bone resorption). In Osteoporosis, osteoclast activity outpaces osteoblast activity, resulting in a net loss of bone mineral density and degradation of the trabecular microarchitecture.
  - Supporting Quote: "Osteoporosis: characterized by a decrease in bone mass... resorption exceeds deposition... trabeculae become thin and fragile." (Cartilage and Bone study guide, Page 22)

Tempting but wrong: Excess unmineralized osteoid is osteomalacia; osteoporosis is resorption exceeding deposition, with net loss of normally mineralized bone.

questions.stem: What are the characteristic microscopic and optical findings when analyzing synovial fluid from a joint affected by Gout?

choices.A: Sheets of simple squamous cells that have peeled off the synovial membrane.
choices.B: Abundant multinucleated osteoclasts actively digesting the articular surface.
choices.C: Rhomboid-shaped, positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals, often found phagocytosed by neutrophils and triggering acute synovial inflammation.
choices.D: Needle-shaped, positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals deposited in the articular cartilage, with few neutrophils because the crystals are not phagocytosed.
choices.E: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, which are often found phagocytosed by neutrophils, initiating a severe inflammatory response.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Gout is a metabolic joint disease caused by the crystallization of uric acid within joints. Synovial fluid analysis under polarized light microscopy shows diagnostic needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, which trigger a severe acute inflammatory response dominated by neutrophils.
  - Supporting Quote: "Synovial fluid analysis... Gout... needle-shaped crystals... negatively birefringent... monosodium urate." (SG1 post-session answers, Page 3)
Part 4: Small Group 2 Answers

Tempting but wrong: Gout crystals are needle-shaped monosodium urate that are negatively birefringent and phagocytosed by neutrophils (Small Group 1).

questions.stem: How do the histopathological findings in the joint space and marrow cavities of a patient with Rheumatoid Arthritis differ from those with Osteoarthritis?

choices.A: Rheumatoid Arthritis shows osteoclasts completely replaced by adipocytes; Osteoarthritis shows bone tissue transformed into dense regular connective tissue.
choices.B: Rheumatoid Arthritis is characterized by needle-shaped crystals, while Osteoarthritis is characterized by a complete loss of Type II collagen.
choices.C: Rheumatoid Arthritis shows cartilage wear and subchondral bone remodeling with osteophytes and little inflammation, while Osteoarthritis shows a dense lymphocyte and plasma cell synovitis with a destructive pannus.
choices.D: Rheumatoid Arthritis (an inflammatory arthritis) shows a dense neutrophil-rich acute infiltrate in the synovium and marrow with urate crystals eroding the cartilage; Osteoarthritis shows the same infiltrate but milder, without crystals.
choices.E: RA shows a dense chronic infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells) in synovium and marrow with a destructive pannus; OA shows cartilage wear and subchondral remodeling without a primary inflammatory synovitis.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease characterized by a proliferative synovitis, where chronic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes and plasma cells) infiltrate the synovium and adjacent bone marrow, replacing normal yellow fat with a destructive pannus. Osteoarthritis is a mechanical, degenerative disease characterized by cartilage erosion and subchondral bone remodeling, without a primary chronic inflammatory infiltrate.
  - Supporting Quote: "No, there's no fat tissue in the marrow spaces... the marrow space is filled with dark blue cells - this represents a dense inflammatory infiltrate... osteoarthritic knee? No... this slide represents rheumatoid arthritis\!" (SG2 post-session answers, Page 1)

Tempting but wrong: RA is chronic inflammation (lymphocytes and plasma cells) with a pannus; neutrophils with urate crystals describe gout, and OA lacks a primary inflammatory synovitis.

A.passage: 4) What tissue have we learned about where the nuclei are compressed flat by all the pink fibers outside the cell? Dense regular connective tissue!! The fibroblasts get smushed by all the collagen they’ve put out into the tissue and all you can see of them are little smashed nuclei.

C.passage: 4) What do you think is happening in this case, and how might this affect the patient? These changes are seen often in older adults, and develops over years of wear and tear on the joints. The articular cartilage can be damaged, and sometimes the bone underlying the cartilage is also damaged. The cartilage tries to repair, but eventually it ends up being all irregular, which just upsets joint function. This is an an example of osteoarthritis of the knee joint. Over time there is increasing pain and restricted movement of the joint.
C.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

E.passage: 2) Examine the spongy bone and marrow spaces deeper in the tissue. Older adults usually have mostly yellow marrow (fat), with some red marrow (developing blood cells) - is that what you see here? No, there’s no fat tissue in the marrow spaces, and we haven’t yet learned blood cell development (heme system block next spring) but it’s not there either!

questions.stem: What structural features determine the stability of an advanced atherosclerotic plaque, and what events trigger an acute arterial thrombosis (occlusion)?

choices.A: The size of the lipid core alone; a large core narrows the lumen so much that blood flow stops and clots, so plaques with thick fibrous caps are the ones most likely to occlude suddenly.
choices.B: The size of the tunica adventitia; if too thick, it compresses the lumen from the outside, stopping all blood flow.
choices.C: The number of valves in the lumen of the elastic artery; if the valves fail, blood pools and clots.
choices.D: The thickness of the fibrous cap (smooth muscle and collagen) over the thrombogenic lipid core; a thin cap can rupture, exposing the core and triggering platelet aggregation and coagulation.
choices.E: The thickness of the tunica media; if the smooth muscle layers are too thick, they compress the intima from outside and narrow the lumen until flow stops without any thrombus forming.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: In advanced atherosclerosis, smooth muscle cells migrate into the tunica intima to lay down a fibrous cap of collagen over a necrotic, lipid-rich core. The thickness and stability of this cap determine plaque stability. If the cap is thin and ruptures, highly thrombogenic lipids and tissue factor are exposed to blood, triggering rapid occlusion via thrombosis.
  - Supporting Quote: "Clinical correlation: Atherosclerosis... Smooth muscle cells then migrate from the tunica media into the intima, where they proliferate and secrete collagen, forming a fibrous plaque... plaque rupture can lead to thrombosis..." (Vascular study guide, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: Stability depends on the fibrous cap: thin caps rupture and expose the thrombogenic core, triggering platelet aggregation and thrombosis (Small Group 2).

A.passage: is simply a list of possible diagnoses that you refine later) We now know that this person’s coronary arteries were diseased, so we can add “Atherosclerosis present, affecting coronary arteries” to our disease list- these changes put the patient at risk for a problem with blood flow to the heart. If the vessel is suddenly completely blocked (usually b/c a plaque suddenly bursts apart into the lumen), all of the heart muscle cells fed by that vessel could die - which is a heart attack. (You will get a TON of more details on this in subsequent blocks)
A.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

The ‘guts’ of the plaque are covered by endothelium, so the guts aren’t exposed to the blood flow. (you'll get plenty of details about plaques and plaque formation in a later block).

questions.stem: Describe the chronological histopathological changes that occur in the myocardium 3 to 4 days following an acute Myocardial Infarction (heart attack).

choices.A: The infarct is filled with granulation tissue (new capillaries and fibroblasts) with early collagen deposition and no remaining necrotic cardiomyocytes.
choices.B: The myocardium is completely restored to normal with newly regenerated, healthy cardiomyocytes.
choices.C: Multinucleated giant cells accumulate to synthesize a temporary cartilage callus over the damaged ventricle.
choices.D: There is a dense infiltration of neutrophils, accompanied by necrotic, hypereosinophilic cardiomyocytes that have lost their nuclei and striations (coagulative necrosis).
choices.E: There is a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells around cardiomyocytes that still have nuclei and striations, because coagulative necrosis does not appear until about two weeks.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: At 3 to 4 days post-myocardial infarction, the necrotic cardiomyocytes have undergone coagulative necrosis, presenting as hypereosinophilic (bright pink) fibers lacking nuclei and striations. This tissue triggers an intense acute inflammatory response, characterized by a dense infiltration of neutrophils to clear the dead tissue.
  - Supporting Quote: "Case 3: Myocardial Infarction... dense neutrophil infiltrate... necrotic cardiomyocytes (no nuclei, hypereosinophilic, loss of striations)..." (SG2 post-session answers, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: By 3–4 days the infarct shows coagulative necrosis (anucleate, hypereosinophilic myocytes) with a dense neutrophil infiltrate; granulation tissue comes later.

C.passage: 4) What do you think is happening in this case, and how might this affect the patient? These changes are seen often in older adults, and develops over years of wear and tear on the joints. The articular cartilage can be damaged, and sometimes the bone underlying the cartilage is also damaged. The cartilage tries to repair, but eventually it ends up being all irregular, which just upsets joint function. This is an an example of osteoarthritis of the knee joint. Over time there is increasing pain and restricted movement of the joint.
C.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

D.passage: 4) What tissue have we learned about where the nuclei are compressed flat by all the pink fibers outside the cell? Dense regular connective tissue!! The fibroblasts get smushed by all the collagen they’ve put out into the tissue and all you can see of them are little smashed nuclei.
D.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

questions.stem: What tissue eventually replaces dead cardiomyocytes 2 to 3 months post-myocardial infarction, and what are its mechanical properties?

choices.A: Loose mucous connective tissue containing cardiac stem cells that slowly differentiate into new cardiomyocytes and restore most of the contractile function within a year.
choices.B: A dense, non-contractile collagenous scar composed of dense connective tissue, which stabilizes the ventricular wall but cannot contract, predisposing the patient to heart failure.
choices.C: Hyaline cartilage, which provides rigid, non-yielding support to prevent cardiac rupture.
choices.D: Highly contractile skeletal muscle fibers that fully restore cardiac pump function.
choices.E: Hypertrophied surviving cardiomyocytes that divide and fill the infarct, restoring wall strength but with weaker contraction than the original muscle.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Cardiomyocytes are permanent cells and cannot regenerate. Dead heart tissue is cleared by macrophages and replaced via granulation tissue with a dense irregular connective tissue scar rich in Type I collagen. This scar prevents ventricular rupture but is non-contractile, which can compromise heart function and lead to heart failure.
  - Supporting Quote: "Infarcted myocardium is replaced by a collagenous scar (dense irregular connective tissue)... does not contract... can lead to heart failure." (SG2 post-session answers, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: Cardiomyocytes are permanent cells that cannot divide; the infarct is replaced by a dense, non-contractile collagenous scar.

B.passage: 6) Does this finding in this person's heart suggest anything about their medical condition? (also tricky, more details iin future blocks) They’ve had damage to the heart muscle in the past (and in fact, they must've had a heart attack, with this part of the heart muscle dying and being replaced by fibrous scar tissue)
B.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

E.passage: 1) The large pink bands are the muscular wall - what kind of muscle would you expect in the GI tract? Smooth muscle – slow and weak contraction
E.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

questions.stem: In the metastatic colon cancer case discussed in Small Group 2, how did tumor cells reach and alter the structure of the draining lymph nodes?

choices.A: They invaded the muscularis externa, entered local blood capillaries, traveled to the node in the arterial supply, and grew in the paracortex while sparing the normal lymphoid follicles and sinuses.
choices.B: Cancerous epithelial cells invaded lymphatic vessels in the colon wall, reached the node via efferent lymphatics, entered at the hilum, and grew as solid sheets within the medullary cords while the cortex stayed normal.
choices.C: They triggered a localized autoimmune reaction that forced normal lymphocytes to differentiate into cancerous glandular epithelium.
choices.D: They traveled via peripheral nerves and physically replaced the paracortical T-cell zones.
choices.E: Tumor cells invaded lymphatics in the colon wall, reached the node by afferent lymphatics into the subcapsular sinus, and grew as abnormal gland-like structures that replaced the normal architecture.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Colon cancer cells can invade local lymphatic vessels in the submucosa of the colon wall. They travel with the lymph fluid to regional draining lymph nodes, entering via the subcapsular sinus. They then proliferate and organize into abnormal gland-like structures that mimic the colon mucosa, displacing and destroying normal lymphoid tissue.
  - Supporting Quote: "This node was draining the area of the tumor, some cancerous cells got into a lymphatic vessel, traveled to the node, entered the node via the subcapsular sinus, and then decided to hang out here and grow. This is colon cancer metastatic to a lymph node." (SG2 post-session answers, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: Tumor cells reach a node through afferent lymphatics into the subcapsular sinus and replace the normal architecture with abnormal glands (Small Group 2).

B.passage: 4) Bonus question: This small rounded structure was dissected out from the fat attached to the colon, and bisected - can you guess what it might be (it is very abnormal) and why it looks like it does? Small and round – it’s a lymph node – but its hard to recognize because the architecture has been completely overtaken, and there’s hardly any normal lymphocyte areas remaining. Instead, there are some cells in there making gland shapes – these are cancerous epithelial cells again.
B.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

C.passage: 5) Any ideas what is happening here? (kinda tricky) This epithelium is cancerous – it has grown too thick, and is very disorganized and crowded.
C.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

E.passage: This node was draining the area of the tumor, some cancerous cells got into a lymphatic vessel, traveled to the node, entered the node via the subcapsular sinus, and then decided to hang out here and grow. This is colon cancer metastatic to a lymph node.
E.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

questions.stem: Under low-power light microscopy, what key architectural changes distinguish colon adenocarcinoma (cancer) from normal, healthy colon tissue?

choices.A: The crypts keep their normal single-layered architecture, but the epithelial cells become pale and eosinophilic as they fill with mucin, and the tumor stays confined above the muscularis mucosae.
choices.B: The muscularis externa is completely replaced by a thick layer of elastic cartilage.
choices.C: The cancerous colon tissue shows a complete absence of blood vessels and a massive accumulation of subcutaneous fat.
choices.D: The mucosal epithelium becomes thinner and flattened, with fewer goblet cells, while the crypts keep their normal single-layered test-tube arrangement in the lamina propria.
choices.E: The organized single-layer crypt architecture is lost; the epithelium becomes thickened, crowded, disorganized and deeply basophilic as it invades deeper layers of the wall.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Under low power, colon adenocarcinoma shows a complete loss of the normal, orderly, single-layered crypt architecture. The cancerous mucosa appears significantly thickened, crowded with cells, highly disorganized, and intensely basophilic (dark blue due to nuclear crowding and active protein synthesis) as it invades the submucosa and muscularis layers.
  - Supporting Quote: "The layer with epithelium is too thick, very blue... disorganized and crowded... mass or tumor." (SG2 post-session answers, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: Adenocarcinoma destroys the organized crypt architecture; the epithelium becomes crowded, disorganized and basophilic as it invades deeper layers (Small Group 2).

A.passage: 2) Do you see any portion of the tissue that looks more pale that the rest? (ask instructor for help if needed) In the upper left aspect of the tissue there is a more pale area.
A.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

B.passage: In the third, top of the layer is falling apart ( this is menstrual – nearly all of the layer will be shed during menstruation)
B.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

C.passage: 1) In some areas of the heart there is normally some fat on the outside of the organ. The first (slow-loading) slide has some; can you find the fat? Along upper edge of tissue there is some fat on the outside of the heart (there’s a coronary artery in the fat too fwiw)
C.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

D.passage: You'll learn more specifics about the colon later, but in general the epithelium is simple columnar, arranged into straight gland structures called "crypts." Some of the columnar cells are absorptive and not very exciting- looking, and some make/secrete mucus and have a big pale blob of mucus in their cytoplasm - these are "goblet cells."
D.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

E.passage: 4) How would you describe the epithelial layer here? It’s thicker, more blue, busy looking; on higher power the epithelium is very disorganized and crowded, with not much space beween the gland shapes.
E.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf
