questions.stem: What histopathological changes are observed in bone marrow during acute osteomyelitis (bone infection)?

choices.A: Ependymal cells line the marrow cavities to pump cerebrospinal fluid through the trabecular spaces.
choices.B: The normal fatty marrow is replaced by a dense infiltrate of eosinophils and mast cells, with marrow edema and congestion but no bone necrosis or sequestra.
choices.C: The fatty marrow is replaced by a suppurative, neutrophil-rich infiltrate with congestion, necrosis, and sometimes fragments of dead bone (sequestra).
choices.D: Osteoclasts undergo rapid apoptosis, leading to an overgrowth of dense, mineralized osteons.
choices.E: The marrow cavity fills with lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages forming granulomas, with gradual fibrosis and new bone formation but no necrosis.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Acute osteomyelitis is a bacterial infection of the bone marrow. Histologically, it is characterized by the replacement of normal yellow fatty marrow with a suppurative inflammatory infiltrate composed of sheets of neutrophils, accompanied by vascular congestion, edema, and fragments of dead bone (sequestra).
  - Supporting Quote: "Osteomyelitis: bone marrow infection... suppurative inflammation... neutrophils... necrosis... sequestrum." (SG2 post-session answers, Page 2)

Tempting but wrong: Acute osteomyelitis is suppurative: neutrophil-rich infiltrate with congestion, necrosis and sometimes dead bone fragments (sequestra).

A.passage: 3)Describe what you see in the marrow spaces. Could this be related to the overall disease process? The marrow spaces have fibrous tissue in them - the body often scars down damaged areas with fibrous tissue, so this indicates that the bone underlying the articular cartilage has experienced damage, and the marrow spaces have been replaced with fibrous scar. (Details of wound healing and scar formation are coming up in block 2).
A.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

B.passage: We looked at this slide last session (the toe) and most of the toe was quite diseased, but this zoomed in area of an articular surface is actually pretty normal - observe how it is of uniform thickness, and the surface is smooth. The marrow space in the underlying bone is fatty, which is appropriate for an older patient.
B.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

C.passage: 2) Examine the spongy bone and marrow spaces deeper in the tissue. Older adults usually have mostly yellow marrow (fat), with some red marrow (developing blood cells) - is that what you see here? No, there’s no fat tissue in the marrow spaces, and we haven’t yet learned blood cell development (heme system block next spring) but it’s not there either!
C.file: SG2_ post-session answers_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

questions.stem: During the mechanical process of bone fracture healing, what structural transition occurs as the temporary callus is remodeled into mature bone?

choices.A: The organized, mechanically strong lamellar bone of the callus is progressively remodeled by osteoclasts and osteoblasts into woven bone, whose random collagen fibers make it more flexible and resistant to refracture.
choices.B: Hyaline cartilage transforms directly into skeletal muscle fibers via transdifferentiation.
choices.C: Elastic fibers proliferate to turn the bone into a highly flexible, un-fracturable structure.
choices.D: Weak woven bone (random collagen fibers, many osteocytes) is remodeled by osteoclasts and osteoblasts into organized, stronger lamellar bone.
choices.E: Dense regular connective tissue in the callus mineralizes directly into compact bone without osteoclast activity, so the woven bone stage is skipped entirely.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: During fracture healing, osteoblasts first produce a temporary callus composed of woven bone, which is mechanically weak and characterized by randomly arranged collagen fibers and disorganized osteocytes. Over time, coordinated remodeling by osteoclasts and osteoblasts replaces this woven bone with highly organized, mechanically strong lamellar bone.
  - Supporting Quote: "woven bone (immature, disorganized)... remodeled into lamellar bone (mature, organized, concentric)..." (Cartilage and Bone study guide, Page 23)

Tempting but wrong: Remodeling runs the other way: weak woven bone (random collagen, many osteocytes) is replaced by organized, stronger lamellar bone.

B.passage: 4) What do you think is happening in this case, and how might this affect the patient? These changes are seen often in older adults, and develops over years of wear and tear on the joints. The articular cartilage can be damaged, and sometimes the bone underlying the cartilage is also damaged. The cartilage tries to repair, but eventually it ends up being all irregular, which just upsets joint function. This is an an example of osteoarthritis of the knee joint. Over time there is increasing pain and restricted movement of the joint.

questions.stem: What is the cellular origin of the "foam cells" found within the tunica intima during early atherosclerosis, and what do they ingest to acquire their characteristic foamy appearance?

choices.A: They are derived from medial smooth muscle cells that migrate into the intima and ingest elastic fibers fragmented by matrix metalloproteinases.
choices.B: They come from blood monocytes that enter the damaged intima, become macrophages, and engulf oxidized LDL through scavenger receptors.
choices.C: They are derived from endothelial cells that absorb excess triglycerides from the vasa vasorum.
choices.D: They are derived from circulating blood neutrophils that enter the damaged tunica intima and engulf native (non-oxidized) LDL through LDL receptors until they swell with lipid.
choices.E: They are derived from neutrophils that phagocytose necrotic cardiac muscle cells.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: Endothelial injury allows low-density lipoprotein (LDL) to enter the subendothelial space (tunica intima), where it becomes oxidized. Circulating monocytes migrate into the intima, differentiate into macrophages, and express scavenger receptors that internalize large amounts of oxidized LDL, transforming them into lipid-laden "foam cells."
  - Supporting Quote: "This damage allows low-density lipoproteins (LDL) to enter the tunica intima, where they become oxidized. Monocytes/macrophages enter the intima and phagocytose the oxidized LDL, becoming 'foam cells'" (Vascular study guide, Page 3)

Tempting but wrong: Foam cells come mainly from monocytes that become macrophages and take up oxidized LDL through scavenger receptors (Small Group 2).

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the correct chronological sequence of tissue changes in the colon wall during the progression of colon cancer?

choices.A: Formation of a localized adenoma (polyp) $\rightarrow$ Metastasis to regional lymph nodes $\rightarrow$ Dysplasia in the polyp's epithelial cells $\rightarrow$ Invasion through the muscularis mucosae and submucosa.
choices.B: Invasion of the muscularis externa $\rightarrow$ Epithelial cell dysplasia $\rightarrow$ Formation of a benign polyp $\rightarrow$ Perforation of the serosa.
choices.C: Mutation/dysplasia in mucosal epithelial cells $\rightarrow$ Formation of a localized adenoma (polyp) $\rightarrow$ Adenocarcinoma invading through the muscularis mucosae and submucosa $\rightarrow$ Invasion of lymphatic or blood vessels to metastasize.
choices.D: Mutation/dysplasia in mucosal epithelial cells $\rightarrow$ Adenocarcinoma invading the submucosa $\rightarrow$ A localized adenoma (polyp) forming on top of the invasive tumor $\rightarrow$ Invasion of lymphatic or blood vessels to metastasize.
choices.E: Endothelial cell damage in the vasa vasorum $\rightarrow$ Accumulation of foam cells in the mucosal crypts $\rightarrow$ Transcytosis of B-cells into the lumen.

questions.explanation:
- Explanation: The progression of colon cancer (adenocarcinoma) begins with genetic mutations in mucosal epithelial cells, leading to dysplasia and the formation of a benign adenomatous polyp. Over time, additional mutations drive transition to adenocarcinoma, which invades through the muscularis mucosae and into lymphatic or blood vessels to metastasize.
  - Supporting Quote: "adenocarcinoma... mucosal epithelium... dysplastic changes... invades through the muscularis mucosae... metastasis to lymph nodes." (SG2 post-session answers, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: The adenoma (polyp) stage comes before invasion; carcinoma is defined by invasion through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa.

questions.stem: During spermatogenesis, which cell type undergoes the transitional movement from the basal compartment into the adluminal compartment of the seminiferous tubule, and what cellular mechanism accommodates this shift?

choices.A: Primary spermatocytes; via the transient opening and closing of tight junctions (zonula occludens) between adjacent Sertoli cells.
choices.B: Secondary spermatocytes; by utilizing amoeboid motility to cross the interstitial fenestrations.
choices.C: Early spermatids; via the secretion of matrix metalloproteinases that dissolve the regional basement membrane.
choices.D: Spermatogonia; by establishing temporary hemidesmosomes with the basement membrane.
choices.E: Type B spermatogonia; via the transient opening and closing of desmosomes anchoring them to the basal lamina, so they enter the adluminal compartment before dividing.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Primary spermatocytes must pass the blood-testis barrier formed by the tight junctions of Sertoli cells to move into the adluminal compartment.

      - Exact Quote: “Tight junctions (zonula occludens) between basolateral membranes of adjacent Sertoli cells form BTB... 1ry spermatocyte opens tight junction and moves to adluminal compartment” [Slide 18].

Tempting but wrong: Type B spermatogonia divide in the basal compartment; their daughters, the primary spermatocytes, cross through Sertoli tight junctions that open and reseal.

A.passage: Blood-Testis barrier (BTB) • A physical barrier provided by Sertoli cells • Prevents exposure of maturing germ cells to the blood • Tight junctions (zonula occludens) between basolateral membranes of adjacent Sertoli cells form BTB – Prevents autoimmune reaction against non-diploid sperms – Spermatogonium is NOT contained within BTB – 1ry spermatocyte opens tight junction and moves to adluminal compartment 18

B.passage: They then undergo the first meiotic division, which yields two haploid secondary spermatocytes (N). The secondary spermatocytes rapidly complete meiosis II, yielding four spermatids (N). The four resulting spermatids are now up near the lumen of the tubule; they are all still attached to each other via intracytoplasmic bridges, their cytoplasmic structure is not yet mature, and they have not been released into the lumen.
B.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

C.passage: • 4 spermatids are attached by intercellular bridges forming spermatogenic syncytium

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q1

questions.stem: How do the roles of Luteinizing Hormone (LH) and Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) contrast regarding their direct cellular targets and mechanical actions in maintaining intra-tubular hormone environments?

choices.A: LH elevates regional temperatures to $34^\circ\text{C}$, while FSH triggers the golgi phase of spermiogenesis.
choices.B: LH targets Leydig cells to produce testosterone, while FSH targets Sertoli cells to produce androgen-binding protein (ABP) which keeps testosterone localized.
choices.C: LH induces interstitial myoid cell contraction, while FSH directly regulates the tight junctions of the blood-testis barrier.
choices.D: LH targets Sertoli cells to release androgen-binding protein (ABP), while FSH targets Leydig cells to stimulate testosterone production.
choices.E: LH targets Leydig cells to produce testosterone, while FSH also targets Leydig cells to make androgen-binding protein (ABP) that carries testosterone into the lumen.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: LH stimulates Leydig cells for testosterone production, whereas FSH acts on Sertoli cells to synthesize ABP to concentrate testosterone locally.

      - Exact Quote: “Luteinizing Hormone (LH):... targets Leydig cells to produce Testosterone... Follicular Stimulating Hormone (FSH):... targets Sertoli cells to produce Androgen Binding Protein (ABP) • ABP binds to testosterone and keeps it within the seminiferous tubule” [Slide 20].

Tempting but wrong: ABP is a Sertoli-cell product made in response to FSH; Leydig cells respond to LH by making testosterone.

A.passage: Spermiogenesis • Process of cytoplasmic maturation in Sertoli cell cytoplasm (temp. sensitive, requires 34oC) 1. Golgi phase • Acrosomal cap starts from proacrosomal vesicles produced by Golgi apparatus • Centrioles move to opposite pole to form basal body of flagellum 2. Cap phase • The acrosomal cap expands & covers ½ of nucleus (contains hyaluronidase and acrosin to break ovum wall); flagellum develops 3. Acrosomal phase • Elongation of nucleus, mitochondria aggregate at middle portion (provide ATP for flagellum movement) 4.

B.passage: • Follicular Stimulating Hormone (FSH): – Produced by anterior pituitary, targets Sertoli cells to produce Androgen Binding Protein (ABP) • ABP binds to testosterone and keeps it within the seminiferous tubule 20

C.passage: Question A Which cell provid es blood- testis B barrier C ? 36

D.passage: Beginning at puberty, testosterone promotes spermatogenesis and exerts masculinizing effects in other regions of the body. The Leydig cells secrete this into the connective tissue, but it needs to be concentrated in the tubules. The Sertoli cells, when stimulated by follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) from the pituitary, secretesthe androgen binding protein (ABP) that binds testosterone and holds it within the tubule.
D.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

E.passage: Endocrine influences • Luteinizing Hormone (LH): – Produced by anterior pituitary, targets Leydig cells to produce Testosterone • Promotes spermatogenesis & secondary male sex characteristics • Testosterone production begins at puberty • In fetal period, produced temporarily in 3 rd and 4th gestational months to develop sex organs

questions.stem: A patient presents with an autoimmune response targeting sperm cells within the lumen of the seminiferous tubules. If the pathogenic autoantibodies are specifically reacting to haploid germ cells, which cellular assembly has failed, and which cell stage remains structurally exempt from this local barrier?

choices.A: The tunica albuginea; secondary spermatocytes are exempt.
choices.B: The blood-testis barrier (BTB) provided by Sertoli cells; primary spermatocytes are exempt because they stay in the basal compartment.
choices.C: The intercellular cytoplasmic bridges; late spermatids are exempt.
choices.D: The interstitial myoid layer; primary spermatocytes are exempt.
choices.E: The blood-testis barrier (BTB) provided by Sertoli cells; spermatogonia are exempt.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Sertoli cell tight junctions provide the BTB to prevent autoimmune actions against haploid cells, while diploid spermatogonia sit outside this barrier.

      - Exact Quote: “A physical barrier provided by Sertoli cells... Prevents autoimmune reaction against non-diploid sperms – Spermatogonium is NOT contained within BTB” [Slide 18].

Tempting but wrong: Only spermatogonia sit below the Sertoli tight junctions in the basal compartment; primary spermatocytes move into the adluminal compartment.

A.passage: They then undergo the first meiotic division, which yields two haploid secondary spermatocytes (N). The secondary spermatocytes rapidly complete meiosis II, yielding four spermatids (N). The four resulting spermatids are now up near the lumen of the tubule; they are all still attached to each other via intracytoplasmic bridges, their cytoplasmic structure is not yet mature, and they have not been released into the lumen.
A.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

B.passage: Sertoli cells also nourish and protect developing sperm. On microscopy, spermatocytes may appear to be inside Sertoli cells (they are not) because the Sertoli cell forms a deep pocket in its membrane that nearly entirely surrounds the spermatocyte. This further serves to protect the spermatocyte. The developing sperm remains nestled in a deep fold of the Sertoli cell, moving towards the lumen, until the end of spermiogenesis when they are released into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule.
B.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

C.passage: • 4 spermatids are attached by intercellular bridges forming spermatogenic syncytium

D.passage: Seminiferous tubules Germ cells dwell inside the cytoplasmic pockets of Sertoli cells Myoid cells

E.passage: Blood-Testis barrier (BTB) • A physical barrier provided by Sertoli cells • Prevents exposure of maturing germ cells to the blood • Tight junctions (zonula occludens) between basolateral membranes of adjacent Sertoli cells form BTB – Prevents autoimmune reaction against non-diploid sperms – Spermatogonium is NOT contained within BTB – 1ry spermatocyte opens tight junction and moves to adluminal compartment 18

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q3

questions.stem: During the specific sub-phases of spermiogenesis, what structural mechanism drives the mechanical modification of the spermatozoon head and flagellum before it is released into the lumen?

choices.A: Cytoplasmic bridges break prematurely during the Golgi phase to allow independent motility within the Sertoli cytoplasm.
choices.B: The acrosomal cap undergoes a transient reaction that utilizes hyaluronidase to expand the cell's flagellar length.
choices.C: Acrosomal vesicles from the Golgi apparatus form a cap covering half the nucleus, the nucleus elongates, mitochondria aggregate in the middle piece, and extra cytoplasm is shed.
choices.D: Acrosomal vesicles from the rough ER cap the whole nucleus, the nucleus rounds up and condenses, mitochondria gather at the tip of the tail, and the extra cytoplasm is kept as fuel.
choices.E: The centrioles dissolve to condense chromosomal DNA, while the residual body transforms into an acrosomal cap.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Spermiogenesis is a differentiation process involving the creation of the acrosomal cap, nuclear condensation/elongation, mitochondrial localization, and loss of cytoplasm.

      - Exact Quote: “Golgi phase: Golgi releases 'acrosomal vesicles' that aggregate to form a 'cap'... Cap phase: Acrosomal cap expands and covers half of the 'head'... Acrosomal phase: Nucleus elongates, mitochondria aggregate in middle of cell... Maturation phase: Extra cytoplasm is shed as 'residual body'” [Top Hat Guide, Page 4].

questions.stem: What unique cytological and organizational characteristic defines the relationship between developing spermatids during the final stage of maturation before spermiation occurs?

choices.A: They are linked to Leydig cells by transient gap junctions that supply direct ATP.
choices.B: They exist as fully isolated cells surrounded by a thick, non-permeable zona pellucida.
choices.C: They are held together as a spermatogenic syncytium via intercellular cytoplasmic bridges.
choices.D: They complete cytokinesis and separate, but each stays embedded in its own Sertoli cell pocket by tight junctions until spermiation.

Explanation: Developing spermatids fail to complete cytokinesis entirely, remaining physically continuous as a syncytium to coordinate development.

      - Exact Quote: “4 spermatids are attached by intercellular bridges forming spermatogenic syncytium” [Slide 20].

Tempting but wrong: Developing germ cells never finish cytokinesis; they stay linked as a syncytium by intercellular cytoplasmic bridges until release.

A.passage: tissue between the seminiferous tubules; in this connective tissue are small groups of Leydig cells. Leydig cells (interstitial cells of Leydig) are endocrine cells and produce hormones (more on these in a bit). The cells seen in the seminiferous tubules are predominantly germ cells in various stages of maturation; the most primitive sit along the basal layer (furthest towards the outside) of the tubule. As they mature, they move towards the lumen of the tubule. Once mature, they travel the length of the tubule towards the exit of the testis.

They are fairly large columnar cells that sit along the base of the tubules, and have a large nucleus and prominent nucleolus. They are attached to each other by tight occluding junctions towards the basal aspect of their lateral aspects. These tight junctions are essential to establishing the blood-testis barrier, which protects the developing sperm. questions.stem: What structural components constitute the glomerular filtration barrier, and how does its mechanical and biophysical configuration regulate the movement of components from blood into urine?

choices.A: Extraglomerular mesangial cells, fenestrated Bowman's capsule, and loop of Henle cells; it filters based on positive charge attraction.
choices.B: Afferent arteriolar myocytes, macula densa tight junctions, and podocyte foot processes; it filters via active transcellular transport.
choices.C: Fenestrated capillary endothelium, a thin glomerular basement membrane, and podocyte filtration slits; it filters by size and favors passage of negatively charged proteins such as albumin.
choices.D: Fenestrated capillary endothelium, a thick fused glomerular basement membrane, and podocyte filtration slits; it filters based on molecular size and negative charge.
choices.E: Parietal epithelial cells, mesangial matrix, and proximal tubule microvilli; it filters based on hydrostatic pressure and lipophilicity.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Glomerular filtration uses a multi-layered molecular sieve that restricts elements based on size and negative charge density.

      - Exact Quote: “Glomerular filtration barrier (GFB)... 3 layers: 1. Fenestrated capillary endothelium 2. Glomerular basement membrane (GBM)... 3. Podocytes (visceral layer of Bowman’s capsule)... Properties: • Molecular size... • Electrical charge (negative charge of GFB repels negatively charged molecules)” [Urinary Guide, Page 4-5].

Tempting but wrong: The barrier's negative charge repels anionic proteins such as albumin, and the GBM is thick and fused (Urinary System study guide).

C.passage: 1. Fenestrated glomerular endothelium 2. Basement membrane (BM)(sandwiched in between): This basement membrane prevents large and negatively charged proteins from exiting the blood.

They sit on top of the external surface of the glomerular capillaries. Mesangium: Supporting cells called mesangial cells are found within extracellular matrix in between capillary loops. Mesangial cells are usually clustered closer to the vascular pole.

questions.stem: If a patient develops an autoimmune disorder that selectively destroys the negative electrical charge of the glomerular basement membrane without altering physical pore size, which clinical finding is expected, and why?

choices.A: Glycosuria; because glucose molecules require negative charge gradients for reabsorption.
choices.B: Proteinuria; because proteins like albumin are normally repelled by the negative charge of the barrier.
choices.C: Hematuria; because red blood cells are normally held back by the negative charge rather than by the size of the pores.
choices.D: Hematuria; because red blood cells are repelled by positive charges.
choices.E: Anuria; because blood filtration entirely ceases when the charge is neutralized.

Tempting but wrong: Red cells are excluded by size; losing the charge barrier mainly lets anionic albumin through, causing proteinuria.

questions.stem: How do the mechanical structural features of the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) correlate with its high capacity for bulk reabsorption compared to the distal convoluted tubule (DCT)?

choices.A: Both have a prominent brush border, but the DCT has more mitochondria and tighter junctions, so it reabsorbs the larger share of filtered sodium and water.
choices.B: The PCT possesses a very prominent brush border of microvilli and abundant mitochondria, whereas the DCT has a clean lumen with a less developed brush border.
choices.C: The PCT is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, whereas the DCT is lined by transitional epithelium containing umbrella cells.
choices.D: The PCT lacks a basement membrane to permit passive paracrine flow, whereas the DCT is heavily encapsulated.
choices.E: The PCT contains podocytes with filtration slits, whereas the DCT relies on fenestrated endothelial walls.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: The structural phenotype of the PCT is custom-tailored for extensive active and passive fluid absorption via a massive microvillar brush border.

      - Exact Quote: “Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)... Simple cuboidal epithelium with VERY prominent brush border (microvilli)... Distal convoluted tubule (DCT)... Simple cuboidal epithelium, clean lumen (brush border not well developed)” [Urinary Guide, Page 6].

Tempting but wrong: The PCT, with its tall brush border and abundant mitochondria, does the bulk reabsorption; the DCT has a clean lumen and fine-tunes the urine.

A.passage: The macula densa is a small cluster of specialized epithelial cells lining the wall of the DCT, found adjacent to the JG cells. Macula densa cells are sensitive to fluctuations in sodium (Na+) levels in the DCT fluid.

B.passage: Similar to the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), the DCT is a coiled structure lined with simple cuboidal epithelium. The DCT cells have little or no microvilli, compared to the PCT cells.

C.passage: The ureters then conduct urine to the urinary bladder, also lined with transitional epithelium, which is designed to withstand cytotoxic materials found in urine.

D.passage: 1. Fenestrated glomerular endothelium 2. Basement membrane (BM)(sandwiched in between): This basement membrane prevents large and negatively charged proteins from exiting the blood.

E.passage: Podocytes in the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule have primary and secondary foot processes (“pedicels”) that cling to the surfaces of glomerular capillaries. Filtration slits are found between adjacent secondary pedicels of podocytes. Within filtration slits are slit diaphragms which form a selective barrier

questions.stem: What are the primary functional subdivisions of the nephron, and how do their structural compartments map across the architectural zones of the kidney?

choices.A: The renal corpuscle filters blood and sits in the medulla alongside the loops of Henle, while the convoluted tubules that reabsorb and secrete are confined to the cortex.
choices.B: The calyces are responsible for filtration and reside in the medulla; the loop of Henle resides exclusively in the fibrous capsule.
choices.C: The renal pelvis is responsible for secretion and spans the renal pyramids; the corpuscle resides in the corticomedullary junction.
choices.D: The corpus (filtration) sits in the cortex; the tubule (PCT, loop of Henle, DCT) does reabsorption and secretion and spans cortex and medulla.
choices.E: The minor calyx is responsible for concentration and resides in the cortex; the major calyx resides in the renal column.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: A nephron is systematically divided into a cortical filtration corpuscle and an extended segmented tubular reabsorption pathway spanning multiple zones.

      - Exact Quote: “Functional unit of kidney: Nephron = A + B • A) Renal corpuscle (cortex) $\rightarrow$ Filtration • B) Renal tubule (cortex and medulla) $\rightarrow$ Reabsorption, Secretion... tubules = PCT --> Loop of Henle --> DCT” [Slide 8, 5].

Tempting but wrong: Renal corpuscles are in the cortex; the tubule portion is what extends from cortex into medulla (Urinary System slides: Nephron = corpuscle + tubule).

A.passage: A - Renal corpuscle → B1- Proximal convoluted tubule → B2- Loop of Henle → B3- Distal convoluted tubule

B.passage: Loop of Henle - primarily in medulla, along with collecting ducts - Sets up osmotic concentration gradient in medulla - Thin part of loop of Henle is squamous (flat nuclei, “T”)

C.passage: Nephron: the renal corpuscle • Renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman’s capsule + mesangium) ~ 200 m • Filtration

D.passage: B) Renal tubule (cortex and medulla) • Reabsorption • Secretion B

E.passage: nephron = 1 renal corpuscle + 1 renal tubule. Notice in the slide below how one is located in the cortex and the other traverses both cortex and medulla.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q16

questions.stem: What unique cytological specialization distinguishes the superficial epithelial layer of the ureter and urinary bladder, and what mechanical property does it confer to these organs?

choices.A: Stratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells; secretes highly alkaline mucus to neutralize metabolic acids.
choices.B: Transitional epithelium with surface umbrella cells; provides a barrier against hypertonic urine and allows distension.
choices.C: Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; allows rapid transcellular water absorption during low pressure.
choices.D: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with cilia; coordinates unidirectional urine flow toward the urethra.
choices.E: Transitional epithelium whose surface cells are linked by gap junctions; lets water and urea pass freely so the urine is concentrated during storage.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Transitional epithelium utilizes highly specialized surface umbrella cells to withstand osmotic gradients and expand dynamically without losing integrity.

      - Exact Quote: “Ureters and urinary bladder... Lined by urothelium / transitional epithelium... Surface cells = 'umbrella cells'... Protects against hypertonic/cytotoxic effects of urine • Allows for distension” [Urinary Guide, Page 7].

Tempting but wrong: Umbrella cells form a barrier against hypertonic urine and let the wall distend; they do not let water and urea pass freely.

A.passage: and in response, JG cell secretes renin which ultimately (via activation of RAAS) ↑ blood pressure

B.passage: The ureters then conduct urine to the urinary bladder, also lined with transitional epithelium, which is designed to withstand cytotoxic materials found in urine.

C.passage: stratified columnar and pseudocolumnar Bladder epithelium ➔ Urethra non-keratinized Prostate squamous epithelium (distally) Female Male

D.passage: Ureters, Bladder, Urethra Urine in the collecting ducts ultimately reaches the renal pelvis of each kidney and then exits via paired ureters, muscular tubes that are lined by transitional epithelium.

E.passage: Collecting duct cells are water permeable due to their sensitivity to antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which is also known as vasopressin. (As noted in the Endocrine Histology study guide - where is ADH made and stored?) ADH promotes reabsorption of water from the urine; this water makes its way into the vasa recta (capillary plexus), leaving a more concentrated urine.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q17

questions.stem: How does the epithelial lining of the urethra shift morphologically along its pathway from the proximal segment near the bladder to its distal exit point?

choices.A: Stratified cuboidal $\rightarrow$ Simple columnar $\rightarrow$ Transitional epithelium.
choices.B: Keratinized stratified squamous $\rightarrow$ Transitional $\rightarrow$ Endothelium.
choices.C: Simple squamous $\rightarrow$ Pseudostratified ciliated columnar $\rightarrow$ Simple cuboidal epithelium.
choices.D: Transitional epithelium $\rightarrow$ Pseudostratified ciliated columnar $\rightarrow$ Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
choices.E: Transitional epithelium $\rightarrow$ Stratified columnar and pseudocolumnar $\rightarrow$ Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: The urethral pathway exhibits a dynamic morphological shift from urinary transitional patterns to structural stratified squamous cells near the external environment.

      - Exact Quote: “Urethra Epithelium shifts from Proximal to Distal: From transitional $\rightarrow$ stratified columnar and pseudocolumnar epithelium $\rightarrow$ non-keratinized squamous epithelium (distally)” [Slide 41].

Tempting but wrong: The urethra goes from transitional to stratified/pseudostratified columnar to non-keratinized stratified squamous; it has no ciliated or keratinized segment.

A.passage: Within the cortex of the kidney, Bowman’s capsule leads into the PCT, which is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with tall microvilli. This provides increased surface area to promote reabsorption of specific molecules from the filtrate in the tubular lumen back into blood circulation.

B.passage: The ureters then conduct urine to the urinary bladder, also lined with transitional epithelium, which is designed to withstand cytotoxic materials found in urine.

C.passage: Similar to the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), the DCT is a coiled structure lined with simple cuboidal epithelium. The DCT cells have little or no microvilli, compared to the PCT cells.

D.passage: Ureters, Bladder, Urethra Urine in the collecting ducts ultimately reaches the renal pelvis of each kidney and then exits via paired ureters, muscular tubes that are lined by transitional epithelium.

E.passage: stratified columnar and pseudocolumnar Bladder epithelium ➔ Urethra non-keratinized Prostate squamous epithelium (distally) Female Male

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q18

questions.stem: Where are mesangial cells located within the renal corpuscle, and what are their primary physiological and structural functions?

choices.A: They are positioned exclusively within the macula densa; they transport sodium into the distal convoluted tubule.
choices.B: They are located within the extracellular matrix between capillary loops; they provide structural support and phagocytose filtration debris.
choices.C: They form the parietal layer of Bowman's capsule; they maintain the filtration space clear of urine.
choices.D: They line the inner wall of the afferent arteriole; they act as high-pressure baroreceptors.
choices.E: They form the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule around the capillaries; their foot processes create the filtration slits.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Mesangial cells fill the core spaces between capillary loops to clean the filtration apparatus and provide mechanical reinforcement.

      - Exact Quote: “Mesangium: Supporting cells called mesangial cells are found within extracellular matrix in between capillary loops... clean the GFB (phagocytosis)” [Urinary Guide, Page 3, 5].

Tempting but wrong: Podocytes form the visceral layer and filtration slits; mesangial cells sit in the matrix between the capillary loops, supporting them and clearing debris.

A.passage: A - Renal corpuscle → B1- Proximal convoluted tubule → B2- Loop of Henle → B3- Distal convoluted tubule

B.passage: There are unique, highly specialized epithelial cells called podocytes, which are part of the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule. They sit on top of the external surface of the glomerular capillaries. Mesangium: Supporting cells called mesangial cells are found within extracellular matrix in between capillary loops. Mesangial cells are usually clustered closer to the vascular pole.

C.passage: Histology, 13e, 2013 = glomerulus + Bowman’s capsule + mesangium Notes: (we won’t go into detail on ▪ “tubular pole” = urinary pole, which is opposite the vascular pole mesangium) ▪ “glomerular capsule” = “Bowman’s capsule” ▪ “capsular space” = where the initial filtrate (an “early” form of urine) accumulates 14

D.passage: Juxtaglomerular cell (in afferent arteriole) JG cell responds to: ↓ in blood pressure in afferent arteriole (“AA”) or ↓ Na+ detected by macula densa

E.passage: Podocytes in the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule have primary and secondary foot processes (“pedicels”) that cling to the surfaces of glomerular capillaries. Filtration slits are found between adjacent secondary pedicels of podocytes. Within filtration slits are slit diaphragms which form a selective barrier

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q19

questions.stem: Which physiological feature accurately distinguishes juxtamedullary nephrons from cortical nephrons within the renal parenchyma?

choices.A: Their renal corpuscles sit near the corticomedullary junction and their long loops of Henle reach deep into the medulla.
choices.B: Juxtamedullary nephrons have renal corpuscles located near the cortical surface and feature very short loops of Henle.
choices.C: Juxtamedullary nephrons are completely devoid of a glomerular filtration barrier and filter blood via the vasa recta.
choices.D: Juxtamedullary nephrons have renal corpuscles near the corticomedullary junction but short loops of Henle that stay in the outer medulla, leaving deep concentration to cortical nephrons.
choices.E: Juxtamedullary nephrons lack a proximal convoluted tubule and feed directly into the minor calyx.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons have specialized long loops that penetrate deep into the inner medulla, optimizing the concentration gradient.

      - Exact Quote: “Nephron locations: • cortical nephrons (near cortical surface) • juxtamedullary (near the corticomedullary junction) nephrons... feature long loops of Henle” [Slide 8 / Urinary Guide Text Context].
Female Reproductive System Explanations

Tempting but wrong: Juxtamedullary nephrons are the ones with long loops of Henle reaching deep into the medulla; cortical nephrons have the short loops.

A.passage: • Each nephron = 1 corpuscle + 1 tubule • Nephron locations: • cortical nephrons (near cortical surface) • juxtamedullary (near the corticomedullary junction) nephrons

B.passage: Bonus fact: A histologic cross-section of renal medulla will show a mix of collecting ducts and loops of Henle (thick and thin portions).

C.passage: The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule are integral parts of the glomerular filtration barrier. Every renal corpuscle has a glomerular filtration barrier that is composed of 3 elements (in order):

D.passage: Loop of Henle - primarily in medulla, along with collecting ducts - Sets up osmotic concentration gradient in medulla - Thin part of loop of Henle is squamous (flat nuclei, “T”)

E.passage: A - Renal corpuscle → B1- Proximal convoluted tubule → B2- Loop of Henle → B3- Distal convoluted tubule

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q20

questions.stem: During the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle, how do the microenvironmental cells of the developing follicle collaborate biochemically to synthesize estrogen?

choices.A: Surface epithelial cells produce cholesterol, which is actively converted into estrogen within the clear zone of the zona pellucida.
choices.B: Granulosa cells produce androgens under LH stimulation, which theca interna cells then convert to estrogen using aromatase under FSH stimulation, before secreting it into the antrum.
choices.C: Granulosa cells produce progesterone under FSH stimulation, which is then metabolized into androgens by the tunica albuginea.
choices.D: Theca externa cells secrete LH directly into the follicular antrum, stimulating the primary oocyte to release estradiol.
choices.E: Theca interna cells make androgens under LH; granulosa cells convert them to estrogen with aromatase under FSH.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Glandular estrogen production requires an active enzymatic collaboration between the androgenic theca interna layer and the aromatase-rich granulosa layer.

      - Exact Quote: “Theca interna cells produce androgens... Under the influence of FSH, granulosa cells express the enzyme aromatase, which converts these theca-derived androgens to estrogen (specifically, estradiol).” [Female Guide, Page 3].

Tempting but wrong: The roles are swapped: theca interna makes androgens (LH) and granulosa cells aromatize them to estrogen (FSH).

A.passage: The oocyte itself is surrounded by the corona radiata, a "halo” of granulosa cells ("CR" in above image). Between the corona radiata and the oocyte there is a thick pink ring (seen on H&E slides) called the zona pellucida (ZP). The zona pellucida is acellular and consists of extracellular glycoprotein matrix surrounding the oocyte. For successful fertilization, sperm must bind to ZP proteins in order to penetrate the zona pellucida.

C.passage: Next to the granulosa cells, there is a layer of cells called theca interna ("TI" in above image), which are significant since they secrete androgens that are taken up by the adjacent granulosa cells, which converted the thecal androgens to estrogen (specifically, estradiol). This occurs in the first half of the menstrual cycle, the ovarian follicular phase.

D.passage: 1 = SECONDARY oocyte, 2 = zona pellucida (it's blue rather than pink here because of the special trichrome stain), 3 = corona radiata (made of granulosa cells), 4 = granulosa cells lining the follicle, 5 = cumulus oophorus (made of granulosa cells)..... 7 = thecal layer (theca interna + theca externa), 8 = fluid filled antrum
D.file: Mini review (Female Reproductive Histology) _ Top Hat.pdf

E.passage: Theca interna: androgens --> to granulosa cells, then granulosa cells convert to estrogens
E.file: Mini review (Female Reproductive Histology) _ Top Hat.pdf

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q21

questions.stem: What precise cytological event occurs to the primary oocyte within a mature (Graafian) follicle just prior to ovulation, and at what stage does the ovulated oocyte remain arrested until fertilization?

choices.A: It completes meiosis I to form a secondary oocyte and a polar body; arrested in metaphase of meiosis II.
choices.B: It undergoes direct cytokinesis to yield four identical spermatid-like ova; arrested in anaphase I.
choices.C: It completes meiosis II entirely; arrested in the zygotic interphase.
choices.D: It completes meiosis I to form a secondary oocyte and a polar body; arrested in prophase of meiosis I until fertilization.
choices.E: It completes mitosis I to form a polar body; arrested in prophase of mitosis II.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: The primary oocyte finishes its first meiotic division within the dominant follicle, releasing a secondary oocyte that halts mid-meiosis II until a sperm fertilizes it.

      - Exact Quote: “Oogenesis... Primary oocyte... completes Meiosis I just prior to ovulation $\rightarrow$ forms secondary oocyte + 1st polar body... Secondary oocyte starts Meiosis II and arrests at Metaphase II until fertilization” [Female Guide, Page 2].

Tempting but wrong: The ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase of meiosis II; the prophase I arrest is the earlier, pre-ovulatory arrest.

A.passage: Secondary oocyte continues into meiosis II and then is “arrested” in metaphase II.

B.passage: Oogenesis This process is high yield for the exam (and for Step 1).

C.passage: Meiosis begins in the fetus. Primary oocytes (2n, 4c) begin meiosis I and are stopped, or “arrested” in prophase I, where they remain diploid. At birth, all the oocytes that are present in the ovary are primary oocytes that are arrested at this stage. Throughout childhood, the ovaries remain inactive. After the onset of puberty, meiosis I resumes. During each menstrual cycle, a small number of primary oocytes complete meiosis I right before ovulation occurs, resulting in secondary oocytes (1n, 2c) with 23 chromosomes.

D.passage: Ovulation occurs, releasing a secondary oocyte from the ovary. This secondary oocyte is still “arrested” in metaphase II. Oocyte travels into fallopian tube, to await potential fertilization. If fertilization does not occur, the secondary oocyte degenerates. If fertilization occurs (when sperm penetrates the zona pellucida ), the secondary oocyte can then complete meiosis II, yielding a haploid ovum (1n, 1c). Bonus fact: Subsequent fusion of maternal and paternal chromosomal material produces a diploid (2n, 2c) cell: the zygote.

E.passage: In fetal life primary oocyte (2N,4C) arrested @ prophase I secondary oocyte haploid ovum After puberty

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q22

questions.stem: Following a surge in luteinizing hormone (LH) and subsequent ovulation, what structural transformation occurs to the remnants of the ruptured follicle, and what is its primary endocrine secretion during the luteal phase?

choices.A: It collapses and forms the corpus luteum, which secretes mainly estrogen and inhibin while progesterone comes from the stroma.
choices.B: It differentiates into the theca externa layer, which produces follicle-stimulating hormone.
choices.C: It degenerates immediately into the corpus albicans, which secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG).
choices.D: It expands into an atretic follicle, which actively clears excess luteinizing hormone from the ovarian cortex.
choices.E: It collapses and forms the corpus luteum, which secretes large amounts of progesterone and smaller amounts of estrogen.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: The physical shell of the ovulated follicle remodels into a highly vascular luteal gland tasked with maintaining early pregnancy conditions via steroid secretion.

      - Exact Quote: “The empty follicle collapses, fills with blood, and forms a structure called a corpus luteum. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and a smaller amount of estrogen).” [Female Guide, Page 3].

Tempting but wrong: The corpus luteum's main product in the luteal phase is progesterone, with smaller amounts of estrogen.

A.passage: menstrual: degenerating glands/blood | (side note: technically menstrual is associated with the very beginning of follicular phase, just based on its timing in the cycle) | (n/a) proliferative: straight, tubular glands | follicular phase | estrogen (made by granulosa cells) secretory: corkscrew/wavy, + secretions | luteal phase | progesterone (made by corpus luteum)
A.file: Mini review (Female Reproductive Histology) _ Top Hat.pdf

B.passage: 1 = SECONDARY oocyte, 2 = zona pellucida (it's blue rather than pink here because of the special trichrome stain), 3 = corona radiata (made of granulosa cells), 4 = granulosa cells lining the follicle, 5 = cumulus oophorus (made of granulosa cells)..... 7 = thecal layer (theca interna + theca externa), 8 = fluid filled antrum
B.file: Mini review (Female Reproductive Histology) _ Top Hat.pdf

C.passage: If pregnancy does not occur, hormone secretion in the corpus luteum drops sharply. At this point, the menstrual cycle reaches its endpoint and eventually, degenerated corpus luteum evolves into a scar-like structure called corpus albicans.

D.passage: When ovulation occurs (prompted by a surge of luteinizing hormone from the pituitary), a dominant mature follicle (located close to the surface of the ovary) ruptures at the ovarian surface (see below) to release the secondary oocyte, along with its zona pellucida and corona radiata.

E.passage: An empty follicle is left in the ovary, which evolves into other distinct structures. This is now the ovarian luteal phase. The empty follicle collapses, fills with blood, and forms a structure called a corpus luteum. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and a smaller amount of estrogen). Progesterone is released in anticipation of a potential pregnancy.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q23

questions.stem: How do the cyclical hormonal changes in the ovary orchestrate the structural remodeling of the uterine endometrium during the transition from the proliferative phase to the secretory phase?

choices.A: Estrogen drives endometrial growth in the proliferative phase; progesterone from the corpus luteum then makes the glands tortuous and glycogen-rich (secretory phase).
choices.B: Progesterone stimulates the shedding of the functional layer; subsequent estrogen induces the spiral arteries to constrict and cause ischemia.
choices.C: Progesterone from the developing follicle drives the proliferative phase; estrogen from the corpus luteum then induces the secretory phase, making the glands tortuous and glycogen-rich before menstruation.
choices.D: FSH induces the sloughing of the basal layer, while LH causes the functional layer to become thin and inactive.
choices.E: Atresia of the follicle leads to high estrogen levels, which mechanically flattens the uterine glands.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Endometrial morphology mirrors ovarian steroid dynamics, transitioning from cellular proliferative repair to rich glandular tortuosity.

      - Exact Quote: “Proliferative phase: driven by estrogen... Secretory phase: driven by progesterone from corpus luteum... glands become highly coiled/tortuous and accumulate glycogen” [Female Guide, Page 4].

Tempting but wrong: Estrogen (follicle) drives proliferation and progesterone (corpus luteum) drives the secretory phase; this option swaps the two hormones.

A.passage: In the proliferative phase, simple tubular (straight) glands in the stratum functionalis develop in response to estrogen. This part of the cycle can be variable (longer or shorter) from person to person Bonus fact: Here is a high-power view of proliferative endometrium glands After ovulation, the secretory phase begins, and endometrial glands respond to progesterone (secreted by the ovarian corpus luteum) to become highly coiled

B.passage: (corkscrew-shaped) and filled with secretions (glycogen and glycoproteins). The endometrium reaches its greatest thickness in the secretory phase. Bonus fact: Here is a high-power view of early secretory endometrium glands (secretory phase can be further subdivided in early, mid and late secretory phases) Leading into the menstrual phase, there is a sharp decrease in progesterone (and estrogen). Spiral arterioles in the stratum functionalis contract, leading to decreased blood flow (ischemia) and tissue degeneration (shedding) of the stratum functionalis layer.

C.passage: menstrual: degenerating glands/blood | (side note: technically menstrual is associated with the very beginning of follicular phase, just based on its timing in the cycle) | (n/a) proliferative: straight, tubular glands | follicular phase | estrogen (made by granulosa cells) secretory: corkscrew/wavy, + secretions | luteal phase | progesterone (made by corpus luteum)
C.file: Mini review (Female Reproductive Histology) _ Top Hat.pdf

E.passage: Identify 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.... and 7, 8 in this mature follicle.... and which stage oocyte is inside this follicle?
E.file: Mini review (Female Reproductive Histology) _ Top Hat.pdf

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q24

questions.stem: If fertilization does not occur, what underlying mechanical and vascular events trigger the onset of the menstrual phase in the uterine wall?

choices.A: A massive surge in progesterone causes vasodilation of the straight arteries, dissolving the basal layer.
choices.B: The myometrium undergoes sustained tetanic contractions that mechanically separate the entire endometrium from the cervix.
choices.C: The corpus albicans secretes proteolytic enzymes that selectively digest the simple columnar epithelium of the perimetrium.
choices.D: Falling progesterone and estrogen cause the straight (basal) arteries to constrict, so the basal layer becomes ischemic and is shed with the functional layer, to be rebuilt from the myometrium.
choices.E: Falling progesterone and estrogen cause spiral artery spasm, ischemia, and shedding of the functional layer.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: When hormonal support drops, spiral arterioles undergo acute ischemic vasospasm, starving the functional layer of oxygen and prompting tissue sloughing.

      - Exact Quote: “Menstrual phase: if no pregnancy occurs... sharp drop in progesterone & estrogen... changes in spiral arteries $\rightarrow$ spasms $\rightarrow$ ischemia $\rightarrow$ shedding of functional layer” [Female Guide, Page 4].

Tempting but wrong: Spiral arteries supply the functional layer and go into spasm; straight arteries keep the basal layer alive so it can regenerate the endometrium.

A.passage: The glands within the endometrium are composed of simple columnar epithelium. There are two layers of endometrium (basalis and functionalis), and our focus will primarily be on stratum functionalis, which undergoes cyclical changes. Stratum functionalis is a physiologically dynamic layer that can range from relatively straight, elongated glands to extensively coiled glands and arteries. These endometrial changes are driven by fluctuating estrogen and progesterone levels during the menstrual cycle.

B.passage: endometrium (lining the uterine cavity) underlying myometrium (smooth muscle layer) outer connective tissue (serosa and adventitia)

C.passage: If pregnancy does not occur, hormone secretion in the corpus luteum drops sharply. At this point, the menstrual cycle reaches its endpoint and eventually, degenerated corpus luteum evolves into a scar-like structure called corpus albicans.

E.passage: (corkscrew-shaped) and filled with secretions (glycogen and glycoproteins). The endometrium reaches its greatest thickness in the secretory phase. Bonus fact: Here is a high-power view of early secretory endometrium glands (secretory phase can be further subdivided in early, mid and late secretory phases) Leading into the menstrual phase, there is a sharp decrease in progesterone (and estrogen). Spiral arterioles in the stratum functionalis contract, leading to decreased blood flow (ischemia) and tissue degeneration (shedding) of the stratum functionalis layer.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q25

questions.stem: What are the distinct structural layers of the uterine wall, and which layer undergoes profound cyclic remodeling and shedding while the other remains stable to regenerate the tissue?

choices.A: Endocervix and Ectocervix; the endocervix sheds its stratified squamous epithelium while the ectocervix remains stable.
choices.B: Functional layer (shed) and Basal layer (retained); both are subdivisions of the Endometrium, which sits on top of the muscular Myometrium.
choices.C: Perimetrium and Myometrium; the myometrium sheds completely during menstruation while the perimetrium remains stable.
choices.D: Functional layer (retained) and Basal layer (shed); both are subdivisions of the Endometrium, which sits on top of the muscular Myometrium.
choices.E: Tunica albuginea and Corona radiata; the corona radiata undergoes cyclic shedding into the uterine lumen.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: The endometrium houses two distinct structural strata: a dynamic functional zone that responds to cycle changes, and a static basal zone that provides regenerative stem cells.

      - Exact Quote: “Endometrium: Simple columnar epithelium + lamina propria... Subdivided into: • Functional layer: undergoes cyclic changes, sheds during menstruation • Basal layer: retained during menstruation, source of cells for regeneration” [Female Guide, Page 3-4].

Tempting but wrong: The functional layer is shed each cycle and the basal layer stays to regenerate it.

A.passage: The surface epithelium is unique. There is an area between the ectocervix and endocervix that is a transformation zone where stratified squamous epithelium (ectocervix) abruptly changes to simple columnar glandular epithelium (endocervix).

B.passage: endometrium (lining the uterine cavity) underlying myometrium (smooth muscle layer) outer connective tissue (serosa and adventitia)

E.passage: • Mature = SECONDARY OOCYTE, single large antrum, cumulus oophorus with corona radiata (see next slide)

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q26

questions.stem: What specific morphological transition defines the cervical transformation zone, and why is this precise histological boundary of major clinical importance?

choices.A: Transitional epithelium shifts to keratinized squamous epithelium; it is the site where Pap smear cells are produced by the basal body.
choices.B: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar shifts to simple cuboidal; it is the site where fertilization typically takes place.
choices.C: Stratified squamous (endocervix) shifts to simple columnar (ectocervix); it is the site where HPV infects cells and is the source of cells sampled by a Pap smear.
choices.D: Simple columnar epithelium shifts to stratified columnar; it is the site where progesterone is converted to active androgens.
choices.E: Simple columnar (endocervix) meets stratified squamous (ectocervix); this is where HPV infects cells, which can lead to dysplasia and cervical cancer.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: The abrupt squamocolumnar boundary at the cervix is highly vulnerable to oncogenic viral integration, making it the primary focal point of screening.

      - Exact Quote: “Cervical transformation zone... Junction where simple columnar epithelium (of endocervix) shifts to stratified squamous epithelium (of ectocervix)... Major site for HPV infection $\rightarrow$ cervical dysplasia $\rightarrow$ cervical cancer. Target of Pap smear screening” [Female Guide, Page 5].

Tempting but wrong: The endocervix is simple columnar and the ectocervix stratified squamous; this option reverses them.

A.passage: This work has been released into the public domain by its author, Euthman at Wikipedia. • Pap smear test: cells squamous cells screen for cervical dysplasia or cancer

B.passage: There are different cell types in the epithelial lining of the tube -- the main ones we will focus on are simple columnar (mostly ciliated), organized in complex maze-like structures (called plicae) that protrude into the lumen (see cross section below). The smooth muscle in the wall of the tube and ciliated columnar cells help to push the oocyte into the uterus. Here is another example (low power) of a cross-section of the tube, showing the complex maze-like pattern formed by protrusions of the plicae (medium power view).

C.passage: Photo by Ed Uthman, MD https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ThinPrep_Pap_smear_HPV.jpeg normal squamous HPV-infected

D.passage: Next to the granulosa cells, there is a layer of cells called theca interna ("TI" in above image), which are significant since they secrete androgens that are taken up by the adjacent granulosa cells, which converted the thecal androgens to estrogen (specifically, estradiol). This occurs in the first half of the menstrual cycle, the ovarian follicular phase.

E.passage: The surface epithelium is unique. There is an area between the ectocervix and endocervix that is a transformation zone where stratified squamous epithelium (ectocervix) abruptly changes to simple columnar glandular epithelium (endocervix).

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — HFD4 Genitourinary, Q27

questions.stem: How do the microscopic features of the fallopian tube (uterine tube) support its dual physiological roles in gamete transport and maintenance?

choices.A: It contains a highly folded mucosa lined by ciliated cells that secrete a nutrient fluid, and peg cells whose cilia sweep the oocyte toward the uterus.
choices.B: It contains large cavernous spaces that fill with blood to physically expand the tube during sperm passage.
choices.C: It contains a highly folded mucosa lined by ciliated cells that sweep the oocyte, and peg cells that secrete a nutrient fluid.
choices.D: It lacks a muscularis layer entirely, relying on the positive hydrostatic pressure of the peritoneal fluid to move the egg.
choices.E: It is lined by an impermeable stratified squamous epithelium that prevents ectopic implantation by blocking all fluid exchange.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Fallopian transport coordinates mechanical ciliary propulsion with metabolic support provided by non-ciliated secretory cells.

      - Exact Quote: “Fallopian tube... Highly folded mucosa... Lined by simple columnar epithelium: • Ciliated cells (sweep oocyte/sperm) • Peg cells (non-ciliated, secretory cells $\rightarrow$ provide nutrient fluid)” [Female Guide, Page 5].

Tempting but wrong: Ciliated cells move the oocyte and peg (secretory) cells produce the nutritive fluid; this option swaps their roles.

A.passage: There are different cell types in the epithelial lining of the tube -- the main ones we will focus on are simple columnar (mostly ciliated), organized in complex maze-like structures (called plicae) that protrude into the lumen (see cross section below). The smooth muscle in the wall of the tube and ciliated columnar cells help to push the oocyte into the uterus. Here is another example (low power) of a cross-section of the tube, showing the complex maze-like pattern formed by protrusions of the plicae (medium power view).

B.passage: Fallopian tube After its release during ovulation, the secondary oocyte enters the fallopian tube. The fallopian tube is open at both ends, with a proximal end leading directly to the uterus and opening into the uterine cavity. The other open (distal) end of the fallopian tube has finger-like projections called fimbriae that sit adjacent to each ovary. As an oocyte is released, the fimbriae pick up and sweep the egg into the lumen of the fallopian tube.

C.passage: The mature (sometimes called Graafian or tertiary) follicle consists of a single fluid- filled antrum ("A" in above image), surrounding and nourishing the growing oocyte. The antrum is lined by mutiple layers of cuboidal granulosa cells ("G" in above image), which secrete nutrients, growth factors, and hormones into the antral space to support the developing oocyte and follicle. In one area of the follicle, granulosa cells pile up to create a prominent heap, called the cumulus oophorus ("CO" in above image), adjacent to the oocyte (appearing to "tether" it to the follicle).

E.passage: Oocytes (the female gamete) are located within follicles, with one oocyte per follicle. Each follicle is lined by epithelium that can range from simple squamous to stratified cuboidal, depending on the stage of follicular maturity.

questions.stem: What structural and cellular alterations distinguish the microscopic appearance of lactating breast tissue from inactive breast tissue?

choices.A: Inactive breast shows abundant enlarged alveoli with scant stroma; lactating breast has sparse ducts separated by abundant fat, because milk is stored in the adipose tissue.
choices.B: Inactive breast contains large, dilated alveoli filled with dense glycogen, while lactating breast tissue shows complete atrophy of the duct system.
choices.C: Inactive breast has sparse glands in abundant connective tissue and fat; lactating breast shows marked gland proliferation, milk-filled alveoli, and little stroma.
choices.D: Inactive breast tissue is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, while lactating breast tissue shifts exclusively to transitional epithelium.
choices.E: Inactive breast contains extensive skeletal muscle bundles, while lactating breast tissue loses all muscular elements to maximize adipose deposition.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: Lactogenesis prompts a massive structural remodeling of breast tissue, maximizing secretory alveoli at the expense of supportive fat and connective tissue.

      - Exact Quote: “Inactive breast: sparse glandular/duct system, abundant connective tissue and adipose stroma... Active/Lactating breast: striking glandular proliferation... Alveoli are enlarged, dilated, and filled with milk secretion. Very little stroma remaining” [Female Guide, Page 6].

Tempting but wrong: This is reversed: inactive breast is mostly stroma and fat with sparse glands, while lactation brings proliferation of milk-filled alveoli.

A.passage: inactive: Small lobules (dotted circle shows 1 lobule) contain small round glands, with connective tissue a) in between glands within each lobule and b) in between lobules. active: Glands within the lobules proliferate and expand each lobule, reducing the visible connective tissue inside each lobule. Note that there is still connective tissue between lobules. lactating: After birth, prolactin (made by which organ ? hover to see answer) stimulates glands in the breast to synthesize lipids and proteins that form milk.

B.passage: Objectives and studying for the exam Objectives 1. Describe key steps in oogenesis 2. List synergistic physiological changes in the uterus and ovary during a menstrual cycle 3. Describe the clinical significance of the cervical transformation zone 4. Identify key histologic features that distinguish inactive vs lactating breast tissue

C.passage: Breast Breast tissue is a modified and specialized glandular structure that is capable of secreting milk. Breast tissue is organized as a branching duct system that contains approximately 15-20 secretory lobes that radiate towards the centrally located nipple. We won't go into the details of the specific branching components. Instead we'll start at a functional unit called the lobule (some references also use the term "terminal duct lobular units" or TDLU).

D.passage: The surface epithelium is unique. There is an area between the ectocervix and endocervix that is a transformation zone where stratified squamous epithelium (ectocervix) abruptly changes to simple columnar glandular epithelium (endocervix).

E.passage: Key points to know • Understand the steps of oogenesis • Recognize an image of a mature ovarian follicle and be aware of its cellular components and functions • Review the correlation between ovarian phases and uterine endometrial phases in the menstrual cycle • Know the significance of the cervical transformation zone • Be familiar with histologic differences between inactive vs. lactating breast

questions.stem: When spermatozoa encounter an egg in the female reproductive tract, what mechanical and enzymatic sequence constitutes the acrosomal reaction required for successful fertilization?

choices.A: The acrosomal cap undergoes rapid mitosis, forming an intercellular syncytium that dissolves the simple columnar epithelium of the fallopian tube.
choices.B: The flagellum sheds its middle piece mitochondria to generate a negative charge that liquefies the polar body.
choices.C: Spermatozoa release progesterone to contract the peg cells, mechanically pulling the oocyte through the vitelline membrane.
choices.D: Spermatozoa bind receptors on the oocyte plasma membrane first, then release acrosin and hyaluronidase from the middle piece to dissolve the corona radiata from the inside.
choices.E: Sperm get through the corona radiata, bind ZP receptors on the zona pellucida, and release hyaluronidase and acrosin from the acrosome to digest the zona.

questions.explanation:
Explanation: To breach the thick barrier of the egg, sperm must selectively bind ZP receptors and execute exocytosis of acrosomal digestive enzymes.

      - Exact Quote: “Spermatozoa encounter the ova... dissociate the cells of the corona radiata... binds specific sperm receptors (ZP receptors) and initiates the acrosomal reaction. This involves release of enzymes (hyaluronidase and acrosin) from the acrosomal cap which digest the zona pellucida” [Top Hat Guide, Page 4].

Best of luck with your studies\! These detailed pathway and mechanism questions will serve as an excellent resource for mastering the complex physiological relationships in your upcoming exam.

Tempting but wrong: The acrosomal enzymes come from the acrosome over the head, and binding to the zona pellucida comes before reaching the oocyte membrane.

A.passage: Fallopian tube After its release during ovulation, the secondary oocyte enters the fallopian tube. The fallopian tube is open at both ends, with a proximal end leading directly to the uterus and opening into the uterine cavity. The other open (distal) end of the fallopian tube has finger-like projections called fimbriae that sit adjacent to each ovary. As an oocyte is released, the fimbriae pick up and sweep the egg into the lumen of the fallopian tube.

C.passage: in oogenesis: primary oocyte (2n, 4c) → secondary oocyte (1n, 2c) → final haploid ovum (1n, 1c)

D.passage: • Mature = SECONDARY OOCYTE, single large antrum, cumulus oophorus with corona radiata (see next slide)

E.passage: The oocyte itself is surrounded by the corona radiata, a "halo” of granulosa cells ("CR" in above image). Between the corona radiata and the oocyte there is a thick pink ring (seen on H&E slides) called the zona pellucida (ZP). The zona pellucida is acellular and consists of extracellular glycoprotein matrix surrounding the oocyte. For successful fertilization, sperm must bind to ZP proteins in order to penetrate the zona pellucida.

questions.stem: During the pathogenesis of cardiac hypertrophy, what specific molecular events link mechanical stress or vasoactive agents to the ultimate morphological change in the cardiomyocyte?

choices.A: Cell-surface receptors activate signal transduction pathways that switch on transcription factors (GATA4, NFAT, MEF2), increasing protein synthesis.
choices.B: Downregulation of BCL-2, allowing BAX to polymerize and synthesize sarcomeric proteins directly in the cytoplasm.
choices.C: Mechanical stress activates mitotic cyclins that drive cardiomyocytes back into the cell cycle, so the heart enlarges by adding new myocytes rather than enlarging existing ones.
choices.D: Rapid depletion of intracellular calcium pools, which triggers the genomic reprogramming of mature cardiomyocytes into embryonic stem cells.
choices.E: Direct activation of caspase-8, which cleaves cytokeratin filaments to allow cellular elongation.

questions.explanation:
- Pathophysiology Breakdown: Cardiac hypertrophy is a form of cellular adaptation to increased hemodynamic load. When cardiomyocytes face mechanical stretch or trophic signals (like endothelin-1 or angiotensin II), cell-surface receptors initiate a cascade of intracellular signal transduction pathways. This activates specific transcription factors (such as GATA4, NFAT, and MEF2) that stimulate the genomic machinery to upregulate protein synthesis, resulting in larger sarcomeres and enlarged cells.
  - Exact Source Quote: > "Mechanism: increase in protein synthesis. Triggers: mechanical sensors (stretch), vasoactive agents (alpha-adrenergic agonists, endothelin-1), growth factors (TGF-beta, IGF-1). These triggers activate signal transduction pathways, which activate transcription factors (GATA4, NFAT, MEF2) to increase synthesis of muscle proteins (hypertrophy)" (Cell injury 1 study guide, Page 4)

Tempting but wrong: Cardiomyocytes are permanent cells: the heart adapts by hypertrophy (bigger cells from more protein synthesis), not by hyperplasia.

A.passage: Some types of injury such as severe DNA damage, marked accumulation of misfolded proteins, or a large increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS – next lecture) after ionizing radiation can cause a cell to activate apoptosis. A withdrawal of growth factors/hormones can also cause dependent cells to activate the intrinsic pathway (e.g. stopping breast feeding triggers apoptosis of breast glandular cells).

questions.stem: Cells undergoing atrophy exhibit a reduction in size and organelles. What are the primary, coordinated cellular pathways responsible for this clearance of structural components?

choices.A: Less protein synthesis plus more degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, together with autophagic vacuoles.
choices.B: Matrix metalloproteinase activation in the extracellular matrix, which triggers cellular shrinkage by compressing the plasma membrane.
choices.C: Activation of executioner caspases (caspases 3 and 6) that selectively digest ribosomal proteins without triggering membrane blebbing.
choices.D: Increased protein synthesis is outpaced by caspase-mediated digestion of organelles, producing apoptotic bodies that neighboring macrophages clear from the shrinking tissue.
choices.E: Saturated lipid peroxidation of the endoplasmic reticulum, leading to the passive shedding of cytoplasmic fragments as residual bodies.

questions.explanation:
- Pathophysiology Breakdown: Cellular atrophy involves a reduction in cell size and mass due to decreased metabolic demands or chronic injury. This is a highly controlled, active biochemical process. First, protein synthesis declines. Second, existing structural proteins are tagged with ubiquitin and systematically degraded by the proteasome. Third, cellular organelles are sequestered into autophagic vacuoles that fuse with lysosomes to be recycled for energy.
  - Exact Source Quote: > "Atrophy is defined as shrinkage in size of cell... mechanism: Decreased protein synthesis (due to decreased metabolic activity) and increased protein degradation (by ubiquitin-proteasome pathway). Autophagy also occurs (autophagic vacuoles fuse with lysosomes to digest cell's own components to try to survive)" (Cell injury 1 study guide, Page 5)

Tempting but wrong: Atrophy is reduced synthesis plus ubiquitin-proteasome degradation and autophagy; caspase activation and apoptotic bodies are apoptosis, a different process.

A.passage: • Muscle is commonly used example • Happens when muscle stops receiving any stimulus • Decreased protein synthesis • Increased protein degradation (via ubiquitin pathway) • → smaller cell size

B.passage: Severe mitochondrial damage Severe plasma membrane damage - loss of the membrane barrier function allows cell to be flooded with extracellular ions (calcium is especially harmful – more on this later)
B.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

C.passage: Caspases act on numerous substrates, including procaspases (inactive forms of caspases), inhibitors of cytoplasmic DNase (results in activity of DNAase), cytoskeletal proteins, and nuclear laminins (scaffold of nuclear envelope). The intrinsic and extrinsic pathways each initially activate different caspases (the ‘initiator’ caspases 9
C.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

D.passage: activates pro-apoptotic protease activating factor-1 (APAF-1) in an ATP dependent fashion. APAF-1 in turn activates caspase 9, which is the initiator caspase for the intrinsic pathway, triggering the caspase cascade.
D.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

E.passage: Examples of intrinsic pathway apoptosis: Example - Endoplasmic reticulum stress

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the correct cellular mechanism of metaplasia, such as the transition from squamous to columnar epithelium in Barrett's esophagus?

choices.A: Chronic irritation causes mature cells to lose their nuclei and revert to a syncytium, which then splits into a different lineage.
choices.B: Severe mitochondrial DNA damage alters ribosomal translation, causing existing squamous cells to synthesize columnar proteins.
choices.C: Fully differentiated, mature squamous cells undergo phenotypic transdifferentiation into columnar cells in response to chronic acid exposure.
choices.D: Metaplasia occurs when columnar cells from the stomach migrate up and replace the squamous epithelium that acid has destroyed, without any reprogramming of local cells.
choices.E: Metaplasia occurs via the genetic reprogramming of tissue stem cells rather than a phenotypic modification of already-differentiated mature cells.

questions.explanation:
- Pathophysiology Breakdown: Metaplasia is a reversible adaptive response where one mature, fully differentiated cell type is replaced by another. This change does not occur because a mature cell physically shifts its structure (transdifferentiation). Rather, chronic irritation or stress reprogram local tissue-specific stem cells (or undifferentiated reserve cells) to differentiate down a new lineage that is better suited to withstand the hostile microenvironment.
  - Exact Source Quote: > "Metaplasia is defined as reversible change in which one adult cell type (epithelial or mesenchymal) is replaced by another adult cell type... mechanism: reprogramming of stem cells (NOT a phenotypic change of already-differentiated mature cells)" (Cell injury 1 study guide, Page 5)

Tempting but wrong: Metaplasia comes from reprogramming of the tissue's own stem cells, not migration of mature cells from another organ (Cell Injury 1 study guide).

A.passage: If the stress that is causing the steatosis is relieved, the cell may revert to normal (i.e., the condition is reversible).
