choices.B: Aspirin (ASA) given during a viral illness compounds a slight mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation defect, causing liver damage and encephalopathy; children with viral illnesses should not get ASA.
choices.C: It represents a direct-acting heavy metal toxicity caused by the combination of lead paint ingestion and viral fever; children require immediate chelation therapy.
choices.D: It is caused by an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to acetaminophen during a viral infection; children should only be given aspirin.
choices.E: It is a direct neurotoxic effect of acetaldehyde generated by the pediatric upregulation of CYP2E1; alcohol-based cough syrups are contraindicated in children.

questions.explanation:
- Pathophysiology Breakdown: Reye's syndrome is a rare, life-threatening pediatric condition characterized by acute non-inflammatory encephalopathy and microvesicular hepatic steatosis. It is strongly linked to the administration of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid or other salicylates) to children or teenagers during an active febrile viral illness (such as influenza A/B or varicella). The interaction between the viral infection and salicylate metabolites leads to severe mitochondrial injury, specifically inhibiting mitochondrial beta-oxidation of fatty acids and oxidative phosphorylation, which triggers systemic metabolic collapse.
  - Exact Source Quote: > "Reye's syndrome occurs in children who are given aspirin (salicylates) during a febrile viral illness (e.g., flu or chickenpox). The toxin causes severe damage to mitochondria, disrupting fatty acid beta-oxidation and resulting in microvesicular steatosis and acute encephalopathy. Therefore, aspirin is contraindicated in children with viral symptoms." (Cell injury 3 study guide, Page 10)

Tempting but wrong: Reye's syndrome is linked to aspirin during viral illness (a mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation problem), so aspirin, not acetaminophen, is avoided in children.

A.passage: Acetylsalicylic acid (ASA, aspirin) and Reye’s syndrome ASA is generally considered a safe compound. In the 1980s it was recognized that some children with a viral illness would develop liver damage when given ASA; this phenomenon was called d h f ll d d h h ld h ld b f

B.passage: • History – 1980’s • Some children recovering from viral illness and given ASA → liver failure • Called Reye’s syndrome • Recommended ASA not be given to kids with viral illness

D.passage: [In case you are wondering why, given the above info, that acetaminophen is still in use – it is a very effective pain reliever and fever reducer, and compared to aspirin and NSAIDS it is easy on the GI tract, and allergic reactions are practically non-existent. Also, upon the recognition of Reye’s syndrome (discussed below), people felt like acetaminophen was a safer drug than aspirin for children. However, if acetaminophen were brought for approval by the FDA today, it would likely be rejected as an over-the-counter medication, because the margin of safety is so narrow (i.e.

E.passage: As discussed above, the secondary pathway (microsomal/oxidation pathway) for metabolism of ethanol involves CYP enzymes (specifically, CYP2E1). Repeated episodes of high blood alcohol levels result in this pathway being used quite frequently, and the cells will respond by generating more CYP2E1 enzymes to handle the increased ethanol load. Another way to say this is that chronic heavy alcohol use “induces” CYP2E1.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the role of EBV in endemic Burkitt lymphoma?

choices.A: EBV drives proliferative conditions in which a host MYC translocation can arise.
choices.B: EBV integrates into chromosome 8 next to MYC, so the translocation is a viral insertion event.
choices.C: EBV provides MYC as a viral oncogene directly inserted into B cells.
choices.D: EBV causes the t(8;14) directly by encoding a recombinase that joins MYC to the immunoglobulin locus.
choices.E: EBV primarily causes lymphoma by destroying p53 and RB through viral ubiquitin ligases.

questions.explanation:
The PDF says EBV “does not appear to insert any viral oncogenes in B lymphocytes, but some of its proteins are known to affect the host cell cycle and increase proliferation, which increases the possibility of DNA errors being passed on to daughter cells.” It then states that “One common genetic lesion... is the translocation t(8;14), which is an activating mutation of MYC proto-oncogene. This is NOT an oncogene from the virus, but evolves as an error during the increased and unchecked B-cell proliferation that the virus is driving.”

Tempting but wrong: EBV drives B-cell proliferation, which raises the chance of a host translocation; it does not cause the translocation directly or by insertion.

A.passage: Of note, the episomal HPV DNA can become integrated into the host chromosome, and this is when neoplasia can arise.

B.passage: In this mutation, the MYC gene (chromosome 8) ends up placed next to the very active promoter for the immunoglobulin heavy chain (chromosome 14). This results in marked over-expression of MYC, which is a transcription factor for numerous pro-growth genes. Once a B-cell clone has MYC oncogene, it is highly likely to become dominant and uncontrolled.

C.passage: • Recognition that RNA viruses can → cancer in animals led to discovery of oncogenes • Retroviruses can cause CA in two ways: – Incorporate host proto-oncogene into viral genome • Host proto-oncogene becomes viral oncogene • Transmitted to other host cells, and to other hosts – Insert viral promoter next to host proto-oncogene • Converts host proto-oncogene to oncogene

D.passage: EBV's role in the other malignancies EBV’s role in other human cancers is also not entirely clear. EBV is known to drive some CNS lymphomas in immunocompromised people, but it doesn’t appear that MYC is involved – and in these patients, restoration of immunocompetence causes the tumor to regress. These phenomenon lends support to the idea that immune dysregulation gives EBV an advantage, as is suspected in endemic Burkitt’s.

E.passage: B-cell lymphomas in immunosuppressed patients (e.g. CNS B cell lymphoma in patients with HIV) Sporadic Burkitt’s lymphoma: only 5-10% of these are associated with EBV. Sporadic Burkitt's lymphoma has a worldwide distribution. These often occur in the abdomen, and can involve kidneys or ovaries. Hodgkin’s lymphoma (to be covered later in systemic pathology) Nasopharyngeal carcinoma: an EBV driven carcinoma that is endemic in the region of Southern China and in some parts of the African continent. 100% of these tumors contain EBV DNA.

questions.stem: Which difference between H. pylori-associated MALToma and H. pylori-associated gastric adenocarcinoma is specifically emphasized in the PDF?

questions.explanation:
For MALToma, the handout says H. pylori acts “via chronic stimulation of the immune system, with germinal centers and nodules of proliferating B cells within the gastric mucosa or submucosa” and that “long-term inflammation and proliferation simply sets the stage for a B-cell to make a DNA error.” For adenocarcinoma, it says there is “continuous inflammation... damages the epithelium, leading to atrophy and ulceration... and then chronic regeneration of the epithelial cells,” progressing to dysplasia and invasive carcinoma.

Tempting but wrong: MALToma is a B-cell lesion driven by chronic immune stimulation; only adenocarcinoma follows the injury, regeneration and dysplasia sequence.

A.passage: • Gastric adenocarcinoma (3% of infected pts) – Repeated inflammation and regeneration • Acute inflamm→ chronic inflamm → atrophy → regeneration and intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma – → accumulation of DNA errors – Evolves over decades – Late changes: K-RAS, p53, APC mutations • ? Certain strains of H. pylori involved – All share a suspect “pathogenicity island” in genome – Contains suspect bacterial gene CagA

B.passage: H. pylori's role in malignancy (lymphoma and adenocarcinoma) Chronic infection with H. pylori is implicated in the development of two different cancers – B-cell gastric lymphoma (also called MALT-omas) and gastric adenocarcinoma. H. pylori is the first bacterium to be considered oncogenic.

C.passage: • Gastric B-cell lymphoma (aka MALToma) – Not well understood – Chronic inflammation – IL-1beta and TNF signaling may be involved – Initially polyclonal B cell proliferation – Eventually a malignant clone emerges

D.passage: Helicobacter pylori H. pylori is a spiral-shaped bacterium that has been implicated in development of human neoplasia (carcinoma and lymphoma). The bacterium infects the gastric mucosa (and sometimes duodenum), and has a particular affinity for the gastric antrum. Persistent infection is accompanied by chronic inflammation (chronic gastritis) followed by mucosal atrophy (thinning) and often ulceration with epithelial regeneration, which may include intestinal metaplasia in the gastric antrum.

E.passage: H. pylori-related gastric adenocarcinoma also relates to long-standing inflammation. Initially there is acute and then chronic gastritis that can progress for decades if untreated. This continuous inflammation that is meant to attack the H. pylori also continually damages the epithelium, leading to atrophy and ulceration of the mucosa, and then chronic regeneration of the epithelial cells at the ulcer site.

questions.stem: Which lesion is correctly classified as a heterotopia rather than a hamartoma?

choices.B: Pancreatic tissue in the jejunum

questions.explanation:
The handout defines “Heterotopia (choristoma): A mass of microscopically normal cells/tissues in an abnormal location” and gives “Heterotopic pancreatic tissue in jejenum” as the example. The slide deck gives the same definition.

Tempting but wrong: A pulmonary chondroid nodule is a hamartoma (native tissues, disorganized); heterotopia is normal tissue in the wrong place, such as pancreas in jejunum.

B.passage: Question #1 A finding of pancreatic tissue in the esophagus would best be characterized by which of the following: a. A hamartoma b. A carcinoma c. A choristoma (aka, heterotopia) d. None of the above

C.passage: Hemangioma: A benign vascular (blood vessel) neoplasm often occurring on the skin of the face or scalp, which may enlarge as the child grows then either persist throughout life or spontaneously regress. A “port wine stain” is a large flat hemangioma which may be associated with various tumor syndromes (von-Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL TSG), Sturge- Webber syndrome, cerebral cavernous malformations).

D.passage: Lymphangioma: A benign vascular (lymphatic vessel) proliferation, which may truly be a neoplasm or hamartoma, often occurring on the neck (cystic hygroma), axilla, mediastinum or retroperitoneum. Cystic hygroma may be associated with Turner syndrome (45,X) or Noonan syndrome (MAP kinase cascade mutations).

E.passage: Tumor-Like Lesions: Tumor-like lesions are essentially an excessive overgrowth of microscopically normal cells/tissues. When the overgrowth is present in the tissue’s native location the term “hamartoma” is used; when the overgrowth is present in a location in which the tissue is not normally present, the term “heterotopia” or “choristoma” is used.

questions.stem: Which histologic feature in a neuroblastic tumor indicates maturation rather than complete undifferentiated neuroblastoma?

choices.A: Tadpole cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm
choices.B: Triphasic blastema-stroma-epithelium pattern
choices.C: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes around an empty lumen
choices.D: Sheets of primitive small round blue cells with no neuropil
choices.E: Neuropil and Homer-Wright rosettes

questions.explanation:
The handout says differentiating neuroblastomas contain “neuropil (aggregates of axons and dendrites) and immature ganglion cells,” and that “Homer-Wright rosettes... is also indicative of differentiation.”

Tempting but wrong: Sheets of primitive cells without neuropil are undifferentiated neuroblastoma; neuropil and Homer-Wright rosettes point to neuroblastic maturation.

A.passage: 2. spindle cells + “tadpole cells” elongated cells with bright red cytoplasm (have actin + myosin)

B.passage: microscopic: (this is important) #1: triphasic pattern: 1. undifferentiated blastemal cells (SRBCs) 2. stroma 3. epithelium

C.passage: 2. Differentiated elements: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (empty central lumen without neuropil)

D.passage: Similar to other primitive neoplasms, the tumor contains sheets of primitive small round blue cells. In ~ 40% of cases Homer-Wright rosettes are seen (the same rosettes seen in neuroblastoma). The tumor arises within the cerebellar vermis and often shows evidence of CNS (spinal cord) spread through the CSF, called “drop metastases.”

E.passage: Homer-Wright rosettes: undifferentiated neuroblasts around neuropil

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — Nemo cancer: radiation/childhood, Q26

questions.stem: A pediatric renal tumor shows blastemal, stromal, and epithelial components recapitulating fetal kidney. Which diagnosis is best supported?

choices.A: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney
choices.B: Wilms tumor
choices.C: Neuroblastoma
choices.D: Medulloblastoma
choices.E: Ewing sarcoma

questions.explanation:
Wilms tumor is described as “derived from nephrogenic blastemal cells... and the tumor contains 3 components (blastemal element, stromal element and epithelial element) which histologically recapitulate the fetal kidney tissue.”

Tempting but wrong: Clear cell sarcoma is a pediatric renal tumor but not triphasic; blastema, stroma and epithelium recapitulating fetal kidney is Wilms tumor.

A.passage: Ewing sarcoma is a primitive small round cell sarcoma that definitionally has a translocation involving EWSR1 and an ETS transcription factor. If this translocation is not present, the tumor is not a Ewing sarcoma. It is the 2nd most common bone tumor in children (after osteosarcoma). Ewing sarcoma usually occurs in the 10-20 year old age group, but it may occur at any age, including older adults.

B.passage: Prognosis of Wilms tumor: The current cure rate of Wilms tumor is ~ 90%.

C.passage: Neuroblastoma: 7% Wilms tumor: 5% Rhabdomyosarcoma: 3% Retinoblastoma: 3%

D.passage: Medulloblastoma: a SRBCT (primitive neurons) of the cerebellum CSF metastasis

E.passage: Ewing sarcoma may occur in the bone (~ 80% of cases) or the soft tissue; primary Ewing sarcoma of the visceral organs is rare.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — Nemo cancer: radiation/childhood, Q27

questions.stem: Which hereditary syndrome-tumor pairing is matched correctly?

choices.A: Denys-Drash — WT1 mutation with high Wilms tumor risk
choices.B: Beckwith-Wiedemann — RB1 mutation with leukocoria
choices.C: WAGR — WT2 imprinting defect at 11p15
choices.D: WAGR — WT1 mutation with high Wilms tumor risk and male pseudohermaphroditism
choices.E: Hereditary retinoblastoma — germline RB1 mutation with low risk of later osteosarcoma

questions.explanation:
The Wilms tumor syndromes section states: “Denys-Drash syndrome... germline point mutation: WT1... risk of Wilms tumor: 90%.” The other options intentionally mismatch details from WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, and hereditary retinoblastoma syndrome.

Tempting but wrong: WAGR is a WT1 deletion with aniridia, GU anomalies and intellectual disability; the WT1 mutation with pseudohermaphroditism is Denys-Drash.

A.passage: 2. Denys-Drash syndrome: Wilms tumor, gonadal dysgenesis (male pseudo hermaphroditism), nephropathy, gonadoblastoma

B.passage: Remember that embryonal RMS may occur in patients with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and ARMS may be seen in patients with hereditary retinoblastoma syndrome.

C.passage: 3. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome: organomegaly, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele mutation: imprinted genes at 11p15 (abnormalities of the WT2 gene; loss of maternal imprinting of WT2 results in overexpression of the insulin like growth factor-2 gene)

D.passage: 1. WAGR syndrome: germline deletion of 11p13 • encodes WT1 and aniridia genes W: Wilms tumor (33% risk of Wilms tumor) A: aniridia (complete or partial absence of iris) G: genital abnormalities (cryptorchidism, hypospadias)

E.passage: 2. hereditary retinoblastoma syndrome: germline RB1 mutation (retinoblastoma, pineoblastoma, ARMS, osteosarcoma)

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — Nemo cancer: radiation/childhood, Q28

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes retinoblastoma from medulloblastoma in the lecture?

choices.A: Both commonly present with leukocoria from posterior fossa spread
choices.B: Retinoblastoma arises in the cerebellar vermis
choices.C: Medulloblastoma is linked to biallelic RB loss and shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes
choices.D: Retinoblastoma is linked to biallelic RB loss and may show Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes
choices.E: Medulloblastoma usually presents with leukocoria

questions.explanation:
The retinoblastoma section says “Nearly 100% of cases have biallelic loss of the RB gene due to mutations” and that differentiation may be shown by “Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (cells surround an empty lumen, without neuropil).” Medulloblastoma instead is a cerebellar tumor with CSF spread and Homer-Wright rosettes.

Tempting but wrong: Biallelic RB loss and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes are features of retinoblastoma; medulloblastoma arises in the cerebellum and spreads through CSF.

A.passage: s/sx: 1. retina: loss of red reflex + development of white reflex (leukocoria)

B.passage: Similar to other primitive neoplasms, the tumor contains sheets of primitive small round blue cells. In ~ 40% of cases Homer-Wright rosettes are seen (the same rosettes seen in neuroblastoma). The tumor arises within the cerebellar vermis and often shows evidence of CNS (spinal cord) spread through the CSF, called “drop metastases.”

C.passage: Microscopically, Ewing sarcoma consist of sheeted SRBCs. Areas with neuropil or rosettes (both Homer-Wright or Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes) may be present.

D.passage: 2. Differentiated elements: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (empty central lumen without neuropil)

E.passage: Medulloblastoma is a malignant cerebellar neoplasm, which usually occurs in children, composed of primitive neuronal cells (SRBCs); cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metastasis is common. Most cases occur in 5-10 year old children and 70% of cases occur before 16 years old. Pre-term delivery increases the risk of developing medulloblastoma.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — Nemo cancer: radiation/childhood, Q29

questions.stem: Which prognostic statement about Ewing sarcoma is most accurate from the PDFs?

choices.A: Metastatic disease at presentation is the most important adverse prognostic factor
choices.B: The main prognostic factor is the specific EWSR1 fusion partner (FLI1 vs ERG)
choices.C: Good prognosis is defined by less than 50% necrosis after neoadjuvant chemotherapy
choices.D: Good prognosis is defined by more than 90% necrosis after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the single most important factor
choices.E: Extra-skeletal tumors have better survival than skeletal tumors

questions.explanation:
The handout says: “The most important prognostic factor is the presence or absence of metastatic disease at presentation and patients with metastatic disease at presentation have a very poor prognosis.” It also notes “if > 90% of the tumor has been destroyed by chemotherapy the patient has a good prognosis.”

Tempting but wrong: Good response to chemotherapy helps, but metastatic disease at presentation is the most important adverse factor.

A.passage: Px-factors: #1: metastatic disease at presentation – very poor px

B.passage: The most common translocation to occur (90% of cases) is t(11;22) which fuses the EWSR1 and Fli1 genes; this is commonly tested, including on boards exams. The second most common translocation is t(21;22) resulting in an EWSR1- ERG fusion.

C.passage: Ewing sarcoma of the skeleton has a better prognosis (cure in ~ 2/3 of patients) than extra-skeletal Ewing sarcoma (5-year survival is only 20%). The most important prognostic factor is the presence or absence of metastatic disease at presentation and patients with metastatic disease at presentation have a very poor prognosis. Ewing sarcoma is treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (chemotherapy before surgery), followed by surgical resection of the tumor. On pathologic assessment, if > 90% of the tumor has been destroyed by chemotherapy the patient has a good prognosis.

D.passage: also important: response to neoadjuvant (before surgery) chemotherapy good response (grade 3 or 4): > 90% tumor destroyed by chemo bad response (grade 1 or 2): < 90% tumor destroyed by chemo

E.passage: Prognosis: skeletal tumors: ~ 2/3 are cured extra-skeletal (soft tissue, visceral): 5-year survival only 20%

questions.stem: A patient treated with an alkylating chemotherapeutic agent for Hodgkin lymphoma later develops acute myeloid leukemia. Which mechanistic feature of this drug class best explains this secondary malignancy?

choices.A: Direct donation of an alkyl group to guanine, causing mispairing
choices.B: Cytochrome P450 conversion of the drug into an epoxide that forms bulky guanine adducts
choices.C: Cytochrome P450–mediated activation of a procarcinogen
choices.D: Formation of N-nitroso compounds that require gastric acid for activation
choices.E: Promotion of proliferation of already-initiated marrow cells without DNA damage

questions.explanation:
Secondary leukemia after alkylating chemotherapy reflects mutagenic DNA damage in normal cells. The handout notes:

  - “Alkylating agents are commonly used as cancer chemotherapy drugs… Alkylation of DNA in normal cells can lead to mutations that cause secondary malignancies many years after the initial treatment.”
    And mechanistically:
  - “Ethylmethane sulfonate EMS, a mustard gas is an alkylating agent that can donate an alkyl group C2H5 to a keto group in guanine. The resulting 6‑ethylguanine acts as an analog of adenine and pairs with thymine leading to transversion mutations.”

Tempting but wrong: Alkylating agents are direct-acting: they donate an alkyl group to guanine without P450 activation.

A.passage: Ethylmethane sulfonate (EMS, a mustard gas) is an alkylating agent that can donate an alkyl group (C2H5) to a keto group in guanine. The resulting 6-ethylguanine acts as an analog of adenine and pairs with thymine, leading to transversion mutations.

B.passage: Hydrocarbons ▪ Metabolized by the cytochrome p450 system to a highly reactive intermediate that causes DNA adducts (addition products)

C.passage: ▪ Do not require metabolic activation by cytochrome P450. ▪ Directly damage cellular DNA Examples:

D.passage: Summary of known health effects for compounds found in smoke particles from tobacco cigarettes and marijuana joints. Numbers indicate the number of tentatively identified compounds which exhibit a given health effect.

E.passage: ▪ Chemicals may also act as tumor promoters and stimulate proliferation of initiated cells.

questions.stem: Ethylmethane sulfonate (EMS) is described as a prototypical direct-acting carcinogen. Which specific DNA-level change does EMS induce?

choices.A: Transversion mutation via 6‑ethylguanine pairing with thymine
choices.B: Frameshift mutation at CpG dinucleotides
choices.C: Frameshift mutation via intercalation of the ethyl group between stacked base pairs
choices.D: Double-strand DNA breaks followed by non-homologous end joining
choices.E: Transversion mutation via 6‑ethyladenine pairing with cytosine

questions.explanation:
The slides specify EMS’s exact lesion:

  - “Ethylmethane sulfonate EMS, a mustard gas is an alkylating agent that can donate an alkyl group C2H5 to a keto group in guanine. The resulting 6‑ethylguanine acts as an analog of adenine and pairs with thymine, leading to transversion mutations.”

Tempting but wrong: The slide's lesion is on guanine (6-ethylguanine acting like adenine and pairing with thymine), not on adenine.

A.passage: Ethylmethane sulfonate (EMS, a mustard gas) is an alkylating agent that can donate an alkyl group (C2H5) to a keto group in guanine. The resulting 6-ethylguanine acts as an analog of adenine and pairs with thymine, leading to transversion mutations.

B.passage: Aflatoxin B1 is a naturally occurring dietary toxin produced by Aspergillus, a fungus. It is metabolized by the liver toa reactive intermediate. Aflatoxin induces a specific mutation (a “signature mutation”) at a particular codon in the p53 gene, resulting in inactivation of the tumor suppressor gene. Co-exposure to persistent viral hepatitis and aflatoxin B1 increases therisk of liver cancer dramatically

C.passage: Ethylmethane sulfonate (EMS, a mustard gas) is an alkylating agent that can donate an alkyl group (C2H5) to a keto group in guanine. The resulting 6-ethylguanine acts as an analog of adenine and pairs with thymine leading to transversion mutations. http://www.nicerweb.com/bio3400/Locked/media/ch15/alkylating.html

E.passage: ▪ Aflatoxin induces a specific mutation (a “signature mutation”) at codon 249 of p53 gene → inactivation.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: carcinogenesis, Q2

questions.stem: A chronic smoker has increased CYP1A1 activity in bronchial epithelium. What is the most direct carcinogenic consequence of this enzymatic induction?

choices.A: Direct alkylation of bronchial DNA by nicotine without metabolic activation
choices.B: Enhanced generation of DNA adduct–forming PAH intermediates
choices.C: Decreased formation of reactive oxygen species by bronchial macrophages
choices.D: Increased glucuronidation and excretion of PAH metabolites in the urine
choices.E: Increased formation of nitrosamines from dietary nitrites

questions.explanation:
CYP1A1 induction in smokers converts PAHs (e.g., benzo[a]pyrene) into reactive intermediates:

  - “They are found in tobacco smoke… These substances are metabolized by the cytochrome P450 system to a highly reactive intermediate that causes DNA adducts.”
    The handout also emphasizes P450 polymorphisms and induction:
  - “Others… are indirect‑acting agents, requiring metabolic activation, primarily through the cytochrome P450 system.”
  - “The activity of these enzymes can also be modulated by non‑genetic mechanisms, e.g., induction of P450 activity by therapeutic drugs or excess alcohol consumption. In chronic smokers, CYP1A1 activity is induced in the lungs accelerating conversion of benzo[a]pyrene into DNA‑reactive metabolites that can induce mutations.”

Tempting but wrong: PAHs such as benzo[a]pyrene are indirect-acting: CYP1A1 turns them into DNA adduct-forming intermediates, and nicotine is not the alkylator.

A.passage: ▪ Do not require metabolic activation by cytochrome P450. ▪ Directly damage cellular DNA Examples:

B.passage: Some chemicals, such as benzo(a)pyrene (a Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon or PAH) and aflatoxin, induce specific mutations (“signature mutations”) in oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes, providing further evidence that chemicals cause cancer.

C.passage: Aflatoxin B1 ▪ It is metabolized by the liver to a reactive intermediate.

E.passage: - Nitrites in food preservatives (form nitrosamines, stomach cancer)

questions.stem: In aflatoxin B1–related hepatocellular carcinoma, which molecular event directly links exposure to this toxin with p53 inactivation?

choices.A: Deletion of the TP53 locus on chromosome 17p
choices.B: Signature mutation at codon 12 of K-RAS that secondarily inactivates p53
choices.C: Aflatoxin-induced HBV integration that deletes the TP53 locus
choices.D: Promoter hypermethylation of TP53
choices.E: Signature mutation at a specific codon of p53

questions.explanation:
Aflatoxin B1 causes a characteristic p53 mutation:

  - “Aflatoxin B1… is metabolized by the liver to a reactive intermediate. Aflatoxin induces a specific mutation a signature mutation at a particular codon in the p53 gene, resulting in inactivation of the tumor suppressor gene.”
    Slides reiterate:
  - “Aflatoxin induces a specific mutation a signature mutation at codon 249 of p53 gene inactivation.”

Tempting but wrong: The lecture's link is a signature mutation at codon 249 of p53, not a deletion or a K-RAS codon 12 change.

A.passage: point mutations at INK4a gene locus: p16 and p14ARF tumor suppressor genes

B.passage: “Signature mutations” associated with exposure to chemical carcinogens in tobacco smoke: Mutations in codon 12 in K-RAS oncogene Lung Cancer G→T transversions in the p53 tumor suppressor gene and many other genes

C.passage: Aflatoxin B1 ▪ It is metabolized by the liver to a reactive intermediate.

D.passage: Promotion – Enhanced proliferation of initiated cells (which may contribute to the development of additional mutations in the cells). A promoter increases the probability of development of a tumor when applied after an initiator. The effects of a promoter are reversible.

E.passage: ▪ Aflatoxin induces a specific mutation (a “signature mutation”) at codon 249 of p53 gene → inactivation.

questions.stem: A worker in an azo dye plant develops bladder cancer. Which mechanistic feature of the agent most likely explains the site-specificity for bladder epithelium?

choices.A: Hormonal co-promotion by androgens in bladder urothelium
choices.B: Direct-acting alkylation of urothelium by the unmetabolized dye in the bloodstream
choices.C: Activation of aromatic amines by bladder CYP1A1 induced by cigarette smoke alone
choices.D: Local activation of PAHs by bladder P450
choices.E: Concentration and prolonged contact of aromatic amine metabolites in urine

questions.explanation:
Site specificity for bladder is linked to aromatic amines used in dye plants:

  - “Aromatic amines… Industrial exposure to aromatic amines such as β‑naphthylamine, occurred in workers at plants that synthesized azo dyes for use in textiles. An increased risk of bladder cancer was noted in these workers.”
    The mechanism is via urinary excretion and urothelial exposure implied by “bladder cancer” as the characteristic tumor site for these chemicals.

Tempting but wrong: Aromatic amines are activated in the liver, and their metabolites are concentrated and held against the bladder urothelium in urine.

A.passage: Prostate cancer growth depends on androgens: responds to anti-androgen therapy

B.passage: Some chemicals are direct-acting agents thatdo not need to be activated metabolically.

C.passage: Asbestos exposure + cigarette smoking → risk of lung cancer increases 50x (synergistic increase). Tobacco Smoke ▪ Uranium miners and cigarette smoke (predominantly Co-Exposures due to exposure to radon gas)

D.passage: ▪ Do not require metabolic activation by cytochrome P450. ▪ Directly damage cellular DNA Examples:

E.passage: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are found in soot and cigarette smoke

questions.stem: A patient with a long history of eating heavily pickled foods develops gastric adenocarcinoma. Which mechanism is most directly responsible for the DNA damage in this setting?

choices.A: Nitrosamines formed from nitrites and amines at acidic gastric pH
choices.B: Direct alkylation of DNA by dietary aflatoxin
choices.C: Benzo[a]pyrene from cooking smoke activated by gastric CYP1A1
choices.D: CagA-mediated direct alkylation of gastric epithelial DNA
choices.E: Estrogen-mediated proliferation of gastric mucosa

questions.explanation:
The nitrite–nitrosamine–gastric cancer pathway is explicit:

  - “Nitrites are preservatives used in pickled or highly salted foods. Nitrites combine with amines present in food at acidic pH in the stomach to form carcinogenic nitrosamines that cause DNA adducts. Nitrosamines are associated with gastric cancer.”
    Slides parallel this:
  - “Nitrites… in pickled or highly salted foods… Nitrites combine with amines present in food in the stomach to form carcinogenic nitrosamines that cause DNA adducts. Nitrosamines are associated with gastric cancer.”

Tempting but wrong: Pickled foods supply nitrites that form nitrosamines at acidic gastric pH; CagA is a bacterial virulence protein, not an alkylator.

A.passage: Nitrites are preservatives used in pickled or highly salted foods. Nitritescombine with amines present in food at acidic pH in the stomach to form carcinogenic nitrosamines that causeDNA adducts. Nitrosamines are associated with gastric cancer.

B.passage: Aflatoxin B1 is a naturally occurring dietary toxin produced by Aspergillus, a fungus. It is metabolized by the liver toa reactive intermediate. Aflatoxin induces a specific mutation (a “signature mutation”) at a particular codon in the p53 gene, resulting in inactivation of the tumor suppressor gene. Co-exposure to persistent viral hepatitis and aflatoxin B1 increases therisk of liver cancer dramatically

C.passage: As you have already learned in the lectures on Cell Injury, people have different polymorphisms in their cytochrome P450 genes. This has been proposed as one reason for individual variation in risk of developing cancer after exposure to carcinogenic chemicals. The activity of these enzymes can also bemodulated by non-genetic mechanisms, e.g., induction of P450 activity by therapeutic drugs or excess alcohol consumption. In chronic smokers, CYP1A1 activity is induced in the lungs accelerating conversion of benzo[a]pyrene into DNA-reactive metabolites that can induce mutations.

D.passage: Direct-Acting Agents ▪ Alkylation of DNA in normal cells can lead to mutations that cause secondary malignancies many years after the initial treatment Alkylating Agents: ▪ Examples: Chemotherapy ▪ Secondary leukemia developing several years Drugs after alkylating agent treatment for Hodgkin’s disease ▪ Thyroid cancer after radiation treatment for Hodgkin’s disease

E.passage: Exposure to high levels of exogenous or endogenous estrogen for prolonged periods of time is associatedwith increased risks of breast cancer and endometrial cancer. Excess estrogen stimulates proliferation of endometrial cells.

questions.stem: A woman on long-term unopposed estrogen therapy develops endometrial carcinoma. In the framework of chemical carcinogenesis, estrogen in this scenario is best classified as:

choices.A: Direct-acting initiator
choices.B: Indirect-acting initiator
choices.C: Progression factor that directly confers invasive and metastatic ability
choices.D: Tumor promoter that stimulates proliferation of initiated cells
choices.E: Complete carcinogen with both initiating and promoting activity

questions.explanation:
Estrogen is framed as a promoter:

  - “Exposure to high levels of exogenous or endogenous estrogen for prolonged periods of time is associated with increased risks of breast cancer and endometrial cancer. Excess estrogen stimulates proliferation of endometrial cells.”
    And under “Promoters – Hormones”:
  - “Endometrial Cancer stimulates cell proliferation… Hormonally‑induced hyperplasia of the endometrium is a precursor lesion of endometrial carcinoma. Fertile ground for carcinogenesis.”
    In the summary:
  - “Endogenous or exogenous hormones may act as tumor promoters.”

Tempting but wrong: Estrogen is a promoter: it drives proliferation of initiated cells and is not itself a mutagenic initiator or progression agent.

A.passage: Some chemicals are direct-acting agents thatdo not need to be activated metabolically.

B.passage: Indirect-Acting 2-Acetylaminofluorene Dimethylaminoazobenzene (butter yellow)

C.passage: Other chemical carcinogens are agents that act either directly or indirectly.

D.passage: Promotion – Enhanced proliferation of initiated cells (which may contribute to the development of additional mutations in the cells). A promoter increases the probability of development of a tumor when applied after an initiator. The effects of a promoter are reversible.

E.passage: • Complete carcinogens are both mutagenic (initiator) and have tumor promoting activity (promoter).

questions.stem: Tobacco smoke is considered a “complete carcinogen” in lung cancer. Which combination best explains this designation?

choices.A: It only acts as an initiator but not a promoter
choices.B: It acts solely by inducing chronic inflammation
choices.C: It is both mutagenic and has tumor-promoting activity
choices.D: It contains only indirect-acting carcinogens that need CYP activation
choices.E: It is a promoter only, acting on cells initiated by radon and asbestos

questions.explanation:
Tobacco smoke is explicitly defined as a complete carcinogen:

  - “Complete carcinogens are both mutagenic initiator and have tumor promoting activity promoter. Tobacco smoke is an example of a complete carcinogen…”
    Slides mirror:
  - “Complete carcinogens are both mutagenic initiator and have tumor promoting activity promoter. Tobacco smoke is an example of a complete carcinogen…”

Tempting but wrong: A complete carcinogen has both initiating (mutagenic) and promoting activity.

A.passage: Promotion – Enhanced proliferation of initiated cells (which may contribute to the development of additional mutations in the cells). A promoter increases the probability of development of a tumor when applied after an initiator. The effects of a promoter are reversible.

B.passage: Many carcinogens induce chronic tissue injury resulting in persistent inflammation: •Tobacco smoking or chewing Inflammation: •Asbestos fibers •Persistent bacterial or viral infections (discussed Enabler of tomorrow) Malignancy Cancers were described as “wounds that do not heal” by the pathologist, Harold Dvorak and chronic inflammation is described as an “enabler of malignancy.”

C.passage: • Complete carcinogens are both mutagenic (initiator) and have tumor promoting activity (promoter).

D.passage: ▪ Direct-acting agents (do Environmental not need to be activated metabolically) Carcinogens ▪ Indirect-acting agents (e.g. tobacco smoke, require metabolic activation, primarily through the cytochrome P450 system)

E.passage: Promotion: enhanced proliferation of initiated cells (which may contribute to the development Mechanism of of additional mutations in the cells). A promoter increases the probability of development of a Carcinogenesis tumor when applied after an initiator. The effects of a promoter are reversible.

questions.stem: A former smoker quit 10 years ago but now develops a second primary lung carcinoma. Which concept best explains the presence of multiple independent neoplastic clones after cessation of exposure?

choices.A: Epigenetic field reprogramming
choices.B: Promoter-dependent reversible hyperplasia that persists after cessation
choices.C: Bystander effect from radiation-damaged neighboring cells
choices.D: Field effect with persistence of initiated cells in exposed epithelium
choices.E: Metastasis of the first primary tumor to the contralateral lung

questions.explanation:
The handout describes a “field effect” and persistence of initiated cells after cessation:

  - “Exposure of bronchial epithelium to cigarette smoke results in a field effect because of the wide extent of carcinogen exposure. Many cells are mutated or damaged, though one clone may emerge after many years as a preneoplastic/neoplastic clone.”
  - “It is worth noting that initiated cells may persist in the exposed field and a secondary malignancy may occur later on, even after a person stops smoking.”

Tempting but wrong: Promoter effects reverse after exposure stops; a second independent primary arises from initiated cells persisting in the exposed field.

A.passage: Genetic K-RAS mutation, p53 mutations, epigenetic alterations Alterations + ~20,000 other acquired mutations, chromosomal alterations

B.passage: Promotion – Enhanced proliferation of initiated cells (which may contribute to the development of additional mutations in the cells). A promoter increases the probability of development of a tumor when applied after an initiator. The effects of a promoter are reversible.

D.passage: Exposure of bronchial epithelium to cigarette smoke results in a “field effect” because of the wide extent of carcinogen exposure. Many cells are mutated or damaged, though one clone may emerge after many years asa preneoplastic/neoplastic clone. It is worth noting that initiated cells may persist in the “exposed field” and a secondary malignancy may occur later on, even after a person stops smoking.

E.passage: Multiple biochemical and molecular events lead to the development of lung cancer:

questions.stem: A shipyard worker with asbestos exposure and heavy cigarette use has a 50‑fold increased lung cancer risk compared with smoking alone. Which term best describes this interaction?

choices.A: Additive
choices.B: Redundant
choices.C: Antagonistic
choices.D: Synergistic
choices.E: Promotional

questions.explanation:
The asbestos–smoking interaction is explicitly called synergistic and quantified:

  - “Asbestos is associated with a rare cancer of the mesothelium… However, asbestos exposure does increase the risk of lung cancer 5‑fold. When asbestos exposure is added to cigarette smoking, the risk of lung cancer increases 55‑fold over that for smoking alone a synergistic increase.”
    Slides similarly:
  - “Asbestos exposure cigarette smoking risk of lung cancer increases 50x synergistic increase.”

Microbial Carcinogenesis (Q11–Q20)

Tempting but wrong: Neither agent is acting just as a promoter here; a combined risk far above the sum of the separate risks (5x and smoking alone) is synergy.

D.passage: Asbestos exposure + cigarette smoking → risk of lung cancer increases 50x (synergistic increase). Tobacco Smoke ▪ Uranium miners and cigarette smoke (predominantly Co-Exposures due to exposure to radon gas)

questions.stem: Human T‑cell leukemia virus type I (HTLV‑1) is associated with adult T‑cell leukemia/lymphoma. Which feature of HTLV‑1 biology best explains the long latency and low penetrance of this malignancy?

choices.A: Viral integration next to MYC proto-oncogene
choices.B: Direct insertion of a viral oncogene into hepatocyte DNA
choices.C: TAX protein that is a constitutively active CD40-like receptor transforming B cells
choices.D: TAX protein that promotes proliferation but requires additional host “hits”
choices.E: Rapid transformation of infected CD4 T cells through insertional activation of MYC

questions.explanation:
Top-Hat text explains low penetrance and long latency:

  - “Only one retrovirus has been directly linked to a human cancer Human T‑cell Lymphotropic Virus Type I HTLV‑1… Only a low percentage 2.5 of those infected go on to develop the lymphomaleukemia, and other factors in the host or host’s environment are suspected to play a role in the development of the malignancy. There is quite a long latency period decades, up to 40‑60 years\!… The specific molecular mechanisms… are unclear. However, research has identified a unique viral gene called TAX… shown to cause cell proliferation, though this is likely just one piece of the puzzle.”
    Slides summarize:
  - “Human T-cell Leukemia Virus Type I HTLV‑1… Risk of developing the lymphoma is low 2.5… Likely requires additional hits. Latency period of 40‑60 years…”

Tempting but wrong: Single-strand breaks are the most numerous but are easily repaired; double-strand breaks correlate best with lethality.

A.passage: A. Single Strand Break B. Double Strand Break C. Base Damage D. Thymine Dimer Creation

B.passage: Reoxygenation • For “sparsely” ionizing radiations (like x-rays), oxygen is an essential intermediary for DNA damage. • Ionized DNA radical can be resorted by free radical scavengers (thiols) • Oxygen binding to the DNA radical prevents this reversal and the DNA damage is “fixed” or made permanent.

C.passage: A. Single Strand Break B. Double Strand Break C. Based Damage D. Thymine Dimer Creation

D.passage: • 1 Gy single exposure causes on average: • >1,000 Damaged bases • 500-1,000 Single-strand DNA breaks • 40 Double-strand DNA breaks • 30 DNA crosslinks

questions.explanation:
Under reoxygenation: “For sparsely ionizing radiations like x-rays, oxygen is an essential intermediary for DNA damage. Ionized DNA radical can be resorted by free radical scavengers (thiols). Oxygen binding to the DNA radical prevents this reversal and the DNA damage is fixed or made permanent.”

A.passage: Radiation and Drug Interactions Radiation will interact with any drug that: • Directly damages DNA (e.g. alkylating agents) – Repair • Interferes with cellular mechanisms of DNA damage repair (e.g. 5-FU) – Repair • Alters cellular redox (“oxygen mimetic”: misonidazole; porfiromycin; “free radical scavengers”: glutathione) – Re-oxygenation

C.passage: Reoxygenation • For “sparsely” ionizing radiations (like x-rays), oxygen is an essential intermediary for DNA damage. • Ionized DNA radical can be resorted by free radical scavengers (thiols) • Oxygen binding to the DNA radical prevents this reversal and the DNA damage is “fixed” or made permanent.

B.passage: Prodromal Latent Period Manifest Illness Recovery or Death Syndrome

C.passage: Cancer risk and radiation exposure • Data for Cancer Risk • Medical treatments using radiation • Radiation use for ankylosing spondylitis, cradle cap, ache… • Occupational exposure • Uranium miner, watch workers – radium dials, … • Radiation accidents • Chernobyl, Fukushima, … • Atomic bomb survivors • Any type of cancer can be radiation induced. • Radiation related cancers are indistinguishable from sporadic cases.

D.passage: Hematopoietic Syndrome • Total body dose of 0.7-10 Gy • Mechanism: • Mitotic and apoptotic death of hematopoietic precursor cell in the bone marrow resulting in neutropenia, anemia, and bleeding complications. • Onset: 1-6 weeks after exposure • Symptoms: • chills, fever, fatigue, bleeding, ulceration of the mouth, infectious complications. • Not always fatal • Probability of death increases with increasing radiation dose exposure. • LD50 (dose that causes 50% case mortality) is 6 Gy. • Death occurs at ~30 days.

E.passage: Cerebrovascular Syndrome • Total body dose ≥ 50-100 Gy • Mechanism: • Vascular system failure and increase intracranial pressure due to edema from vascular dysfunction and meningitis. • Onset: minutes to hours after exposure • Symptoms: • Severe nausea/vomiting, disorientation, loss of coordination, respiratory distress, seizures, coma • Universally Fatal • Death occurs in 24-48 hours • Treatment: Comfort measures

questions.doc_section: II. Radiation Exposure, Risks, and Safety (10 questions)
questions.stem: Which thyroid cancer–related preventive measure is specifically recommended during nuclear accidents with I-131 release?

choices.A: Administration of radioactive I-131 to ablate the thyroid
choices.B: Thyroid hormone (levothyroxine) to suppress TSH-driven iodine uptake
choices.C: Prolonged fasting to reduce iodine uptake
choices.D: Taking I-131 as potassium iodide to saturate the thyroid
choices.E: Taking I-127 as potassium iodide to saturate the thyroid

questions.explanation:
Thyroid cancer/I-131 slide: “Radioactive I-131 when ingested is taken up and concentrated in the thyroid gland leading to thyroid cancer… Prevention Taking I-127 as potassium iodide during risk of exposure saturates thyroid gland and prevents I-131 uptake.”

Tempting but wrong: Stable I-127 in KI saturates the thyroid; I-131 is the radioactive isotope being blocked.

A.passage: Thyroid Cancer • Radiation induced thyroid cancer tends to be low grade and very treatable with >95% survival. • Children and adolescence particularly at risk. • Short latency period: 5-10 years. • Unlike other solid tumors • High risk of thyroid cancer with nuclear reactor and atomic bomb exposures due to Iodine-131 contamination.

E.passage: Thyroid Cancer • Iodine (I-127) is natural element (not radioactive) that is a key component of thyroid hormone; T3 and T4. • Radioactive Iodine - 131 is a by-product of nuclear reactors. • Nuclear accidents can cause large quantities of I-131 fallout resulting in contamination including food and water. • Radioactive I-131 when ingested is taken up and concentrated in the thyroid gland leading to thyroid cancer. • I-131 has a short half-life of 7 days. • Prevention: Taking I-127 (as potassium iodide) during risk of exposure saturates thyroid gland and prevents I-131 uptake.

questions.stem: For fetal radiation effects, what is the predominant effect of radiation exposure during the preimplantation period, as summarized in the table?

choices.A: Growth disturbances without malformations
choices.B: Increased risk of childhood leukemia without structural anomalies
choices.C: Lethal embryonic death if dose is above threshold; survivors have little/no abnormalities
choices.D: Major congenital malformations with growth retardation
choices.E: Major malformations of the central nervous system with microcephaly and intellectual disability in survivors

questions.explanation:
Fetal effects table: For “Preimplantation Period (From fertilization to attachment to the uterine wall)” the effect is: “Lethal effect, embryonic death If the embryo survives, it will have little/no abnormalities.”

Childhood Tumors

Tempting but wrong: CNS malformations and microcephaly belong to organogenesis and the early fetal period; preimplantation exposure is all-or-none.

A.passage: Fetal Effects of Radiation Exposure • The effects of radiation on an unborn fetus can be broadly divided into 3 categories: • Lethal effects • Malformations • Growth Disturbances without malformations • The principal factors in determination of effects are: • Radiation dose • Gestational stage • Data are derived from animal studies and studying the Japanese survivors of the atomic bombs

B.passage: Cancer risk and radiation exposure • Overall risk: ~5% per Sv (1,000 mSv) • Factors influencing Cancer Risk • Radiation Dose • Time of exposure - short greater risk over long (i.e. slow) exposure. • Age • Cancer risk decreases with increasing age of exposure • Greatest susceptibility during Childhood/Adolescence • Sex • Females at higher risk • Predominately due to breast cancer risk

C.passage: Effects of Radiation by Developmental Period Developmental Period Definition Effects of radiation above threshold Preimplantation From fertilization to attachment Lethal effect, embryonic death Period to the uterine wall If the embryo survives, it will have little/no abnormalities

D.passage: Organogenesis Period in which major organs Major congenital abnormalities, are formed growth retardation

E.passage: • Studies of survivors of the Japanese A-bombs have NOT shown significantly elevated rates of birth malformations/mutations or elevated rates of cancer/non-cancer deaths in offspring. • Human Doubling dose estimated from survivor data is more suggestive of higher than 1 Gy

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: radiation/childhood, Q20

questions.stem: In the childhood tumor handout, how is a hamartoma specifically defined?

choices.A: A mass created by excessive overgrowth of microscopically normal tissues native to the location
choices.B: A benign neoplasm of vascular origin native to the skin
choices.C: A malignant proliferation of mesenchymal cells
choices.D: A mass created by overgrowth of normal tissue in an abnormal location
choices.E: A mass of tissue derived from all three germ layers, often in a midline location

questions.explanation:
Handout definition: “Hamartoma A mass created by excessive overgrowth of microscopically normal cells/tissues native to the location.” The slide deck similarly: “Hamartoma A mass created by excessive overgrowth of microscopically normal cells/tissues native to the location.”

Tempting but wrong: Tissue from all three germ layers is a teratoma; normal tissue in an abnormal location is a heterotopia (choristoma).

A.passage: Hamartoma: A mass created by excessive overgrowth of microscopically normal cells/tissues native to the location

B.passage: Benign neoplasm: A neoplasm that typically remains localized and will not spread (metastasize) to other sites (the tumor acts in an indolent fashion)

C.passage: 2. Sarcoma: tumor cells differentiate towards mesenchymal cells (mesodermally derived cells)

D.passage: Heterotopia (a choristoma) is a mass of microscopically normal cells/tissues in an abnormal location.

E.passage: Teratomas have mature cells/tissues from multiple germ layers

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: radiation/childhood, Q21

questions.stem: Which association between lesion and syndrome is explicitly highlighted in the pediatric benign tumor section?

choices.A: Hemangioma with Li-Fraumeni syndrome
choices.B: Hemangioma with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and hemihypertrophy
choices.C: Port-wine stain with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
choices.D: Cystic hygroma with Turner and Noonan syndromes
choices.E: Cystic hygroma with Down syndrome and WAGR syndrome

questions.explanation:
Lymphangioma/cystic hygroma: “Lymphangioma A benign vascular lymphatic vessel proliferation… often occurring on the neck (cystic hygroma)… Cystic hygroma may be associated with Turner syndrome (45,X) or Noonan syndrome (MAP kinase cascade mutations).” Slides: “Cystic hygroma Turner syndrome X0, Noonan syndrome MAPK pathway mutations.”

Tempting but wrong: The handout links cystic hygroma to Turner and Noonan syndromes.

A.passage: Hemangioma: A benign vascular (blood vessel) neoplasm often occurring on the skin of the face or scalp, which may enlarge as the child grows then either persist throughout life or spontaneously regress. A “port wine stain” is a large flat hemangioma which may be associated with various tumor syndromes (von-Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL TSG), Sturge- Webber syndrome, cerebral cavernous malformations).

B.passage: Remember that embryonal RMS may occur in patients with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and ARMS may be seen in patients with hereditary retinoblastoma syndrome.

C.passage: They like to put cases with port wine stains on boards Port wine stains: often seen in kids with tumor syndromes (you will learn about these in GU and neuro blocks)

D.passage: Cystic hygroma: Turner syndrome (X0), Noonan syndrome (MAPK pathway mutations)

E.passage: Lymphangioma: A benign vascular (lymphatic vessel) proliferation, which may truly be a neoplasm or hamartoma, often occurring on the neck (cystic hygroma), axilla, mediastinum or retroperitoneum. Cystic hygroma may be associated with Turner syndrome (45,X) or Noonan syndrome (MAP kinase cascade mutations).

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: radiation/childhood, Q22

questions.stem: Regarding sacrococcygeal teratomas in children, which combination best matches the handout’s description?

choices.A: Most common pediatric germ cell tumor; usually sacrococcygeal; 4× more common in females; about 10% with hindgut/midline defects
choices.B: Most common pediatric germ cell tumor; usually sacrococcygeal; 4× more common in males; nearly all malignant at birth
choices.C: Most common in boys; often associated with BRCA1 mutation
choices.D: Typically arise in the first trimester and regress before birth
choices.E: Always malignant when diagnosed before age 2

questions.explanation:
Teratoma section: “The most common pediatric germ cell tumor is the mature teratoma… The most common location of mature teratoma in children is the sacrococcygeal region. These sacrococcygeal teratomas are 4 x more common in females and 10% of cases are associated with other congenital anomalies, including birth defects of the cloaca and hindgut such as spina bifida and meningoceles.”

Tempting but wrong: Sacrococcygeal teratomas are 4 times more common in girls, and most are benign at birth (malignancy rises with age).

A.passage: The most common pediatric germ cell tumor is the mature teratoma, which is composed of mature tissue of more than one germ layer, and sometimes of all three (endo-, ecto-, and mesoderm). The most common location of mature teratoma in children is the sacrococcygeal region. These “sacrococcygeal teratomas” are ~ 4 x more common in females and ~ 10% of cases are associated with other congenital anomalies, including birth defects of the cloaca and hindgut such as spina bifida and meningoceles.

B.passage: epidemiology: incidence: 6% of all pediatric cancer • #1 pediatric kidney tumor

C.passage: Location: 1. sacrococcygeal: most common in children < 2 y/o (~ 40%) • 4 x more common in girls

D.passage: At 2 years old (spontaneous regression) px: may enlarge as child grows, then spontaneously regress (or may persist)

E.passage: 3. pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma: ~ 10% of all RMS age: nearly always adults (50-60 y/o)

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: radiation/childhood, Q23

questions.stem: Which molecular alteration is definitional for congenital infantile fibrosarcoma according to the pediatric malignancy section?

choices.A: ETV6–NTRK3 translocation with NTRK3 as a receptor tyrosine kinase
choices.B: N-MYC amplification
choices.C: ETV6–NTRK3 translocation with NTRK3 lost as a tumor suppressor
choices.D: EWSR1–FLI1 translocation creating an aberrant ETS transcription factor
choices.E: PAX3–FOXO1 fusion

questions.explanation:
Congenital infantile fibrosarcoma: “Congenital infantile fibrosarcoma is a malignant tumor of fibroblast-like cells… with a ETV6-NTRK3 gene re-arrangement translocation. The NTRK3 gene is a trans-membrane tyrosine kinase which, when over-expressed due to the translocation, activated the MAP kinase cascade…” Slides: “congenital infantile fibrosarcoma… t(12;15) ETV6-NTRK3 NTRK3 receptor tyrosine kinase.”

Tempting but wrong: The fusion overexpresses NTRK3, a receptor tyrosine kinase; it is not a tumor-suppressor loss.

A.passage: age (most cases): < 1 y/o (40-80% congenital) t(12;15): ETV6-NTRK3 NTRK3: receptor tyrosine kinase px: low-grade malignant (recurrence - common, mets - rare)

B.passage: The most important prognostic factor in neuroblastoma is the presence or absence of N-Myc gene amplification; N-Myc gene amplification always makes a tumor high-risk.

C.passage: (Congenital) infantile fibrosarcoma: (Congenital) infantile fibrosarcoma is a malignant tumor of fibroblast-like cells (not SRBCs) with a ETV6-NTRK3 gene re- arrangement (translocation); the NTRK3 gene is a trans-membrane tyrosine kinase which, when over-expressed due to the translocation, activated the MAP kinase cascade causing the cells to proliferate and create a tumor. (Congenital) infantile fibrosarcoma may be present when the baby is born (congenital cases) or develop early in life (infantile cases).

D.passage: Ewing sarcoma: • a SRBCT characterized by a translocation involving EWSR1 + an ETS transcription factor

E.passage: 2. alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS): ~ 20% of childhood RMS age: 6-10 y/o (children + young adults) genetics: PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 (translocation) microscopic: SRBCs

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: radiation/childhood, Q24

questions.stem: In neuroblastoma, which single factor is emphasized as the most important prognostic factor, and how is it characterized?

choices.A: Site of origin in sympathetic ganglia; adrenal origin has best prognosis
choices.B: N-MYC amplification; always high-risk, overriding stage, age, and histology
choices.C: Presence of Homer-Wright rosettes; indicates benign behavior
choices.D: Tumor stage; advanced stage always has good prognosis
choices.E: Age at diagnosis; under 18 months always has good prognosis regardless of N-MYC status

questions.explanation:
Neuroblastoma prognosis: “The most important prognostic factor in neuroblastoma is the presence or absence of N-Myc gene amplification N-Myc gene amplification always makes a tumor high-risk.” Slides emphasize: “N-Myc gene amplification… the \#1 px factor in neuroblastomas… N-Myc gene amplified tumors are ALWAYS high risk… N-Myc amplification trumps stage, age and histology.”

Tempting but wrong: Young age is favorable, but N-MYC amplification makes the tumor high-risk whatever the age.

A.passage: As expected, the anatomic location of neuroblastic tumors recapitulates the migration of neural crest cells, so tumors are most commonly seen in the adrenal medulla and sympathetic ganglia.

B.passage: A major prognostic factor N-Myc gene amplification (20-30% of neuroblastomas): • the #1 px factor in neuroblastomas (especially if the tumor would otherwise have a good px) N-Myc gene amplified tumors are ALWAYS high risk: • N-Myc amplification trumps stage, age and histology

C.passage: Homer-Wright rosettes: undifferentiated neuroblasts around neuropil

D.passage: Prognosis: • based on stage, age (always poor px in adults), anatomic location and histologic subtype/presence of translocation

E.passage: 3. pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma: ~ 10% of all RMS age: nearly always adults (50-60 y/o)

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: radiation/childhood, Q25

questions.stem: Which triad best characterizes the classic features of WAGR syndrome associated with Wilms tumor?

choices.A: Wilms tumor, hemihypertrophy, organomegaly; imprinting defects at 11p15
choices.B: Wilms tumor, aniridia, GU anomalies, intellectual disability; germline 11p13 deletion
choices.C: Wilms tumor, male pseudohermaphroditism, nephropathy; WT1 dominant-negative point mutation
choices.D: Wilms tumor, microcephaly, café-au-lait spots; NF1 mutation
choices.E: Wilms tumor, ataxia, gonadoblastoma; WT1 point mutation

questions.explanation:
WAGR: “1. WAGR syndrome Wilms tumor, Aniridia, GU abnormalities, and intellectual disability germline mutations 11p13 the site of the WT1 and aniridia genes risk of Wilms tumor 33%.” Slides: “WAGR syndrome germline deletion of 11p13 encodes WT1 and aniridia genes W Wilms tumor… A aniridia… G genital abnormalities… R intellectual disability.”

Tempting but wrong: That triad is Denys-Drash; WAGR is a germline 11p13 deletion with aniridia and intellectual disability.

A.passage: 3. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome: organomegaly, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele mutation: imprinted genes at 11p15 (abnormalities of the WT2 gene; loss of maternal imprinting of WT2 results in overexpression of the insulin like growth factor-2 gene)

B.passage: 1. WAGR syndrome: Wilms tumor, Aniridia, GU abnormalities, and intellectual disability

C.passage: 2. Denys-Drash syndrome: autosomal dominant • germline missense (point) mutation in WT1 1. gonadal dysgenesis (male pseudo-hermophidism) • incompletely masculinized male genitals, 46, XY, testis present

D.passage: Malignant pediatric tumors (Wilms tumor) Associated syndromes: ~ 10% of Wilms tumors

E.passage: Prognosis of Wilms tumor: The current cure rate of Wilms tumor is ~ 90%.

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: radiation/childhood, Q26

questions.stem: For retinoblastoma, which genetic pattern statement is correct as described in the handout?

choices.A: Nearly all cases are sporadic and lack RB gene involvement
choices.B: Familial cases always involve trisomy 21
choices.C: Nearly all cases have biallelic RB loss; about 40% are hereditary with a germline mutation in one allele
choices.D: Nearly all cases have biallelic RB loss; about 90% are hereditary, with both alleles mutated in the germline
choices.E: The RB gene is not a tumor suppressor in this tumor type

questions.explanation:
Retinoblastoma genetics: “Nearly 100% of cases have biallelic loss of the RB gene due to mutations. Approximately 40% of cases are hereditary the patient inherits one mutated RB allele then develops a sporadic mutation in the 2nd allele and 60% are sporadic the patient develops sporadic mutations is both RB alleles.”

Tempting but wrong: About 40% are hereditary, with one germline RB mutation and a second somatic hit.

A.passage: Malignant pediatric tumors (Retinoblastoma) http://www.rsc.org/ Genetics: (important) All retinoblastomas: Have biallelic loss of RB due to mutations (13q14) Sporadic cases: ~ 60% • both alleles have sporadic mutations Familial (inherited cases): ~ 40% • one allele with a germline (inherited) mutation and the 2nd with a sporadic mutation

B.passage: 3. pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma: ~ 10% of all RMS age: nearly always adults (50-60 y/o)

C.passage: Nearly 100% of cases have biallelic loss of the RB gene due to mutations. Approximately 40% of cases are hereditary (the patient inherits one mutated RB allele then develops a sporadic mutation in the 2nd allele) and ~ 60% are sporadic (the patient develops sporadic mutations is both RB alleles). Patients who inherit a mutated RB allele are also at risk to develop osteosarcoma, pineoblastoma, and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (see below).

D.passage: Patients are usually in the 2-5 year old age range (nearly all cases occur before 10 years old).

E.passage: A. The tumor often synthesizes catecholamines B. It is a type of small round blue cell tumor C. Tumors with amplification of the N-myc gene are high-risk D. Tumors often harbor a translocation

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes medulloblastoma in children based on the handout?

choices.A: Malignant supratentorial tumor with no association with prematurity
choices.B: Malignant cerebellar tumor of glial cells that never spreads through CSF
choices.C: Benign cerebellar tumor of astrocytes with no CSF spread
choices.D: Malignant cerebellar small round blue cell tumor with frequent CSF “drop metastases”
choices.E: Malignant cerebral small round blue cell tumor with leukocoria and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes

questions.explanation:
Medulloblastoma: “Medulloblastoma is a malignant cerebellar neoplasm, which usually occurs in children, composed of primitive neuronal cells SRBCs cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metastasis is common.” Slides: “Medulloblastoma a SRBCT primitive neurons of the cerebellum CSF metastasis.”

Tempting but wrong: Leukocoria and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes belong to retinoblastoma; medulloblastoma is cerebellar with CSF drop metastases.

A.passage: Specific malignant pediatric tumors 1. (congenital) infantile fibrosarcoma: a malignant “fibroblast” tumor

B.passage: Medulloblastoma is a malignant cerebellar neoplasm, which usually occurs in children, composed of primitive neuronal cells (SRBCs); cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metastasis is common. Most cases occur in 5-10 year old children and 70% of cases occur before 16 years old. Pre-term delivery increases the risk of developing medulloblastoma.

C.passage: Benign: A neoplasm that typically remains localized and will not spread (metastasize) to other sites

D.passage: Similar to other primitive neoplasms, the tumor contains sheets of primitive small round blue cells. In ~ 40% of cases Homer-Wright rosettes are seen (the same rosettes seen in neuroblastoma). The tumor arises within the cerebellar vermis and often shows evidence of CNS (spinal cord) spread through the CSF, called “drop metastases.”

E.passage: 2. Differentiated elements: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (empty central lumen without neuropil)

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: radiation/childhood, Q28

questions.stem: For rhabdomyosarcoma, which association between subtype and molecular/genetic feature is highlighted as “worth remembering”?

choices.A: Pleomorphic RMS – N-MYC amplification
choices.B: All RMS subtypes share the same non-recurrent mutations
choices.C: Embryonal RMS – EWSR1–FLI1 fusion
choices.D: Alveolar RMS: PAX3–FOXO1 or PAX7–FOXO1 translocation; associated with hereditary retinoblastoma
choices.E: Embryonal RMS: PAX3–FOXO1 or PAX7–FOXO1 translocation; associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann

questions.explanation:
ARMS genetics: “In ARMS, these monotonous SRBCs form nests… ARMS is a translocation sarcoma since most cases contain a PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 gene re-arrangement… ARMS may be seen in patients with hereditary retinoblastoma syndrome.” Slides: “ARMS this is worth remembering… PAX3-FOXO1… PAX7-FOXO1… hereditary retinoblastoma syndrome germline RB1 mutation retinoblastoma, pineoblastoma, ARMS, osteosarcoma.”

Tempting but wrong: The PAX–FOXO1 translocations define alveolar RMS, not embryonal.

A.passage: Embryonal RMS is the least aggressive type of RMS, followed by cases with PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7- FOXO1 gene re-arrangement (ARMS) and pleomorphic RMS is the most aggressive type of RMS.

B.passage: 3. pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma: ~ 10% of all RMS age: nearly always adults (50-60 y/o)

C.passage: The most common translocation to occur (90% of cases) is t(11;22) which fuses the EWSR1 and Fli1 genes; this is commonly tested, including on boards exams. The second most common translocation is t(21;22) resulting in an EWSR1- ERG fusion.

D.passage: 2. alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS): ~ 20% of childhood RMS age: 6-10 y/o (children + young adults) genetics: PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 (translocation) microscopic: SRBCs

E.passage: ARMS: (this is worth remembering) 1. recurrent translocations: most cases 1. PAX3 –FOXO1 (FKHR) – t(2;13) 2. PAX7-FOXO1 (FKHR) – t(1;13)

questions.source: HFD Remediation Questions — PPLX cancer: radiation/childhood, Q29

questions.stem: In Ewing sarcoma, which statement best summarizes the required molecular feature and typical radiographic finding?

choices.A: ETV6–NTRK3 fusion with “sunburst” periosteal reaction
choices.B: BRAF V600E mutation with “soap-bubble” lytic lesion
choices.C: PAX3–FOXO1 fusion with “Codman triangle” periosteal reaction
choices.D: Translocation involving EWSR1 and an ETS factor (e.g., EWSR1–FLI1), often with “onion-skin” periosteal reaction
choices.E: Translocation involving EWSR1 and an ETS factor (e.g., EWSR1–FLI1), often with a "sunburst" periosteal reaction

questions.explanation:
Ewing sarcoma: “Ewing sarcoma is a primitive small round cell sarcoma that definitionally has a translocation involving EWSR1 and an ETS transcription factor. If this translocation is not present, the tumor is not a Ewing sarcoma.” Slides add: “Ewing sarcoma… a SRBCT characterized by a translocation involving EWSR1 an ETS transcription factor… Ewing sarcoma often elicits an onion skin periosteal reaction, as seen on imaging studies.”

Do you want the next batch of questions to focus even more on molecular details (translocations, pathways) versus clinical epidemiology and presentations?

Tempting but wrong: The EWSR1–ETS fusion is right, but Ewing's classic finding is "onion-skin" periosteal reaction; sunburst suggests osteosarcoma.

A.passage: Radiology: “onion skin” periosteal reaction on X-ray Periosteal/subperiosteal reaction: “onion skinning,” “sunburst pattern,” Reactive bone in “Codman's triangle” periosteum (periosteal reaction) Common boards question cortex

C.passage: 2. alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS): ~ 20% of childhood RMS age: 6-10 y/o (children + young adults) genetics: PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 (translocation) microscopic: SRBCs

D.passage: Ewing sarcoma: • a SRBCT characterized by a translocation involving EWSR1 + an ETS transcription factor

E.passage: The most common translocation to occur (90% of cases) is t(11;22) which fuses the EWSR1 and Fli1 genes; this is commonly tested, including on boards exams. The second most common translocation is t(21;22) resulting in an EWSR1- ERG fusion.

questions.stem: How does epithelium receive oxygen and nutrients?

choices.A: By diffusion from vessels in the supporting adjacent connective tissue
choices.B: From lymphatic vessels that penetrate the basal lamina between basal cells
choices.C: Directly from the apical (luminal) surface, with no contribution from deeper tissue
choices.D: From a capillary plexus within the basal lamina itself
choices.E: From capillaries that run between the epithelial cells

questions.explanation:
The study guide: “Epithelium itself does not contain vessels (is avascular) and relies on diffusion of nutrients from vessels located in the supporting adjacent connective tissue.”

Tempting but wrong: The basal lamina is acellular and avascular; vessels stay in the connective tissue below it (epithelium is avascular).

why.A: Correct — diffusion from vessels in the adjacent connective tissue.
why.B: Lymphatics, like blood vessels, stay in the connective tissue; nothing penetrates the basal lamina into the epithelium.
why.C: Some apical uptake happens in particular sites, but epithelium is fed by diffusion from the underlying connective tissue.
why.D: The basal lamina is acellular and avascular; vessels stay in the connective tissue below it (epithelium is avascular).
why.E: Epithelium is avascular — no vessels between its cells.

questions.exam_trap: “Avascular” does not mean poorly nourished — the supply comes from the underlying connective tissue.

questions.stem: Why are carcinomas the most common type of cancer, according to the epithelium study guide?

choices.A: Epithelium is avascular, so its cells divide in hypoxia, which directly mutates their DNA
choices.B: Epithelial cells lack a basal lamina, so they invade the stroma easily
choices.C: Epithelial cells renew frequently, and frequent replication means more chances for genetic errors
choices.D: Epithelium arises only from ectoderm, which has the least stable genome

questions.stem: How do the histological features at different levels of the nephron correlate the major cellular activities or functions at these regions?
questions.model_answer: The longest portion of the nephron, the PCT, consists of simple cuboidal epithelium, the cells of which have great basolateral surface areas due to prominent folding and large apical surfaces due to extensive microvilli. The cells actively remove most material, including water, protein, and small compounds, from the glomerular filtrate and release it from their basolateral surfaces for uptake by peritubular capillaries. Cells of the simple squamous epithelium of the loop of Henle’s thin limb passively reabsorb Na+ and Cl–, while the cuboidal cells of this loop’s thick limb actively reabsorb various other electrolytes. Simple cuboidal cells of the DCT are also engaged largely in electrolyte reabsorption.

questions.stem: What does the juxtaglomerular apparatus do, and how does it do it?
questions.model_answer: Specialized, columnar macula densa cells of the DCT and unique juxtaglomerular smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole make up the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which regulates glomerular blood flow and keeps glomerular filtration rather constant using feedback mechanisms. Briefly, macula densa cells monitor Na+ and Cl– levels within the DCT. When these are elevated, the macula densa releases vasoactive compounds that act on the JG muscle, triggering contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing glomerular pressure and filtration rate until levels of the these ions are again lowered.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has experienced dull pelvic pain for the past 2 months. Physical examination shows a right adnexal mass. An abdominal ultrasound scan shows a 7.5-cm cystic ovarian mass. The mass is surgically excised. The surface of the mass is smooth, and it is not adherent to surrounding pelvic structures. On gross examination, the cystic mass is filled with hair. choices.B: Fibroadenoma

questions.explanation: A teratoma is a neoplasm derived from totipotential germ cells that differentiate into tissues that represent all three germ layers: ectoderm, endoderm, and mesoderm. When the elements all are well differentiated, the neoplasm is “mature” (benign). Adenocarcinomas have malignant-appearing glandular elements. Fibroadenomas have a benign glandular and stromal component; they are common in the breast. Gliomas are found in the central nervous system. Hamartomas contain a mixture of cell types common to a tissue site; the lung is one site for this uncommon lesion. A mesothelioma arises from the lining of thoracic and abdominal body cavities. A rhabdomyosarcoma comprises cells that poorly resemble striated muscle; most arise in soft tissues. PBD10 269–270 BP00 191–192

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has had three episodes of hematuria in the past week. He has a 48 pack- year history of smoking cigarettes. On physical examination, there are no abnormal findings. A urinalysis shows 4+ hematuria, and cytologic examination of the urine shows that atypical cells are present. A cystoscopy is performed and a 4-cm sessile mass with a nodular, ulcerated surface is seen in the dome of the bladder. Which of the following terms best describes this lesion?

choices.A: Carcinoma
choices.B: Papilloma
choices.C: Sarcoma
choices.D: Fibroma
choices.E: Adenoma

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman has noted a nodule on the skin of her upper chest. She reports that the nodule has been present for many years and has not changed in size. It is excised, and the microscopic appearance is shown in the figure. Which of the following neoplasms is this lesion most likely to be?

choices.B: Melanoma
choices.C: Hemangioma
choices.D: Leiomyoma
choices.E: Nevus

questions.explanation: The small, discrete nature of this mass and its slow growth with nearly unchanged size suggest a benign neoplasm. The red color is consistent with vascularity. The figure shows many small, capillary-sized vascular channels in this neoplasm. A hemangioma is a common benign lesion of the skin. Fibroadenomas arise in the breast. Leiomyomas, which are white, arise from smooth muscle and are most common in the uterus. Lipomas are yellow fatty tumors that can occur beneath the epidermis. Melanomas are malignant and tend to increase in size quickly; many are darkly pigmented. The benign counterpart to the melanoma is the nevus, which is quite common, but nevi are usually light to dark brown. PBD10 268–270 BP00 190–192

questions.explanation: The cells shown in the figure show marked pleomorphism and hyperchromatism (anaplasia), and it is difficult to discern the cell of origin because no differentiation is noted. A bizarre tripolar mitotic figure is present. This degree of anaplasia is consistent with an aggressive, high-grade malignancy called anaplastic carcinoma. Apoptosis is single cell necrosis, but the cells shown appear viable and not fragmented. Dysplasia refers to changes within an epithelium that presage a neoplasm. Metaplasia with one epithelial cell type substituted for another may presage dysplasia and malignancy. Well-differentiated neoplasms tend to be less aggressive and slower growing and resemble the cell of origin. PBD10 270–273 BP30 192–194
