questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman has a mammogram showing an irregular spiculated 3 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. A radiotracer is injected near the mass. Surgical excision of the mass is performed along with an axillary lymph node, which, on scanning, contains radiotracer. Microscopic examination of the excised node with immunohistochemical staining reveals subcapsular cells positive for cytokeratin. Which of the following is the most likely interpretation of these cytokeratin positive cells?

choices.A: Metaplasia
choices.B: Invasion
choices.C: Dysplasia
choices.D: Metastasis
choices.E: Atypia

questions.explanation: Lymphatic spread, especially to regional lymph nodes draining from the primary site, is typical of a carcinoma. Cytokeratin is an epithelial cell marker, and there are no epithelial cells in lymph nodes, but carcinomas are epithelial in origin, and the most common form of malignancy in the breast. Thus, metastases were identified in a sentinel lymph node. Atypia is descriptive of abnormal cells but is not by itself indicative of either dysplasia or malignancy. Atypia could occur with inflammation. Dysplasia is a premalignant change identified within an epithelium. Inflammation may result from nodal responses to tumor antigens and by-products of malignant cells, but does not indicate that metastases are present. Invasion occurs locally, and lymphatic invasion in the breast can lead to metastases traveling via lymphatics. Metaplasia occurs in epithelia and may presage dysplasia. PBD10 274–276, 332 BP20 195–196

questions.stem: A Pap smear obtained from a 29-year-old woman during a routine health maintenance examination is abnormal. She is currently asymptomatic. She has a history of multiple sexual partners. Cervical biopsy specimens are obtained and the microscopic appearance is shown in the figure. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Squamous cell carcinoma
choices.B: Dysplasia
choices.C: Metaplastic transformation
choices.D: Carcinoma in situ
choices.E: Adenocarcinoma

questions.explanation: In the figure, the disorderly, atypical epithelial cells involve the entire thickness of the epithelium. They extend through the underlying basement membrane and into the underlying stroma as rounded nests at the right, a process known as invasion. The ectocervix and the squamous metaplasia of endocervix give rise to dysplasia from which squamous cell carcinoma can arise. Carcinoma in situ is confined to the epithelium; if the basement membrane is breached, the lesion is no longer in situ, but rather invasive. An adenocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm arising from glandular epithelium, such as the endocervix or endometrium, not the ectocervix. A dysplastic process could precede development of carcinoma in situ and squamous carcinoma; dysplasia involves only part of the thickness of the epithelium. A hamartoma contains a mixture of cell types common to a tissue site. Metaplasia can occur in response to persistent infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) and other inflammatory conditions. Metaplasia can be the precursor to dysplasia. PBD10 273–274 BP40 194–195

However, hematogenous metastases are possible at sites such as bone marrow, liver, or the opposite lung. About half of all cerebral metastases arise from lung primary carcinomas. questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman has experienced increasing malaise and a 10-kg (22 lb) weight loss over the past year. She dies of massive pulmonary thromboembolism. The gross appearance of the liver at autopsy is shown in the figure. Which of the following best describes the lesions seen in her liver?

choices.A: Invasive angiosarcoma
choices.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma
choices.C: Multifocal hepatic adenomas
choices.D: Leukemic infiltration
choices.E: Metastatic adenocarcinoma

questions.explanation: The figure shows the appearance of multiple variably sized tan metastatic lesions in the liver from hematogenous spread of carcinoma. Adenocarcinomas from abdominal primary sites such as colon, pancreas, and stomach are most likely. Thromboembolism suggests a hypercoagulable state such as a paraneoplastic syndrome. Angiosarcomas of the liver are uncommon. A primary malignancy typically appears as a dominant mass, not multiple masses. Although some benign tumors, such as leiomyomas of the uterus, can be multiple, this is not the rule in the liver, and hepatic adenomas are rare. Although hepatocellular carcinomas can have “satellite” nodules, widespread nodules such as those seen in the figure are more characteristic of metastases. Leukemic infiltrates typically do not produce large mass lesions, though some lymphomas may do so. Resection of multiple metastases is usually futile. PBD10 274–276 BP60 195–196

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a screening mammogram and a 4-cm right breast mass is detected. The mass is excised and on microscopic examination is a poorly differentiated carcinoma. Following genomic analysis of the tumor cells, she is treated with a chemotherapy protocol. The carcinoma initially diminishes in size, but then enlarges and metastases occur. Which of the following molecular events in the carcinoma cells led to more advanced stage of disease despite chemotherapy?

choices.A: Reactivation of telomerase lost during transformation
choices.B: Loss of a tumor suppressor gene
choices.C: Inhibition of apoptosis
choices.D: Accumulation of passenger mutations
choices.E: Activation of a proto-oncogene

questions.explanation:
Passenger mutations may be silent until selective pressure on cancer cells unmasks their potential, such as drug resistance. Neoplasms must initially have driver mutations such as activation of proto-oncogenes to oncogenes or loss of a tumor suppressor gene that enable uncontrolled cell growth. Enhanced cancer cell survival through inhibition of apoptosis or continued division through activation of telomerase further enhance tumor size and growth. A 4-cm cancer has billions of cells, and even if chemotherapy kills 99% of them, there is still a pool of remaining cells selected out with passenger mutations providing selective advantage. PBD10 282–283 BP30 200–201

Tempting but wrong: Telomerase is reactivated during transformation, not lost then regained; resistance and metastasis after an initial response come from selected subclones (passenger mutations, heterogeneity).

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has had easy fatigability and noted a dragging sensation in her abdomen for the past 5 months. Physical examination reveals that she is afebrile. She has marked splenomegaly, but no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show her total WBC count is 250,000/mm 3 with WBC differential count showing 64% segmented neutrophils, 11% band neutrophils, 7% metamyelocytes, 5% myelocytes, 4% myeloblasts, 3% lymphocytes, 2% basophils, 2% eosinophils, and 2% monocytes. A bone marrow biopsy is performed, and karyotypic analysis of the cells reveals a t(9;22) translocation. Medical treatment with a drug having which of the following modes of action is most likely to produce a complete remission in this patient?

choices.A: Delivering normal TP53 into cells with viral vectors
choices.B: Inhibiting nonreceptor tyrosine kinase activity
choices.C: Antibody binding to epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptors
choices.D: Activating cellular caspases
choices.E: Preventing translocation of β-catenin to the nucleus

questions.explanation: This patient has a classic history and t(9;22) translocation with chronic myelogenous leukemia. The translocation causes uncontrolled nonreceptor tyrosine kinase activity of the BCR-ABL fusion gene. These patients undergo remission with drugs such as imatinib that inhibit tyrosine kinases. Agents that activate caspases theoretically may help in many cases, especially when apoptosis is blocked as in tumors with BCL2 overexpression. Antibodies to epithelial growth factor receptors, such as ERBB2 (HER2) receptors, are beneficial in certain breast tumors with amplification of this gene. Delivery of TP53 into cells by viral vectors has not yet been proven to be valuable in cancer treatment, and it is not used in chronic myelogenous leukemia. Translocation of β-catenin to the nucleus occurs in colon cancers when there is mutational loss of APC genes. PBD10 288–289 BP90 202

Physical examination shows a 2-cm mass fixed to the underlying tissues beneath the areola and three firm, nontender, lymph nodes palpable in the right axilla. There is no family history of cancer. An excisional breast biopsy is performed, and microscopic examination shows the findings in the figure. Over the next 6 months, additional lymph nodes become enlarged, and CT scans show nodules appearing in the lung, liver, and brain. choices.A: Fusion of BCR and C-ABL genes
choices.B: Amplification of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene
choices.C: Mutation of one TP53 gene copy
choices.D: Deletion of one RB gene copy

Increased expression of ERBB2 (HER2) can be detected immunohistochemically and by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) in the biopsy specimen. One third of breast cancers may show this change. Such amplification is associated with a poorer prognosis. Detection of a specific gene product in the tissue has value for determination of treatment and prognosis. BRCA1 and TP53 mutations, if inherited in the germ line, can predispose the patient to loss of the second allele, leading to breast cancer and other tumors. With BRCA1, there is family history of breast cancer, often at a young age. The tumor suppressor gene TP53 mutations predispose to many types of cancers. An inherited deletion of RB gene predisposes to retinoblastoma. The BCR-ABL fusion product, seen in chronic myeloid leukemia, often results from t(9;22). PBD10 287, 332 BP20 203, 206

Such mutations can lead to more aggressive behavior, including metastasis. EGFR -TK-inactivators include erlotinib and gefitinib. The CDK gene product involves cell cycle control. An abdominal CT scan shows a 5-cm mass in the head of the pancreas. Fine-needle aspiration of the mass is performed. On biochemical analysis, the neoplastic cells show marked reduction of GTPase activity. Which of the following genes is most likely to be affected in this process?

choices.A: RAS
choices.B: RET
choices.C: MYC
choices.D: TP53
choices.E: APC

questions.explanation: The RAS oncogene is the most common oncogene involved in the development of human cancers. Mutations of the RAS oncogene reduce GTPase activity, and RAS is trapped in an activated GTP-bound state. RAS then signals the nucleus through cytoplasmic kinases. However, RAS is downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases. A mutated APC gene can cause activation of the WNT signaling pathway. The MYC oncogene is a transcriptional activator that is overexpressed in many tumors. The TP53 tumor suppressor gene encodes a protein involved in cell cycle control. The RET proto-oncogene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in neuroendocrine cells of the thyroid, adrenal medulla, and parathyroids. The sis oncogene encodes platelet-derived growth factor receptor-β, which is overexpressed in certain astrocytomas. PBD10 286–288 BP80 206–207

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child has exhibited difficulty with vision in her right eye. On physical examination, there is leukocoria of the right eye, consistent with a mass in the posterior chamber. MR imaging shows a mass that nearly fills the globe. The child undergoes enucleation of the right eye. Molecular analysis of the neoplastic cells indicates absence of both copies of a gene that contributes to control of the cell cycle. Which of the following genes has most likely undergone mutation in this neoplasm?

choices.A: TP53
choices.B: BCL2
choices.C: NF1
choices.D: RB
choices.E: KRAS

questions.explanation: The RB gene is a classic example of the two-hit mechanism for loss of tumor suppression. About 60% of these tumors are sporadic, whereas the rest are familial from inheritance of a mutated copy of the RB gene. Loss of the second copy in retinoblasts leads to the occurrence of retinoblastoma in childhood. The RB gene controls the G 1 to S transition of the cell cycle; with loss of both copies, this important checkpoint in the cell cycle is lost. The BCR-ABL fusion gene in chronic myelogenous leukemia is an example of overexpression of a gene product producing neoplasia. The BCL2 gene is an inhibitor of apoptosis. The hMSH2 gene is present in most cases of hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer and functions in DNA repair. Many cancers have the KRAS gene, which acts as an oncogene. The NF1 gene product acts as a tumor suppressor; this is a component of neurofibromatosis (which usually does not involve the eye), and the neoplasms typically appear at a later age. Many cancers have the TP53 tumor suppressor gene mutation, but this is not typical of childhood ocular neoplasms. PBD10 291–294 BP40 208–209

On examination this 1.3 cm lesion is asymmetric with irregular borders and a rough surface. The lesion is excised and on microscopic examination invades into the dermis. Molecular analysis reveals the malignant cells can pass through the G 1 /S checkpoint due to mutational amplification of a gene. Which of the following genes is most likely to be mutated in this lesion?

choices.B: APC
choices.C: BCL2
choices.D: CDK4

questions.explanation: Cyclin-dependent kinases play a role in cell cycle control. CDK4 mutations involving gain- of-function play a role in carcinomas of breast, esophagus, and liver, among others. CDK4 amplification is characteristic of malignant melanoma, as in this case (A = asymmetry; B = border irregularity; C = color change). The ABL gene when “turned on” by fusion with the BCR gene has increased tyrosine kinase activity, as in chronic myeloid cell proliferations. The APC gene is involved with contact inhibition pathways. BCL2 gene products are involved in apoptotic pathways. RB also controls the G1/S checkpoint, but it is a tumor suppressor and loss of RB function rather than amplification leads to removal of brakes on G1/S checkpoint. PBD10 290, 292, 294 BP40 207–208

Growth factors such as EGF are activators of the cell cycle to promote cell growth. Inability to hydrolyze GTP is a result of RAS oncogene activation. Bronchoscopy is performed, and lung biopsy specimens show small cell anaplastic lung carcinoma. His family history shows three first-degree maternal relatives who developed leukemia, sarcoma, and carcinoma before age 40 years. choices.B: APC (tumor suppressor)

questions.explanation: TP53 is the most common target for genetic alterations in human neoplasms. Most are sporadic mutations, although some are inherited. The inheritance of one faulty TP53 suppressor gene predisposes to a “second hit” that eliminates the remaining TP53 gene. Homozygous loss of the TP53 genes dysregulates the repair of damaged DNA, predisposing individuals to multiple tumors, as in this case. The APC gene is mutated in sporadic colon cancers and in familial polyposis coli. The BCL2 gene is mutated in some non-Hodgkin lymphomas. The HER2 gene is one of the epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptor family members amplified in some breast cancers. The EGF mutation is most often seen in squamous cell carcinomas of the lung. K-RAS mutations are present in many cancers, but not typically in lymphoid malignancies. The NF1 gene mutation is seen in neurofibromatosis type

questions.stem: In an experiment, cells from human malignant neoplasms explanted into tissue culture medium continue to replicate. This allows development of “immortal” tumor cell lines that are extremely useful for the study of tumor biology and responses to therapeutic modalities. choices.B: Telomerase expression
choices.C: Hypoxia-induced factor 1α binding
choices.D: CDK gene methylation

questions.explanation: Chromosomal telomere shortening in normal human cells limits their replicative potential and gives rise to replicative senescence. This occurs because most somatic cells lack the enzyme telomerase. Normal human stem cells do express telomerase. By contrast, 90% or more of human tumor cells show activation of telomerase, explaining continued tumor growth in the body and “immortalized” cell lines in culture. All other pathways listed cannot affect telomerase shortening, which is the rate-limiting step in indefinite replication of cells. PBD10 303–304 BP40 218–219

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has a pheochromocytoma of the left adrenal gland; a sibling had a cerebellar hemangioblastoma. He undergoes adrenalectomy, and on microscopic examination there is extensive vascularity of the neoplasm. Mutational analysis of the neoplastic cells shows that both allelic copies of a gene have been lost, with downstream activation of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) transcription . choices.D: von Hippel–Lindau (VHL)

questions.explanation: Angiogenesis is a key feature of neoplasms because the growing tumor needs a blood supply, and up-regulation of factors such as VEGF and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) help to keep the cancer growing. VEGF may be up-regulated by activation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-α (HIF-1-α). The VHL gene acts as a tumor suppressor, and it normally produces a protein that binds to HIF-1-α so that it is cleared. VHL mutation leads to loss of this binding protein and activation of angiogenesis factors. Individuals with VHL syndrome have various neoplasms, including pheochromocytomas, renal cell carcinomas, and hemangioblastomas. The other listed genes have products that do not directly act on angiogenesis pathways. PBD10 305–306 BP60 219–220

questions.explanation: Several pathologic mechanisms play a role in the development of tumor metastases. The tumor cells first must become discohesive and detach from the primary site, degrade the basement membrane and interstitial connective tissue, and then attach elsewhere to become metastases. Reduced expression of adhesion molecules such as E-cadherins promotes metastases. Tumor cells can elaborate, not reduce, proteases such as metalloproteinases to promote discohesiveness. Expression of estrogen and progesterone receptors predicts breast cancer responsiveness to antihormone therapy, and there is a monoclonal antibody, trastuzumab, that targets HER-2, a form of epidermal growth factor receptor. questions.stem: An epidemiologic study investigates the potential morphologic and molecular alterations that may contribute to the development of cancers in a population. Data analyzed from resected colonic lesions show changes that suggest the evolution of a sporadic colonic adenoma into an invasive carcinoma. Which of the following best describes the mechanism producing these changes leading to colonic malignancies?

choices.A: Overexpression of epithelial cell surface growth factor receptor genes
choices.B: Inheritance of defects in TP53 genes that increase the susceptibility to develop cancer
choices.C: Extensive regeneration of tissues increasing the mutation rate in regenerating cells
choices.D: Stepwise accumulation of multiple proto-oncogene and tumor suppressor gene mutations
choices.E: Activation of proto-oncogenes by chromosomal translocation

questions.explanation: Development of colonic adenocarcinoma typically takes years, during which time multiple mutations occur within the mucosa, including mutations involving such genes as APC (adenomatous polyposis coli), KRAS, and TP53. The accumulation of mutations, rather than their occurrence in a specific order, is most important in the development of a carcinoma. Activation of proto-oncogenes, extensive regeneration, faulty TP53 genes, and amplification of growth factor receptor genes all contribute to the development of malignancies, but they are not sufficient by themselves alone to produce a carcinoma from an adenoma of the colon. Inherited loss of wild-type TP53 contributes to multiple cancers, but not to sporadic adenomas. PBD10 314–315 BP50 204–205

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has noted a feeling of pelvic heaviness for the past 6 months. On physical examination, there is a palpable nontender lower abdominal mass. An abdominal ultrasound scan shows a 12-cm solid mass in the uterine wall. A total abdominal hysterectomy is performed. The mass has the microscopic appearance of a well-differentiated leiomyosarcoma. One year later, a chest radiograph shows a 4-cm nodule in her right lower lung. Cytologic analysis of a fine-needle biopsy specimen of the nodule shows a poorly differentiated sarcoma. The patient’s medical history indicates that she has smoked cigarettes most of her adult life. Which of the following mechanisms best explains these findings?

choices.A: Immunodeficiency with HIV infection
choices.B: Development of a second primary neoplasm
choices.C: Persistent exposure to cigarette smoke
choices.D: Metastasis from an aggressive tumor subclone
choices.E: Inheritance of a defective RB gene

questions.explanation: Although neoplasms begin as monoclonal proliferations, additional mutations occur over time, leading to subclones of neoplastic cells with various aggressive properties. This subcloning may allow metastases, greater invasiveness, resistance to chemotherapy, and morphologic differences to occur. Because sarcomas of the lung are rare, the lung mass is statistically a metastasis. Though second primary malignancies do arise, particularly in persons who have already had a malignancy, the odds favor a metastasis in a person with a prior malignancy. Sarcomas are not related to smoking tobacco. Inheritance of a mutant RB gene is most likely to lead to childhood retinoblastomas and osteosarcomas. Kaposi sarcoma is the sarcoma most often associated with AIDS from HIV infection. PBD10 314–315 BP50 204–205

questions.stem: An investigational study reviews cells harvested from patients 30 to 50 years of age who had right-sided colon cancer with multiple polyps present. These patients typically develop multiple malignant lesions of the colon during middle age. Molecular analysis of the cells from the lesions shows changes in hPMS1, hPMS2, and hMLH1 genes. choices.B: Tumor promoters induce proliferation
choices.C: Many oncogenes are activated by translocations

questions.explanation: Patients with hereditary nonpolyposis colon carcinoma (HNPCC) inherit one defective copy of mismatch repair genes. Several human mismatch repair genes are involved in the development of HNPCC. Mismatch repair defects have microsatellite instability. Microsatellites are tandem repeats found throughout the genome. Normally, the length of these microsatellites remains constant. In HNPCC, these satellites are unstable and increase or decrease in length. Although HNPCC accounts for only 2% to 4% of all colon carcinomas, microsatellite instability can also be detected in about 15% of all sporadic colon carcinomas. Mutations in mismatch repair genes can be detected by the presence of microsatellite instability. The other listed options are not characteristic of HNPCC. PBD10 314–315 BP50 226–227

No axillary adenopathy is noted. A fine-needle aspirate of the mass shows anaplastic ductal cells. The patient’s 30-year- old sister was recently diagnosed with ovarian cancer, and 3 years ago her maternal aunt was diagnosed with ductal carcinoma of the breast and had a mastectomy. questions.explanation: Approximately 5% to 10% of breast cancers are familial, and 80% of these cases result from mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. Onset of these familial cancers occurs earlier in life than the sporadic cancers. The protein products of these genes are involved in DNA repair. BCL2 is overexpressed in some lymphoid neoplasms. The epithelial growth factor receptor ERBB2 (HER2) overexpression is present in some sporadic breast cancers; other epidermal growth factor (EGF) alterations can be seen in lung, bladder, gastrointestinal, ovarian, and brain neoplasms. The HST1 mutation is seen in some gastric cancers. IL2 overexpression is associated with some T cell neoplasms. KRAS overexpression is seen in many cancers, including some breast cancers, but the early age of onset and family history in this case strongly suggest BRCA mutations. Aflatoxins are found in food substances contaminated with Aspergillus. β-naphthylamine is an industrial chemical associated with urinary bladder carcinomas. questions.stem: A study of patients treated with chemotherapy protocols for cancer shows that 10% of them subsequently develop a second cancer, a much higher incidence compared with a control group not receiving chemotherapy. These chemotherapy protocols included the alkylating agent cyclophosphamide. What is the most likely mechanism by which this agent causes carcinogenesis in these treated cancer patients?

choices.A: Direct DNA damage
choices.B: Inhibition of DNA repair
choices.C: Activation of protein kinase C
choices.D: Activation of endogenous viruses
choices.E: Blockage of transforming growth factor (TGF)-β pathways

questions.explanation: Chemical carcinogens can have highly reactive electrophilic groups that can directly damage DNA, leading to mutations. Direct-acting agents, such as alkylating chemotherapy drugs, do not require conversion to a carcinogen. Some environmental toxic agents, such as polycyclic hydrocarbons, require metabolic conversion to a carcinogen and are called indirect-acting agents. Phorbol esters are examples of promoters of chemical carcinogenesis that cause tumor promotion by activating protein kinase C. This enzyme phosphorylates several substrates in signal transduction pathways, including those activated by growth factors, and the cells divide. Forced cell division predisposes the accumulation of mutations in cells previously damaged by exposure to a mutagenic agent (initiator). The TGF-β pathways work via growth inhibition. Proteins such as p53 that function in DNA repair pathways can become nonfunctional through mutation. Viral infections such as hepatitis B and C tend to promote growth by binding to p53 and inactivating its protective function. Telomerase activity is not affected by carcinogens. PBD10 321–322 BP20 229–230

On physical examination, there is a 2-cm, firm, nontender nodule involving the right lobe of the thyroid gland. Sequencing of DNA derived from the nodule shows rearrangement of the RET gene. questions.explanation: Radiation is oncogenic, and the risk increases with higher dosages. Cancers of thyroid and bone as well as leukemias may develop years following environmental radiation exposure. Dosages of therapeutic radiation are carefully controlled, but risk for subsequent malignancy is still increased. The Chernobyl nuclear reactor disaster affecting persons in Belarus and Ukraine is a cautionary tale regarding environmental exposure to radiation. Trauma is not a risk factor for development of cancer, although traumatic episodes often are recalled and irrationally associated with subsequent health problems. Lack of iodine leads to goiter but not to thyroid neoplasia. Hepatocellular carcinomas can arise in cirrhosis caused by chronic alcoholism. Ataxia telangiectasia is an inherited syndrome that carries an increased risk of development of leukemias and lymphomas. Arsenic exposure, which is uncommon, leads to lung and skin cancers. questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with multiple sexual partners has had vaginal bleeding and discharge for the past 5 days. On physical examination, she is afebrile. Pelvic examination shows an ulcerated lesion arising from the squamocolumnar junction of the uterine cervix. A cervical biopsy is performed and microscopic examination reveals an invasive tumor containing areas of squamous epithelium, with pearls of keratin. In situ hybridization shows the presence of human papillomavirus type 16 (HPV-16) DNA within the tumor cells. Which of the following molecular abnormalities in this tumor is most likely related to infection with HPV-16?

choices.A: Increased expression of epidermal growth factor receptor
choices.B: Trapping of the RAS protein in a GTP-bound state
choices.C: Inability to repair DNA damage
choices.D: Epigenetic silencing of the RB gene
choices.E: Functional inactivation of the RB protein

questions.explanation: The oncogenic potential of HPV, a sexually transmissible agent, is related to products of two early viral genes— E6 and E7. E7 protein binds to RB protein to cause displacement of normally sequestered transcription factors, which nullifies tumor suppressor activity of the RB protein. E6 protein binds to and inactivates the TP53 gene product. Increased epidermal growth factor receptor expression is a feature seen in many pulmonary squamous cell carcinomas, and the related ERBB2 (HER2) receptor is seen in some breast carcinomas. Epigenetic modifications include DNA methylation and histone modifications which, depending on their nature, may enhance or inhibit gene expression. Inability to repair DNA damage plays a role in some colon and skin cancers. Trapping of GTP-bound RAS protein can occur in many tumors but is not related to HPV infection. PBD10 324–325 BP50 232–233

Serologic studies for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and anti-hepatitis C virus (HCV) are positive. He develops hepatocellular carcinoma 15 years later. Which of the following viral characteristics best explains why this patient developed hepatocellular carcinoma?

choices.C: Viral inactivation of RB and TP53 gene expression

questions.explanation: Although the hepatitis B virus (HBV) and HCV genomes do not encode for any transforming proteins, the regenerating hepatocytes are more likely to develop mutations, such as inactivation of TP53. HBV does not have a consistent site of integration in the liver cell nuclei, and it does not contain viral oncogenes. Many DNA viruses, such as human papillomavirus (HPV), inactivate tumor suppressor genes, but there is no convincing evidence that HBV or HCV can bind to p53 or RB proteins. Also, the HBV-encoded regulatory element, called HBx, disrupts normal growth of infected hepatocytes. Neither HBV nor HCV infects immune cells. PBD10 326–327 BP70 234–235

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with a history of chronic viral hepatitis has noted a 6-kg weight loss over the past 5 months. Physical examination shows no masses or palpable lymphadenopathy. An abdominal CT scan shows a nodular liver with a 10-cm mass in the right lobe. A stool guaiac test result is negative. An elevation in which of the following laboratory tests is most likely to be present in this man?

choices.A: Carcinoembryonic antigen
choices.B: Immunoglobulin M
choices.D: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
choices.E: Calcitonin

questions.explanation: Some chronic hepatitis B and C viral infections progress to hepatocellular and/or cholangiocarcinoma. AFP is an oncofetal protein that is a tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinomas and some testicular carcinomas. AFP is normally present in fetal life but not in adults. A serum immunoglobulin level with protein electrophoresis aids in the diagnosis of myeloma. Gastrointestinal tract adenocarcinomas, including those arising in the stomach, colon, and pancreas, as well as some lung carcinomas, may be accompanied by elevations in the serum carcinoembryonic antigen level. CA-19-9 is a tumor marker for colonic and pancreatic carcinomas. Some thyroid carcinomas produce calcitonin. Unfortunately, the sensitivity and specificity of tumor marker tests for detection of cancers, when they are small, is not high. PBD10 326–327 BP70 234–235

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has noticed blood in his urine for the past week. Cystoscopy shows a 4-cm exophytic mass involving the bladder mucosa near the trigone. After biopsy specimens are obtained, he undergoes a radical cystectomy. Examination of the excised specimen shows an anaplastic carcinoma that has infiltrated the bladder wall. Which of the following techniques applied to the cells from his neoplasm is most likely to categorize the cell of origin?

choices.A: Immunohistochemistry
choices.B: DNA microarray
choices.C: Chromosomal karyotyping
choices.D: Flow cytometric analysis
choices.E: Cytologic smear

questions.explanation: Histologic sections from malignant neoplasms are frequently assessed with a panel of immunostains to detect antigenic characteristics, such as protein expression, to aid in characterizing the cell of origin, as well as to provide information in selection of treatment protocols. In this case, the immunostains are likely to reveal that this neoplasm is a high- grade urothelial carcinoma. A cytology smear shows light microscopic findings helpful to screen for malignancy, but the findings often fall short of diagnosing a specific cell type. The other listed techniques are best for determination of treatment and prognosis. PBD10 332 BP20 238

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man has noted a chronic cough for the past 3 months. On physical examination, there is mild stridor on inspiration over the right lung. A chest radiograph shows a 5-cm right hilar lung mass, and a fine-needle aspiration biopsy specimen of the mass shows cells consistent with small cell carcinoma. If staging of this neoplasm is denoted as T2N1M1, which of the following findings is most likely in this man?

choices.A: Elevated corticotropin level
choices.B: Poorly differentiated tumor cells
choices.C: Brain metastases
choices.D: Obstruction of a mainstem bronchus
choices.E: Infiltration of the chest wall

questions.explanation: The M1 designation indicates that distant metastases are present. N1 means local lymph nodes are positive for carcinoma. Elevated corticotropin levels indicate secretion of an ectopic hormone that may produce a paraneoplastic syndrome, but this is not part of staging. A T2 designation indicates that the overall size of the tumor is not large; it is still within the lung parenchyma and not impinging upon margins of the lung. The TNM system is used for staging, not microscopic grading of cellular differentiation. PBD10 330 BP00 236–237

questions.stem: A 57-year-old healthy woman has a check of her health status and the only abnormal finding is occult blood in her stool. A colonoscopy is performed at the splenic flexure is a 4-cm mass with rough, eroded, hemorrhagic surface. Biopsies of this mass are obtained and on microscopic examination show crowded columnar cells with hyperchromatic and pleomorphic nuclei and invasion into submucosa. Which of the following terms best describes this woman’s colonic lesion?

choices.A: Adenocarcinoma
choices.B: Leiomyoma
choices.C: Adenoma
choices.D: Leiomyosarcoma
choices.E: Hamartoma

questions.explanation: The large size and microscopic features suggest malignancy, but the invasion is diagnostic of malignant behavior. The columnar appearance mimics the colonic epithelial cell of origin (endoderm embryologically), so adenocarcinoma applies. The benign counterpart is adenoma. A hamartoma is a “tumor” producing mass effect but consists of more than one tissue cell type found at the site of origin. Smooth muscle neoplasms can arise in many locations but are not common in bowel; leiomyoma is the benign version and leiomyosarcoma the malignant counterpart. A teratoma exhibits neoplastic cells derived from all three embryologic cell lines formed at gastrulation: ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm. PBD10 268– 270 BP00 190–192

questions.stem: A 32-year-old healthy woman with a history of multiple sexual partners since age 15 has a check of her health status. A cervical sample is obtained and positive for a high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) subtype. She undergoes colposcopy with cervical biopsies and microscopic examination shows loss of uniformity and architectural orientation of individual squamous epithelial cells involving the lower third of the epithelium. The basement membrane is intact. Which of the following terms best describes her cervical lesion?

choices.A: HPV cytopathic change
choices.B: Dysplasia
choices.C: Well-differentiated carcinoma
choices.D: Poorly differentiated carcinoma
choices.E: Carcinoma in situ

questions.explanation: Partial thickness atypical changes represent dysplasia that could progress to full thickness (carcinoma in situ) and to invasion through the basement membrane (invasive carcinoma). HPV is a driving force, but the cytopathic effect, such as koilocytosis, is only a marker and more likely to be found with HPV subtypes that are low-risk for cancer. Dysplasias are potentially reversible, and most women clear the virus. PBD10 272–273 BP30 194

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman notes abdominal enlargement for the past 5 months despite a diet and exercise program. On physical examination there is a left adnexal mass. Abdominal ultrasound scan shows a 9-cm mass in the region of the left ovary. Paracentesis is performed and 600 mL of cloudy fluid is obtained that on microscopic examination shows malignant cells present. Through which of the following mechanisms have the malignant cells appeared in the fluid obtained?

choices.A: Seeding
choices.B: Multiple primary neoplasms
choices.C: Lymphatic spread
choices.D: Hematogenous spread
choices.E: Vein invasion

questions.explanation: Ovarian cancers often spread by seeding through the peritoneal cavity, and enlargement from ascites may be, unfortunately, the initial sign. Hematogenous metastases appear in distant organs such as liver and lung. Lymphatic spread involves lymph nodes with lymphadenopathy detected on physical exam or radiologic imaging. Malignancies can undergo necrosis, but necrotic cells are difficult to analyze cytologically and are nonviable for the establishment of metastases. Renal cell carcinoma has a propensity for invasion of the renal vein, but this is essentially a localized form of hematogenous spread. PBD10 274–275 BP50 195–196

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man has become increasingly fatigued and has had multiple infections over the past 7 months. Laboratory studies show anemia along with large numbers of abnormal neoplastic white blood cells. The tumor cells have hyperactive tyrosine kinase activity. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) shows a fusion gene. Which of the following is the most likely karyotypic abnormalities in his tumor cells?

choices.A: Deletion
choices.B: Amplification
choices.C: Translocation
choices.D: Duplication of Y
choices.E: Autosomal aneuploidy

questions.explanation: The mechanism of oncogenic gene rearrangement in chronic myeloid leukemia is described, wherein the BCR locus on chromosome 22 is translocated next to the ABL locus on chromosome 9 with formation of BCR-ABL fusion gene with potent tyrosine kinase activity. As your parents warned when you were young, don’t go over to the house of a certain child, or “the two of you together will just cause trouble.” With amplification, there are multiple copies of an oncogene producing too much of a product to drive cell proliferation. Aneuploidies are often seen in cancers, but are likely the consequence of an unstable genome, not the cause, and impart additional malignant characteristics. Deletions could take out a tumor suppressor gene, but the allelic number would be abnormal. The Y chromosome has few genes that do not play a role in neoplasia. PBD10 288 BP80 201–203

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man enjoys grilling meats over an open flame. He follows screening recommendations and undergoes colonoscopy. A 2-cm polyp is found in the sigmoid region. The excised polyp is examined microscopically and has adenocarcinoma confined to the polyp. Molecular analysis reveals lack of GTP breakdown by hydrolysis at the cell membrane. Which of the following genes most likely underwent point mutation to drive these events?

choices.A: MYC
choices.B: TP53
choices.C: BCL2
choices.D: RAS
choices.E: Transforming growth factor (TGF)-β

questions.explanation: RAS mutations greatly reduce the GTPase its activity, thereby trapping RAS in the GTP bound active state with consequent activation of downstream growth promoting pathways. Such oncogenic activity of RAS underlies transformational events in many cancers, particularly adenocarcinomas. The BCL2 family of genes plays a role in apoptosis. MYC may be affected downstream of RAS. TGF-β is growth inhibiting. TP53 is a tumor suppressor gene. Though the char on grilled meats imparts interesting flavors, high-temperature cooking of meats from animals, such as over an open flame, generates heterocyclic amines and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons that are mutagenic. One could counter this via consumption of high fiber foods reducing colonic transit time. PBD10 286–288 BP80 206– 207

questions.stem: A family has a history of cancer involving multiple persons at multiple organ sites, including lung, breast, colon, ovary, and brain. Cell cycle arrest in response to DNA damage is impaired. Men and women are equally involved. The cancers have been diagnosed from childhood to young adulthood. In this patient an inherited mutation most likely leads to tumorigenesis through which of the following mechanisms?

choices.A: Loss of tumor suppression
choices.B: Amplification of growth factor receptor
choices.C: Point mutation in a proto-oncogene
choices.D: Chromosomal translocation
choices.E: Epigenetic modification of histones

questions.explanation: The Li Fraumeni syndrome is described. TP53 mutations underlie many sporadic cancers, which typically have onset in adulthood. However, an inherited mutation is the first “hit” and the second “hit” can occur early in life. The inheritance pattern appears autosomal dominant. HER2 mutation in breast cancers is an example of growth factor receptor amplification. Chronic myelogenous leukemia is an example of translocation with BCR-ABL fusion gene. Epigenetic modifications can occur but are unlikely to be in definable patterns. RAS point mutations can lead to oncogenic growth promotion. PBD10 294–297 BP70 211– 212

Colonoscopy is performed and the mucosal surface is covered by hundreds of 0.3- to 1-cm polyps. A larger 4-cm mass is present in transverse colon. Two of four teenage siblings are found to have colonic polyps. Molecular analysis of neoplastic cells obtained by biopsy shows loss of E-cadherin expression with reduced contact inhibition. choices.B: Cyclin

questions.explanation: This family has an APC gene mutation driving adenomatous polyposis coli, and adenocarcinoma arises within the first two decades in nearly all involved persons, so screening is performed and total colectomy can be curative. Loss of APC gene reduces degradation of β–catenin which translocates to the nucleus and triggers transcription of growth-related genes. The autosomal dominant inheritance pattern is in keeping with a tumor suppressor gene. Caspases are involved with apoptosis. Cyclins are involved in cell cycle control. GTP is involved in RAS signaling. Tyrosine kinases can be growth promoting. PBD10 297–299 BP90 213–215

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has felt an enlarging lump in his left armpit for 6 months. On examination there is a 3-cm movable painless mass in his right axillary region. The mass is excised and on microscopic examination consists of well-differentiated lymphocytic cells forming irregular follicles. Immunohistochemical staining shows intense BCL2 protein positivity. Through which of the following mechanisms has this mass most likely enlarged slowly in this man?

choices.A: Defective DNA repair
choices.B: Increased telomerase
choices.C: Sustained angiogenesis
choices.D: Upregulated aerobic glycolysis
choices.E: Diminished apoptosis

questions.explanation: The BCL2 family of genes is involved with apoptosis, and overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL2 protein favors cell survival with accumulation of more cells, and this mechanism is common in follicular lymphomas, which tend to be slow-growing and indolent, but difficult to eradicate. The other foils involve mechanisms other than BCL2. DNA repair involves TP53 , and a variety of other mechanisms. Telomerase activity is normally present in human stem cells, but when cancer cells have this activity, they have almost unlimited replicative potential. Angiogenesis provides a supporting framework for continued malignant cell growth. The Warburg effect provides cancer cells with a biochemical advantage via aerobic glycolysis. PBD10 302–303 BP30 217–218

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast carcinoma and receives a course of chemotherapy with a protocol including doxorubicin and tamoxifen. Her malignancy shrinks in size over the next 6 months. However, a year later the mass is still present and larger in size. The chemotherapy led to selection of malignant cells resistant to apoptosis. This resistance to chemotherapy is most likely mediated via mutation with loss of function involving which of the following genes?

choices.A: RAS
choices.B: BCL2
choices.C: MYC
choices.D: TP53
choices.E: IDH

questions.explanation: Wild-type TP53 encodes p53 protein that provides protection against cellular proliferation following DNA damage by initiating the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis. Overexpression of mutated TP53 with reduced or abolished p53 function can explain resistance to chemotherapy agents such as cisplatin, doxorubicin, gemcitabine, and tamoxifen. BCL2 protein is anti-apoptotic and overexpression reduces apoptosis. IDH mutations lead to epigenetic changes in oncometabolism. Amplification of MYC results in oncogenic activity by transcription of genes, such as CDK genes that promote cell proliferation. MYC also promotes cell growth by switching the cell towards aerobic glycolysis. RAS point mutations interfere with breakdown of GTP, driving cell proliferation. PBD10 302– 303 BP30 217

questions.stem: A 61-year-old nulliparous woman with a family history of cancer is found to have a right breast mass on mammographic screening. A biopsy of the mass shows carcinoma. Laboratory studies show Hgb 14.1 g/dL, WBC count 7440/mm 3 , platelet count 223,000/mm 3 , sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, HCO 3 25 mmol/L, glucose 100 mg/dL, calcium 12.1 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.2 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, and total protein 6.2 g/dL. Which of the following is most likely being elaborated by the carcinoma cells in this woman?

choices.A: Parathormone-related peptide
choices.B: Erythropoietin
choices.C: Arginine vasopressin
choices.D: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-like substance
choices.E: Insulin-like substance

questions.explanation: The abnormal laboratory finding is hypercalcemia, which can be part of a paraneoplastic syndrome when malignant cells “turn on” genes that produce a hormone or hormone-like substance. Squamous cell lung carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and breast carcinoma are the most likely to upregulate parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP). ACTH production by a neoplasm leads to Cushing syndrome with hyperglycemia and hypokalemia. Increased arginine vasopressin (anti-diuretic hormone) will reduce free water excretion and lead to hyponatremia. Erythropoietin production leads to increased red blood cell mass and high Hgb. Elaboration of an insulin-like substance leads to hypoglycemia. PBD10 328–330 BP00 236–237

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has passed darker urine over the past 2 months. On physical examination he has no abnormal findings. Urine microscopic examination reveals numerous red blood cells (RBCs). Cystoscopy is performed, and a 2 × 3 cm raised, rough-surfaced red lesion is noted just above the trigone. Biopsies are taken and, on microscopic examination, show urothelial carcinoma extending into the smooth muscle. Which of the following is the most important indicator of his overall prognosis?

choices.A: Grade
choices.B: Risk factor
choices.C: Age
choices.D: Genetic profile
choices.E: Stage

questions.explanation: Local resection may suffice for lower-grade urothelial carcinomas that are minimally invasive and localized. The risk for recurrence may be reduced with bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) installation into the bladder. Just being human, becoming old, and having encountered multiple external factors in life have more to do with cancer risk than minor genetic variations among groups of humans. The risk for cancer increases with age and exposure to risk factors such as carcinogenic agents (cigarette smoke, aniline dyes, cyclophosphamide) but does not determine prognosis because the most important factor is the extent of the neoplasm at the time of diagnosis. Urothelial carcinomas are virtually all high grade when invasive. Genetic variations in the cancer such as TP53 mutations might inform therapeutic options. The larger and more invasive the cancer, the more likely it has acquired more aggressive characteristics. Moreover, the risk for additional urothelial cancer anywhere in the urinary tract informs follow-up. PBD10 957–962 BP20 702–704

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has noted passing darker urine within the past 3 weeks. On physical examination, there are no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows blood is present. Cystoscopy is performed, and there is a 0.5 × 1.7 cm reddish area on the dome of the bladder. Biopsies are obtained and have the microscopic appearance shown in the figure. What is the most likely risk factor for his disease?

choices.A: Inherited gene mutation
choices.B: Congenital urachal remnant
choices.C: Smoking
choices.D: Schistosomiasis
choices.E: Obesity

questions.explanation: Urothelial carcinoma in situ is shown in the figure. Smokers are at increased risk. Urothelial malignancies can be recurrent and multifocal; they are far more likely to be sporadic than familial, although gene mutations such those in TP53 may be the same. Familial malignancies often present much earlier in life. The embryologic allantois extends from the developing bladder and may persist as a urachal remnant forming a diverticulum, cyst, or fistula to the umbilicus, and there is a low risk for adenocarcinoma. Obesity increases the risk for malignancy, but correlation with a specific malignancy is difficult to draw. Schistosomiasis can lead to squamous metaplasia and increased risk for squamous carcinoma of the bladder. PBD10 957–962 BP20 702–704

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man recently retired after many years in a job that involved exposure to aniline dyes, including β-naphthylamine. One month ago, he had an episode of hematuria that was not accompanied by abdominal pain. On physical examination, there are no abnormal findings. Urinalysis shows 4+ hematuria and no ketones, glucose, or protein. Microscopic examination of the urine shows red blood cells (RBCs) that are too numerous to count, 5 to 10 white blood cells (WBCs) per high- power field, and no crystals or casts. The result of a urine culture is negative. Cystoscopy is performed, and biopsy of a lesion reveals the microscopic appearance in the figure. Which of the following neoplasms is he most likely to have?

choices.A: Urothelial carcinoma
choices.B: Renal cell carcinoma
choices.C: Rhabdomyosarcoma
choices.D: Adenocarcinoma
choices.E: Squamous cell carcinoma

questions.explanation: Exposure to arylamines markedly increases the risk of urothelial carcinoma with papillary appearance shown in the figure, which can occur decades after the initial exposure. After absorption, aromatic amines are hydroxylated into an active form, which is detoxified by conjugation with glucuronic acid and then excreted. Urinary glucuronidase splits the nontoxic conjugated form into the active carcinogenic form. Adenocarcinoma is a complication of the congenital condition known as exstrophy of the bladder. Rhabdomyosarcoma of the pelvis is typically a pediatric neoplasm and not associated with chemical exposures. Renal cell carcinomas also may manifest as painless hematuria, but exposure to aniline dyes is not a risk factor. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy of the urethra, but it is rare and has no relation to carcinogens. PBD10 957–962 BP20 702–704

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has noted over the past month a change in the way his scrotum feels as he showers. On examination, only a left testis is palpable, and it is larger than average for his age. An ultrasound examination reveals a solid 4-cm mass with a rim of normal echogenicity in the testis. Laboratory studies show no elevation of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), or human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). Orchiectomy is performed, and microscopic examination of the mass shows a uniform population of large cells that form sheets and nests separated by thin bands of connective tissue, along with lymphocytic infiltrates, multinucleated cells, and syncytiotrophoblasts. Which of the following additional findings is the most likely risk factor for his testicular mass?

choices.A: Mumps viral infection
choices.B: Cryptorchidism
choices.C: Varicocele
choices.D: Cirrhosis of the liver
choices.E: Karyotype with 47, XXY

questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism results from failure of the testis to descend from the abdominal cavity into the scrotum during fetal development. One or both testes may be involved, with risk for neoplasia, especially germ cell tumors, and most often seminoma as in this case, even in the descended testis. An undescended testis eventually atrophies during childhood. Unilateral cryptorchidism may lead to infertility because it may be associated with atrophy of the contralateral descended testis. Isolated cryptorchidism is a developmental defect that is usually sporadic and is not inherited in the germline. After 34 years as in this case, the cryptorchid testis is atrophic and nonfunctional for spermatogenesis, but likely visible with computed tomography (CT) imaging as part of his work-up, looking for possible metastases. However, testicular cancer, cirrhosis, and mumps are risks for testicular atrophy. Klinefelter syndrome carries an increased risk for germ cell tumors but not to the degree of cryptorchidism. A varicocele increases the likelihood for infertility but not cancer. PBD10 966–967, 970–971 BP10 692–693, 694

questions.stem: A 23-year-old, previously healthy man suddenly develops severe pain in the scrotum. The pain continues unabated for 6 hours, and he goes to the emergency department. On physical examination, he is afebrile. There is exquisite tenderness of a slightly enlarged right testis, but there are no other remarkable findings. The representative gross appearance of the right testis is shown in the figure. Which of the following conditions is most likely to cause these findings?

choices.A: Obstruction of blood flow
choices.B: Previous vasectomy
choices.C: Mycobacterial infection
choices.D: Hemorrhagic choriocarcinoma
choices.E: Lymphatic obstruction

questions.explanation: The markedly hemorrhagic appearance in the figure results from testicular torsion that obstructs venous outflow to a greater extent than the arterial supply. Doppler ultrasound shows reduced or no vascular flow in the affected testis. An abnormally positioned or anchored testis in the scrotum is a risk factor for this condition. Testicular carcinomas do not obstruct the blood flow and are not likely to produce an acute event. Parasitic infestation, typically filariasis, obstructs the flow of lymph, leading to gradual enlargement of the scrotum with thickening of the overlying skin. Tuberculosis can spread from the lung through the bloodstream, producing miliary tuberculosis, seen as multiple pale, millet-sized lesions, most often involving the epididymis with chronic granulomatous inflammation. A previous vasectomy may lead to a small leakage of fluid and sperm, producing a localized sperm granuloma. PBD10 968 BP80 693

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man has noted asymmetric enlargement of the scrotum over the past 4 months. On physical examination, the right testis is twice its normal size and has increased tenderness to palpation. The right testis is biopsied. The epididymis and the upper aspect of the right testis have extensive granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and caseous necrosis. Which of the following infections is the most likely cause of these findings?

choices.A: Mumps
choices.B: Gonorrhea
choices.C: Chancroid
choices.D: Syphilis
choices.E: Tuberculosis

questions.explanation: Tuberculosis with mycobacterial infection is uncommon in the testes, but it can occur with disseminated disease. The infection typically starts in the epididymis and spreads to the body of the testis. Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi leads to ulcerated nodules of the external genitalia. Mumps produces patchy orchitis with minimal inflammation, which heals with patchy fibrosis. Syphilis involves the body of the testis, and there can be gummatous inflammation with neutrophils, necrosis, and some mononuclear cells. Gonococcal infections produce acute inflammation. PBD10 373, 968 BP80 693

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man has had increasing difficulty with urination for the past 10 years. He now has to get up several times each night because of a feeling of urgency, but each time the urine volume is not great. He has difficulty starting and stopping urination. On physical examination, the prostate is enlarged to twice its normal size but is not tender to palpation. One year ago, his serum prostate- specific antigen (PSA) level was 6 ng/mL, and it is still at that level when retested. Which of the following drugs is most likely to be effective in treatment of this man?

choices.A: Prednisone (corticosteroid)
choices.B: Finasteride (5α-reductase inhibitor)
choices.C: Estrogen (hormone)
choices.D: Nitrofurantoin (antibiotic)
choices.E: Mitoxantrone (chemotherapy agent)

questions.explanation: The clinical features are typical of benign prostatic hyperplasia causing a slight elevation of the PSA level. A PSA level that remains unchanged for 1 year, as in this case, is less likely to be found with a prostate cancer. Finasteride is a 5α-reductase inhibitor that decreases formation of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) that binds to androgen receptors in prostatic stromal and epithelial cells, driving proliferation with prostate gland enlargement. However, α 1 -adrenergic blockers that diminish smooth muscle tone are somewhat more effective in treating nodular hyperplasia. Estrogen therapy has been used as antihormonal therapy in prostate cancer. Mitoxantrone is a chemotherapy agent that, when given with prednisone, has been shown to be effective in treating advanced prostate cancers. Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic that is often used in treating urinary tract infections. PBD10 976–977 BP70 698–699

questions.stem: A 71-year-old African American man visits his physician for a checkup because he is worried about his family history of prostate cancer. Physical examination does not indicate any abnormalities. Because of the patient’s age and family history, his prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level is measured and is 8 ng/mL. Six months later, the PSA level is 10 ng/mL. A urologist obtains transrectal biopsy specimens, and microscopic examination shows multifocal areas of glandular hyperplasia and the appearance shown in the figure. Which of the following statements applies best to this clinical and pathologic scenario?

choices.A: Related to an inherited tumor suppressor gene mutation
choices.B: Responsive to 5α-reductase inhibitor therapy
choices.C: Associated with increased risk for invasive cancer
choices.D: Chronic inflammation from urinary tract obstruction
choices.E: Normal microscopic finding of the peripheral zone

questions.explanation: Prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) shown here has dysplastic features including hyperchromatic cells crowded into a pseudo-multilayer appearance, with preservation of gland architecture. PIN is a potential precursor of prostatic adenocarcinoma. By itself, it does not warrant therapy because only approximately one-third of patients diagnosed with PIN develop invasive cancer within 10 years. Conversely, in approximately 80% of cases in which prostate cancer is present, PIN can be found in the surrounding tissue. PIN usually does not increase the PSA levels. In this case, the elevation in PSA levels may have been caused in part by the coexistent hyperplasia. Although prostatitis may increase PSA levels, no inflammation is seen here. Although PIN can be found in the peripheral zone, it is not a normal finding. Although there is a family history, specific risk factors are difficult to identify; BRCA2 mutations account for a small number of prostate cancers. Prostatic hyperplasia may respond to inhibition of diminished dihydrotestosterone (DHT) synthesis, but not PIN or cancer. PBD10 977–982 BP20 699–701

questions.stem: A 57-year-old previously healthy man has observed his urine to become darker over the past month. On physical examination there are no abnormal findings. Urine dipstick analysis shows 1+ blood. Cystoscopy is performed and a 1-cm area of erythema is present in the dome of the bladder. Biopsies are obtained and the microscopic appearance is shown in the figure. Which of the following is his most likely risk factor for this lesion?

choices.A: Chronic alcohol abuse
choices.B: Opioid use
choices.C: Smoking
choices.D: Vitamin A deficiency
choices.E: Urinary tract infections

questions.explanation: The figure shows urothelial carcinoma in situ (CIS), and the arrow points to a mitotic figure. At his age a history of smoking is the likely risk, and there is a field effect upon the entire urothelium, so additional malignancies may occur anywhere in the urinary tract with urothelium, and subsequent follow-up is required. Alcohol abuse mainly affects liver, brain, and heart. Opioids can be blamed for many problems, mainly behavioral, but neoplasia is not one of them. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are very common but are not linked to cancer; schistosomiasis with Schistosoma hematobium carries a risk for bladder cancer for persons residing in endemic regions. PBD10 957–962 BP20 702–704

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has noted increasing frequency of need to urinate over the past 2 years. When he urinates there is difficulty starting the stream, which is weak. On digital rectal examination there is no tenderness, but he has the finding represented by the image. Which of the following pharmacologic therapies is most useful in treating this man?

choices.A: β 1 -Adrenergic agonist
choices.B: Corticosteroid
choices.C: Antibiotic
choices.D: Chemotherapy agent
choices.E: 5α-Reductase inhibitor

questions.explanation: This enlarged prostate is nodular, consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The hyperplasia of glands and stroma begins in the transitional zone but enlargement continues, compressing the prostatic urethra, leading to symptoms of frequency and hesitancy. Increased sensitivity to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) drives the cellular proliferation, so the 5α-reductase inhibitor reduces conversion of testosterone to DHT. β 1 -Adrenergic agonists aid in treating bronchial asthma. α-Adrenergic blockers relax prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle to enhance urination. Docetaxel, a taxane derivative chemotherapy agent, binds to microtubules and prevents androgen receptor nuclear translocation, but he has hyperplasia, not prostate cancer. Corticosteroids reduce inflammation, but BPH is not an inflammatory process. Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic used to treat urinary tract infections secondary to obstruction from BPH. PBD10 976– 977 BP70 698–699

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had fever, pelvic pain, and a feeling of pelvic heaviness for the past week. Pelvic examination shows a palpable painful left adnexal mass. Laparoscopy shows an indistinct left fallopian tube that is part of a 5-cm circumscribed, red-tan mass involving the left adnexal region. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely to produce these findings?

choices.A: Haemophilus ducreyi
choices.B: Herpes simplex virus
choices.C: Treponema pallidum
choices.D: Chlamydia trachomatis
choices.E: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

questions.explanation: Sexually transmitted diseases are the most common cause of inflammation of the fallopian tube. When the incidence of gonorrhea caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae decreases in a population, the proportion of cases of salpingitis caused by Chlamydia and Mycoplasma increases. The fallopian tube can become distended and adherent to the ovary and may form a tubo-ovarian abscess. These are features of pelvic inflammatory disease. Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, which can produce erythematous papules of the external genitalia or vagina, but grossly visible lesions may not be present in women. Herpes simplex virus most often involves the external genitalia, but it may produce vaginal or cervical lesions; it is unlikely to advance farther. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an uncommon cause of salpingitis. Treponema pallidum infection causes syphilis, which does not produce florid inflammation with mass effect, just a chancre. PBD10 988–989, 1015 BP50 726– 727

questions.stem: A 24-year-old transgender man has had multiple sexual partners for the past 5 years with receptive and insertive anal intercourse. On examination acetic acid application to his perianal area identifies a 0.5-cm flat pale area of squamous epithelium. A swab of the lesion is obtained and by molecular analysis is positive for human papillomavirus (HPV) subtype 18. Viral oncoproteins are most likely inactivating which of the following host epithelial cell genes to reduce cellular senescence, contributing to cell genomic instability?

choices.A: EWS
choices.B: RAS
choices.C: APC
choices.D: TP53
choices.E: BCL2

questions.explanation: The HPV oncoproteins E6 and E7 are overexpressed when the virus integrates into host cells, leading to inactivation of products of tumor suppressor genes RB and TP53 , along with inactivating cyclin/CDK complexes. The ongoing effects of HPV infection along with other factors can promote oncogenesis. APC mutations underlie development of colonic adenocarcinomas. The BCL2 gene encodes an anti-apoptotic protein. Chromosomal translocation brings EWS and FLI1 together for a fusion gene encoding a transcription factor driving Ewing sarcoma. RAS mutations contribute to oncogene mediated carcinogenesis in many cancers, particularly adenocarcinomas. PBD10 986, 991, 996 BP60 717–718

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman comes to her nurse practitioner for a routine health maintenance examination. On physical examination, there are no abnormal findings. A Pap smear shows abnormalities; colposcopy and a biopsy are performed. The figure shows the microscopic appearance of the biopsy specimen. Which of the following is the best strategy to prevent the development of this lesion?

choices.A: Avoidance of tobacco products
choices.B: Consumption of a diet rich in vegetables
choices.C: Vaccination for human papillomavirus
choices.D: Use of oral contraceptives
choices.E: Maintenance of an ideal body weight

questions.explanation: The figure shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) termed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) III because the dysplasia involves the full thickness of the cervical epithelium. Such lesions arise more frequently in women who have had first intercourse at an early age, have multiple sexual partners, or have a male partner with multiple sexual partners. These factors are believed to increase the risk of infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 16 and 18, which have high risk for dysplasias and carcinomas of the cervix. Because of the causal relationship with HPV infection, the use of HPV vaccines has been shown to prevent disease progression. Cervical squamous neoplasia has not been shown to be associated with smoking, diet, body weight, or hormonal influences. PBD10 997–999, 1000–1001 BP10 718–720

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. No abnormalities are found on physical examination. A screening Pap smear shows cells consistent with a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL). Subsequent cervical biopsy specimens confirm the presence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) I. Which of the following risk factors is most likely related to her Pap smear findings?

choices.A: Multiple sexual partners
choices.B: Diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure
choices.C: Oral contraceptive use
choices.D: Vitamin B 12 (cobalamin) deficiency
choices.E: Prior treatment for a malignancy

questions.explanation: CIN I represents minimal (mild) dysplasia (LSIL) and is a potentially reversible process. Dysplasias are preneoplastic and may progress to carcinomas if not treated. Risk factors for cervical dysplasias and carcinoma include early age at first intercourse, multiple sexual partners, and a male partner with multiple previous sexual partners. These factors all increase the potential for infection with human papillomavirus. DES exposure is a factor in the development of clear cell carcinomas of the vagina and cervix. Use of oral contraceptives, which contain very low amounts of hormonally active compounds, does not cause cervical dysplasia or carcinoma. Treatment of cancers does not typically result in dysplasias, although the atypical changes in epithelial cells from radiation and/or chemotherapy may be challenging to distinguish from cancer. A vitamin B 12 deficiency may produce some megaloblastic epithelial changes, but not dysplasia. PBD10 997–999, 1000–1001 BP10 718–720

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has a Pap smear as part of a routine health maintenance examination. There are no remarkable findings on physical examination. The Pap smear shows cells consistent with a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) with human papillomavirus type 18. Cervical biopsy specimens are obtained, and microscopic examination confirms the presence of extensive moderate dysplasia (CIN II) along with intense chronic inflammation with squamous metaplasia in the endocervical canal. What is the most likely explanation for proceeding with cervical conization for this patient?

choices.A: Her reproductive years are over
choices.B: HPV infection cannot be treated
choices.C: Perimenopausal state
choices.D: Presence of chronic cervicitis
choices.E: Risk for invasive carcinoma

questions.explanation: This patient’s CIN II is an HSIL that may progress to invasive carcinoma in several years if not treated, particularly because she has a high-risk subtype of HPV. Infection with HPV often drives this process, but the presence of HPV alone does not determine therapy. HPV infection cannot be eradicated with antibiotics, but patients may clear the virus. Chronic cervicitis with squamous metaplasia is not a malignant lesion and does not determine therapy in this case. The conization can preserve fertility in women who are of childbearing age. PBD10 997–999, 1000–1001 BP10 718–720

questions.stem: A 28-year-old sexually active woman comes to her physician’s assistant for a routine health maintenance examination. There are no abnormal findings on physical examination. She has been taking oral contraceptives for the past 10 years. A Pap smear shows a high-grade squamous epithelial lesion (HSIL), also termed moderate dysplasia, or cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) II. What is the most likely molecular pathogenesis for this finding?

choices.A: Recurrent gonococcal cervicitis
choices.B: Inheritance of a tumor suppressor gene mutation
choices.C: Viral inactivation of the RB1 gene product
choices.D: Estrogenic stimulation of cell proliferation
choices.E: Up-regulation of antiapoptosis genes

questions.explanation: Dysplasias of the cervix should not be ignored because they naturally progress to more severe dysplasias and to invasive carcinomas. Although not all cases progress, the physician should not take this chance. Dysplasias are strongly related to human papillomavirus (HPV) infections, and HPV DNA can be found in up to 90% of cases. Viral E6 and E7 proteins bind to Rb to up-regulate cyclin E. In about 10% to 15% of cases, there is no evidence of HPV, and other factors may play a role in the development of the dysplasia. With such HPV infection, the Pap smear may show changes of CIN I (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, or LSIL). Oral contraceptives with low- dose estrogens and progestins do not increase the risk of dysplasia significantly. Though the RB1 gene is involved, this is not an inherited problem, and retinoblastomas are not seen with HPV infection. Cervicitis usually is due to bacterial or fungal organisms and is not a significant risk for dysplasia or carcinoma. Antiapoptosis genes such as BCL2 do not play a role in cervical carcinogenesis. PBD10 997–999, 1000–1001 BP10 718–720

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had a small amount of vaginal bleeding and a brownish, foul-smelling discharge for the past month. On pelvic examination, there is a 3-cm lesion on the ectocervix, shown in the figure. Microscopic examination of the lesion is most likely to show which of the following?

choices.A: Clear cell carcinoma
choices.B: Chronic cervicitis
choices.C: Squamous cell carcinoma
choices.D: Adenocarcinoma
choices.E: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia

questions.explanation: The cervical lesion shown in the figure is large and ulcerative and projects into the vagina. It is most likely an invasive squamous cell carcinoma that has infiltrated the subepithelial region. Dysplastic changes confined to the epithelium represent cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and do not form mass lesions. Glandular invasive lesions indicate an adenocarcinoma, which is much less common than squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. Chronic cervicitis has erythema, but no mass effect. Clear cell carcinomas are uncommon and most likely found arising in the vagina. Extramammary Paget disease usually arises on the vulva, producing an eczematous lesion, not a mass, because the neoplastic cells are confined to the epithelium and to adjacent skin adnexa. PBD10 998–1000 BP00 720

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman has had postcoital bleeding for 6 months. She experienced menarche at age 11 years and has had 12 sexual partners during her life. She continues to have regular menstrual cycles without abnormal intermenstrual bleeding. Pelvic examination shows a focal, slightly raised area of erythema on the cervix at the 5 o’clock position. A Pap smear shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), also termed severe cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN III). Analysis of cells from the cervix shows the presence of human papillomavirus type 16. Which of the following malignancies is she at greatest risk of developing if the lesion is not treated?

choices.A: Leiomyosarcoma
choices.B: Clear cell carcinoma
choices.C: Squamous cell carcinoma
choices.D: Sarcoma botryoides
choices.E: Immature teratoma

questions.explanation: This woman has several risk factors for the development of cervical squamous cell carcinoma, including multiple sexual partners, documented infection of the cervix with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) type 16, and diagnosis of an HSIL. The remaining choices are not related to HPV infection. Clear cell carcinomas of the cervix are uncommon; some are associated with maternal use of diethylstilbestrol (DES) in pregnancy. An immature teratoma arises in the ovary. A Krukenberg tumor is a form of metastasis to the ovary. Leiomyosarcomas are rare and typically arise in the myometrium, although they can occur in the cervix. Sarcoma botryoides is a vaginal lesion that typically occurs in young girls. PBD10 998–1000 BP00 720

questions.stem: A 49-year-old perimenopausal woman has had menometrorrhagia for the past 3 months. On physical examination, there are no remarkable findings. The microscopic appearance of an endometrial biopsy specimen is shown in the figure. The patient undergoes a dilation and curettage, and the bleeding stops, with no further problems. What condition is most likely to produce these findings?

choices.A: Ovarian mature cystic teratoma
choices.B: Pregnancy with missed abortion
choices.C: Use of oral contraceptives
choices.D: Chronic endometritis
choices.E: Repeated failure of ovulation

questions.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia with numerous crowded glands as shown in the figure results from excessive estrogenic stimulation. This lesion often occurs with failure of ovulation about the time of menopause. Hyperplasias do not develop from endometritis. Estrogen-secreting ovarian tumors also may produce endometrial hyperplasia, but teratomas are not known for this phenomenon. A secretory pattern of the endometrium is seen in pregnancy, not the proliferative pattern shown in the figure. Oral contraceptives contain small doses of estrogenic compounds that do not lead to hyperplasia. PBD10 1006–1008 BP80 723

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has had menometrorrhagia for the past 2 months. She has no history of prior irregular menstrual bleeding, and she has not yet reached menopause. On physical examination, there are no vaginal or cervical lesions, and the uterus appears normal in size, but there is a right adnexal mass. An abdominal ultrasound scan shows the presence of a 7-cm solid right adnexal mass. Endometrial biopsy shows hyperplastic endometrium but no cellular atypia. What is the most likely lesion that underlies her menstrual abnormalities?

choices.A: Granulosa-theca cell tumor
choices.B: Mature cystic teratoma
choices.C: Corpus luteum cyst
choices.D: Endometrioma
choices.E: Metastasis

questions.explanation: The mass is probably producing estrogen, which has led to endometrial hyperplasia. Estrogen- producing tumors of the ovary typically have granulosa or theca cells. Teratomas can contain various histologic elements, but not estrogen-producing tissues. Endometriosis can give rise to an adnexal mass called an endometrioma, which enlarges over time. Endometrial glands are hormonally sensitive, but they do not produce hormones. Corpus luteum cysts are common, but they are unlikely to produce estrogens. Metastases to the ovary do not cause increased estrogen production. Polycystic ovarian syndrome would involve both ovaries. PBD10 1006–1008, 1026 BP60 723, 731
