atlas.title: Introduction to tissue types: Epithelium
atlas.body: Objectives: Describe the general characteristics and functions of epithelium. Identify and describe the six common subtypes of epithelium. Describe how the type of epithelial structure relates to function in particular tissues/organs. Describe glands, both exocrine (with ducts) and endocrine (without ducts) Name and describe the three types of exocrine glandular secretion. NOTE: There are four main tissue types: epithelium, connective tissue, muscle, and neural tissue. Over the next few sessions, we’ll introduce all four types.

atlas.title: Forms unicellular and multi-cellular glands (secretion)
atlas.body: Origin: any of the three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) – depends on location Blood supply: Epithelium itself does not contain vessels (is avascular) and relies on diffusion of nutrients from vessels located in the supporting adjacent connective tissue (more on this soon!) Renewal: Epithelial cells tend to renew themselves frequently as compared to other tissue types – they may be exposed to harsh environment (skin vs external environment, stomach lining vs stomach acid) or extremely metabolically active (liver) - and cells routinely die and are replaced. Frequent replication to make new cells means more chances to make genetic errors, which can result in cancer.

atlas.title: Classification – Subtypes of epithelium
atlas.body: Initial subtyping is by the number of cell layers: simple (single layer) or stratified (multiple layers) Simple epithelium is one cell layer thick, and is useful for filtration, diffusion, absorption, and secretion. The subclassifications are simple squamous, simple cuboidal, simple columnar, and pseudostratified. Stratified epithelium is more than one cell layer thick, and is most useful for protection and frequent renewal. The shape of the cells at the apical layer (top) gives the subtype the name. The subclassifications are: stratified squamous, stratified cuboidal (only rarely found), stratified columnar (only rarely found), and transitional.

atlas.title: Simple epithelium
atlas.body: Simple squamous epithelium– the root of the word squamous means “scale” (like a fish scale), which describes their shape. They are very thin, and when cross-sectioned often only the nucleus stands out – the cytoplasm is too thin to be appreciated. This type of epithelium is good for making a thin surface allowing diffusion and transport of molecules. Examples include: inner lining of blood vessels, the lining of alveoli (air sacs of lung), and Bowman’s capsule (urine filtration in the kidney). In each of these settings, some small molecules (ions, H2O) can simply diffuse through the body of the cell (e.g.

atlas.title: Stratified epithelium
atlas.body: Stratified squamous epithelium is named after the flat, scale-shaped cells in the top layer. The most basal layer is the growth zone,  generating new cells; the cells mature as they move upwards and eventually are sloughed off at the top. This is the strongest and most protective of all the epithelial types. This epithelium type may be keratinizing (making keratin to protect against moisture loss) where exposed to the elements, or non-keratinizing when found inside the body. Examples include: epidermis (epithelial layer of the skin,) which is keratinized, and lining of the oral cavity, tongue, esophagus, and vagina, all of which are non-keratinized.

atlas.title: Gland formation - exocrine and endocrine
atlas.body: Now that we’ve introduced the subtypes of epithelium, we’ll talk more specifically about glands – glands are of groups of epithelial cells that are specialized for secretion (biosynthesis and release of complex molecules). Glands initially develop as an invagination of surface epithelium down into the adjacent connective tissue, establishing a cluster of cells deep to the epithelial surface that then specialize. There are two main classes of glands - exocrine and endocrine. Exocrine glands maintain a connection to the epithelium above them, and this connection forms a duct;  secretions made by the glandular cells travel up the duct to the epithelial surface.

atlas.title: Exocrine glands
atlas.body: The specialized epithelial cells of a gland (glandular cells) are typically columnar cells that synthesize product that collects in their apical cytoplasm (examples are mucus, sweat, saliva, digestive enzymes, etc). The cells then release their product apically into a duct. Ducts are also lined by epithelial cells (ductal cells) that differ in function from the glandular cells. The duct transports the product (and in some cases the duct cells may modify the contents) to the epithelial surface, and the contents are dumped onto the surface. Exocrine glands may form a variety of shapes, including straight tubules, coiled tubules, branching tubules, or clusters (aka acini).

atlas.title: Sidedness
atlas.body: Epithelial cells exhibit “sidedness;” their apical, lateral, and basal surfaces are distinct and non- interchangeable regions. Sidedness is essential to the function of both individual epithelial cells and an epithelium as a whole. The specific subtype of epithelium at different locations in the body relates to the function performed at that location. Depending on the location and organ, epithelial cells may be found in sheets or in glands, and may be specialized to perform diffusion, secretion, absorption, protection, etc. Some of these specificities will be covered in the general epithelium lecture, with a deeper dive as we address the histology of each organ system.
atlas.file: 25_08_08 - Epithelial Surface Specializations_ Review _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Characteristics of distinct epithelial cell surfaces
atlas.body: LATERAL specializations: Junctions There are four types of junctions found at the lateral surfaces of epithelial cells: Tight junctions (or zonula occludens; zonula means “belt”) are not especially strong, but form a fully sealed band between cells that prevents anything from seeping between the cells. This sealing junction is usually found up near the apical aspect of the lateral surfaces. Primary proteins  are claudins and occludens. Adherens junctions (or zonula adherens) form a strong band of adhesion between the lateral aspects of the cells. Proteins are cadherins, catenins, and actin filaments.
atlas.file: 25_08_08 - Epithelial Surface Specializations_ Review _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: APICAL specializations
atlas.body: Microvilli are regular membrane foldings containing an actin core, and serve to increase the cell’s apical surface area. Cells with microvilli are typically involved in a high level of absorption or secretion at their apical aspect. Example: In the intestine, many cells have microvilli, enhancing the absorption of nutrients. On routine microscopy the microvilli appear as a blurry edge to the apical surface, referred to as the “brush border” (more on this in the gastrointestinal lecture!). Cilia are motile, and perform a sweeping action to move substances along the apical surface of the epithelium. Cilia are cell membrane-covered structures extending from the cell surface.
atlas.file: 25_08_08 - Epithelial Surface Specializations_ Review _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: The primary cell – the FIBROBLAST
atlas.body: The primary cell found in all basic connective tissue (but not in the specialized types) is the fibroblast. The fibroblast synthesizes, https://app.tophat.com/e/470724/content/course-work/item/13 9f88f95-7a49-4470-801c-432ba26621ae?open_fullscreen=true 8/12/25, 4 29 AM Page 2 of 18 : 5 exudes, and attaches to the fibers of the ECM. It also generates the ECM macromolecules, which interact with the fibers and with other cell types residing there. Fibroblasts are stellate-shaped cells which can be difficult to visualize microscopically in a background of many ECM fibers and other cell types.

atlas.title: Extracellular matrix – the MACROMOLECULES
atlas.body: The macromolecules are sometimes referred to as the “ground substance” (as in “background”). They cannot be seen with the regular microscope. Like the fibers, the macromolecules are produced by the main cell. Different macromolecules are found in https://app.tophat.com/e/470724/content/course-work/item/13 9f88f95-7a49-4470-801c-432ba26621ae?open_fullscreen=true 8/12/25, 4 29 AM Page 7 of 18 : 5 different types of connective tissue and lend to the properties of that tissue type. There are two main classes of macromolecules in the ground substance – glycoproteins and proteoglycans. Glycoproteins consist of a globular protein base with an attached branched carbohydrate.

atlas.title: HISTOLOGY OF CONNECTIVE TISSUE
atlas.body: Now we'll look at connective tissue microscopically. It is found throughout the body – wherever a vessel passes through tissue, there’s a little bit of connective tissue helping hold it in place. Connective tissue can also be found in large deposits in some locations. https://app.tophat.com/e/470724/content/course-work/item/13 9f88f95-7a49-4470-801c-432ba26621ae?open_fullscreen=true 8/12/25, 4 29 AM Page 11 of 18 : 5 There are three histologic types/patterns of connective tissue, which have distinct microscopic appearances, and relate to the function of the tissue. These are loose, dense regular, and dense irregular connective tissue.

atlas.title: OTHER CELLS found in connective tissue
atlas.body: Immune cells are found in many sites, such as bone marrow, lymph nodes, circulating in the blood, and living within other tissues. Here we will introduce a few types of immune cells that are commonly found in tissues (you'll hear more about them later also). https://app.tophat.com/e/470724/content/course-work/item/13 9f88f95-7a49-4470-801c-432ba26621ae?open_fullscreen=true 8/12/25, 4 29 AM Page 13 of 18 : 5 We’ll use the loose connective tissue supporting the epithelium of the intestines as the example. The primary job of the of the intestines is to absorb nutrients from the diet (more specifics on this process later).

atlas.title: ADIPOSE TISSUE/FAT
atlas.body: Fat, or adipose tissue, is classified as a connective tissue, although it doesn't exactly fit the "cells embedded in a matrix" definition. There are two types of fat – white and brown. The fat cell is called the https://app.tophat.com/e/470724/content/course-work/item/13 9f88f95-7a49-4470-801c-432ba26621ae?open_fullscreen=true 8/12/25, 4 29 AM Page 16 of 18 : 5 adipocyte, and contains a large amount of fat in the cytoplasm – this is melted away during processing to make slides, so the blank “white” cytoplasm in fat cell represents where lipids used to be. White fat (aka unilocular fat) is by far the more common of the two.

atlas.title: CARTILAGE
atlas.body: Cartilage is a specialized connective tissue, and is most often derived from mesoderm. Cartilage can function as a shock absorber(at the articular surfaces of joints) and as a semi- rigid but flexible support (as in the trachea, the nose, the external ear). Cartilage is avascular, meaning there are no vessels penetrating the tissue, and nutrients for the cells are only available by diffusion from adjacent tissues, or from synovial fluid in the joint space. This limits cartilage to forming only thin plates or small masses.
atlas.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

atlas.title: Cartilage: cells and matrix
atlas.body: Immature, developing cartilage cells are called chondroblasts ; once they are mature they are called chondrocytes (we’ll see a similar nomenclature in bone). These cells produce the extracellular matrix elements (fibers and macromolecules) and exude them into the extracellular space. The immature chondroblasts produce a lot of matrix materials while forming cartilage, but the mature chondrocyte that lives in completed cartilage only produces a little maintenance-level amount of matrix.
atlas.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

atlas.title: Cartilage growth (two patterns)
atlas.body: First, some background: In the fetus, most of the skeleton is initially cartilaginous. During development, primitive precursor tissue (sometimes called “mesenchyme”) condenses in appropriate places and differentiates along a cartilage pathway, forming initial small foci of cartilage. Once there is a piece of cartilage formed, there is a residual thin lining around the edges of the piece that is called the perichondrium, which contains cartilage progenitor cells that can make more chondroblasts if needed. There are two ways in which cartilage can grow: appositional growth and interstitial growth. In both settings, young chondroblasts are initially close to each
atlas.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

atlas.title: BONE
atlas.body: Bone is also a specialized connective tissue. The origin is largely mesoderm, except for cranial bones, which are neural crest-derived. Bone has a variety of functions, as follows: Provides attachment points for muscles, allowing locomotion Protects visceral organs (rib cage) and the brain (skull) Houses the marrow, where blood cells develop Is a calcium store
atlas.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

atlas.title: Bone: Cells and matrix
atlas.body: Bone’s matrix is hard and partially inorganic, but is not static https://app.tophat.com/e/470724/content/course-work/item/13 35c6e8-4da4-4ead-9128-a301b8cc89a1?open_fullscreen=true 8/11/25, 10 34 AM Page 9 of 24 : 5 and can grow, repair, and regenerate. By weight, a little more than half of the matrix is organic and contains type I collagen and macromolecules. The macromolecules of bone, particularly the glycoproteins, attract and bind calcium. The inorganic portion of the matrix consists of calcium, phosphorus (often complexed as “hydroxyapatite crystals”), and other trace minerals.
atlas.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

atlas.title: The Epiphyseal Plate
atlas.body: In the long bones, a region of growing cartilage remains between the epiphyses and the diaphysis; this is called the https://app.tophat.com/e/470724/content/course-work/item/13 35c6e8-4da4-4ead-9128-a301b8cc89a1?open_fullscreen=true 8/11/25, 10 34 AM Page 17 of 24 : 5 epiphyseal plate and allows for growth of long bone during childhood and young adulthood. The cartilage in the plate proliferates (via interstitial growth), which effectively pushes the diaphysis away from the epiphysis, creating length. Since a thick cartilage plate cannot be sustained due to avascularity, some of it dies and is replaced by bone (endochondral ossification). The result is a lengthened bone.
atlas.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

atlas.title: More bone vocabulary/concepts
atlas.body: When new bone is first developed, it is called is primary/immature bone. The osteocytes may be slightly https://app.tophat.com/e/470724/content/course-work/item/13 35c6e8-4da4-4ead-9128-a301b8cc89a1?open_fullscreen=true 8/11/25, 10 34 AM Page 20 of 24 : 5 crowded, the collagen fibers of the matrix are disorganized, and matrix mineralization is low. Because of the irregular collagen arrangement, it is also sometimes called “woven” bone by pathologists.
atlas.file: 25_08_11 - Cartilage and Bone study guide (Top Hat).pdf

atlas.title: The Haversian system
atlas.body: The Haversian system architecture is seen only in compact https://app.tophat.com/e/470724/content/course-work/item/13 35c6e8-4da4-4ead-9128-a301b8cc89a1?open_fullscreen=true 8/11/25, 10 34 AM Page 22 of 24 : 5 configuration of mature bone. A Haversian system, also referred to as an osteon, is a repeating microarchitectural unit of compact bone organization, and allows adequate nutrients for all osteocytes within a thick piece of bone. (if it helps, the cross- sectional diameter of an osteon is ~0.2 mm). The Haversian canal is a small channel running parallel to the long axis of the bone, containing very small blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.

atlas.title: SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS
atlas.body: Muscle Tissue SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS There are three major types of muscle: (1) skeletal or striated muscle, (2) cardiac muscle, and (3) smooth or visceral muscle. Skeletal muscle cells are very long, multinucleated fibers, cylindrically shaped and with diameters up to 100 μm. The sarcolemma of each fiber is surrounded by an external lamina and thin connective tissue, endomysium, containing capillaries.

atlas.title: Organization of Skeletal Muscle Fibers
atlas.body: Groups of fibers called fascicles are surrounded by perimysium; all fascicles are enclosed within a dense connective tissue epimysium. Internally, each muscle fiber is filled with myofibrils, composed of thousands of thick myosin filaments and thin actin filaments, highly organized into contractile units called sarcomeres. Within sarcomeres, thick and thin filaments interdigitate; globular myosin heads project from the thick filaments toward the F­actin filaments, which are associated with tropomyosin and troponin. Sarcomeres are separated by Z discs that bisect the light­staining I bands that contain mainly the thin filaments attached to α­actinin in the Z disc.

atlas.title: Sarcoplasmic Reticulum & Transverse Tubule System
atlas.body: In the sarcoplasm between parallel myofibrils are mitochondria and cisternae of smooth ER, called the sarcoplasmic reticulum (S R) specialized for C a2+ sequestration and release. At each sarcomere, two terminal cisterns of SR contact a deep invagination of the sarcolemma called a transverse or T­tubule, forming a triad that triggers Ca2+ release when the sarcolemma is depolarized.

atlas.title: Mechanism of Contraction
atlas.body: C a2+ binding to troponin causes tropomyosin to change shape and allow the myosin heads to bind the actin subunits, forming crossbridges between thick and thin filaments. The myosin heads then pivot with ATP hydrolysis, which pulls the thin filaments along the thick filaments. With Ca2+ and ATP present, a contraction cycle ensues in which myosin heads repeatedly attach, pivot, detach, and return, causing the filaments to slide past one another, shortening the sarcomere. When the membrane depolarization ends, Ca2+ is again sequestered, ending contraction and allowing the sarcomeres to lengthen again as the muscle relaxes.

atlas.title: Muscle Spindles & Tendon Organs
atlas.body: These are both sensory proprioceptors in which sensory axons wrap around intrafusal fibers in small specialized fascicles or around When the membrane depolarization ends, Ca2+ is again sequestered, ending contraction and allowing the sarcomeres to lengthen again as the muscle relaxes. Access Provided by: Synapses of motor axons with skeletal muscle are called MEPs, NMJs, or myoneural junctions; the neurotransmitter is acetylcholine. A motor axon may form many terminal branches, each ending on an MEP of a muscle fiber; all fibers innervated by branches of that axon comprise a motor unit.

atlas.title: Cardiac Muscle
atlas.body: Cardiac muscle fibers are also striated, but they consist of individual cylindrical cells, each containing one (or two) central nuclei and linked by adherent and gap junctions at prominent intercalated discs. Sarcomeres of cardiac muscle are organized and function similarly to those of skeletal muscle. Contraction of cardiac muscle is intrinsic at nodes of impulse­generating pacemaker muscle fibers; autonomic nerves regulate the rate of contraction.

atlas.title: Smooth Muscle
atlas.body: Smooth muscle fibers are individual small, fusiform (tapering) cells, linked by numerous gap junctions. Thin and thick filaments in smooth muscle fibers do not form sarcomeres, and no striations are present. Thin actin filaments attach to α­actinin located in dense bodies that are located throughout the sarcoplasm and near the sarcolemma; contraction causes cells to shorten individually. Sarcoplasmic reticulum is less well­organized in smooth muscle fibers, and there is no transverse tubule system. Troponin is lacking in smooth muscle; proteins controlling the sliding filaments here include myosin light­chain kinase (MLCK) and the Ca2+­binding protein calmodulin.

atlas.title: Regeneration of Muscle Tissue
atlas.body: Repair and regeneration can occur in skeletal muscle because of a population of reserve muscle satellite cells that can proliferate, fuse, and form new muscle fibers. Cardiac muscle lacks satellite cells and has little capacity for regeneration. Regeneration is rapid in smooth muscle because the cells/fibers are small and relatively less differentiated, which allow renewed mitotic activity after injury.

atlas.title: Introduction to tissue types: Muscle
atlas.body: Objectives: Once you have digested this lecture, you should be able to: 1. List the three types of muscle; describe functional and structural similarities/di!erences 2. Describe the similarities/di!erences in the histologic appearance of the three types, and be able to recognize microphotographs of classic, clear examples of each type 3. Describe the hierarchy of organization of skeletal muscle, from gross all the way down to molecular 4. Describe the function of the sarcomere as the basic unit of contraction in striated muscle

atlas.title: Basics
atlas.body: Introduction to tissue types: Neural tissue/nervous system Lecture/powerpoint presentation by: Dr. Michael Punsoni This study guide is prepared by your Histology course directors For questions regarding the lecture, please reach out to Dr. Punsoni. For questions on the study guide, please email our course directors. Optional reference: Chapter 9 (Nervous system) in Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas, 17th Edition

atlas.title: Neuroanatomy - a few notes
atlas.body: The general function of the nervous system is to regulate and coordinate the functions of other tissues. The nervous system has two main divisions: the central nervous system (CNS), and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Here are the components of both CNS and PNS (which will be described in deeper detail in each respective section below). The CNS consists of the 1) brain (which includes the cerebrum and cerebellum) and 2) spinal cord. The CNS acts as the central control region, accepting inputs, processing information, and issuing outgoing “commands”.

atlas.title: The Somatic Nervous System (motor and sensory)
atlas.body: The Autonomic Nervous System (maintains the body’s homeostasis – regulation of heartbeat, blood vessels, digestive, respiratory and urinary tracts; stimulates glands to secrete mucus, tears, and digestive enzymes). In the following sections, we'll look @ some basic morphologies of key cell types in the CNS and PNS.

atlas.title: Glial Cells
atlas.body: In addition to neurons, nervous tissue contains supporting cells known as glial or neuroglial cells. There is very little connective tissue in the CNS, so it is these cells that provide support and protection for neurons. They also supply nutrients to neurons, and modulate the transmission of nerve impulses. Glial cells cannot transmit nerve impulses themselves, and do not form synapses. However, they form the myelin sheaths around axons, and they are able of dividing (they are therefore the source of nervous system tumors). In the brain, glial cells (or “glia”) are estimated to outnumber neurons by >10:1.

atlas.title: Ependymal cells
atlas.body: Astrocytes Astrocytes are found only in the CNS. They are the largest of the neuroglia, and are the most abundant neuroglial cells. They have many long processes that help anchor neurons to their blood supply. They are therefore believed to play an important role in the blood-brain barrier, which serves a protective filter against pathogens and toxins.

atlas.title: Supplying glucose needed for nerve activity
atlas.body: Oligodendrocytes These glial cells are found in the CNS and are smaller than astrocytes. They surround (wrap around) the axons of neurons forming a “myelin sheath” which insulates and supports neural conduction. They have a characteristic morphology (a clear "halo" surrounding the nucleus as shown below):

atlas.title: Schwann cells (the PNS counterpart of oligodendrocytes)
atlas.body: Schwann cells in the PNS (peripheral nervous system) serve the same purpose as oligodendrocytes in the CNS-- they form myelin sheaths. In addition, they also have phagocytic activity and help clear cellular debris. 🩺Clinical correlation: myelin Multiple sclerosis is the most common demyelinating disease in the CNS. There is significant variability in how the disease evolves (including a "relapsing and remitting" pattern of disease). The etiology is currently thought to be immune-mediated. Also refer back to the Panopto lecture recording for additional details on this topic when studying for the exam.

atlas.title: Microglia
atlas.body: Microglia are specialized brain macrophages that are derived from blood-borne monocytes (mesodermal origin). They are phagocytic cells that act as the “first line of defense” against foreign invaders. Microglia are small cells with elongated bodies, elongated nuclei, dense chromatin and relatively few processes. They are found throughout the CNS). These cells make up ~15% of the cells of the CNS.

atlas.title: Ependymal cells
atlas.body: These are cuboidal or low-columnar cells that form a single layer lining the internal cavities (ventricles) of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord. The apical surfaces of ependymal cells are covered with cilia, which helps to circulate the CSF through the ventricles and central canal. Within the brain's ventricles, modified ependymal cells, loose connective tissue and capillaries together form the choroid plexus, which produces CSF. 🩺Clinical correlation: CSF Abnormal accumulations of CSF can lead to expansion of the ventricular spaces within the brain, also known as hydrocephalus. There are different ways of classifying hydrocephalus: congenital vs.

atlas.title: Meninges: pia mater, arachnoid, dura mater ("PAD")
atlas.body: The meninges are a system of membranes, or specialized connective tissue, that envelops the CNS. The meninges consist of 3 layers: the the pia mater, arachnoid, and dura mater or “dura”. (These layers "PAD" the brain.) A key function of the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is to protect the brain and spinal cord. Dura mater: this is the outermost layer and is made up of very dense fibrous connective tissue that is fairly impermeable and tough. Arachnoid: this layer of very loose connective tissue lies in between the dura and the pia. CSF (Cerebrospinal Fluid, see below) occupies spaces within the arachnoid layer.

atlas.title: Histology of Skin
atlas.body: Lecture/powerpoint presentation: Dr. Leslie Robinson-Bostom This study guide is prepared by your Histology course directors For questions regarding the lecture, please reach out to Dr. Robinson-Bostom. For questions on the study guide, please email your course directors. Optional reference: Chapter 18 (Skin) in Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas, 17th Edition

atlas.title: Big picture: the microscopic anatomy of skin
atlas.body: Skin is the outer covering of living tissues and is the largest organ of the integumentary system. The integumentary system includes the surface (skin) and specialized skin structures and appendages (hair, nerves, glands).

atlas.title: Skin: General structure
atlas.body: The skin is composed of 1. stratified squamous epithelium (epidermis - quick link back to our epithelium study guide) 2. overlying connective tissue (dermis- quick link back to CT study guide) with a layer of subcutaneous fat immediately adjacent (deep) to the dermis. Skin can be thick and non-hairy or thin and hairy (bonus fact: skin can have a variable thickness between 0.075 and 1.4 mm). The skin also has specialized structures including hair, nerve endings, and sebaceous and sweat glands. These have important contributions to the biological function of skin.

atlas.title: Epidermis
atlas.body: The epidermis consists of stratified squamous epithelium. Skin thickness varies based upon the number of cell layers and the number of dead cells on the surface. (Related to the bonus fact above: Eyelid skin is extremely thin (~0.075mm), whereas the skin on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet can be 1.4mm thick!) The epidermis has five distinct histological strata/layers, composed of keratinocytes passing through their life cycle. These, in order from most basal are 1. stratum basale (proliferative layer) 2. stratum spinosum (cell adhesion) 3. stratum granulosum (anti-dessicant) 4. stratum lucidum (transition to dead cells) 5. stratum corneum (dead cells sloughing off)

atlas.title: Stratum Basale (or germinativum)
atlas.body: This basal layer is the renewal layer (epidermis is renewed every 15-130 days). These cells can be considered the "stem cells" of all epidermis, undifferentiated, proliferating, and creating daughter cells that migrate upward, beginning the process of differentiation.

atlas.title: Stratum Spinosum
atlas.body: These keratinocyte cells have “spiny” processes filled with bundles of tonofilaments. The “spines” form intercellular junctions that result in cohesion in the epidermis. Many desmosomes are present, creating a “prickly” cell appearance. Keratinization begins in this layer.

atlas.title: Stratum Granulosum
atlas.body: The stratum granulosum consists of layers of flattened, granule-filled keratinocytes. This layer is about 2-5 layers thick. The cells contain keratohyalin granules, which contain substances that bind tonofilaments. The cells also contain membrane-coating granules, which are secretory vesicles whose product (GAGS & lipids) creates the sealing, anti-dessicant property of skin.

atlas.title: Dermis
atlas.body: This is the mesodermal connective tissue layer deep and adjacent to epidermis. It exerts an inductive effect on overlying ectodermal tissue, influencing development of skin characteristic to a particular area (i.e. sole, palm, etc.) The basal lamina between (i.e. at the interface of) the epidermis and dermis follows the contour of the dermal papillae, which has ridges that increase surface area for adhesion. Hemidesmosomes are very plentiful at this interface.

atlas.title: Skin: Functions
atlas.body: As discussed earlier, the skin has protective functions, conferring protection from injury, resistance to abrasion and protection from UV radiation. It is important for thermoregulation via evaporative cooling, blood shunting and insulation. This is because the skin contains a blood supply far greater than its requirements, which allows control of energy loss by radiation, convection and conduction. Dilated blood vessels increase perfusion and heat loss while constricted vessels greatly reduce cutaneous blood flow and conserve heat. The skin also contains receptors for environmental stimuli, such as heat and cold, touch, pressure, vibration, and tissue injury.

atlas.title: Sweat glands (eccrine and apocrine)
atlas.body: Most sweat glands are eccrine (merocrine) type, i.e. they don't lose cytoplasmic components during secretion, in contrast with apocrine type noted below. Eccrine glands are simple, coiled tubular glands that produce a mixture of water, salt, urea, NH3 (aka the precursor to sweat, which is an ultrafiltrate of plasma). Eccrine sweat glands are found at border between dermis and hypodermis, and play a role in regulation of body temperature via evaporative cooling. A specialized type of sweat gland in the skin of the axilla and groin is of the apocrine type (i.e. pieces of the gland cells break off and are lost with the secretory product).

atlas.title: The Circulatory System SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS
atlas.body: Heart The heart has three major layers: (1) the inner endocardium of endothelium and subendothelial connective tissue; (2) the myocardium of cardiac muscle; and (3) the epicardium, connective tissue with many adipocytes and covered by mesothelium. The cardiac conducting system stimulates rhythmic contractions and consists of modified cardiac muscle fibers forming the sinoatrial (SA) and atrioventricular (AV) nodes, the atrioventricular bundle (of His), left and right bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers.
atlas.file: Circulatory System - SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS.pdf

atlas.title: Vasculature
atlas.body: Macroscopically visible blood vessels have three major layers or tunics: (1) The intima includes the endothelium, connective tissue, and an internal elastic lamina in larger vessels; (2) the media contains alternating layers of smooth muscle and collagen or elastic lamellae; and (3) the adventitia (or externa) contains connective tissue, small vessels (vasa vasorum), and nerves. Through the vasculature, endothelial cells are not simply heart and vessel liners; they actively produce factors that prevent blood clotting, factors that cause adjacent smooth muscle cells to contract or relax, and factors that initiate inflammation at sites of damage or infection.
atlas.file: Circulatory System - SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS.pdf

atlas.title: Lymphatic Vessels
atlas.body: Interstitial fluid that is not pulled into venules by colloidal osmotic pressure drains as lymph into blind vessels called lymphatics, or lymphatic capillaries, which have very thin endothelial cell walls with spaces between the cells. Lymphatics converge into larger, thin­walled lymphatic vessels in which lymph is propelled by movements of surrounding muscles and organs, with intimal valves keeping the flow unidirectional. The largest lymphatic vessels, the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, both with walls having tunics like those of veins, return lymph to the circulatory system by joining veins near the heart.
atlas.file: Circulatory System - SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS.pdf

atlas.title: Histology of the Vascular System
atlas.body: Objectives Once you have digested this material you should be able to: Name and describe the cells that line the entire inner surface of the cardiovascular system. Describe the general structure of arteries and veins. Describe features of different sizes of arteries (including elastic features where present), and the importance of arterioles. Describe the general differences between arterial and venous vessels, and distinguish between them on histologic sections. Describe the structural differences between different capillary types. Relate the structure of the different types of capillaries to their respective functions/locations. Briefly explain the two clinical correlations described.

atlas.title: Overview
atlas.body: The vascular system functions to physically transport blood to and from organs and tissues. The smallest-caliber vessels of the system, the capillaries, allow the exchange of fluids, ions, and molecules between the blood and tissues. We will discuss generalities of the vascular system, the structure of arteries and veins, differences between the two, and end with a discussion of capillary types. When discussing the vascular system, the term lumen refers to the interior space where the blood travels. The entire lumen of the cardiovascular system (heart and vessels) is lined by a simple squamous epithelium called the endothelium; the individual cells are called endothelial cells. While some

atlas.title: The heart
atlas.body: The heart muscle proper is composed entirely of cardiac muscle cells, with a small amount of loose connective tissue and collagen type III present between cells to support the small vessels within the muscle. As you’ve already learned, some of the muscle cells are specialized to conduct impulses (the Purkinje fibers). All of the inner surfaces of the chambers are lined by endothelium. The heart valves are composed of dense regular connective tissue, with dense irregular connective tissue at the sites of attachment to the heart muscle.

atlas.title: Vessels: General structure
atlas.body: Arteries and veins (but not capillaries) share a general structure, consisting of three layers: the tunica intima, the tunica media, and the tunica adventitia. The tunica intima is the innermost layer, sitting next to the lumen and in contact with the blood. It is composed of the endothelium (simple squamous epithelium) and a relatively thin underlying layer of connective tissue. The tunica media is the middle layer and is composed of a variable number of smooth muscle cells arranged in a circular pattern around the lumen. The smooth muscle cells allow for constriction or dilation of the lumen. There are also a small number of fibroblasts, collagen fibers, and ground substance.

atlas.title: ARTERIES
atlas.body: Arteries are classified by size. The largest are the elastic arteries , and are close to the heart (e.g. aorta, pulmonary artery); these experience widely fluctuating high pressure, and in addition to having internal and external elastic lamina, they contain large amounts of elastic fibers throughout the tunica media. These are arranged in sheets (lamellae) that alternate with layers of smooth muscle and collagen fibers in the media.

atlas.title: VEINS
atlas.body: Veins are not strictly categorized and are usually just referred to by large, medium, and small. A very small vein that is just exiting a capillary bed can be called a venule. Veins experience relatively low pressures as compared to arteries, and their walls are considerably thinner, largely due to a thin tunica media. This results in them being somewhat “floppy,” and on histologic sections they often appear collapsed. There is not much elastic tissue on the venous side of the system; the largest vein (the vena cava) has a very thin internal elastic lamina.

atlas.title: CAPILLARIES – the “microcirculation”
atlas.body: The microcirculation deals with the flow of blood from the arterioles, through capillaries, into venules. Meta-arteriolar precapillary sphincters control the flow of blood between the arteriole and capillaries. When the sphincters are closed, blood is not allowed to travel into capillary beds. This allows blood to be distributed where most needed. In some cases there may be a channel directly connecting the arteriole to the venule (arteriovenous anastomosis), allowing the blood to simply bypass the bed entirely and circulate back to the heart.

atlas.body: IMS 1: HFD: Histology and Function of Blood/Blood Cells ILM/powerpoint presentation: Dean Mather This study guide is prepared by your Histology course directors Optional: Chapter 12 (Blood Cells) in Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas, 17th Edition

atlas.title: Serum vs plasma 🧪
atlas.body: Blood collected in the presence of an anticoagulant and then centrifuged will separate by weight into layers: 1. an RBC layer (~45% by volume), known as hematocrit; 2. a thin layer of wbc & platelets (“buffy coat”), and 3. PLASMA  Blood collected without an anticoagulant will coagulate (clot), leaving a combination of Clot + SERUM.
atlas.file: 25_08_14 - Blood Cells study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: The blood smear
atlas.body: Blood cells can be examined microscopically by making a peripheral blood smear, in which a drop of blood is placed onto a glass microscope slide and smeared to make a very thin layer of blood. The slide is air dried and stained with a mixture of stains. With the mixture of dyes used, pink staining on the slide is due to cellular components that are acidophilic (they bind to acidic dyes like eosin). Bluish staining is due to cellular components that bind to basic dyes.
atlas.file: 25_08_14 - Blood Cells study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Red blood cells (RBCs) = erythrocytes
atlas.body: Normal concentration in blood: ~5 million/μL. Mature RBCs are anucleate biconcave discs with a diameter of 7-8 μm (you do NOT need to memorize the specific sizes of the blood cells, but be aware of relative differences in size between RBC/WBC/platelets). The biconcave shape results in a 20-30% increase in surface area (as compared to a sphere). The very large surface area to volume ratio allows for efficient gas transfer.
atlas.file: 25_08_14 - Blood Cells study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Normal WBC count ~ 6,000-10,000/μL
atlas.body: There are two categories of WBC: Granulocytes (aka polymorphonuclear cells, see the 3 starred * types below) and Agranulocytes (mononuclear-- the 2 nonstarred types). There are five types of WBCs. Remember, 🙊 NLMEB = “Never let monkeys eat bananas!" -  in order of frequency (while you do not need to learn the specific % values noted here, do know the order): 1. Neutrophils: 50-70% * 2. Lymphocytes: 25-35% 3. Monocytes: 3-7% 4. Eosinophils: 1-3% * 5. Basophils: 0-1% *
atlas.file: 25_08_14 - Blood Cells study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Have a short lifespan (1-2 d)
atlas.body: Are a dominant component of “pus” Characteristic microscopic appearance:  Irregularly shaped, multi-lobed (segmented ) nucleus (normally 3-5 lobes ) connected by thin "strings" 🩺Neutrophils: Clinical correlation 48 hours after a myocardial infarction, polys (neutrophils) flood into dead heart muscle to clean up the mess (significant increase in acute inflammation can be seen microscopically, below). This is a high power photo of damaged heart muscle, post-myocardial infarction ("MI"), with multiple neutrophils infiltrating the bottom half of this photo. The neutrophils are a pathologic (abnormal) finding. They appear as a response to acute injury to the heart.

atlas.title: Lymphocytes
atlas.body: Small lymphocytes are ~6-8 μm in diameter (but when “activated” by particular antigens they can reach sizes up to 18μm). They have a lifespan of hours to years and are produced in the bone marrow (like other WBCs). Lymphocytes migrate to specific areas of the body to become  mature:

atlas.title: Eosinophils
atlas.body: Eosinophils comprise ~ 1-3% of WBCs and are about same size as a neutrophil (12- 15μm in diameter). They remain in circulation for 3-8 hours before migrating to skin, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract.

atlas.title: Basophils
atlas.body: Basophils are the least common wbc (<1% of blood leukocytes) and are around same size as neutrophils (12-15μm in diameter).  Functions: see slide above. Note that basophil degranulation releases a significant amount of histamine into peripheral blood.

atlas.title: Platelets
atlas.body: Blood platelets (aka thrombocytes) are anucleate, disk-like cell fragments measuring 2-4μm in diameter, with a lifespan of 7-10 days. They are formed from fragments of megakaryocytes. Megakaryocytes are large precusor cells that live in bone marrow. atlas.title: Histology: Lymphatic system
atlas.body: IMS 1: Histology – Lymphatic System (aka Lymphoid System): ILM /powerpoint presentation: Dr. Luba Dumenco (Professor Emerita) This study guide is prepared by your Histology course directors Optional reference: Chapter 14 (Lymphoid System) in Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas, 17th Edition

atlas.title: Big picture: Lymphatic/Lymphoid system
atlas.body: The general functions of the lymphatic system are to provide the sites for the differentiation of lymphocytic cells (including their ability to recognize “non-self” or foreign cells or invaders; as well as their ability to distinguish “self” from “non-self”) and to provide regions for blood and lymph filtration. Origin of the lymphatic tissues is mesoderm, with the exception of the unusual thymic stroma, which is composed of endodermal epithelial cells that are derived from pharyngeal pouches 3 & 4.

atlas.title: Cells
atlas.body: Cells in the lymphatic system include B & T lymphocytes and Antigen-presenting cells (APCs). B-cells: form from bone marrow sites; generate memory cells and plasma cells; account for approximately 10-20% of circulating lymphocytes T-cells: approximately 70-80% of circulating blood lymphocytes. NK (Natural Killer) cells: comprise remainder of circulating lymphocytes APCs: Antigen presenting cells – these include macrophages, Langerhans cells (in the skin), dendritic cells, and B-cells. A note on "cortex" and "medulla": You'll see these terms used throughout many organs (not just in the lymphoid system).

atlas.title: Lymphatic vessels
atlas.body: The lymphatic vessels can be considered to be a “one-way street back to the Superior Vena Cava”. They originate as “blind” lymphatic capillaries in connective tissue beds and continue as vessels interrupted by lymph nodes on their path back to the venous system. Lymphatic endothelial cells line these lymphatic vessels. Interstitial fluid forms at the arterial end of the capillaries because of the higher pressure of blood there; most of it returns to the venules. The rest (~10-20%) enters the lymphatic capillaries as lymph, a watery, clear liquid with the same composition of interstitial fluid. The lymphatic vessels ultimately converge on the Right Lymphatic Duct and the Thoracic Duct.

atlas.title: Immunity
atlas.body: Cellular immunity (or cell-mediated immunity) is mediated by T cells. It is the arm of the adaptive immune system that does not involve antibodiesor complement, but rather involves the activation of T lymphocytes, macrophages, and Natural Killer cells (NK cells), and the release of various cytokines in response to an antigen. Humoral immunity is mediated by B cells and antibody production. Exposure to specific antigen results in activation of B cells, which differentiate into antibody-producing plasma cells and memory cells. Circulating antibodies react with antigen to increase phagocytosis and neutralize invaders. Note that an “antigens” elicit immune responses.

atlas.title: Primary and Secondary Organs of the Lymphatic
atlas.body: System The primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow and thymus) are the sites where B and T lymphocytes originate. (B cells originate in the bone marrow, and T-cells in the thymus). The secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, spleen and tonsils) are locations where further lymphocyte differentiation may occur; lymphocytes reside in secondary lymphoid organs. Additionally, there are localized areas of unencapsulated lymphoid tissue throughout the body, known as “MALT” that also serve this purpose near mucosal surfaces. Some of these organs are fully encapsulated, while others are not.

atlas.title: Bone Marrow
atlas.body: The bone marrow is the origin of all hematopoietic cells (more details on bone marrow/blood cell development in a future course). For this course, you will not be tested on the microscopic histology of bone marrow cells. However, do be aware of which bone marrow cell type gives rise to platelets (look back to the blood cells module).

atlas.title: Thymus
atlas.body: General facts The thymus is located in the mediastinum (middle cavity within thorax) near the great vessels. It has a dual embryonic origin: the stroma is of epithelial origin (from endoderm cells of pharyngeal pouches 3 & 4). The T cell progenitor population is of mesodermal origin (originally from the bone marrow). Thymus growth peaks in youth and the thymus involutes with age. The lymphocytes of the fetal thymus are gradually replaced by loose connective tissue and fat in the adult. The thymus is a lobulated, encapsulated organ. Its connective tissue capsule trabeculae extend into the thymus creating lobules. Each lobule has a cortical region and a medulla.

atlas.title: Cells in thymus
atlas.body: Thymocytes: These precursor-T cells are derived from stem cells produced by the bone marrow. In the thymic cortex, they are surrounded by the epithelial reticular cell framework and they undergo an intense selection process through interactions with the epithelioreticular cells. Most cells die in the cortex; less than 5% of the lymphoid progenitors that originally entered the thymus from the bone marrow will mature, leave the thymus, and enter the peripheral immune system. Note that several thymic growth factors (such as thymosin) control the maturation of T cells. The “good” T-cells that emerge from the cortex then travel to the bloodstream.

atlas.title: Unique stromal structure of thymus
atlas.body: The thymus' stroma is made up of special cells called “epithelial reticular cells” that create the framework of the stroma. Unique facts about these cells: 1) they are actually of epithelial origin, arising from endoderm of pharyngeal pouches 3 and 4, 2) they are attached to each other via desmosomes, and 3) these cells are also involved in the selection, proliferation and/or death of thymocytes. (Despite the word "reticular" in the name, there are actually no reticular fibers in the stroma.) To convey outgoing T-cells, some efferent lymphatic vessels originate close to the trabeculae and leave through them.

atlas.title: Lateral aspects: the junctions and their functions
atlas.body: Tight/occluding junction, or zonula occludens: the most apical of the lateral junctions, makes a complete seal but not very strong (primary proteins are claudins and occludens) The adherens junction, or zonula adherens: located deeper, a very strong band of adhesion (primary proteins cadherins, catenins, and actin filaments) Desmosomes: “spot welds” between cells, very strong, on the internal aspect they connect to the cytoskeleton (the cytoskeletal protein is a keratin, the desmosome primary proteins are cadherins) Gap junctions: allow ions/small molecules to move between cells (protein is a connexon with connexin subunits) 2.

atlas.title: Development and anatomy
atlas.body: Development The gonad (testis) and associated ducts (efferent ducts, epididymis, and vas deferens) arise from the intermediate mesoderm in the region of the genital (gonadal) crest. In the 4th week of gestation, primordial germ cells migrate to the genital ridge; at this point the gonadal tissue is indifferent (not committed to testis or ovary). In humans with sex chromosomes XY, a region on the Y chromosome determines differentiation towards a male phenotype. Production of “testis determining factor” induces the gonad to develop seminiferous tubules (the testicular structures within which sperm develop).
atlas.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Anatomy
atlas.body: The male reproductive system involves structures in the scrotum, the abdomen/pelvis, and the penis. All the contents of the scrotal sac are contained within a sac-like extension of the peritoneum called the tunica vaginalis, which has visceral and parietal layers. Within the sac, the testis is immediately surrounded by another connective tissue wrapping which grossly appears white and is called the tunica albuginea. Leading to the sac is the spermatic cord, which includes vessels, nerves and the vas deferens as it exits the scrotum to the pelvis. The pampiniform plexus is a venous plexus in the spermatic cord which helps draw heat away from the scrotum.
atlas.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Testis
atlas.body: The bulk of the testis consists of seminiferous tubules (about 1000), where primordial germ cells develop into sperm; at the hilum of the testis there is a region of ducts that collect the sperm to exit the testis. There is a small amount of connective tissue between the seminiferous tubules; in this connective tissue are small groups of Leydig cells. Leydig cells (interstitial cells of Leydig) are endocrine cells and produce hormones (more on these in a bit).
atlas.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis
atlas.body: Development of sperm At reproductive maturity (puberty), development of germ cells begins within the seminiferous tubule. Primordial germ cells (diploid) sit along the base of the tubules. The process of spermatogenesis involves meiosis, and generates haploid spermatids sitting near the lumen of the tubules. Another process called spermiogenesis follows, which modifies the cytoplasm and generates structurally mature spermatozoa which are released into the lumen. These can leave the seminiferous tubules and exit the testis. Details of spermatogenesis: The primordial germ cells, called spermatogonia, sit along the base of the seminiferous tubules.
atlas.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Sertoli cells
atlas.body: Sertoli cells live within the seminiferous tubules and support the developing germ cells. They are fairly large columnar cells that sit along the base of the tubules, and have a large nucleus and prominent nucleolus. They are attached to each other by tight occluding junctions towards the basal aspect of their lateral aspects. These tight junctions are essential to establishing the blood-testis barrier, which protects the developing sperm. If this barrier is breached, immune cells may become sensitized to components of the flagella or the acrosomal cap.
atlas.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Endocrine activity in the testis
atlas.body: The testis is influenced by the hypothalamic- pituitary axis. Leutinizing hormone (LH, aka interstital cell stimulating hormone) from the pituitary stimulates the interstitial Leydig cells to secrete testosterone. This happens briefly during the fetal period during genital tract development, then resumes at puberty. Beginning at puberty, testosterone promotes spermatogenesis and exerts masculinizing effects in other regions of the body. The Leydig cells secrete this into the connective tissue, but it needs to be concentrated in the tubules.
atlas.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Getting out of the testis
atlas.body: From the seminiferous tubules the spermatozoa move on to epithelial lined ducts near the hilum of the testis. These structures are all within the testis proper, but are often not visible on testis slides (depends on where the section is taken from). From the seminiferous tubules the sperm enter the straight tubules (tubuli recti), which are are very short, are lined by Sertoli cells, and lead to the rete testis, which removes excess fluid, concentrating the sperm. Next are the efferent ducts lined by ciliated columnar cells and surrounded by a band of smooth muscle that helps propel the sperm (as do the cilia).
atlas.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Epididymis and Vas Deferens
atlas.body: The epididymis consists of a long coiled tube, and is found curled alongside the testis. The start of the epididymis is markedly coiled and forms a mass-like, palpable lump; this region is called the ‘head’ of the epididymis, and the remainder is called the tail. The epithelium is pseudostratified columnar with stereocilia (recall these are more like large microvilli); the cells are called “principal cells.” Sperm are stored in the epididymis, and in the epididymis the final spermatozoa maturation takes place, with flagella becoming motile. By the time they leave the epididymis, the spermatozoa are completely mature in both structure and function.
atlas.file: 01-Male Reproductive System study guide _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Introduction
atlas.body: Within the urinary system, we will be focusing on the following organs and components, with an emphasis on kidney: kidney anatomic components and introductory notes on function nephron corpuscle tubules blood flow through kidney closer look @ a glomerulus and Bowman's capsule glomerular filtration barrier (and clinical correlation) closer look @ a tubule (consisting of PCT --> Loop of Henle --> DCT) juxtaglomerular apparatus (and clinical correlation) renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) collecting ducts ureters, bladder, urethra

atlas.title: Kidney
atlas.body: Structure In order to filter blood, each kidney is highly vascularized to provide an extensive interface between blood and the parts of the kidney that perform filtration, reabsorption, and secretion functions. These activities are carried out by a functional unit in the kidney called a nephron (see below). The structures in the nephron are highly specialized to fine-tune blood and maintain homeostasis. The final product of filtration, urine, is a concentrated waste product that exits kidneys via paired ureters. Each kidney is divided into an outer cortex and inner medulla, with a corticomedullary junction sitting @ the interface between the two.

atlas.title: Henle, distal convoluted tubule (DCT)
atlas.body: Blood flow through kidney (high yield for exam): Arterial blood flows under high pressure from the aorta to the renal artery which enters the kidney at the hilum. The renal artery branches (see above, interlobar artery --> arcuate --> interlobular --> afferent arterioles) and forms capillary tufts (glomerulus, 1 per nephron). After filtration occurs in the renal corpuscle (more below), blood exits the efferent arteriole and can divide into 2 capillary beds that are associated with tubules: peritubular (surrounds PCT and DCT in the cortex), and vasa recta (surrounding loop of Henle in the medulla). Blood then exits the kidney (via interlobular vein --> arcuate --> interlobar --> renal vein).

atlas.title: Function
atlas.body: Key functions of the kidney include: 1. filtration (of water and small molecules out of blood) <----- occurs in renal corpuscle 2. reabsorption (of water and selective molecules back into blood) <----- occurs in renal tubule 3. secretion (waste and larger metabolites out of blood) <----- occurs in renal tubule

atlas.title: Glomerulus + Bowman's capsule
atlas.body: A renal corpuscle has a vascular pole (where afferent and efferent arterioles enter and exit, respectively) and a urinary pole, where the initial filtrate leaves the capsular space and enters the renal tubule. We'll look closer @ the components of the corpuscle: glomerulus Within the corpuscle, a glomerulus consists of a rounded cluster of capillary loops. The endothelium of these capillaries are fenestrated (without diaphragms) and have a continuous basal lamina.

atlas.title: Bowman's capsule
atlas.body: This structure has been referred to as a "two-walled pouch" or "cup-shaped sac" that consists of a 1) parietal layer the forms the outer edge of the "pouch/sac" and 2) a visceral layer, which envelopes the exterior surface of the glomerular capillary loops to form Bowman's space. See the parts drawn/shaded in blue in lecture slide below. There are unique, highly specialized epithelial cells called podocytes, which are part of the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule. They sit on top of the external surface of the glomerular capillaries.

atlas.title: Glomerular filtration barrier
atlas.body: FUNCTION: The glomerular filtration barrier allows *selective* filtration of blood from the afferent arteriole into Bowman’s space. Filtration occurs at the interface between glomerular capillaries and podocytes (remember the BM is sandwiched in between). Details on specifically filtered components will be presented in a separate lecture.

atlas.title: Tubule: PCT --> Loop of Henle --> DCT
atlas.body: We've looked @ filtration. Now let's move into the renal tubule (the 2nd half of the nephron), where reabsorption and secretion occur. Early filtrate flows from Bowman's space --> Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) --> Loop of Henle --> Distal convoluted tubule (DCT). While we don't dive deeply into the details of reabsorption and secretion here (I'll include a few bonus facts just for context), we will examine how certain parts of the tubule (the DCT) contribute to a key function of the kidney -- maintenance of blood pressure.

atlas.title: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)
atlas.body: The release of renin is an essential component of the renin-angiotensin- aldosterone system (RAAS), which regulates intravascular volume and blood pressure. This slide is included for context -- for this exam, you will only be responsible for the green highlighted parts and details noted above. Be aware that RAAS is high-yield for Step 1.

atlas.title: Collecting ducts
atlas.body: The distal convoluted tubules merge with collecting tubules in the renal medulla and eventually converge into collecting ducts. With the help of the osmotic concentration gradient set up by the Loop of Henle, the (near-final) urine is now concentrated in collecting ducts. Epithelial cells of the collecting ducts are cuboidal/low columnar cells that show sharp, well-defined cell borders. Collecting duct cells are water permeable due to their sensitivity to antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which is also known as vasopressin.

atlas.title: Cervix and Vagina
atlas.body: Breast The female reproductive system is notable for the tightly coordinated biochemical and physiological changes that prime the system for potential fertilization and subsequent support of a developing fetus. The components of the female reproductive tract addressed in this lecture include the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina. (Vulvar histology will not be covered here.) Breast (mammary) tissue will also be covered in this lecture. An important feature of this system is that several of its organs (ovary and uterus) have dynamic histology and physiology that vary in a cyclical pattern.

atlas.title: Menstrual cycle: introduction
atlas.body: While we will not dive into the full details of the physiology of the 28-day (estimated) menstrual cycle, it's useful to highlight a few concepts and facts: During a menstrual cycle (see slide below), there is coordinated synchronization between ovarian and uterine physiology. Ovarian and anterior pituitary hormones are released and regulate maturation of ovarian oocytes and follicles cyclical evolution of the uterine epithelial lining (aka endometrium). During a "textbook" 28-day menstrual cycle, ovaries produce fluctuating levels of estrogen and progesterone, which influence the uterine endometrium to transition from proliferative ➔ secretory ➔ menstrual phases (see Uterus section).

atlas.title: Ovary
atlas.body: The ovary is divided into cortex and medulla. Follicles (which “house” oocytes) are found embedded in the connective tissue of the cortex. The medulla contains mostly loose connective tissue and vessels that enter at the hilum of the ovary. Oocytes (the female gamete) are located within follicles, with one oocyte per follicle. Each follicle is lined by epithelium that can range from simple squamous to stratified cuboidal, depending on the stage of follicular maturity. Both oocytes and follicles undergo a number of maturation steps. At birth, it is estimated that there are up to ~1-2 million oocytes present, a number that diminishes to ~300,000 - 400,000 at puberty.

atlas.title: Maturation of the follicle
atlas.body: Big picture: During each menstrual cycle, a small number of ovarian follicles undergo maturation from primordial follicle ➔ primary follicle ➔ secondary (antral) follicle ➔ mature follicle. Remember, each follicle contains one oocyte. Within the follicle, an oocyte grows larger during follicular maturation.

atlas.title: Uterus
atlas.body: The uterus, a pear-shaped organ, consists of endometrium (lining the uterine cavity) underlying myometrium (smooth muscle layer) outer connective tissue (serosa and adventitia) The glands within the endometrium are composed of simple columnar epithelium. There are two layers of endometrium (basalis and functionalis), and our focus will primarily be on stratum functionalis, which undergoes cyclical changes. Stratum functionalis is a physiologically dynamic layer that can range from relatively straight, elongated glands to extensively coiled glands and arteries. These endometrial changes are driven by fluctuating estrogen and progesterone levels during the menstrual cycle.

atlas.title: Fallopian tube
atlas.body: After its release during ovulation, the secondary oocyte enters the fallopian tube. The fallopian tube is open at both ends, with a proximal end leading directly to the uterus and opening into the uterine cavity. The other open (distal) end of the fallopian tube has finger-like projections called fimbriae that sit adjacent to each ovary. As an oocyte is released, the fimbriae pick up and sweep the egg into the lumen of the fallopian tube. There are different cell types in the epithelial lining of the tube -- the main ones we will focus on are simple columnar (mostly ciliated), organized in complex maze-like structures (called plicae) that protrude into the lumen (see cross section below).

atlas.title: Cervix & Vagina
atlas.body: Cervix = endocervix and ectocervix The cervix is a tubular structure that is continuous with the inferior aspect of the uterus, and consists of an outer portion (ectocervix) that faces the vagina and an inner portion (endocervix) that is continuous with the uterus. The surface epithelium is unique. There is an area between the ectocervix and endocervix that is a transformation zone where stratified squamous epithelium (ectocervix) abruptly changes to simple columnar glandular epithelium (endocervix). Bonus facts: Unlike uterine endometrium, cervical epithelium does not undergo the same types of epithelial changes in response to hormones.

atlas.title: Vagina
atlas.body: The vagina is covered by stratified squamous epithelium that is similar to the ectocervix. It also displays a prominent smooth muscle layer. At the distal end of the vagina, the mucosa gradually transitions into the epidermis of the skin that covers the external genitalia.

atlas.title: Breast
atlas.body: Breast tissue is a modified and specialized glandular structure that is capable of secreting milk. Breast tissue is organized as a branching duct system that contains approximately 15-20 secretory lobes that radiate towards the centrally located nipple. We won't go into the details of the specific branching components. Instead we'll start at a functional unit called the lobule (some references also use the term "terminal duct lobular units" or TDLU). Within each lobule, there are multiple glands and a duct. The epithelium that lines ducts and glands is predominantly simple cuboidal, surrounded by a discontinuous layer of myoepithelial cells (smooth muscle-derived) and basement membrane.

atlas.title: Death
atlas.body: Optional reading: Robbins, Basic Pathology Chapter 2, p 31-41, skipping 'morphologic patterns of tissue necrosis' [will be covered in ischemia lecture], p 45-47 (ER stress and DNA damage), and p 48-51 (cell adaptations)
