atlas.title: Introduction/overview
atlas.body: This first lecture will address general principles of cell adaptation, injury, and death. We are going to address all parts of the adjacent diagram. Cells constantly adapt to physiological demands to maintain what is called a “homeostatic steady state”. Depending on the stimulus, cells may adapt by performing excess work, replicating, decreasing function, or altering genetic expression. The main cell adaptations to a persistent stimulus are cellular hypertrophy, hyperplasia and metaplasia. Decrease or loss of normal stimuli (e.g., workload, hormones) may result in cellular atrophy. Depending on the specific conditions, adaptive reactions by cells can eventually produce tissue/organ damage.
atlas.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

atlas.title: Hypertrophy – increase in cell size
atlas.body: Hypertrophy is most often discussed in terms of muscle cells. Striated muscle cells cannot divide, so when the cell senses the mechanical stress brought on by increased work demand, it responds by making more sarcomeres, more sarcoplasmic reticulum, and more mitochondria to do the work. This increases cell size, or causes “cell hypertrophy.” If pronounced, all the individual cells bulking up can make the entire organ (heart, bicep, etc) grossly larger. Hypertrophy can be physiologic or pathologic. Studies on cardiac muscle have shown that physical exercise (particularly ‘cardio’ type) that results in physiologic hypertrophy is accompanied by increased microvasculature within the heart, which
atlas.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

atlas.title: Hyperplasia – increase in cell number
atlas.body: Hyperplasia can occur in tissues that are capable of replication, and can be physiologic or pathologic. An example of physiologic hyperplasia is the proliferation of glandular epithelium in breast tissue at puberty and in pregnancy. Another example is the regeneration of liver parenchyma after partial resection. Both of these hyperplasias are due to 'normal' physiologic responses. An example of pathologic hyperplasia is endometrial hyperplasia, which occurs as a result of excess estrogen, either endogenous (adipose tissue can make estrogen, and obese individuals are at risk for endometrial hyperplasia), or exogenous (hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms).
atlas.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

atlas.title: Atrophy – decrease in tissue or cell size
atlas.body: An example of atrophy is the decrease in gross muscle size and decrease in individual muscle cell size when a limb is immobilized in a cast or when a person is bed-ridden (called ‘disuse atrophy’). Muscle cells that have lost communication from nerves will similarly have a decrease in cell size (‘denervation atrophy’). Atrophy can also be seen in the brain in some neurodegenerative changes, where cells wither to disease. Atrophy results from decreased protein synthesis and/or increased degradation of proteins in cells. Degradation of cellular proteins occurs mainly by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.
atlas.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

atlas.title: Metaplasia – reversible change in cell differentiation
atlas.body: Metaplasia reflects a change in cell differentiation Metaplasia - Normal due to certain pseudostratified columnar epithelium (on external the left) becomes more stressors. One squamous-like (on the right) example is squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium in smokers. The chronic insult to the bronchial mucosa causes the stem cells of the epithelium to change their differentiation to squamous. The conversion to a more squamous phenotype helps protect against the offensive substances in the cigarette smoke. In cases of metaplasia, the tissue will revert to its original, appropriate epithelial type if the insult
atlas.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

atlas.title: Cell injury
atlas.body: Causes of cell injury range from gross trauma to single gene defects, and many different aspects of cell function may be affected. Insufficient oxygen is a common cause of cell injury, whether due to traumatic transection of a vessel, a thrombus blocking an artery as in myocardial infarction (heart attack), or cyanide poisoning, which paralyzes the electron transport chain in the mitochondria. The degree of injury to the cell and the cell’s response is dependent on the nature of the injury, the speed of onset, the duration of the injurious stimulus, and the severity of the insult.
atlas.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

atlas.title: Reversible injury
atlas.body: When a cell receives an injurious stimulus, it will try to shift its biochemical processes to live with the injury. The cell has a certain amount of reserve to tolerate injury, and if the stimulus is eventually removed, the cell may be able to shift back to normal processes and have survived the insult. This type of injury is termed reversible injury. However, if over time the stimulus persists, the cell’s attempts at adaptation may ‘tip over’ into a state that cannot be resolved; the cell is then in a state of irreversible injury and will proceed to cell death. Some features of reversible injury are appreciated with the light microscope.
atlas.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

atlas.title: Reversible injury: steatosis (fatty change)
atlas.body: Steatosis refers to an accumulation of fats inside cells – often seen in stressed liver, heart, muscle, or kidney cells - and appears as a clear droplet within the cytoplasm that Liver cells containing may displace the large (and some and small) fat droplets nucleus to the (example of MASLD, next section) side. The liver cell plays a large role in fat metabolism, and steatosis is easily appreciated in hepatocytes. There are many clinical situations that can result in steatosis, including chemical/drug toxicity, obesity, diabetes mellitus, anoxia, protein malnutrition, and
atlas.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

atlas.title: Clinical correlation, steatosis (MASLD and MASH)
atlas.body: Clinical correlation: Metabolic Dysfunction Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) (previously called Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)) is the most common liver disease worldwide, with a prevalence in developed countries of 25- 30%. Predisposing conditions include obesity and insulin resistance (type 2 diabetes). The steatosis is potentially reversible if the patient can lose weight, which often also reverses the insulin resistance. The histopathology of MASLD shows both small vacuoles of fat in the liver cells (microvesicular steatosis) and large vacuoles (macrovesicular steatosis). Many patients do not develop any further liver changes.
atlas.file: 04-Cell injury 1 - Adaptation, Injury, Death study gude.pdf

atlas.title: Intro/definitions
atlas.body: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are potentially damaging molecules that are generated during routine cellular function, and which are normally neutralized by the cell. Increased generation or decreased ‘management’ of ROS leads to an excess of ROS; this situation is called oxidative stress. Most ROS are a type of free radical (specifically, an oxygen-derived free radical). Free radicals are molecules that have a single unpaired electron. They are very reactive and engage fairly violently with surrounding molecules. Molecules that are ‘attacked’ by free radicals may themselves be converted to free radicals, thus compounding the problem.
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: NADPH-oxidase
atlas.body: Cytochrome P450 mixed-function oxidases: enzymes that metabolize drugs, hormones, and chemicals in the sER (the liver does a LOT of this). Two types of free radicals can be generated in this process – ROS as by-products of the oxidase, and free radicals generated as intermediates in the metabolism of exogenous chemicals, such as carbon tetrachloride (covered below) Insults that can generate large amounts of ROS are massive inflammation, hyperoxia, ionizing radiation, reperfusion of ischemic tissues (sudden return of oxygenated blood to injured cells), and some toxins. Pathologic and normal sources of ROS (do NOT memorize the names of the ROSs)
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: Metal chelators/carrier proteins
atlas.body: Transition metals such as copper and iron donate or accept free electrons during intracellular reactions, and this can yield free radicals, as in the Fenton reaction. [ H2O2 + Fe2+ --> Fe3+ + .OH + OH- ] Iron must be in the ferrous state (Fe2+) to participate in this reaction. Most of intracellular free iron is in the ferric state (Fe3+) and will not participate, but small amounts of the ferrous state are found within cells and during transport in the bloodstream. To help manage ferrous iron, carrier proteins such as ferritin, transferrin, or hemoglobin shield the iron from surrounding molecules and keep them from acting as free radicals.
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: Superoxide dismutase (SOD)
atlas.body: Found in many cells; there are of various types. A manganese-SOD is in mitochondria, and copper-SOD and Zinc-SODs are found in the cytosol. They catalyze the following reaction: 2O2.- +2H ----> H2O2+O2
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: Lipid peroxidation
atlas.body: ROS will attack the double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids in membranes, yielding peroxides, which are also unstable and will attack other fatty acids. Damage to the plasma membrane disrupts the electrolyte balance of the cell and can lead to cell necrosis. Damage to membranes of lysosomes is also particularly harmful, as degradative enzymes spill into the cytosol. Damage to mitochondrial membranes disrupts oxidative phosphorylation and will typically lead to cell necrosis.
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: Protein crosslinking, fragmentation
atlas.body: There are several ways proteins can be affected by ROS. ROS may induce inappropriate crosslinking of residues, leading to misfolding (which can induce ER stress) and/or loss of needed enzymatic activity. ROS may also attack and fragment proteins.
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: DNA damage/breaks
atlas.body: ROS attack on thymine residues in both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA can cause breaks. This may lead to triggering of apoptosis, and has been implicated in the malignant transformation of cells in some cancers.
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: Basic principles of toxicology
atlas.body: Toxicology is the study of poisons. Xenobiotics are substances in the environment to which a person may be exposed via ingestion, inhalation, or skin contact; if these are known to be harmful, they may be described as toxins. Xenobiotics may be excreted and/or accumulate in tissues, may act at the site of entry or at more distant locations in the body, and may or may not undergo metabolism (via CYP enzymes, discussed below). The classic measure of toxicity of a substance is the LD50 – the lethal dose that kills 50% of the study population. The lethal dose is usually expressed as mg of toxin per kg of body weight.
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: Metabolism of drugs and toxins, CYP enzymes
atlas.body: Much of the metabolism of drugs and toxins occurs in the hepatocyte, since the liver receives portal tract contents absorbed in the GI tract. The hepatocyte is well- equipped with metabolic enzymes to handle many ingested (or otherwise absorbed) chemicals. Metabolism of chemicals, drugs and toxins occurs in two phases.
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: Mechanism of action
atlas.body: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) is a solvent once used (now banned) in the dry- cleaning industry, and is a prototype for indirectly-acting toxins. It belongs to a class of chemicals called hydrocarbons, which are fairly abundant in modern society, and are used in fuels, paints, lubricants, rubber cement, and various solvents. Carbon tetrachloride is specifically a halogenated hydrocarbon (as is chloroform). The hepatotoxicity of carbon tetrachloride occurs once it has undergone phase I metabolism by CYP, and thus it is an indirect toxin. The resulting molecules are a free radicals, which interact with hepatic macromolecules and are particularly damaging to membranes via lipid peroxidation.
atlas.file: 05-Cell Injury 2 - ROS, Intro to Toxins study guide.pdf

atlas.title: Cell Injury 3: Alcohol and other toxins
atlas.body: Optional reading: Baby Robbins, 10th ed. Ch. 2 Effects of alcohol p310-312; Ch. 8 Effects of alcohol p310-312; Ch. 16 Alcoholic and nonalcoholic liver disease p652-655; Ch. 8 Acetaminophen, Aspirin p314 Note: all photos/diagrams in this handout are from Robbins.

atlas.title: Ethanol (EtOH) - Introduction
atlas.body: Alcohol consumption is estimated to contribute to more than 100,000 deaths per year in the US. Approximately 50% of these deaths are alcohol-related accidents, homicides, and suicides, and approximately 15% are due to end-stage liver disease (cirrhosis) due to chronic alcohol use. Some diseases associated with ethanol abuse include the following: Oral cavity and esophageal cancers, degenerative brain damage, skeletal and cardiac muscle damage, gastritis, pancreatitis, impaired intestinal absorption, testicular atrophy, fetal alcohol syndrome, and assorted liver damage including fatty change, inflammation, and cirrhosis.

atlas.title: Biochemical mechanisms
atlas.body: Three mechanisms (ADH, MOS, catalase) Most ingested ethanol is metabolized in the liver, although some may be metabolized in the gastric mucosa. There are three possible ‘first-step’ pathways by which ethanol is metabolized, all of which produce acetaldehyde. 1. Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) catalyzes the main pathway of EtOH metabolism requires NAD+ is located in the cytosol 2. Microsomal EtOH-oxidizing system (MOS) is the secondary pathway, and becomes active when BAC is high uses a CYP enzyme (specifically CYP2E1) is located in the sER 3. Catalase contributes minimally to EtOH metabolism. is located in peroxisomes.

atlas.title: Individual differences in ethanol metabolism
atlas.body: Varying isoforms of ADH and ALDH exist among different populations around the world. The existence of ADH and ALDH isoforms were first identified in Japan while investigating the phenomenon of “alcohol intolerance,” which affects a significant proportion of the Japanese population. Affected persons experience significant discomfort after ingestion of even a small amount of alcohol; symptoms include flushing of the face and neck, general discomfort, nausea, headache, tachycardia, and hyperventilation. The different isoforms of the ADH and ALDH enzymes have widely varying kinetics.

atlas.title: Pathology and pathogenesis of alcoholic liver disease
atlas.body: Fatty liver Fatty liver (hepatosteatosis) due to alcohol is a reversible liver injury. Intracellular accumulation of fat causes enlargement of the hepatocytes without clinical symptoms There are several ways in which ethanol causes fatty change: 1. The metabolism of ethanol by ADH involves NAD+, which is also needed for mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation. When NAD+ is depleted by alcohol metabolism, mitochondria are less effective at processing fatty acids, and they accumulate in the cell. This is the main contributor to steatosis in the setting of ethanol abuse. 2. Ethanol impairs the mechanisms for packaging and secreting lipoproteins; this results in lipid retention within the cell.

atlas.title: Alcoholic hepatitis
atlas.body: This is a potentially reversible liver injury and is often accompanied by steatosis (steatohepatitis). Clinical findings may include fever, liver tenderness, and jaundice. Hepatocytes swell and show alcoholic ‘hyaline’ (Mallory’s hyaline, Mallory bodies) in the cytoplasm; these are collections of intermediate filaments. Under the light microscope, Mallory’s hyaline appears as eosinophilic globules in the cytoplasm. Affected hepatocytes may already be well on their way to necrosis, and responding neutrophils may seen. The pathways leading to alcoholic hepatitis are not entirely understood, but several factors are suspected to contribute. 1.

atlas.title: Fibrosis and cirrhosis
atlas.body: Some chronic heavy drinkers (why only some and not all is not well-understood Cirrhotic liver ith nodular and is under gross texture investigation) will develop fibrosis in the areas of previous necrosis/inflammation. This typically starts in the centrilobular area (zone 3); we previously discussed that the highest concentrations of CYP enzymes are in the centrilobular area, and this area seems to be where the fibrosis develops first (eventually it can involve all zones). When there is a lot of fibrosis in the liver, to the point that much of the volume has been replaced by fibrous tissue, the term cirrhosis is used.

atlas.title: Ethanol abuse and CYP enzymes
atlas.body: As discussed above, the secondary pathway (microsomal/oxidation pathway) for metabolism of ethanol involves CYP enzymes (specifically, CYP2E1). Repeated episodes of high blood alcohol levels result in this pathway being used quite frequently, and the cells will respond by generating more CYP2E1 enzymes to handle the increased ethanol load. Another way to say this is that chronic heavy alcohol use “induces” CYP2E1. As a result, any chemicals (drugs, anesthetics, carcinogens, and industrial solvents) that are also metabolized by CYP2E1 will undergo increased/more rapid metabolism.

atlas.title: Other common toxins – Pain relievers
atlas.body: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is commonly found in households, and acetaminophen is an ingredient in over 300 over-the-counter ‘cold and flu’ type medications as well. The drug has been implicated in both accidental and intentional overdoses, and acetaminophen overdose or suspected overdose results in over 50,000 emergency department visits in the US each year. There is a relatively narrow margin of safety between a therapeutic dose of acetaminophen and a toxic dose.

atlas.title: Acetaminophen and EtOH
atlas.body: Acetaminophen is particularly toxic to individuals who drink regularly (as little as 2 drinks/day). The upregulation of CYP in response to elevated blood EtOH levels can lead to increased processing of acetaminophen by CYP, resulting in markedly increased NAPQI, and cell necrosis. Even a small dose of acetaminophen can be toxic to regular drinkers and chronic heavy drinkers. There is now a “black box” warning on over-the-counter medications containing acetaminophen that alerts users to this danger.

atlas.title: Morphologic patterns of tissue necrosis p 36-37
atlas.body: Objectives: Describe the sequence of events within a cell deprived of oxygen Explain which events yield irreversible injury, and why Describe the benefits and possible drawbacks of reperfusion Recognize and name different gross appearances of infarcts and necrotic tissue Note: All photos and diagrams from Robbins uless otherwise stated.

atlas.title: Hypoxia and ischemia
atlas.body: Hypoxia is a state of decreased oxygen availability, and is an extremely common cause of cell injury and death. Most often, a tissue will be hypoxic beacuse of ischemia, or lack of sufficient blood flow to the affected tissue. However, hypoxia can also be due to overall poor oxygenation secondary to poor pulmonary function. The brain and cardiac muscle are extremely vulnerable to low blood oxygen content and/or decreased blood flow. In the brain, irreversible injury happens within minutes of oxygen deprivation, and cardiac myocytes are irreversibly damaged within about thirty minutes.

atlas.title: Biochemical events in ischemia
atlas.body: General biochemical changes Keep in mind that the biochemical changes and injury resulting from oxygen deprivation may be reversible. The tipping point into necrosis usually relates to insurmountable damage to mitochondria and/or membranes. The initial metabolic response of cells to lack of oxygen is to shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis, which generates some ATP (but a lot less than ox phos).

atlas.title: Calcium influx
atlas.body: Influx of calcium resulting from ion pump failure can cause denaturing of proteins and can also cause activation of many enzymes including phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases. The resulting damage to the plasma membrane and mitochondria often tips the cell over to irreversible injury and necrosis.

atlas.title: Clinical correlation: detection of cellular damage
atlas.body: One result of damage to the plasma membranes is leakage of cell contents into the local area and eventually into the bloodstream. In some cases, cell components may be detected by laboratory testing and help deduce organ damage. In the case of cardiac ischemia, the cardiac isoform of troponin (involved in actin-myosin interactions of muscle contraction) is leaked, and can be measured in the peripheral blood. Serum troponin is a very sensitive and specific test, and is currently the best laboratory marker of myocardial infarction (and has replaced older testing such as CK-MB and myoglobin).

atlas.title: Restoring blood flow/Reperfusion
atlas.body: The goal of early intervention in cardiac ischemia is restoration of blood flow, either by physically stenting open the affected coronary artery, or by pharmacologic thrombolysis of the obstructing clot. Animal studies have shown that the faster blood flow returns, the more cells are saved from necrosis (up to a point – after about six hours of hypoxia, return of blood flow saves a negligible number of cells). The optimum amount of muscle is saved if blood flow is restored within the first 90 minutes after the ischemic event.

atlas.title: Pathology descriptors of infarcts and necrosis
atlas.body: Infarct – describes area of ischemic insult The term infarct refers to a localized area of ischemic tissue. Grossly, infarcts are often wedge- shaped. The wedge shape delineates the area fed by the vessel that is blocked. The tip of the wedge is approximately the area of blockage, while the body of the wedge contains all the tissue fed by downstream branches of that vessel. Microscopically the tissue consists of necrotic cells. Infarcts may be described as white or red; this refers to the gross appearance of the infarcted tissue.

atlas.title: Necrosis – describes patterns of dead tissue
atlas.body: While the term “necrosis” is used to describe a form of cell death, it is also used to describe the overall pattern of tissue death. There are several descriptive types used when talking about the overall patterns:

atlas.title: Atherosclerosis
atlas.body: NOTE!! This topic is under construction, and the lecture portion has not yet been replaced. The older recorded videos cover what is in the TopHat, but they also contain a lot of additional information that will be covered elsewhere in the curriculum. atlas.title: Arteriolosclerosis
atlas.body: Note the extra "olo" in the word! This is normally found in the elderly, but in patients with chronic hypertension it develops earlier and can be more widespread. It affects small arteries and arterioles. The altered hemodynamics of hypertension cause stressed endothelial cells to leak plasma proteins into the tunica media, where the proteins deposit. The smooth muscle cells are also stressed, and deposit extracellular matrix within the wall. Overall the tunica media is thicker and less compliant, and the lumen is decreased in diameter, which causes restriction of blood flow to the downstream capillary beds.

atlas.title: Atherosclerosis
atlas.body: This also falls under the umbrella of "arteriosclerosis." It affects large elastic arteries, large muscular arteries, and medium muscular arteries, and is characterized by lipid deposition in the tunica intima, causing thickening of the intima, and can cause thinning of the underlying tunica media. These depositions can decrease the size of the lumen, compromise blood flow, and result in significant downstream effects. The remainder of this study guide will focus on this specific type of arteriosclerosis.

atlas.title: Atherosclerosis
atlas.body: Atherosclerosis is characterized by development of lesions within the tunica intima called "atheromas" or atherosclerotic plaques." The athero- prefix derives from Greek for "gruel"and describes the porridge-like, often gritty consistency of plaque contents. These lesions occupy space, decreasing the lumenal cross- sectional area (causing a stenosis) and the blood flow through the vessel.

atlas.title: Pathogenesis of atherosclerosis
atlas.body: The current thinking about atherosclerosis is that overall it is a "response to injury," and that it is a sort of chronic inflammatory response of the arterial wall to an endothelial insult which goes through several stages to arrive at a mature plaque. The cells involved are dysfunctional endothelial cells, macrophages, lymphocytes, and the smooth muscle cells of the tunica media, some of which migrate to the intima during this process. The diagram here is a summary; the individual steps are below. The basic steps are as follows (diagram of steps is below): 1.

atlas.title: Platelets adhere to endothelium or to leukocytes
atlas.body: Increased permeability allows lipoproteins to access and accumulate in the tunica intima 3. Macrophage activation, smooth muscle recruitment, more accumulation of lipids in the walls Macrophage and platelet products (PDGF, FGF, TGF-alpha) stimulate smooth muscle cell migration into intima Accumulating cholesterol crystals and free fatty acids are sensed by macrophage cytosolic innate immune receptors Inflammasome activation leads to IL-1 secretion, attracting leukocytes Local T cells are also activated, and produce IFN-gamma, which further activates macrophages, smooth muscle cells, and endothelial cells 4.

atlas.title: Smooth muscle cells accumulate lipoproteins
atlas.body: Oxidized (modified) LDL Is readily ingested by macrophages through the scavenger receptor Is chemotactic for circulating monocytes, increases monocyte adhesion, and inhibits motility of macrophages already in the lesion (both attracts and retains macrophages in lesion) Stimulates release of growth factors and cytokines Is cytotoxic to endothelial cells (causing further dysfunction) and to smooth muscle cells 5.

atlas.title: Effects of plaques
atlas.body: Plaques will occupy space and decrease the cross-sectional area of the lumen (a stenosis), which will compromise blood flow, Some stenotic arteries can be stented (mechanically propping the vessel open) restoring blood flow.

atlas.title: Specific diseases related to atherosclerotic plaques
atlas.body: Peripheral vascular disease In vessels that serve the extremities, like the iliac arteries that arise from the most distal aorta, plaques may reduce the blood flow to the point that the distal lower extremities are cool, with weak pulses, and these patients are at risk of tissue death necessitating amputation. Some patients may require a bypass (e.g. from aorta to the femoral arteries, bypassing the diseased iliacs) to preserve their lower extremities.

atlas.title: Aneurysms
atlas.body: Aneurysms are abnormally dilated vessels with a thin tunica media. They can be congenital, but many are due to vessel damage by plaques. Plaque-related aneurysms can develop anywhere, but the distal aorta is a common location. Large plaques will thin/weaken the tunica media, resulting in dilation of the vessel and loss of elasticity; this dilation is referred to as an aortic aneurysm, which is an example of a "complicated lesion" of atherosclerosis. The lumen of an aortic aneurysm is usually narrow, despite the dilation of the artery, since there is usually a large volume of plaque within it, and clots may also develop.

atlas.title: Hormones and Feedback Mechanisms
atlas.body: Protein hormones typically interact with target cells via cell membrane-bound receptors. Steroid hormones interact with receptor within their target cells. Steroid hormones easily pass through the hydrophobic environment of cell membranes. Feedback mechanisms (FM), also referred to as feedback loops, are an important part of maintaining biological homeostasis. There are positive and negative FMs.

atlas.title: Negative FM
atlas.body: Results in the maintenance of hormone levels within an appropriate physiological range (homeostasis) If a hormone level rises or falls beyond a certain physiological "normal" level (also known as a setpoint), a negative FM activates to bring that level back to "normal". Hormone release is regulated primarily via the negative feedback mechanism. Negative Feedback Mechanism/Loop (copied from link). Here "set point" = homeostatic "normal" Positive FM is also present in the endocrine system, but is uncommon --> see oxytocin (pituitary section) below

atlas.title: Pituitary
atlas.body: Also called the "Hypophysis"; weight: 0.5 g pituitary hormones are protein hormones The pituitary has 2 distinct halves (anterior/posterior) and an "intermediate" area in between anterior pituitary = "adenohypophysis" or "pars distalis" multiple cell types synthesize different hormones (see slide below for summary, and refer to Dr.

atlas.title: The link between Hypothalamus + Pituitary
atlas.body: The Hypothalamic-Hypophyseal Tract: a bundle of axons that connect hypothalamus and neurohypophysis of the pituitary gland The Hypothalamic-Hypophyseal Portal System/circulation: blood supply that carries small regulatory peptides from the hypothalamus to the adenohypophysis The tract and portal system enable the transport of hormones and allow fast communication between hypothalamus, pituitary gland and target organs. Some references also refer to this as the "Hypothalamic-pituitary axis". For now, just be aware of the links between these 2 organs and facts noted above. You'll cover the physiology later on (and yes, this will be another high yield topic)!

atlas.title: Parathyroid
atlas.body: There are 4 small parathyroid glands sitting on the posterior side of thyroid. Each parathroid gland consists primarily of "principal cells" (also called "chief cells") that are the main functional cells, which secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH). (There is another cell type, the oxyphil cell, which we won't go into detail here.) A key function of PTH: to maintain homeostasis of blood calcium (Ca2+) levels.

atlas.title: Adrenal Cortex
atlas.body: The cortex is futher subdivided into 3 layers, in order from superficial to deep, with their main hormone products (steroid hormones) listed: zona glomerulosa (adjacent to capsule, most "superficial") mineralocorticoids (main one = aldosterone) -------------> "salt" (see memory tip below) zona fasciculata glucocorticoids (main one = cortisol) -------------> "sugar" zona reticularis (adjacent to medulla) androgens (DHEA ) -------------> "sex" Be aware that the above list is simplified -- there are other hormones released by these layers, but only the most prominent ones are listed above.

atlas.title: Adrenal Medulla
atlas.body: The medulla is centrally located, and contains preganglionic sympathetic fibers that release catecholamines (main ones = epinephrine, norepinephrine). You will not be responsible for recognizing the images of individual adrenal cell types histologically, but DO know the names of the layers and their associated key hormones. 🩺Clinical correlations - adrenal Diving a little deeper into 2 specific adrenal hormones:

atlas.title: Pineal gland
atlas.body: This small gland sits in the posterior wall of the 3rd ventricle of the brain. Pinealocytes (the main cell type) in this gland are responsible for the secretion of melatonin, which has both photosensory and neuroendocrine functions in the regulation of circadian rhythms (such as our sleep-wake cycles).

Last year he was started on a PPI (proton pump inhibitor) for a year which has helped somewhat, but he still experiences some symptoms. He is referred to gastroenterology for further workup, and they schedule an upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy). On endoscopy, the gastroenterologist notes that the GE junction mucosa appers irregular (below right, normal on the left), with extensions of salmon-colored mucosa up into the distal esophagus (often described as "tongues" of salmon-colored mucosa).

atlas.title: Introduction
atlas.body: A total of 2 million new cancer cases and 611,000 cancer deaths were projected to occur within the United States in 2024. Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the IS, accounting for about 18% of deaths from all causes. It is also a leading cause of death in children aged 5-14 in the US.
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Terminology
atlas.body: The term "tumor" literally means swelling, from the Latin tumere, "to swell." The term "tumor" is often used interchangeably with the term "neoplasm" which means "new growth." Tumors/neoplasms may be benign (generally harmless) or malignant (potentially harmful). The distinction between benign and malignant is based on judgement of a neoplasm's potential behavior (we'll discuss this more below) A tumor is said to be benign when its gross and microscopic characteristics are considered to be relatively innocent, meaning that it will remain a localized growth, will not metastasize to other sites, and is typically treatable with surgical excision.
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Osteoma - benign tumor of bone
atlas.body: Lipoma - benign tumor of fat Leiomyoma - benign smooth muscle tumor (leio = smooth, myo = muscle ) Rhabdomyoma - benign striated muscle tumor (rhabdo = striped) The nomenclature for benign tumors of epithelial origin is more complex and often consists of more than one word. The name may include the cell/tissue of origin, the microscopic architecture, and/or the gross appearance.
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Leiomyosarcoma - malignant smooth muscle tumor
atlas.body: Rhabdomyosarcoma - malignant striated muscle tumor Carcinomas are cancers arising from epithelial cells, and are the most common types of cancer. Lung, breast, prostate, and colon carcinomas are the most common cancers in the US. Since there can be different epithelial types in one organ, additional descriptors are often used.
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Hepatocellular carcinoma is a malignant tumor of hepatocytes
atlas.body: Papillary carcinoma is an example of nomenclature that describes the microscopic appearance of finger-like growths, but it doesn't tell you the cell of origin/location, so a descriptor would be needed. Thyroid papillary carcinoma is the most common cancer to use this terminology (malignant thyroid follicular cells grow in finger-like projections). OTHER malignancies that are not mesenchymal or epithelial use a variety of terms: Lymphoma - malignancy of lymphocytes, found in lymph nodes and other immune tissues Leukemia - malignancy of immature WBCs in the marrow, can be found circulating in the blood
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Melanoma - malignancy of melanocytes
atlas.body: Characteristics of benign versus malignant tumors The distinction between benign and malignant is critical for treatment and prognosis, and is based on clues to the tumor's biologic behavior, including gross and microscopic findings. The following features are used to help determine if a tumor is benign or malignant.
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Rate of tumor growth
atlas.body: Rate of tumor growth can be appreciated by repeat physical exam (if the tumor is palpable) or by repeat imaging. On microscopy, pathologists look for and count the number of visible mitoses to estimate growth rate. Benign tumors typically undergo slowly progressive growth. Growth in a benign neoplasm may even halt, and occasionally will even regress (shrink). On microscopy, there are rare or no mitoses found on the slides, and when one is found, it is normal in appearance. Malignant tumors may grow erratically with periods of slow and fast growth, although some specific types of malignant tumors are known to grow especially quickly.
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Metastasis
atlas.body: Benign tumors do not metastasize, while malignant tumors have the ability to metastasize. If metastases are identified in lymph nodes or other organs, the original tumor must be malignant. The liver is a common site of metastasis from malignancies of the gastrointestinal tract, and the lung is another organ that will often develop metastases from elsewhere in the body. Both of these organs "see" a lot of blood, and have extensive capillary beds, where traveling tumor cells can lodge and begin growing.
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Local invasion
atlas.body: Benign tumors do not invade or infiltrate local tissues. They are usually well-demarcated masses with a distinct edge, which may be appreciated on imaging and/or gross exam. They may push against/compress adjacent normal tissue, which can sometimes cause damage. When excising a benign tumor, it is often easy to extract them from the surrounding tissue.
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Cellular characteristics
atlas.body: There are a number of microscopic features that pathologists analyze to determine if a tumor is malignant. Finding just one feature usually isn't enough to call a tumor malignant, and pathologists consider all features together when diagnosing a tumor. Most of these changes are seen in the neoplastic cells themselves, but changes in the stromal (non-neoplastic supporting tissue) component can also be helpful clues. Loss of polarity: This refers to loss of normal cell and tissue organization, loss of normal relationships, and disorganized growth.
atlas.file: 25_10_27 - Intro to Cancer 1_ Terminology _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Introduction
atlas.body: This lecture is an introduction to the molecular basis of cancer to prepare you for the next set of lectures that will further investigate specific examples of the topics covered here. This lecture covers the fundamental principles of cancer's molecular basis, and the acquisition of some of the "hallmarks of cancer."
atlas.file: 25_10_28 - Intro to Cancer 2_ Biology of Cancer _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Fundamental principles
atlas.body: Non-lethal genetic damage Non-lethal DNA damage is the root of carcinogenesis. The cell has mechanisms to repair DNA so that it does not get passed on to daughter cells, but occasionally an error does slip through, and this can be the start of a neoplastic process. Genetic damage can be acquired (e.g. via environmental exposures, viral-induced mutations) or more rarely inherited/germ-line.
atlas.file: 25_10_28 - Intro to Cancer 2_ Biology of Cancer _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Transformation
atlas.body: Cancer develops as a consequence of transformation of a single progenitor cell that has incurred genetic damage and then undergoes clonal expansion with numerous generations of daughter cells carrying the same damaged genes (i.e. numerous clones of the original). The monoclonal nature of tumors is now readily demonstrated using molecular techniques, it was originally determined by analysis of an X-linked polymorphic enzyme (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, G6PD):
atlas.file: 25_10_28 - Intro to Cancer 2_ Biology of Cancer _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Tumor Progression and Heterogeneity
atlas.body: Though a malignant tumor is originally/initially a monoclonal population of cells, over time it becomes heterogenous. Since tumor cells grow rapidly and without normal checks on growth, each tumor cell may accumulate an additional genetic error. This new error could be fatal to the cell, or it could enhance its ability to proliferate unchecked (we will discuss this type of error in the next few lectures). This new error will then be passed on to the progeny of that specific tumor cell, creating a subclone within the tumor with its own new survival advantage.
atlas.file: 25_10_28 - Intro to Cancer 2_ Biology of Cancer _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Main classes of genes affected in cancer
atlas.body: There are four classes of normal regulatory genes that are often seen damaged in cancerous growth. We will be discussing these in more depth in the upcoming lectures. These classes of genes and their products' functions are: Growth-promoting proto-oncogenes: their products promote progression of the cell replication cycle or signal within pro-growth pathways Growth-inhibiting tumor suppressor genes: their products inhibit the cell replication cycle or inhibit signaling down pro-growth pathways Genes that regulate apoptosis: their products recognize intracellular imbalances/errors or trigger/execute apoptosis Genes involved in DNA repair: their products recognize DNA errors, or halt cell cycl…
atlas.file: 25_10_28 - Intro to Cancer 2_ Biology of Cancer _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Cancer"
atlas.body: Tumors that become malignant acquire multiple fundamental changes in cell physiology and function. Subsequent lectures will explore specific examples of the ones towards the top of this list, so here we will explore the bolded items towards the bottom: 1. Genomic instability resulting from defects in DNA repair (mutator phenotype) 2. Self-sufficiency in growth signals (sustaining proliferative signaling) 3. Insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals (evading growth suppressors) 4. Evasion of apoptosis (resisting cell death) 5. Avoiding immune destruction 6. Metabolic changes in cancer (deregulating cellular energetics, e.g. Warburg effect) 7.
atlas.file: 25_10_28 - Intro to Cancer 2_ Biology of Cancer _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Limitless replication potential
atlas.body: This ability relates to telomeres and telomerase. Telomeres are DNA and protein 'caps" attached to the ends of the chromosomes, and function as a "clock. Telomeres progressively shorten with each cell division, until they are "too short" and growth arrest and/or cell senescence occurs (this is important in human aging). The limit for any given cell is 50-70 cell divisions. Telomerase is an enzyme that can add to the length of telomeres, extending the functional life of the cell. Somatic cells (the majority of cells in the body) do not have telomerase, so they will eventually run down their telomeres and become senescent.
atlas.file: 25_10_28 - Intro to Cancer 2_ Biology of Cancer _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Inducing angiogenesis
atlas.body: The growth of a tumor mass is dependent on its ability to recruit new blood vessels. The induction of blood vessel growth is called angiogenesis. Without angiogenesis, a tumor cannot enlarge beyond a size of 1-2 millimeters. Neovascularization provides a new source of oxygen and nutrients needed for tumor survival and growth, and may deliver growth factors and.or hormones that may also speed tumor growth (depending on the specific tumor type). Angiogenesis also allows the tumor intimate contact with the vasculature, increasing the likelihood of vessel invasion by tumor and subsequent metastasis.
atlas.file: 25_10_28 - Intro to Cancer 2_ Biology of Cancer _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Angiogenic switch
atlas.body: Neovascularization of a tumor involves sprouting of new vessels from previously existing ones, and VEGF action on vessels induces this new growth. The amount of available VEGF is modulated by HIF-1alpha and VHL (von-Hippel-Lindau) protein. Hypoxia induces an increased amount of HIF-1alpha (hypoxia-induced factor) which is a transcription factor for VEGF and other pro-angiogenic factors. HIF-1alpha normally undergoes post-translational modification by an oxygen-dependent hydroxylase, which allows it to bind to VHL protein. VHL is a ubiquitin ligase complex which causes destruction of HIF-1alpha.
atlas.file: 25_10_28 - Intro to Cancer 2_ Biology of Cancer _ Top Hat.pdf

atlas.title: Angiogenic inhibitors in clinical use
atlas.body: The chemotherapy agent Bevacizumab (Avastin) is a monoclonal antibody that recognizes and binds to VEGF so that it becomes unable to engage with VEGF-receptors on target vessels. This drug is used in combination with other chemotherapy agents that target other aspects of tumor growth and survival. There are also other drugs (Sunitinib, Sorafenib) that are inhibitors of VEGF-receptor tyrosine kinase activity within the target cells.

atlas.title: TERMINOLOGY – genetic errors
atlas.body: Driver mutation: a mutation that directly alters the expression/function of a gene/protein, leading to cancer Passenger mutation: other genetic mutations that accumulate during uncontrolled proliferation. Many neoplasms “collect” DNA errors as they rapidly replicate. Accumulation of a passenger mutations can result in more aggressive tumor growth, or resistance to certain treatments. If a passenger mutation is especially powerful, it may become the new driver mutation for a particular tumor. Activating/gain-of function mutation: mutation that results in increased or enhanced activity of a protein.

atlas.title: CYCLINS/CDKs/CDK inhibitors
atlas.body: Recall that there are checkpoints and restriction points in the cell cycle where the DNA is surveyed for damage before proceeding further. If a cell successfully passes the G1 restriction point, it is then committed to replicating. Recall that the proteins that help out at the restriction points and checkpoints are the Cyclins, which regulate Cyclin-dependent-kinases (CDKs), whose actions can be inhibited by the aptly-named CDK-inhibitors (CDKIs). Cyclins and CDKs are "pro- growth" and will push the cycle forward, while the CDKIs will try to stop the cycle from progressing.

atlas.title: GROWTH FACTORS and their RECEPTORS
atlas.body: GROWTH FACTORS: Far upstream from the cell replication cycle proper are the growth factors (and inhibitors) that modulate cell entrance into the replicative cycle. Mutations in some growth factors (e.g. EGF) and inhibitors (e.g. TGF-beta) have been implicated in human cancers. Elevated levels of a growth factor (or too little inhibitor) results in constant stimulation of the receptor and downstream pathways, pushing the cells to replicate. Most often, growth factors are secreted by neighboring cells and act in a paracrine (but not autocrine) fashion, since most often the secreting cell doesn’t display the target receptor.

atlas.title: RAS/RAF mutations
atlas.body: RAS and RAF are both proto-oncogenes, and mutations in either one can cause them to become oncogenes whose proteins inappropriately signal downstream, driving growth. Mutations in the RAS or RAF genes, the genes for other associated proteins, or genes for downstream cascade proteins can lead to a constitutively active signaling cascade.

atlas.title: ABL (tyrosine kinase signal transducer) - translocation
atlas.body: ABL is a proto-oncogene that can mutate to behave as an oncogene. The gene is located on chromosome 9, where it is appropriately regulated. The protein Abl is another signal transduction molecule involved in pro-growth pathways. It is a tyrosine kinase that is not a receptor (aka non-receptor tyrosine kinase).

atlas.title: Myelogenous
atlas.body: Leukemia (CML) is a prototypical example of a malignancy resulting from a specific hallmark translocation, t(9;22). The gene ABL on 9 translocates with BCR (a breakpoint cluster region) on chromosome 22, resulting in a derivative 22 chromosome known as the Philadelphia chromosome (first described at UPenn in 1960; this was the first fusion gene ever identified and investigated). The gene from 22 that is involved is BCR (named for the breakpoint cluster region it is near), but the normal function of this gene is still not elucidated. The BCR-ABL fusion gene produces a fusion protein Bcr-Abl.

atlas.title: HER2 (growth factor receptor) - amplification
atlas.body: HER2 gene codes for a a growth factor receptor in the ERBB family (which also includes EGFR). It is a receptor tyrosine kinase, located in the cell membrane, whose ligand is unknown. Dimerization enhances ligand binding and promotes kinase activity, which then signals down pro- growth pathways (specifically MAPK and PI3K). The HER2 gene is found on chromosome 17 (17q12) and is amplified in about 20-30% of breast cancers; these tumors are usually high-grade. These cancer cells show many copies of the HER2 protein in the membranes, which result in increased downstream signaling of MAPK (pro-growth) and PI3K/AKT (pro- growth and anti-apoptotic) pathways.

atlas.title: Vignette 1 – self-palpated breast mass
atlas.body: A 60 year-old woman presents to her PCP with concern about a self-palpated breast mass. She is not entirely up to date on her mammograms but did have a negative mammogram three years ago. Her PCP also palpates the mass, expresses concern, and sends the patient to radiology for a mammogram. Mammography shows a radio-opaque spiculated mass measuring at least 5 cm, and the radiologist performs a core biopsy of the mass. The biopsy shows a proliferation of malignant cells forming some small ducts, but mostly as small solid nests, invading through the tissue.

atlas.title: Her2 gene amplification
atlas.body: Recall that the Her2 protein is a member of the ERRB family of growth receptors. Amplification of the HER2 gene produces excessive her2 receptors, which are bound by (unknown) ligand, leading to overstimulation of MAPK and PI3K/ERK growth pathways. The drug trastuzumab (trade name Herceptin) blocks and holds the her2 receptors so that they cannot bind with their (unknown) ligand and signal downstream. The drug also (somehow, not elucidated) appears to initiate antibody-dependent cell-mediated toxicity, resulting in eventual destruction of the tumor cell.

atlas.title: Tumor Suppressors
atlas.body: Objectives: Once you digest this lecture, you should be able to: Define a tumor suppressor and explain the “two-hit” hypothesis Discuss functions of Rb protein and its modulators; what happens if Rb fails Discuss functions of p53 protein and its modulators; what happens if p53 fails Explain (briefly) the role of SMAD4 in the TGF-beta inhibitory pathway Explain the concept of contact inhibition, and example of e-cadherin/beta-catenin/APC Describe syndromes associated with germline mutations of RB, TP53, APC Explain the adenoma-carcinoma sequence with colon cancer as example

atlas.title: Inhibitory Signals: Tumor Suppressor Genes” pp208-214
atlas.body: Introduction Last lecture we discussed how proto-oncogenes can be affected by a genetic error and behave as oncogenes, driving uncontrolled growth. The current lecture will discuss the flip-side of that, looking at genes/proteins that usually function to inhibit or “hit the brakes” on cell proliferation – these are the tumor suppressors. We’ll explore some examples of how disruption of these genes and their protein products can result in uncontrolled proliferation.

atlas.title: The two-hit hypothesis
atlas.body: Recall that in the last lecture we discussed oncogenes, which as proto-oncogenes act to promote growth, but as oncogenes they promote uncontrolled growth. In most cases, one allele bearing a mutated oncogene is sufficient to cause the disease, and the fact that the other allele has a perfectly normal copy of the gene doesn’t make any difference. However, if a tumor suppressor gene is mutated, the other allele’s non-mutated gene copy can often produce enough normal protein to keep growth in check and the cell functioning properly. It follows that a single allele mutation of a tumor suppressor gene is not necessarily sufficient to generate the disease.

atlas.title: RB gene/protein function
atlas.body: The RB allele can be mutated by point mutations that cause a non-functional protein, or a deletion of the gene. RB mutation can be found in other tumors besides retinoblastoma. In addition, some viral proteins can bind the Rb protein and cause inactivation (more on this in the microbial carcinogenesis lecture). In short, the Rb protein: Is a classic example of tumor suppressor Integrates inputs from a diversity of signaling pathways Is a key negative regulator of cell proliferation cycle Governs G1/S checkpoint

atlas.title: CDK4 activating mutation
atlas.body: CDK-inhibitor (often p16) deletion or silencing TP3 gene/p53 protein – the guardian of the genome TP53 is the most commonly mutated gene in human cancers overall. The gene is located on chromosome 17 (17p13) and encodes p53, a transcription factor that is a main actor when a cell is stressed. It can act to halt the cell cycle and initiate DNA repair. If the DNA is beyond repair it can initiate apoptosis or induce a permanent non- replicative state (senescence).

atlas.title: Regulation and activity of p53 protein
atlas.body: The p53 protein is found in the cytoplasm but also can travel to the nucleus to perform its transcription-factor actions. It is active when it is phosphorylated. When it is non-phosphorylated, it is bound, held, and prevented from acting by its main regulator, the protein MDM2. Under normal conditions, MDM2 maintains the half-life of p53 at about 20 minutes via several mechanisms. MDM2 can: target p53 for degradation block p53's transcription-factor-activity in the nucleus cause p53 to be expelled from the nucleus into the cytoplasm There is also a protein called p14ARF that can interact with MDM2 and help stabilize p53 and prevent MDM2 from targeting p53 for degradation.

atlas.title: Impairment of TP53 gene/p53 protein
atlas.body: There are a number of ways to impair p53 performance. There are a variety of TP53 gene mutations (missense, frame shift, nonsense) that lead to an impaired protein, or the gene may be entirely deleted. If only one allele is affected, the other allele can be relied upon, unless that allele takes a second-hit, which will then allow uncontrolled proliferation. Other ways to impair p53 function include the following: overexpression of MDM2, causing cause over-inhibition of p53. deletion of the stabilizing molecule p14ARF, leading to increased degradation of p53 by

atlas.title: Germline mutation of the p53 gene: Li-Fraumeni syndrome
atlas.body: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is the clinical manifestation of a germline p53 mutation. Similar to RB families, one damaged allele alone is insufficient to cause disease, but these patients already have ‘one hit’ in every cell in the body, requiring only one additional hit to knock the protein out entirely. Germline mutation of p53 confers a 25-times greater risk of malignancy by age 50. Patients develop multiple different primary tumors at a relatively young age. The spectrum of tumors is very diverse, including bone and soft tissue sarcomas, leukemia, brain cancer, breast cancer, and adrenal cortical carcinomas, among others.

atlas.title: TGF-beta pathway, contains SMAD proteins
atlas.body: TGF-beta is a member of a family of growth factors. In most cells and under normal conditions, TGF-beta is a potent inhibitor of cell growth when binding to its receptors (TGF-R1 and 2). Binding causes the receptor to signal down a cascade that ultimately increases transcription of CDK-inhibitors and blocks transcription of pro-growth genes (CDK4, MYC, etc). TGF-beta signaling is altered in many cancers, often by mutation of the TGF-R2 (found in colon, stomach, and endometrial carcinomas), or by inactivating mutations of downstream molecules, one of which is SMAD4. The SMAD4 gene is often mutated in pancreatic cancers, and is a current hot topic for investigation.

atlas.title: APC
atlas.body: Contact inhibition Normal epithelial cells, when replicating under normal conditions, will stop proliferating once they form their expected structure – a single sheet of stratified squamous across the oral cavity, a sheet of simple columnar cells in the colon that invaginates into crypt structures, etc. Research has shown that most normal cells in culture will stop proliferating when they bump up against other existing cells, which has led to the idea of “contact inhibition.” Contact inhibition implies that there is some sort of signal or communication between cells as they contact each other that inhibits further replication.

atlas.title: A. Overview of Chemical Carcinogens
atlas.body: The first association between chemicals and carcinogenesis was made by Sir Percival Pott, who observed a high incidence of scrotal cancer in chimney sweeps, which he attributed correctly to chronic soot exposure. Danish Chimney Sweeps Guild required members to bathe daily soon after.

atlas.title: IMS-I
atlas.body: Dr. Adina Badea, PhD Environmental Carcinogens Epidemiological and biological evidence indicatesthat up to 80% of all cancers are environmental inorigin. Environment includes exposures to industrial carcinogens, occupational exposures, diet, tobacco use, sun exposure, and risky personal behaviors. The major causes of cancer are chemicals, radiation, and biological agents, such as viruses. The role of industrial chemicals in the burden of cancer has been subject of an intense debate for many decades, which is still unresolved. A variety of synthetic and naturally occurring chemicals are involved in cancer, some of whichare quite specific for particular tumors.

atlas.title: Exposures to Other
atlas.body: Carcinogens • Asbestos is associated with a rare cancer of the mesothelium (most often of the pleural/peritoneum) called mesothelioma. [Note that there is no association between mesothelioma and smoking]. However, asbestos exposure does increase the risk of lung cancer 5-fold. When asbestos exposure is added to cigarette smoking, the risk of lung cancer increases 55-fold over that forsmoking alone (a synergistic increase). Asbestos also causes laryngeal cancer.

atlas.title: Introduction
atlas.body: Worldwide, viruses are estimated to cause approximately 15% of all cancers in humans. However, it is clear that most viral infections do not lead to the development of cancer, suggesting there must be additional factors required in addition to viral infection alone. This lecture will cover some RNA tumor viruses (retroviruses) and DNA tumor viruses (HPV, EBV, HBV), and their relationships to cancer development. We’ll also look at how chronic infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori contributes to gastric malignancies; this is the first (and so far the only) bacterium implicated the pathogenesis of human neoplasia.

atlas.title: RNA virus: the retrovirus HTLV-1
atlas.body: The recognition that RNA viruses can cause cancer in animal models led to the discovery of oncogenes. The retrovirus subset of RNA viruses are known to cause cancer in two ways: A retrovirus may incorporate a proto-oncogene from a host into its own genome, resulting in a "viral oncogene." Subsequent viral infection of other hosts will carry this oncogene into the host cell, and may cause malignancy. A retrovirus can insert a promoter next to a proto-oncogene in a host cell, resulting in conversion of the host proto-oncogene into an oncogene. Several animal retroviruses are known to cause cancers in animals.

atlas.title: HHV-8 (Human herpes virus 8): Kaposi's sarcoma
atlas.body: Human papilloma virus (HPV) Cervical cancer is caused by a persistent infection with certain strains of HPV; these strains are called "high-risk HPV" (HR-HPV). Approximately 42 million Americans are currently infected with HR-HPV, and another 13 million become newly infected each year (data retrieved from CDC July 2025). HR-HPV is sexually transmitted, and it is estimated that up to 80% of sexually active people will be infected with HR-HPV at some point in their lifetime. While HR-HPV infection of the genital tract is quite common, neoplasia develops in only a small portion of those infected. HR-HPV is also the causative agent for most anal cancers, and about 20% of oropharyngeal cancers.

atlas.title: Natural history of HPV infection
atlas.body: Most HR-HPV infections are transient and asymptomatic. 70% of new infections are cleared spontaneously by the host’s immune system within a year, and as many as 90% clear within two years. Younger patients, especially those <25 yo, are more likely to clear the infection. Those with compromised immune systems, such as those co-infected with HIV, are less likely to clear the infection and are at higher risk of developing neoplasia. Smokers also are less likely to clear the infection. Transient infection may result in mild cytologic abnormalities that may be seen on pap smear, but doesn't last long enough to cause cancer.

atlas.title: Life cycle of HPV
atlas.body: We will specifically discuss cervical dysplasia, but the pathogenesis is similar for other HPV- driven carcinomas of vagina, vulva, penis, anus, and oropharyngeal lesions. The HR-HPV subtypes have a tropism for mucosal squamous epithelium, such as the cervix, vagina, labia minora, under the foreskin of the penis, the columnar- to-squamous transition in the anus, and oral cavity/pharyngeal mucosa. They are able to infect skin (e.g. of vulva or penis) but prefer a non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. HPV viruses gain access via an abrasion or microscopic wound on the cervix, and first infect the cells at the basal layer of the squamous mucosa.

atlas.title: Pathogenesis of HPV-driven dysplasia/neoplasia
atlas.body: The development of cancer associated with HR- HPV subtypes is dependent on viral inactivation of tumor suppressor proteins p53 and Rb, resulting in increased host DNA damage and risk of developing neoplasia. Inactivation of p53 and pRb is mediated by the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7, and the transcription of E6 and E7 is regulated by the early viral protein E2.

atlas.title: The E7 protein also inhibits the CDKI p21
atlas.body: The affected host cells now lack most of their p53 and Rb proteins, both of which are major tumor suppressor proteins that inhibiting cell proliferation. (Note that the genes for p53 and Rb may be fine and functioning well, and it's the proteins that are being destroyed). The E6 protein also increases telomerase expression, and the E7 protein also inhibits the CDKI p21 so CyclinD/CDK4 operate without regulation.

atlas.body: The nomenclature for cervical dysplasia is complicated, since the information is reported differently depending on whether it is being observed on a cytology specimen (pap smear) or on a tissue biopsy. You do NOT need to worry about this nomenclature for the exam, nor will you be asked to diagnose photos!! You should be familiar with the differences between mild/low-grade dysplasia and severe/high-grade dysplasia, and what is happening within the cells in those respective situations. [IF you are interested: Cytology (pap smear) reports abnormalities seen in individual cells as low- grade dysplasia or high-grade dysplasia.

atlas.title: Detection of cervical dysplasia
atlas.body: Cervical dysplasia may be detected by cytologic examination commonly called the pap smear (the Papanikolaou test), in which cells are collected by scraping and brushing of the cervical transformation zone during a pelvic exam. These can be smeared directly on a slide, but these slides can be thick and/or obscured by blood and mucus; more often the brush is placed in a fluid, making a cell suspension. This suspension is processed to make a very thin layer of cells, for easy cytologic evaluation, and a portion of the suspension can be used for detection of HR-HPV DNA.

atlas.title: Latency Period
atlas.body: Breast cancer • Risk of breast cancer after radiation is highest during breast development in adolescent years. • Long term data from Hodgkin’s Lymphoma survivors treated with chest radiation • Risk Parallels that of a BRCA 1 gene mutation • 20% risk by age 40-45 yr (average risk 1%) • 60-80% lifetime risk (average risk 8%) • Patients with high dose radiation exposure to the chest/breasts at age <25yr should undergo high risk screening or can considered prophylactic mastectomies.

atlas.title: Disaster
atlas.body: Chernobyl Nuclear Disaster • The most severe accident in the history of nuclear power industry. • April 25, 1986. • Explosions during a safety test led melt down and massive release of radioactive materials into the environment for 10 days. • Very high radiation exposures (2-20 Gy) to ~1,000 on-site staff and emergency workers responding to initial fires. • Exposures to additional people working in recovery and cleanup, estimated total 600,000. • Resettlements of 336,000 people in surrounding regions. • Contaminated areas affecting over 5 million people.

atlas.title: Childhood Tumors
atlas.body: Hart Introduction Tumors in children encompass a wide spectrum of benign and malignant lesions with vastly different clinical behaviors. Malignant tumors are rare in children, affecting ~ 0.002% of the pediatric population. It is estimated that ~ 2% of all malignant tumors occur during childhood (between 1 - 18 years old). Malignant tumors account for ~ 12% of deaths in children between 1 - 4 years old and ~ 20% of death in children between 5 -14 years old. Benign Tumors and Tumor-Like Lesions (Hamartomas and Heterotopias): Benign tumors are much more common than malignant tumors in both children and adults.

atlas.title: Hart
atlas.body: Nearly 100% of cases have biallelic loss of the RB gene due to mutations. Approximately 40% of cases are hereditary (the patient inherits one mutated RB allele then develops a sporadic mutation in the 2nd allele) and ~ 60% are sporadic (the patient develops sporadic mutations is both RB alleles).

atlas.title: Childhood Tumors
atlas.body: Hart Microscopically, both childhood types of rhabdomyosarcoma contain SRBCs. In the embryonal type, skeletal muscle differentiation may be seen in some of the cells that are in latter stages of myogenesis. These cells are termed tadpole cells (cells with eccentric nuclei on one end and bright red cytoplasm on the other). Less differentiated (more immature) cells in both embryonal and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma have a typical SRBC appearance. Immunohistochemical stains are necessary to prove skeletal muscle differentiation. Embryonal RMS Tadpole cell

atlas.title: Hart
atlas.body: Ewing sarcoma: Ewing sarcoma is a primitive small round cell sarcoma that definitionally has a translocation involving EWSR1 and an ETS transcription factor. If this translocation is not present, the tumor is not a Ewing sarcoma. It is the 2nd most common bone tumor in children (after osteosarcoma). Ewing sarcoma usually occurs in the 10-20 year old age group, but it may occur at any age, including older adults.

atlas.title: Case 1: routine colonoscopy
atlas.body: A 60 yo presents for a routine screening colonoscopy; their last colonoscopy was ten years ago and was normal. They have type 2 diabetes that is well-controlled, and hyperlipidemia. They have no GI concerns. There is family history of colon cancer in a paternal grandfather at age 70 and in a maternal aunt at age 65. There is no family history concerning for a genetic predisposition to cancer. Colonoscopy reveals one polyp in the distal descending colon, and two polyps in the ascending colon; all three are retrieved and submitted to pathology.

atlas.title: Case 2: a growing mole
atlas.body: A 45 year old presents with concern about a "growing mole" on their left upper back that appeared six months ago. They report significant history of sun exposure to the area. Physical examination reveals a 1.2 cm hyperpigmented lesion with irregular borders and variable brown-to-black coloration seated over the left shoulder blade.

Local anesthetic is administered, and the lesion plus 0.5 cm of surrounding normal-appearing skin is excised, down to the level of the subcutis, and is submitted to pathology. One of the slides of the lesion is shown HERE. Unaffected skin for comparison is HERE. 1) Examine the lesion (you've seen this slide before). Describe what you see. What do you think this lesion is? There is a tumor invading down from the epidermis into the dermis, replacing the normal dermal connective tissue with atypical cells, some of which contain brown pigment, suggesting a melanocytic origin.

atlas.title: CASE 3: A palpable mass
atlas.body: A 60 yo presents with a concern for a self-palpated breast mass. She is in generally good health. Her last mammogram was two years ago, and was unremarkable. Family history is remarkable for a paternal aunt with breast cancer in her 60s and a maternal grandmother with breast cancer at age 70. The clinician is able to palpate the area of concern, which feels relatively superficial and 1-2 cm in size. A core biopsy is performed by palpation, and given the results of the core biopsy, the patient is scheduled for and undergoes a partial mastectomy (lumpectomy).
atlas.file: SG7_ post-session answers (study guide for exam)_ MD29 Histopathologic Foundations of Disease.pdf

atlas.title: PHOTO EXAMPLE OF HER2 IHC NEG AND POS
atlas.body: If the results of the IHC are not definitively positive or negative (i.e. equivocal), pathologists will then test the tumor with fluorescent in-situ hybridization (FISH), looking for abnormality. What abnormality is the pathologist is looking for on these tests? Why is this useful information? Review how this abnormality can drive neoplasia. HER2 is member of the EGFR family of receptor tyrosine kinases (more about EGFR in pulmonary block), and signals down pro-growth pathways. The IHC looks for overexpression of her2 protein, and ISH looks for amplification of the HER2 gene on chromosome 17.

atlas.title: CASE 4: abnormal pap
atlas.body: A 34yo presents for routine gyn care. Her last pap smear was three years ago, and was negative for squamous cell atypia. HPV DNA testing at the time was positive for HPV16. She also reports pelvic discomfort and fullness, and has been told she probably has uterine fibroids (leiomyomas). The bimanual pelvic exam reveals a somewhat bulky uterus, consistent with fibroids. There are no gross abnormalities on visualization of the ectocervix. A pap smear is collected and submitted for cytology and HPV DNA testing.
